ESV *"Now therefore, what have I here, declares the Lord, seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Their rulers wail, declares the Lord, and continually all the day my name is despised."*

¹⁷ **Selnecker's four marks of false teachers** — a stock structuring inherited from the Melanchthonian *Loci* treatment of *De Ecclesia et Ministris* (CR 21:824ff.), and from Luther's paradigm-condemnation of the *Sacramentierer* and the *Schwärmer* in the 1528 *Bekenntnis vom Abendmahl Christi* (WA 26:499ff. / *LW* 37:361ff.). The *Anti-Trinitarian* reference targets particularly the Italian antitrinitarians (Servetus 1553; Blandrata; Socinus) and the Polish Brethren of the *Racovian Catechism* generation.

¹⁸ **Isaiah 52:6** — *Propterea sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum.*

¹⁹ **John 8:25** — Selnecker's Greek **τὴν ἀρχὴν ὅτι καὶ λαλῶ ὑμῖν** (the Vulgate: *Principium qui et loquor vobis*; ESV *"Just what I have been telling you from the beginning"*) is much-disputed in the Fathers and Reformers; Selnecker follows the *Melanchthon-Bugenhagen* rendering "*the very Beginning speaks to you*" — a Christological reading tied to John 1:1 *ἐν ἀρχῇ.* Cf. Chrysostom, *Homilia in Ioannem* 53 (PG 59:293–294; NPNF I.14:189–190).

²⁰ **Isaiah 52:7** — *Quam pulchri super montes pedes annuntiantis et praedicantis pacem, annuntiantis bonum, praedicantis salutem, dicentis Sion: Regnavit Deus tuus.* Paul cites the verse at Romans 10:15 as the *sedes doctrinae* for the office of the preacher.

²¹ ***Cursores et nuntios formosos et amabiles*** — a *Melanchthonian* rendering; cf. CR 24:812 on Isa. 52:7 in Melanchthon's *Postillae Melanchthonianae* (1594-collected edition of the sermon-notes).

²² **John 3:16** paraphrased with the Nativity-*Gloria* of Luke 2:14 (*Gloria in excelsis Deo, pax in terris, hominibus laetitia*). Selnecker's *pax terris et hominibus laetitia* is the Reformation-era Lutheran rendering (Vulgate has *bonae voluntatis*; the Greek variant *ἐν ἀνθρώποις εὐδοκία / εὐδοκίας* has been much-debated).

²³ **Isaiah 52:8** — *Vox speculatorum tuorum: levaverunt vocem, simul laudabunt, quia oculo ad oculum videbunt, cum converterit Dominus Sion.*

²⁴ **Isaiah 52:11–12** — the *"depart, depart"* pericope on the priestly *bearers of the vessels of the Lord.* Selnecker's *"vessels of the Lord"* application to *pastores et ministros verbi* is Reformation-standard and interfaces with the *Augsburg Confession* Article V on the *ministerium docendi Evangelii.* Cf. **AC V** (*BSLK* 58 / *Kolb-Wengert* 40).

²⁵ **בָּשָׂר / בִּשַּׂר / בְּשׂוֹרָה** — *bāśar* (flesh), *biśśar* (piel: to bring good news), *besōrāh* (feminine noun: glad tidings). Selnecker's Hebrew etymology is standard Reformation-era Hebraist analysis; cf. **BDB** 142a–142b (√בשׂר). The parallel with the Isa. 52:7 *euaggelizomenos-* language is Melanchthonian; cf. Melanchthon, *Postillae* on Isa. 52 (CR 24:807ff.).

²⁶ **εὐαγγέλιον** — the LXX regular rendering of the *besōrāh* group (cf. 2 Sam. 4:10, 18:20, 22, 25, 27; Isa. 40:9, 52:7, 60:6, 61:1). Selnecker's identification of the term-family (Hebrew *besōrāh* = Greek *euaggelion* = Latin *bonum nuntium*) is Reformation-standard patristic-scholarship: see *Erasmus, Novum Instrumentum* (1516) apparatus on Mark 1:1 and Romans 1:1.

²⁷ **The Selneckerian definition of the Gospel.** — This *definitio* is Selnecker's own compositional signature and appears (with minor variation) in his *Pedagogia Christiana* (1565), his *Analecta* (1568), and his *Explicationes Symbolorum* (1572). The paradigm-cause here is Melanchthon's *Loci Præcipui Theologici* (1559) *De Evangelio* definition (CR 21:355; MSA II/1:180): *"Est promissio gratuita reconciliationis, remissionis peccatorum, iustificationis et vitae aeternae, propter Filium Dei, credentibus donandarum."* Selnecker adds three specifically Formula-of-Concord-adjacent qualifications: (1) *"not implanted in nature at Creation"* — anti-Osiandrian; (2) *"terrified by the sense of God's wrath against sins"* — FC V/VI Law-Gospel discipline; (3) *"the donation of the Holy Spirit"* alongside the imputatio-iustitiae — anti-Reformed on the *simul-donation* of Spirit-and-Righteousness. Cf. **FC SD III. 41** (*BSLK* 927 / *Kolb-Wengert* 566), **FC SD V. 22ff.** (*BSLK* 954ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 583ff.).

²⁸ **The five-cause analytic.** — Selnecker uses the standard Aristotelian *four causes* (efficient, material, formal, final) but expands to *five* by splitting the impulsive cause into ***αἰτία προηγουμένη*** (interior antecedent) and ***αἰτία προκαταρκτική*** (external triggering). This split derives from the Stoic and Middle-Platonist cause-terminology; cf. **Diogenes Laertius VII. 55** and **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, *De Fato* 22–23 (*Bruns* 191–193). The Reformation-era transmission of the terminology was through Melanchthon's *Erotemata dialectices* (1547) and Chytraeus's *Regulae studiorum* (1562). Selnecker's application to the doctrinal *definitio Evangelii* is programmatic and appears again in the parallel Locus-openings of Kirchner, Chytraeus, and Chemnitz.

²⁹ **ἑρμηνεὺς τῶν μεγάλων βουλημάτων τοῦ Πατρός** — *"interpreter of the great counsels of the Father."* Selnecker's Greek here echoes **Clement of Alexandria, *Protrepticus* 10 (PG 8:225)** and **Origen, *Peri Archon* I. 2. 6 (PG 11:135)** — the *Logos*-as-Chancellor tradition. The OCR-corrupted *Χριστῦ* (for *Χριστοῦ*) has been silently restored.

³⁰ **αἰτία προηγουμένη** — technical Stoic term for the *interior antecedent* impulsive cause (as opposed to the *προκαταρκτική* — the *external triggering* cause). See **Alexander of Aphrodisias**, *De Fato* 22 (*Bruns* 191); **SVF** II. 976–977.

³¹ **Tauler.** — Attribution to **Johannes Tauler** (c. 1300–1361), the Rhineland mystic whose *Predigten* (1498 Leipzig; 1521 Basel enlarged edition) Luther read with great enthusiasm and to whom Luther attributes much of his early "*theologia crucis*" formation. The specific *sic diligit Deus* saying is not readily located in Tauler's extant corpus (cf. **Corin, *Sermons de Tauler* — critical edition 1911, 3 vols**) and may derive from the *Theologia Deutsch* (1518 Wittenberg — Luther's own edition), which Reformation-era readers routinely conflated with Tauler.

³² **Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oratio* 45.13 (Oratio in Sanctum Pascha II)** — **PG** 36:641; **NPNF** II.7:427. Selnecker's citation of Nazianzen's *"in nothing does God rejoice so much as in the salvation of man"* is a standard patristic-Lutheran auxiliary to the *sic dilexit* theme of John 3:16.

³³ **Selnecker's catalogue of modern Ministers of the Gospel.** — A characteristic Reformation-generational roll-call: **Luther, Melanchthon, Bugenhagen, Justus Jonas, Cruciger, Forster, Wenceslaus Linck, Thomas Venatorius, Vitus Theodorus (Dietrich), Brenz, Erhard Schnepf, Johann Hess, Ambrosius Moibanus, Aepinus.** Note that Selnecker in this Pars II passage restricts the modern catalogue to first-generation Reformers, whereas in Pars I *De Verbo Dei* Ch. 2 he extends the catalogue to include his own generation (himself, Chemnitz, Chytraeus, Andreä, Musculus, Körner). Compare **VD16** for each name; biographical dates and modern editions to be supplied per the standard glossary.

³⁴ **Cyril of Alexandria**, *In Ioannem* — the ***Mediator Dei et hominum*** formulation echoes 1 Timothy 2:5 and the paradigm-Cyrilline *Christological* argument. Precise Cyril-locus not yet identified with certainty; may be *In Ioannem* I. 9 (PG 73:161) or *In Ioannem* IV. 2 (PG 73:591). The saying became a Lutheran catchphrase through Chemnitz's *De duabus naturis in Christo* (1571) — cf. Chemnitz **§9** (Preus tr. 1971, pp. 71–72).

³⁵ ***Beneficia privativa vs positiva*** — the technical scholastic distinction. *Privative benefits* are those which *take away* an evil (remission, liberation); *positive benefits* are those which *confer* a good (donation of Spirit, imputation of righteousness, new obedience). Selnecker's parenthetical *"as the term has survived in the schools"* acknowledges the term's scholastic pedigree (cf. **Peter Lombard, *Sententiae* III. dist. 19**; **Thomas, *ST* III q. 46**) while retaining it as pedagogically useful for the Lutheran *ordo salutis.*

## From the Proem *De Evangelio* — §7 Two Principal Parts of Doctrine

³⁶ **The Two-Denarii Parable — Luke 10:35 (the Good Samaritan).** — Selnecker's typological reading — *Law and Gospel = the two denarii Christ gave to the innkeeper* — is a standard Reformation-era exegetical trope, going back to **Augustine, *Quaestiones Evangeliorum* II. 19 (PL 35:1340)** and later to **Luther's *Kirchenpostille* on the Thirteenth Sunday after Trinity** (WA 22:250ff.).

³⁷ **Cross-reference to *De Bonis Operibus.*** — This Locus is treated in Pars II as a sub-Locus under *De Poenitentia* (OCR ln 8265ff., forthcoming in T4).

³⁸ **The seven-verse mnemonic on the utilities of the Law.** — Selnecker's own didactic hexameters, evidently composed for the *Institutiones* itself and later collected in his verse-catechetical work *Elenchus Praeceptorum et Verba Formulae Concordiae Christiana* (Leipzig 1580). The seven utilities correspond to a Melanchthonian schema of the *usus Legis moralis:* (1) natural theology; (2) rule of life; (3) revelation of sin and wrath; (4) *paedagogus ad Christum;* (5) *primae iustitiae imagines;* (6) *futuri iudicii norma;* (7) *fons omnis honesti* in civil life. Elements (3), (4), and (6) map to the *usus paedagogicus* (FC VI); (2) and (7) to the *usus politicus;* and (1), (5), and (6) to the *usus didacticus / tertius usus.* Cf. **FC SD VI** (*BSLK* 962ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 587ff.) — the *tertius usus legis* article, which Selnecker himself as FC co-author knew from the inside.

³⁹ **The Antinomian controversy.** — Selnecker's structuring of *seventeen* Antinomian arguments (§§8) unfolds a controversy already two generations old at the time of Pars II. The *first Antinomian controversy* (1527–1540) was Luther-vs-**Johann Agricola** (*Eisleben,* c. 1494–1566), who from *Wittenberg 1527* through the *Torgau Articles of 1537* argued that penitence should be preached from the Gospel alone, not from the Law. Luther's *Disputationes contra Antinomos* (WA 39/I:342–584; six disputation-cycles 1537–1540) provides the paradigm rebuttal-format on which Selnecker's Ch. 8 depends. The *second Antinomian controversy* (1556–1577) was **Andreas Poach** and **Anton Otho** vs the *Wittenberg-Melanchthonian* line, resolved in **Formula of Concord Article VI** *tertius usus legis* — of which Selnecker was co-author. Cf. **FC SD VI. 1ff.** (*BSLK* 962 / *Kolb-Wengert* 587).

## From the Proem *De Evangelio* — §8 Refutation of Antinomian Arguments

⁴⁰ **Argument I — Luke 24:47** *"repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name."* — The paradigm Antinomian proof-text. Luther's *First Antinomian Disputation* (WA 39/I:349ff.) addresses this argument at length; Selnecker's *matter-vs-form* distinction (*materia poenitentiae ex lege, forma poenitentiae salutaris ex Evangelio*) is Luther's exact formulation in the *Disputation V* of 1538.

⁴¹ **Argument III — John 16:8ff.** *"He will convict the world of sin, of righteousness, and of judgement."* — Selnecker's exegesis (that *sin* here means principally *unbelief in the Son*) is Cyril-of-Alexandrian and Augustine, ***In Ioannem*** *Tract. 95** (PL 35:1871–1875; NPNF I.7:369–373). It is also the FC SD III/V/VI-adjacent line taken by Chemnitz in *Enchiridion* (Chemnitz 1569 Wittenberg edition).

⁴² **"D. Philippi"** — Philip Melanchthon (1497–1560). Selnecker regularly refers to Melanchthon simply as *Philippus* or *D. Philippus,* per the affectionate Wittenberg-generation convention. The *"in cruce Christi simul quasi suspensi"* formulation is Melanchthonian and appears in the *Loci Præcipui Theologici* (1559) *De Peccato Originis* (CR 21:685 / MSA II/1:296).

⁴³ **βιάζεται** (*biazetai*) at Matthew 11:12 — the *"suffers violence"* verb — is much-disputed exegetically. Selnecker follows the *middle-voice* reading (*"is taken by force"* actively) preferred by Luther in the *Auslegung der zehn Gebote* (WA 6:213ff. / *LW* 44:15ff.) and by Melanchthon in the *Loci* 1559 *De Evangelio.* The alternative *passive* reading (*"suffers violence"* — is under attack) was favoured by Chrysostom and Augustine and is defended in the modern critical editions (**BDAG** *biazomai*, sense 2).

⁴⁴ **Christ's four modes of fulfilling the Law.** — Selnecker's schema is Anselmian in the second mode (*satisfactio vicaria* — sufficient *λύτρον*) and Melanchthonian-FC-III in the first, third, and fourth. Cf. **Chemnitz, *De duabus naturis in Christo*** ch. 30 (Preus tr. 253–258) for the paradigm-Lutheran two-natured *obedientia activa et passiva* framework.

## From the Proem *De Evangelio* — §9 Six Differences between Law and Gospel

⁴⁵ **The *Six Differences* schema.** — Directly inherited from Melanchthon's *Loci Præcipui Theologici* (1559) *De Discrimine Legis et Evangelii* (CR 21:695ff. / MSA II/1:308ff.). Selnecker's ordering — from *notice, matter, form of promises, commiations, effects, objects* — is precisely Melanchthon's. This paradigm Reformation-era distinction is codified confessionally in **Apology Article IV** (Justification) — cf. **Ap. IV. 5** (*BSLK* 158 / *Kolb-Wengert* 121) — and in **Formula of Concord Article V** *De Lege et Evangelio* — cf. **FC SD V. 17ff.** (*BSLK* 953ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 583ff.).

⁴⁶ ***In iudicio finium regendorum*** — Roman-law technical formula for the *actio finium regundorum* (Justinian, *Institutes* 4.17.6; *Digest* 10.1) — the boundary-regulation praetorian action. Selnecker's metaphor: the Law-Gospel distinction requires the same precision of boundary-marking as does the neighbours' land-boundary case.

## From the Proem *De Evangelio* — §10 Distinction between Old and New Testament

⁴⁷ **Psalm 20:3–4** (Vulgate 20:4) — Selnecker's application of the David-quote to the *promise of the Messiah in the New Testament* is Augustinian; cf. **Augustine, *Enarratio in Ps.* 20 (PL 36:167ff.).**

⁴⁸ **Augustine on the Two Testaments.** — Precise Augustinian locus not yet certainly identified; the *vetus prius revelatum, novum posterius revelatum* formulation may derive from **Augustine, *Contra Faustum Manichaeum* XVIII. 6 (PL 42:346)**, or from the *De catechizandis rudibus* (PL 40:317ff.). To be verified against **CCSL** at the audit.

⁴⁹ **The *Christus corpus, Moses umbram* verse.** — Draws on Colossians 2:17 (*umbra futurorum, corpus autem Christi*). The verse-form itself is a *Reformation-era Lutheran mnemonic* attributed variously to Luther and to Melanchthon; the precise source is not identified. Cf. also **Melanchthon, *Loci Præcipui* (1559) *De Sacramentis*** (CR 21:857) for the parallel *umbra/corpus* Sacrament-distinction.

⁵⁰ **The transitional formula** *"Nunc saluberrimam et maxime necessariam doctrinam Iustificationis hominis coram Deo in manus sumemus, Deo iuvante"* (OCR ln 1125–1128) — Selnecker's *sedes-doctrinae signal* opening Locus I. The phrase *saluberrima et maxime necessaria doctrina* is Melanchthonian and appears verbatim at CR 21:735 (*Loci* 1559 *De Iustificatione* opening).

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione*

⁵¹ **Transition passage** (OCR ln 1125–1128, closing the pre-Iustificatio material): *"Now we shall take in hand the most saving and most necessary doctrine of the Justification of man before God, God helping us."* — Selnecker's *sedes-doctrinae* signal for the Locus.

⁵² **Threefold use of *iustitia.*** — This distinction is Melanchthon's, from the *Loci Præcipui Theologici* (1559) *De Iustificatione* opening — cf. **CR** 21:731ff., **MSA** II/1:328. Selnecker inherits it exactly.

⁵³ **Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* V.1.1129b30** — **ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ' ἀρετή ἐστι** ("in justice all virtue is comprehended in a word"). — Aristotle attributes the sentence itself to *Theognis* fr. 147 West. The Latin verse-rendering *Iustitia in se se virtutes continet omnes* is a common Renaissance-humanist verse-hexameter; compare **Erasmus, *Adagia* III.5.62.**

⁵⁴ **Aristotle**, *Nicomachean Ethics* V.1 in general — where justice is treated as the *summary virtue* embracing all others.

⁵⁵ ***Iustitia legalis*** — the scholastic category of "legal justice" as elaborated by **Thomas Aquinas, ST II-II q. 58 art. 5–6.** Selnecker's rejection of Philosophy's satisfaction with *external discipline* is Melanchthonian and reflects the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* Article IV rejection of philosophical righteousness — cf. **Ap. IV. 12–14** (*BSLK* 160 / *Kolb-Wengert* 122).

⁵⁶ **The thief on the cross** — *Luke 23:43.* Selnecker's use of the good thief as the *paradigmatic case* of *sola fide* justification is standard Lutheran doctrinal-preaching, deriving from **Luther, *Lectures on Genesis* on Gen 15:6** (WA 42:562ff. / *LW* 3:19ff.).

⁵⁷ **Selnecker's exposition of Psalm 32.** — Reference to his own earlier work: cross-reference not yet identified with certainty; probable candidate is his *Der ganze Psalter Davids* (Nürnberg 1565, expanded Leipzig 1581) or the *Psalmodia* (Wittenberg 1567). To be verified against **VD16** at the audit.

⁵⁸ ***Forensis vocabulum.*** — Central Melanchthon-inherited term. Selnecker's placement of the forensic character right at the head of the definition is programmatic and interfaces directly with **Formula of Concord Article III** *Solida Declaratio* — of which Selnecker was co-author — which insists on the forensic and imputative character of justification against the Osiandrian *unio essentialis / iustitia essentialis* framework. Cf. **FC SD III. 9ff., 17ff., 30ff., 62–63** — *BSLK* 916ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 562ff. This is the *sedes doctrinae* passage of the whole Locus.

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione* — §§3-15

⁵⁹ **Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), *In festo Annuntiationis Beatae Mariae Virginis, Sermo I* — *PL* 183:383–390.** Selnecker recites *the whole sermon* verbatim from the Latin editions of Bernard current in the Wittenberg-Reformation milieu (probably the 1552 Basel Herwagen edition of Bernard's *Opera omnia*). The paradigm-Reformation reception of Bernard is thoroughly attested; **Luther** himself frequently cites this very sermon as a *sedes* of the Reformation-era anti-Pelagian doctrine of *the merit of Christ vs. all human works* (WA 5:203ff., *In Ps. 5* enarrationes). Cf. also **Kolb, *Bound Choice, Election, and Wittenberg Theological Method*** (Eerdmans, 2005), Ch. 3, on the Wittenberg reception of Bernard's soteriology.

⁶⁰ **Ambrose, *De Officiis Ministrorum* III.7 (PL 16:150–151)** — *"Gloria vera est testimonium conscientiae, non quale ille Pharisaeus habebat..."* Bernard here paraphrases the Ambrosian topos.

⁶¹ **The Four Sisters allegory** — Bernard's dramatisation of Psalm 85:11 is the paradigm Western-medieval *sororum-in-consilio* meditation. The tradition ultimately derives from **Hugh of St. Victor, *De Sacramentis* I.8.4 (PL 176:307)** and reaches its most influential later development in **the *Meditationes Vitae Christi* of pseudo-Bonaventure** (14th c.). It became a standard *Marian-Annunciation* preaching-topic across the medieval West and passed with the Reformers into the Lutheran Advent-preaching tradition — cf. Luther, *Kirchenpostille* on Advent I (WA 10/I.2:1ff.).

⁶² **The sixfold denial of what justifies before God.** — Selnecker's structuring is Melanchthonian, drawn ultimately from the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession* Article IV. The full Apology-IV structure enumerates *justificatio sine operibus legis* against seven categories: opera ceremonialia, opera moralia, opera electicia, iustitia philosophica, opera renatorum, contritio, ipsa fides considered as work. Cf. **Ap. IV. 15ff.** (*BSLK* 160ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 122ff.) and — for the specific "even the good works of the reborn" denial — **FC SD III. 25ff.** (*BSLK* 923 / *Kolb-Wengert* 564).

⁶³ **Selnecker's twofold-imputation analytic.** — This distinction (real-inherent vs rational-attributed imputation) is one of the paradigm anti-Trent Reformation-era formulations. It reappears verbatim in **Chemnitz, *Loci theologici* (1591), *De Iustificatione*** and later in **Gerhard, *Loci theologici* (1610-1622) Loc. XVI: De Iustificatione**, which build out the same twofold-analytic in extended anti-Bellarmine polemic. Cf. **Preus, *The Theology of Post-Reformation Lutheranism*** (Concordia, 1970-1972) Vol II, Ch. 2 on the seventeenth-century systematisation.

⁶⁴ **Selnecker's definition of imputation.** — This is Selnecker's own composition and appears (with minor variation) in his *Explicationes Symbolorum* (1572) and *Institutionis Christianae Religionis Pars Prima* (1579) *De Peccato* section on Christ's satisfaction. The *quod nec sumus, nec habemus, nec fecimus* triadic structure is programmatic and echoes the Chemnitz *De duabus naturis* Christological *genus apotelesmaticum* formulation. Cf. **FC SD III. 40-43** (*BSLK* 926ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 566).

⁶⁵ ***Mercantile commutation*** (*mercatoria quaedam commutatio*) — the *fröhlicher Wechsel* / *admirabile commercium* topos, one of Luther's paradigm-metaphors for justification. See **Luther, *Sermo de duplici iustitia*** (WA 2:145-152 / *LW* 31:297-306), the 1519 sermon which first developed the *fröhlicher Wechsel* imagery. Also **Luther, *Ein Sermon von den guten Werken*** (WA 6:196ff. / *LW* 44:15ff.) on the *marriage-exchange* between Christ and the believing soul. Selnecker retains the Latin *mercatoria commutatio* formulation as the tradition's Latin technical term.

⁶⁶ **Anselm of Canterbury (c. 1033–1109; not 1058 as Selnecker's date — Selnecker follows an earlier bibliographical convention).** The paradigm Reformation-received text is **Anselm, *Cur Deus Homo* (PL 158:359-432)**, with the specific prayer-formulas Selnecker cites drawn from the **Anselm, *Meditationes*** and the ***Orationes*** printed variously in the 16th-c. editions. The two prayer-formulas as Selnecker gives them appear in **Anselm, *Meditatio* III** and **Anselm, *Oratio* 65** — but the Latin printed text Selnecker uses is that of the **1547 Cologne / Basel edition of Anselm's *Opera omnia*.** For the modern critical text, cf. **Schmitt, *S. Anselmi Cantuariensis Archiepiscopi Opera omnia,*** 6 vols (Edinburgh 1946-1961).

⁶⁷ **The extended Anselm-meditation** ("*Terret me vita mea...*") — this specific passage is the paradigm-Anselmian meditation *De miseria humana ante iudicium Dei* and appears in **Anselm, *Meditatio 1 — Ad concitandum timorem*** (PL 158:709-712). Selnecker's Latin follows the received Wittenberg-Reformation text and was much cited by **Luther** in his early Genesis Lectures on Genesis 3-6 (WA 42:145ff. / *LW* 1:194ff.) and by **Melanchthon** in the *Loci Præcipui* on *De Iustitia hominis coram Deo* (CR 21:731ff. / MSA II/1:328ff.).

⁶⁸ **The *Cum sis ipse nocens* verses.** — This is an anonymous late-medieval anti-Reformation distich, quoted by Luther in the *Disputatio de iustificatione* of 1536 (WA 39/I:78ff.) and cited by **Bellarmine, *De iustificatione* II.1** as a paradigm-Catholic objection. Selnecker's Latin transmission of the verses follows the received Reformation-era anti-Tridentine polemical corpus.

⁶⁹ **The *gratia et donum* distinction.** — Paul at Romans 5:15 distinguishes ***ἡ χάρις καὶ ἡ δωρεά*** (*hē charis kai hē dōrea,* the grace and the gift). The Reformation-era Lutheran systematisation of this distinction into *iustificatio (= gratia, imputation)* and *renovatio (= donum, inhabitatio Spiritus)* is paradigmatically set out in **Luther, *Rationis Latomianae confutatio*** of 1521 (WA 8:43ff. / *LW* 32:133ff.) — the *Antilatomus,* which Selnecker knew thoroughly. Cf. also **FC SD III. 32-40** (*BSLK* 924ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 565ff.) on the *gratia/donum* distinction as it interfaces with the anti-Osiandrian question of *iustitia essentialis.*

⁷⁰ **Osiander controversy.** — **Andreas Osiander** (1498–1552), *Von dem einigen Mittler Jesu Christo und Rechtfertigung des Glaubens* (Königsberg 1551), taught that man is justified not by the imputed obedience of Christ, but by the *indwelling essential righteousness of the divine nature of Christ* (*iustitia essentialis*) infused into the believer. The Osiandrian controversy 1549–1566 was resolved confessionally in **FC SD III** which explicitly rejects the Osiandrian *iustitia essentialis* framework and confirms the imputative-forensic model. Selnecker as FC co-author was directly involved. Cf. **FC SD III. 17-19, 60-63** (*BSLK* 920ff., 940-941 / *Kolb-Wengert* 563, 572).

⁷¹ **Sedes doctrinae de iustificatione.** — The paradigm-Lutheran Reformation-orthodoxy identification of Romans + Galatians as the *sedes* for the justification-doctrine is programmatic and traces to **Melanchthon's *Loci Præcipui Theologici*** (1559) *De Iustificatione* opening (CR 21:731ff. / MSA II/1:328ff.). Selnecker structures the whole exposition as an *analytical commentary* on the two Epistles.

⁷² **The ten arguments from Romans 4.** — Selnecker's numbered-argument schema tracks Melanchthon's *Commentarii in Epistolam Pauli ad Romanos* (1540 Wittenberg; **CR** 15:493-796 / **MSA** V:35-231) on Rom. 4 quite closely. For the modern critical treatment, cf. **Cranfield, *A Critical and Exegetical Commentary on the Epistle to the Romans*** (Edinburgh: T&T Clark, 1975-1979), Vol I, on Rom. 4:1-25 (pp. 224-260); and **Dunn, *Romans 1-8*** (WBC 38A, 1988), pp. 195-229.

⁷³ **Rom. 9 as anti-Pelagian rather than anti-conditional-election.** — Selnecker's reading of Rom. 9 — *the Pauline discourse targets Jewish-election-vs-Gentile-election in the *ordo salutis,* not a supralapsarian double-decree* — is the paradigm-Lutheran FC XI hermeneutic. Selnecker himself was co-author of FC XI *De Praedestinatione,* which explicitly rejects both the Reformed *decretum absolutum* and the Calvinist *supralapsarian* readings of Rom. 9. Cf. **FC SD XI. 4ff., 33-42, 76-90** (*BSLK* 1064ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 640ff.).

⁷⁴ **Rom. 9:16 — *"Non est volentis..."*** — a paradigm-anti-Pelagian text, the *sedes* for the *sola gratia* strand of the Reformation-era doctrine of grace. Augustine's exegesis at *De praedestinatione sanctorum* 6-9 (PL 44:965ff. / NPNF I.5:498ff.) is the paradigm reference-point, but Selnecker deliberately does *not* follow the Augustinian double-predestinarian reading — retaining instead the Chrysostomean-cooperative reading which the FC XI framework then confirms.

⁷⁵ **The hardening-terminology.** — Selnecker's exhaustive philological analysis of the four hardening-verbs (*qāšāh, ḥāzaq, kābad,* and the LXX renderings *sklērynō / katischyō / barynō*) is a paradigm sixteenth-century humanist-Hebraist procedure and is remarkable for its philological accuracy. Selnecker draws on **Sebastian Münster's *Hebraica Biblia*** (Basel 1534-1535, revised 1546) and **Sanctes Pagninus, *Thesaurus Linguae Sanctae*** (Lyon 1529; revised 1575) for the Hebrew semantic-field analysis.

⁷⁶ **Oecumenius (c. 990–1050 by traditional attribution)** — the Byzantine commentator whose *Catena in Pauli Epistolas* (PG 118:325ff. for Romans) was much used by Reformation-era exegetes as a Greek-Fathers-catena. The specific formulation **ὁ θεὸς σκληρὸν καὶ ἀπειθῆ εἶναι συγχωρεῖ** ("*God concedes him to be hard and disobedient*") appears in Oecumenius on Rom. 9:18 (PG 118:509).

⁷⁷ **Augustine, *De correptione et gratia* 14-15 (PL 44:942-946)** for the *God-willing-to-be-obeyed-or-punished* formulation; and **Augustine, *Enchiridion* 100-104 (PL 40:279-282; CCSL 46:103-105)** for the passage Selnecker cites on the *will-of-God-fulfilled-in-both-ways.*

⁷⁸ **Luther's *Enarrationes in Genesin* on Genesis 26** (WA 43:459ff. / *LW* 5:41ff.) — the ***Swan-Song*** of the aging Luther (1544-1545, published posthumously 1550-1552). The specific *retraction*-passage Selnecker excerpts is at **WA 43:459-463** on Gen. 26:9 and represents the mature Luther's programmatic clarification of the *De Servo Arbitrio* (1525; WA 18:600-787 / *LW* 33) — namely, that the *hidden God / revealed God* distinction must not be used to feed *predestinarian speculation* but always to *drive the anxious conscience to the vocative Christ.* The FC XI *Solida Declaratio* — Selnecker co-authored — canonises this Luther-*Enarratio*-26 hermeneutic as the confessional-Lutheran doctrine of predestination.

⁷⁹ **The vessels-of-wrath / vessels-of-mercy exegesis** — Selnecker's *"God has created no men for destruction"* is the paradigm-Lutheran FC XI reading of Rom. 9:22-23 against the Reformed *reprobation ante praevisa peccata* framework. Cf. **FC SD XI. 76-90** (*BSLK* 1091ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 649ff.).

⁸⁰ **Selnecker's definition of faith.** — This is Selnecker's own compositional signature; the *firma et certa cognitio divinae erga nos benevolentiae* language is a *Concord-generation* Lutheran technical formulation, appearing verbatim in Chemnitz *Loci* (De Fide justificante) and Selnecker's own *Explicationes Symbolorum* (1572). It is the paradigm formulation against the *fides implicita* / *fides informis* Papist framework.

⁸¹ **The *synergon* controversy.** — Selnecker's careful *ordo/subject/matter*-analytic of the human will in conversion is the Second Antinomian Controversy's *synergism controversy* (1560-1577) working itself out toward FC II *De Libero Arbitrio.* Selnecker was co-author of FC II. Cf. **FC SD II. 44-90** (*BSLK* 890ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 552ff.) — the *doctrine-of-the-servile-will* article confirming Luther's *De Servo Arbitrio* while resisting both *Manichaeism* (which makes man a stone) and *Melanchthonian synergism* (which makes man a co-cause). Selnecker's *materia rationalis / non-brutum / συνεργὸν = subjectum non otiosum* formulation is the paradigm FC II compromise-language.

⁸² **The *Nil sum, nulla miser* verses** — attributed by Selnecker to *D. Philippus* (Philip Melanchthon), and appearing in **Melanchthon, *Selectarum Declamationum Philippi Melanthonis... liber tertius*** (Strassburg 1546-1553), as part of the *Preces Ecclesiasticae.* The *massam humanam / massam Christi* metaphor here is the paradigm-Melanchthonian *incarnation-solidarity* topos.

⁸³ **Georg Spalatin (1484–1545) — the paradigm-Wittenberg court-preacher and Luther-collaborator.** The *Sola fides hominem caelesti donat honore* verses were composed by Spalatin as an epistolary poem to **Eobanus Hessus** (1488–1540), the paradigm-Wittenberg humanist-poet, and printed in **Eobanus's *Sylvae*** (Frankfurt 1539). Selnecker frequently draws on these Wittenberg-Reformation Latin verses as pedagogical mnemonics; compare his own *Elenchus Praeceptorum* (Leipzig 1580) which uses similar didactic-hexameter forms.

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione* — §§16-22

⁸⁴ **The four reasons for the exclusive *Sola Fide*.** — Selnecker's schema is paradigm-Lutheran and directly parallels **Melanchthon, *Loci Præcipui Theologici* (1559) *De Iustificatione*** (CR 21:741ff. / MSA II/1:340ff.). Cf. also **Chemnitz, *Examen Concilii Tridentini* (1565-1573), Pars I *De Iustificatione*** — the paradigm Reformation-orthodoxy anti-Trent handbook, structured as a rebuttal of Trent Session VI (1547) canon by canon; and **Apology of the Augsburg Confession Article IV** (*BSLK* 158ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 120ff.) on the same four-reason apparatus. Note also **FC SD III. 32-45** (*BSLK* 924ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 565ff.).

⁸⁵ **Chrysostom on Luke 8:50** — the *"only believe"* / *πίστιν εἰσάγωμεν* saying appears in **John Chrysostom, *Homilia in Lucam*** — precise locus not certainly identified; the Latin transmission is via the medieval *Catena aurea* of **Thomas Aquinas** on Luke 8 (*S. Thomae Aquinatis Opera*, Parma 1863, XII:99). The paradigm sixteenth-century transmission is through **Erasmus's *Novum Instrumentum*** apparatus on Luke 8:50.

⁸⁶ **Basil the Great (c. 330-379), *Homilia de Humilitate*** — PG 31:525-540; the *sola fide iustificari* saying is at PG 31:532. Reformation-era transmission via the **1532 Basel Herwagen** edition of Basil's *Opera*.

⁸⁷ **Gregory Nazianzen (329-390), *Oratio* — "de taxias"** — precise locus not certainly identified; the Latin transmission is via the **Wittenberg-Reformation patristic catena** and appears in similar form at **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Iustificatione*** (CR 21:735) with attribution to Nazianzen's *Orationes.*

⁸⁸ **Photius of Sirmium** — Selnecker here appears to conflate two Photii: **Photius of Constantinople** (c. 810-891), whose *Amphilochia* and homiletic corpus are in PG 101-104, and the earlier **Photinus of Sirmium** (d. 376), the anti-Trinitarian condemned at the Councils of Sirmium 351 and Constantinople 381. The specific Galatians-3 quotation appears in **Photius of Constantinople's *Amphilochia*** (PG 101:1265ff.) rather than in any extant Photinus text; the *Sirmiensis* attribution in Selnecker's 1579 imprint is a Reformation-era bibliographic confusion.

⁸⁹ **Origen (c. 185-254), *Commentarii in Epistolam ad Romanos* III.3 (PG 14:942ff.)** — the *sola fides iustificat* saying at PG 14:952. The paradigm-Reformation-orthodox transmission is through **Erasmus's 1536 edition of Origen** and later through **Merlin's 1512 Paris edition.**

⁹⁰ **Ambrose (c. 340-397) — but properly *Ambrosiaster*** — *Commentarium in Epistolam ad Romanos* (PL 17:47ff., attributed pseudonymously to Ambrose in the manuscript tradition Selnecker uses). The paradigm-Reformation quotations from *"Ambrose on Romans"* are almost all from *Ambrosiaster,* whose true identity was only settled by **Erasmus's 1527 Basel edition of Augustine** (which noted the *pseudo-Ambrose* attribution). See **Souter, *A Study of Ambrosiaster*** (Cambridge 1905) and **Bammel, *Der Römerbriefkommentar des Ambrosiaster*** (in various *Reihe Judentum und Christentum,* 1963-1970). The *sola fide* citations are all authentic Ambrosiaster and are among the most important Reformation-era *sola-fide* patristic testimonies.

⁹¹ **Hilary of Poitiers (c. 315-367)** — the *fides sola iustificat* attribution — precise locus not identified in Hilary's extant corpus; may be **Hilary, *De Trinitate*** or **Hilary, *Tractatus super Psalmos*** (PL 9-10). Melanchthon similarly cites *Hilary sola fide* in *Loci* 1559 (CR 21:735). The specific dictum may be a Reformation-era Hilarian *florilegium* attribution rather than a verifiable Hilarian source.

⁹² **Victor Poeta** — likely **Claudius Marius Victor** (5th c. Gaul), author of the *Alethia,* a paraphrase of Genesis in three books. The specific Abraham couplet is at *Alethia* II (PL 61:963ff.). Reformation-era transmission via the **1560 Basel Fabricius edition** of Christian Latin poets.

⁹³ **Council of Trent, Session VI (13 January 1547), Canon 9 *De Iustificatione***: *"Si quis dixerit, sola fide impium iustificari, ita ut intelligat, nihil aliud requiri, quo ad iustificationis gratiam consequendam cooperetur, et nulla ex parte necesse esse, eum suae voluntatis motu praeparari atque disponi: anathema sit."* — Latin text in **Denzinger-Hünermann §1559**; English in **Tanner, *Decrees of the Ecumenical Councils*** II:679. Chemnitz's *Examen* Pars I *De Iustificatione* — Section on *Solus vs Sola Fide* — is the paradigm-Lutheran rebuttal of the whole Trent VI apparatus.

⁹⁴ **Selnecker, *Analectus*** (Leipzig 1568, expanded 1572) — one of Selnecker's earlier didactic-doctrinal works, referenced here by cross-reference; a companion to the *Institutio* as a compendium of dogmatic *loci-notes.* Cf. **VD16** S 5559 for the first edition.

⁹⁵ **Luther, *Rationis Latomianae confutatio*** (1521; WA 8:43-128 / *LW* 32:133-260) — the ***Antilatomus,*** Luther's paradigm treatise on the *sola fide* against Jacobus Latomus of Louvain. The *ring/gem* metaphor for faith-and-Christ is a stock Reformation-era Lutheran homiletic image, appearing frequently in **Luther, *Kirchenpostille*** on the Epiphany and Purification-of-Mary pericopes (WA 10/I.1:207ff.).

⁹⁶ **The *analogia geometrica* on Ephesians 4:7** — the paradigm-Melanchthonian rhetorical figure. Cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559** *De Ministerio* (CR 21:824). Selnecker's *"analogy in geometric-proportion, distributing to each what is congruent to his vocation"* echoes Melanchthon's rhetorical *loci-partitio* method.

⁹⁷ **Augustine on general vs special grace** — cf. **Augustine, *De correptione et gratia* 6-15** (PL 44:921-946); **Augustine, *De praedestinatione sanctorum* 3-11** (PL 44:962-975). The **operating/co-operating** distinction is at **Augustine, *De gratia et libero arbitrio* 17** (PL 44:901).

⁹⁸ **Pelagius (c. 354-420)** and the paradigm anti-Pelagian controversy — condemned at the Council of Carthage (418), Ephesus (431), Orange II (529). Selnecker's *"as today the Jesuits do the same"* is a paradigm sixteenth-century Reformation-era anti-Jesuit polemical trope, deriving from Melanchthon's *Antitheses adversus veterem Ecclesiam* (1552) and reiterated in Chemnitz's *Examen* Pars I. The Jesuit-Pelagian parallel became a standard confessional-Lutheran polemical *topos* through the 1580s-1620s (Selnecker at Leipzig, Hunnius at Wittenberg, later Gerhard at Jena).

⁹⁹ **Augustine, *De gratia et libero arbitrio* 17** (PL 44:901) — *"Deus operatur quidem in nobis velle, sed cum incipimus velle, tunc etiam nostrum est velle."* Also **Augustine, *Enchiridion* 32** (PL 40:248) — *"Nolentem praevenit ut velit, volentem subsequitur ne frustra velit."* These are the paradigm-Lutheran *anti-synergist* Augustinian citations in the FC II framework.

⁹⁹ᵃ **The three Papist grounds for doubt** — Selnecker's tripartite structure of the Papist objection is Chemnitz-*Examen*-standard and appears in **Chemnitz, *Examen* Pars I *De Certitudine Gratiae*** (Preus tr. 1971, I:428ff.).

¹⁰⁰ **The Hebrew *yēṣer sāmûk* / *ποίημα* Isa 26:3 analysis** — draws on **Sebastian Münster, *Hebraica Biblia*** (Basel 1534-1535) on Isaiah, and on **Johann Forster (1495-1558), *Dictionarium Hebraicum novum*** (Basel 1557) — Forster's Hebrew lexicon was the standard Wittenberg-Reformation Hebraist reference-work of Selnecker's generation. Forster taught Hebrew at Wittenberg 1548-1558 and produced the Hebrew apparatus for Luther's late Old Testament lectures. See **Newman, *Jewish Influence on Christian Reform Movements*** (Columbia 1925), ch. 8, on Forster's role.

¹⁰¹ **Council of Trent, Session VI, Canon 13 *De Iustificatione***: *"Si quis dixerit, omni homini ad remissionem peccatorum assequendam necessarium esse, ut credat certo et absque ulla haesitatione propriae infirmitatis et indispositionis peccata sibi esse remissa: anathema sit."* — **Denzinger-Hünermann §1563**. And Canon 14: *"Si quis dixerit, hominem a peccatis absolvi et iustificari ex eo, quod se absolvi et iustificari certo credat, aut neminem vere esse iustificatum, nisi qui credat se esse iustificatum: anathema sit"* — **§1564**. Chemnitz's *Examen* Pars I *De Certitudine* section is the paradigm-Lutheran anti-Trent rebuttal.

¹⁰² **Bernard, *De Fragmentis Septem, Sermo* 3** — precise reference not confidently identified in Bernard's *Opera*; the *charitas adoptionis, veritas promissionis, potestas redditionis* triadic structure is characteristic Bernardine and appears in various forms in his **Sermones in Cantica Canticorum** (PL 183:783ff.) and **Sermones de tempore.** Selnecker's citation matches the *Sermones super quaedam Verba* group in the *S. Bernardi Opera Omnia*, Paris 1544.

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione* — §§23-25 (4 grades of necessity + predestination objections + fructus fidei)

¹⁰³ **Augustine on foresight and moral responsibility.** — The paradigm Augustinian formulation ("*Deus omnia praescit quorum ipse auctor est, nec tamen omnium quae praescit ipse auctor est*") comes from **Augustine, *De libero arbitrio* III.4** (PL 32:1276f. / CCSL 29:279ff.) — the classical distinction between divine foreknowledge as *cognitive* and divine causality as *volitional.* Also **Augustine, *De civitate Dei* V.9-10** (PL 41:148-153 / CCSL 47:135-140) on foreknowledge vs necessity. The memory-analogy Selnecker attributes to Augustine ("*nemo memoria sua cogit facienda*") is a Reformation-era paraphrase of the Augustinian argument-form.

¹⁰⁴ **Chrysostom, *Homiliae in Matthaeum* 59 on Matt. 18:7** (PG 58:575ff.) — the Chrysostomean anti-Stoic hermeneutic of *οὐκ ἀνάγκη ἀλλὰ γνώμη* (*not necessity but the intention*) as the ground for the *"Woe to that man"* pronouncement. The Latin Reformation transmission is via the ***Homiliae in Matthaeum*** of the 1517 Erasmus Basel edition.

¹⁰⁵ **The critique of "monkey Augustinians."** — Selnecker's *simiarum more* passage targets the **supralapsarian double-predestinarian** wing of the Reformed tradition — specifically **Beza's *Tabula praedestinationis*** (1555; expanded in the *Aphorismi* and *Quaestiones et responsiones*) — and the **Zanchi** / **Perkins** / **Piscator** Reformed-Orthodox systematisation that would culminate at Dordt (1618-19). The Chrysostomean-cooperative reading of Rom. 9 is the paradigm-Lutheran FC XI alternative. Cf. **FC SD XI. 33-42** (*BSLK* 1074-1078 / *Kolb-Wengert* 645-647).

¹⁰⁶ **Augustine on God as debtor by promise.** — The dictum ***"Deus se debitorem fecit non aliquid a nobis accipiendo, sed quod ei placuit promittendo"*** is at **Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 32, Sermo 1** (PL 36:277 / CCSL 38:247). Also **Augustine, *Sermo* 158.2** (PL 38:863) — *"Debitor factus est non aliquid a nobis accipiendo, sed quod ei placuit promittendo."* Paradigm Augustinian formulation of the *promissio-debitor* topos, central to the Wittenberg-Reformation understanding of the Evangelical covenant.

¹⁰⁷ **Tertullian on demanding the debt with faith.** — The dictum comes from **Tertullian, *De patientia* 15** (PL 1:1272 / CCSL 1:317ff.) — the *De patientia* was one of the most cited Tertullian works in the Reformation era, especially in the Wittenberg-Melanchthonian patristic-catena tradition. Cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559** (CR 21:747f. / MSA II/1:346ff.) for the same *Tertulliana vox*.

¹⁰⁸ **The three anti-Stoic Latin distichs** — *"Fata movere Deus…"*, *"Non plus fata tamen…"*, and *"Non Deus est numen Parcarum carcere clausum…"* — are drawn from the Wittenberg-Reformation Latin-poetic canon against Stoic fatalism. The middle line (*"pia vota valent"*) appears in **Eobanus Hessus, *Hymni* on Divine Providence** (Wittenberg 1539). The final quatrain (*"Non Deus est numen…"*) is likely Melanchthonian in origin — cf. **Melanchthon, *Selectarum Declamationum liber tertius*** (Strasbourg 1546) on divine providence. The paradigm anti-Stoic-God cluster in the Wittenberg humanist-classical curriculum.

¹⁰⁹ **Augustine on the will glorying in the Lord.** — *"Absit ut sit vel dicatur voluntas bona, quae in aliis vel in seipsa, et non in Domino gloriatur"* — a paradigm-Augustinian anti-Pelagian formulation, appearing in **Augustine, *De gratia et libero arbitrio* 6, 15** (PL 44:894, 899) and **Augustine, *Contra Iulianum* IV.3** (PL 44:743). The *Quid habes quod non accepisti?* (1 Cor. 4:7) locus is the paradigm anti-Pelagian *sedes* — cf. **Augustine, *De praedestinatione sanctorum* 3-5** (PL 44:962-968).

¹¹⁰ **The twelve grounds for universal grace.** — Selnecker's *duodecim rationes* schema for the *voluntas antecedens salvifica universalis* is the paradigm Concord-generation Lutheran defence against both the Catholic-Molinist middle-knowledge and the Reformed double-decree frameworks. Cf. **FC SD XI. 15-24, 76-90** (*BSLK* 1068ff., 1091ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 642ff., 649ff.) — Selnecker himself co-authored FC XI. The paradigm *voluntas antecedens vs voluntas consequens* distinction traces to **Damascene, *De fide orthodoxa* II.29** (PG 94:964ff.) and enters the Wittenberg-Reformation tradition via **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Praedestinatione*** (CR 21:912ff. / MSA II/2:242ff.).

¹¹¹ **The Great Commission language.** — Selnecker cites *μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη* (Matt. 28:19) with the observation that the aorist imperative + accusative direct object (rather than partitive genitive) has universal-collective force — "make disciples of *all* the nations," not merely "make disciples out from among the nations." This is a paradigm 16th-c. Wittenberg-humanist exegetical move against the Reformed *ex numero electorum* restriction of the Great Commission. Cf. **Chemnitz, *De duabus naturis in Christo*** (Jena 1570), Ch. 25, on the *pantes* of the Great Commission.

¹¹² **Ambrose on faith as the root of good works.** — *"Fides est radix bonorum operum"* — a paradigm-Ambrosian formulation appearing in **Ambrose, *De officiis ministrorum* I.29** (PL 16:69) and elsewhere in the Ambrosian corpus. Widely cited in Reformation-era Lutheran systematics as the *sedes* for the *fructus-fidei* framework. Cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Bonis Operibus*** (CR 21:775ff.).

¹¹³ **Augustine on incepted obedience.** — *"Omnia mandata Dei facta deputantur, quando quicquid non fit ignoscitur"* — from **Augustine, *Retractationes* I.19** (PL 32:614 / CSEL 36:104ff.) — one of the paradigm-Augustinian formulations of the *inchoatio-obedientiae* topos which the Reformation carries over into the doctrine of the *iustitia inchoata* of the regenerate. Also **Augustine, *Ad Bonifacium* (*Epistola* 185)** (PL 33:792ff. / CSEL 57:1-44) for the *studium praeceptorum servandi + ignoscendi* framework.

¹¹⁴ **Erhard Schnepf (1495-1558), the Württemberg reformer.** — Snepfius the elder taught at **Marburg** (1527-34) and **Tübingen** (1544-58), and was a paradigm Wittenberg-generation South German Lutheran. The *pater-filiolus* metaphor Selnecker recalls is a characteristic Schnepfian homiletic image from his lectures on the Psalms and the Pauline Epistles. Selnecker as a young Wittenberg student (matriculated 1550) knew Snepfius in the last years of Schnepf's life. Cf. **T. Kolb, *Erhard Schnepf: Studien zu seinem Leben und Wirken*** (Tübingen: Mohr Siebeck, 1990).

¹¹⁵ **The third use of the Law — anti-Antinomian.** — Selnecker's polemic here targets the *Second Antinomian Controversy* (1556-1580) — specifically **Andreas Poach** and **Anton Otto**, who rejected the *tertius usus legis* as *diabolicum phantasma*. The Concord-generation Lutheran resolution is in **FC SD VI** (*BSLK* 962-970 / *Kolb-Wengert* 587-591), which affirms the third use against both the *Antinomian* and the *Papist* positions. Selnecker as FC co-author signed on to the *tertius usus* framework here. Cf. **Elert, *Morphologie des Luthertums*** (München 1931-32) II:39-58 on the Second Antinomian Controversy.

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione* — §26 *Recapitulatio* Capita §§I–XLIV

¹¹⁶ **Luther on the *articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesiae*.** — The classical Lutheran topos *"stante et salvo articulo iustificationis, stat et manet vera doctrina, fides et religio"* traces to **Luther, *Disputatio pro declaratione virtutis indulgentiarum* (95 Theses commentary)** and above all to the **1535 Galatians Commentary** (WA 40/I:441 / *LW* 26:283): *"quia isto articulo stante stat Ecclesia, ruente ruit Ecclesia."* Also **Luther, *Schmalkaldische Artikel* II.1** (*BSLK* 415f. / *Kolb-Wengert* 301) — "*Auf diesem Artikel steht alles*." This is the paradigm-Lutheran formulation of the *centrality* of the doctrine of justification, and Selnecker (as FC co-author of Art. III on Justification) carries the topos over as the opening thesis of the Recapitulatio.

¹¹⁷ **The verse ***"ἐν δὲ δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ᾿ ἀρετή ᾿ ὅτι"*** is from **Theognis of Megara, *Elegiae* 147** (6th c. BC), cited by **Aristotle, *Nicomachean Ethics* V.1** (1129b) as a definition-of-justice topos: *"in righteousness all virtue is comprehended in sum."* The paradigm Reformation-era transmission is through **Melanchthon, *Enarratio Ethicorum Aristotelis*** (Wittenberg 1544; CR 16:277ff.), which uses this same Theognidean-Aristotelian dictum as the definition-of-*iustitia*-universalis pivot. Selnecker as Melanchthon's student inherits the citation.

¹¹⁸ **The Pelagian controversy — chronology.** — Pelagius was condemned at the **Council of Carthage (418)**, the **Council of Ephesus (431)**, and definitively at the **Second Council of Orange (529)** — which is the paradigm anti-Pelagian confessional-Western text. Selnecker's dating "*about the year 400*" refers to the initial phase of the controversy — the arrival of Pelagius in Rome c. 400 and his encounter with Augustine at Carthage 411-412. The Pelagian → Semi-Pelagian → Anti-Pelagian arc runs from Pelagius (d. c. 420) through **Cassian** and **Faustus of Riez** (5th c.) to the resolution at Orange II. Cf. **B. Rees, *Pelagius: A Reluctant Heretic*** (Woodbridge: Boydell, 1988).

¹¹⁹ **Augustinian gratia distinctions.** — The distinction between **gratia praeveniens / operans** (preceding grace, working faith without the will's cooperation) and **gratia subsequens / cooperans** (subsequent grace, cooperating with the renewed will) is the paradigm-Augustinian framework at **Augustine, *De gratia et libero arbitrio* 17** (PL 44:901): *"Ut enim velimus, sine nobis operatur; cum autem volumus et sic volumus ut faciamus, nobiscum cooperatur"* — *"That we may will, He worketh without us; but when we will, and so will as to do, He co-worketh with us."* Cf. also **Augustine, *Enchiridion* 32** (PL 40:248). The distinction between *gratia generalis* (God's benevolent providence toward all) and *gratia specialis* (justifying grace given to the elect) is Melanchthonian systematisation of the Augustinian framework — cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Gratia*** (CR 21:657ff. / MSA II/1:243ff.).

¹²⁰ **The Isaiah 26:3 *Yēṣer sāmūch* meditation.** — The paradigm-Lutheran Reformation exegesis is drawn from **Luther, *Enarratio in Isaiam*** (WA 25:171-172 / *LW* 16:189-190) — where Luther explicates the *Yēṣer sāmūch* as *"cogitatio firma quae sustinetur a Deo"*. Selnecker's development — through **D. Forster's Hebrew** apparatus (see note ¹⁰⁰ above) and through the *Sāmach*-as-*sustainer* etymology — is the Wittenberg Hebraist reception of the Lutheran Isaiah-lecture. Cf. also **Melanchthon, *Commentarii in Isaiam*** on Isa. 26 (CR 13:989ff.). The Mark 9:24 *"credo, adiuva incredulitatem meam"* is the paradigm consolation-*locus* in the Lutheran *Anfechtung*-tradition.

¹²¹ **The Greek Scholiast on Hebrews 11.** — The extended Greek passage which Selnecker quotes is from the **Catena in Epistolam ad Hebraeos** as preserved in **Oecumenius** (PG 119:341) and **Theophylact** (PG 125:325-328). Selnecker follows the received sixteenth-century Wittenberg Greek-patristic transmission — likely through the **1532 Basel Herwagen Basil-Chrysostom-Cyril** edition and through **Erasmus's 1516 Novum Instrumentum** apparatus on Hebrews 11.

¹²² **Basil the Great on faith as *πληροφορία*.** — From **Basil, *De fide*** (PG 31:676-692), specifically **Ch. 1**: *"τί γὰρ ἴδιον τῆς πίστεως..."* — the paradigm Basilian definition of faith as *indiscriminate fullness of assurance of the God-breathed sayings*. Widely cited in the Reformation-era Lutheran *πληροφορία*-tradition. Cf. also **Basil, *Homilia in Psalmum 115*** (PG 30:104-116) on faith and the Word.

¹²³ **Augustine on the certitude of confidence.** — *"Totius fiduciae certitudinem in pretioso Christi sanguine positam esse"* — this Augustinian dictum appears in various forms in the Augustinian corpus, especially at **Augustine, *In Psalmum 55* Enarratio 3** (PL 36:648) and **Augustine, *De doctrina Christiana* I.14** (PL 34:24) on the blood of Christ as the ground of Christian confidence. The Reformation-era transmission is through **Luther, *Postilla* on Passiontide** (WA 10/I.2:143ff.) — an Augustinian-Lutheran commonplace.

¹²⁴ **The Fathers on ***sola fide***.** — Selnecker's catena — *Basil, Nazianzus, Origen, Ambrose (i.e. Ambrosiaster), Augustine, Athanasius, Hilary* — is the paradigm Reformation-era ***sola fide*** patristic testimony-list. See notes ⁸⁵-⁹¹ above (already cited at §17) for the specific loci in each Father. The catena tradition traces to **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559** (CR 21:735ff.) and **Chemnitz, *Examen* Pars I *De Iustificatione* — Section on Patristic Testimonies**. The *"μόνον πίστευε"* of Luke 8:50 (Christ to Jairus) is the paradigm New Testament *sola fide* dominical *sedes*.

¹²⁵ **Luther on faith and works — the flame-analogy.** — The paradigm-Lutheran dictum *"impossibile est ut fides non operetur..."* is from **Luther, *Vorrede auf die Epistel S. Paul: an die Römer*** (Preface to Romans, 1522; WA DB 7:10 / *LW* 35:370-371): *"O es ist ein lebendig, geschäftig, tätig, mächtig Ding um den Glauben, dass es unmöglich ist, dass er nicht ohn Unterlass sollte Gutes wirken."* Also in Latin form in **Luther, *In Epistolam ad Galatas Commentarius* (1535)** (WA 40/I:266 / *LW* 26:155). Cf. **FC SD IV. 10-11** (*BSLK* 942f. / *Kolb-Wengert* 575) on the same Lutheran fides-vera-numquam-sine-fructibus formulation.

¹²⁶ **Luther's *ex fide in fidem* insight — the tower experience.** — Selnecker's exposition of Rom. 1:17 *"ex fide in fidem"* — the *iustitia Dei passiva* — recapitulates Luther's own *"tower experience"* narrative from the **Preface to the Latin Writings** (1545; WA 54:179ff. / *LW* 34:336ff.): the recognition that the *iustitia Dei* in Rom. 1:17 is not God's punitive righteousness but the righteousness which God gratuitously imputes unto the believer. This is the *paradigm Reformation-hermeneutic breakthrough* which Selnecker as second-generation Wittenberg student inherited. Cf. **Luther, *Vorlesung über den Römerbrief*** (WA 56:171-173 / *LW* 25:151-153) for the 1515-16 Romans lectures — the original *reformatorische Grundeinsicht.*

## From Locus I *De Iustificatione* — §26 *Recapitulatio* Capita §§XLV–LXXXV + closing Christ-hymn

¹²⁷ **Luther's "tower experience" reminiscence.** — Selnecker here transmits an oral tradition from his own preceptors at Wittenberg (matriculated 1550) — the paradigm-Lutheran reminiscence of the *turmerlebnis* narrative which Luther himself set down definitively in the **1545 Preface to the Latin Writings** (WA 54:179-187 / *LW* 34:336-338): *"tandem miserente Deo, meditabundus dies et noctes, connexionem verborum attendi, nempe: Iustitia Dei revelatur in illo, sicut scriptum est: Iustus ex fide vivit. Ibi iustitiam Dei coepi intellegere eam qua iustus dono Dei vivit, nempe ex fide."* Selnecker's version — through Melanchthon's mediation — preserves the same *iustitia passiva* recognition. Cf. **Bornkamm, *Luthers geistige Welt*** (Lüneburg 1953) and **Oberman, *Luther: Man Between God and the Devil*** (New Haven 1989), Ch. 5, for the historical-theological analysis of the tower-experience.

¹²⁸ **Active and passive obedience of Christ — the *τέλος νόμου* framework.** — Selnecker's rejection of the *sola passive obedientia* framework (which he attributes to "certain novel opinions") targets **Johannes Piscator** (1546-1625) — the Reformed theologian who would later fully develop this position in his *Theses de fide iustificante* (1616) and *De iustitia Christi passiva et activa* (1620). But the position was already circulating in the 1570s Reformed and Radical circles. Selnecker's *τέλος νόμου εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι* (Rom. 10:4) framework — that the *τέλος* signifieth *both consummation and perfection, or entire satisfaction, and both active and passive obedience* — is the paradigm-Lutheran FC-generation formulation. Cf. **FC SD III. 32-63** (*BSLK* 924-943 / *Kolb-Wengert* 565-573) on the *iustitia Christi activa et passiva* imputed together. Also **Chemnitz, *Loci Theologici*** on *De Iustificatione* (Preus tr. 1989, II:445-491) for the paradigm Concord-generation exposition.

¹²⁹ **Bernard on the three-fold gratuitous nature of grace.** — *"Necesse est primo omnium credere, quod peccatorum remissionem habere non possis nisi per indulgentiam Dei; deinde quod nihil boni operis habere possis nisi et hoc dederit ipse; postremo quod aeternam vitam nullis possis operibus promereri nisi gratis detur et illa"* — this Bernardine triad is drawn from **Bernard, *De gratia et libero arbitrio* 14** (PL 182:1015ff. / *S. Bernardi Opera Omnia,* Rome 1957ff., III:187). One of the paradigm Reformation-received Bernardine testimonies for the *sola gratia* framework. Cf. **Luther, *De servo arbitrio*** (WA 18:786 / *LW* 33:294) for the same Bernardine dictum used against Erasmus.

¹³⁰ **The FC IV framework — necessity of good works.** — Selnecker's careful triage of the phrase *bona opera necessaria sunt ad salutem* — which he rejects because of *merit*-implications, while affirming that *good works are necessary secundum gradus necessitatis* — is the paradigm Concord-generation resolution of the **Major-Amsdorf controversy** (1552-1560). Georg Major had said *"bona opera necessaria sunt ad salutem"*; Nikolaus von Amsdorf countered *"bona opera perniciosa sunt ad salutem"*; both formulations rejected in **FC SD IV** (*BSLK* 940-951 / *Kolb-Wengert* 574-581), which affirms that *good works are necessary as fruits of faith and as witness of salvation, but not as cause or merit of salvation*. Selnecker as FC IV co-author here transmits the Concord-formula compromise.

¹³¹ **Augustine on human vs divine righteousness — the candle-in-sunlight image.** — *"Humana iustitia, diuinae iustitiae comparata, iniuftitia est, quia et lucerna in tenebris fulgere cernitur, sed in Solis radium posita tenebratur"* — this Augustinian dictum in this precise form is not extant in the received Augustinian corpus, but the substance appears in various forms at **Augustine, *In Iohannem Tractatus* 3.19** (PL 35:1404 / CCSL 36:29ff.) and **Augustine, *Enarrationes in Psalmos* 143** (PL 37:1857ff.). The *lucerna-vs-Sol* comparison is a Reformation-era Augustinian *sententia* transmission — likely through **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559** *De Iustificatione* (CR 21:757). Cf. also **Isaiah 64:6** *"omnes iustitiae nostrae quasi pannus menstruatae"* — the paradigm biblical *sedes* for the *iustitiae-nostrae-immundae* topos.

¹³² **Augustine on God crowning His own gifts.** — *"Deus dona sua coronat in nobis, non merita nostra"* — from **Augustine, *Epistola* 194 *ad Sixtum*** (PL 33:874-891 / CSEL 57:176ff.), specifically Ch. 5.19: *"Cum Deus coronat merita nostra, nihil aliud coronat quam munera sua"* — the paradigm-Augustinian formulation of the *sola gratia* framework against Pelagianism, widely cited in Reformation-era Lutheran systematics. The Bernardine *"sufficit ad meritum scire quod non sufficit meritum"* (Bernard, *Sermones super Cantica* 68.6, PL 183:1112) is a Cistercian recapitulation of the same Augustinian topos. The Pontifical scholastic distinction between *meritum de congruo* (merit of congruity — pre-justification human works that merit grace *congrue* rather than *strictly*) and *meritum de condigno* (merit of condignity — post-justification human works that merit reward *strictly* and *by proportion*) is the Sentences-tradition scholastic framework, systematised by **Thomas Aquinas, *ST* I-II q. 114 aa. 1-9** and by **Duns Scotus, *Ordinatio* I d. 17**. Chemnitz's *Examen* Pars I *De Bonis Operibus* rebuts this entire framework as unbiblical.

¹³³ **Chrysostom on love and faith — mutual dependence.** — *"οὐδὲν ὄφελος ἀγάπης πίστεως χωρίς, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδ᾿ ἂν γένοιτο ἀγάπη ἡ ἑτέρα"* — the paradigm Chrysostomean formulation of the *fides-charitas* mutual dependence. Precise locus not certainly identified in Chrysostom's extant corpus; the Latin transmission is via the medieval *Catena aurea* of Thomas Aquinas on 1 Cor. 13. The paradigm sixteenth-century transmission is through the **1517 Erasmus Basel Chrysostom edition** and through **Melanchthon, *Enarratio Epistolae Prioris ad Corinthios*** (CR 15:1050ff.) on 1 Cor. 13.

¹³⁴ **Trent Session VI, Canon 13 — the certitude-anathema — again.** — Selnecker's polemical broadside against *Papist doubting* recapitulates the substance of §21-22 (already-cited note ¹⁰¹ on **Trent Sess. VI, Canons 13-14**, *Denzinger-Hünermann* §§1563-1564). The Concord-generation Lutheran response is at **FC SD III. 30-31, 60-63** (*BSLK* 923f., 940-941 / *Kolb-Wengert* 564-565, 572) affirming the *πληροφορία* certitude of faith against the Tridentine anathema. Cf. also **Chemnitz, *Examen* Pars I *De Certitudine Gratiae*** (Preus tr. 1971, I:428ff.) for the paradigm anti-Trent handbook on this point.

¹³⁵ **The *Christe Deus nobis in mundi faecibus assis* — closing Christ-hymn.** — This is Selnecker's own composition, in the tradition of Wittenberg-humanist Latin Christian verse. The verses recapitulate the paradigm-Selneckerian pastoral concerns of the *Institutio* — the *conservation of pure doctrine* against heretics (Antinomians, Sacramentarians, Osiandrians, and Papists — the four groups against whom Selnecker had preached throughout his career), the *Emmaus-companionship* (*Vespera iam venit, nobiscum Christe maneto*, cf. Luke 24:29), the *sanguis Christi* Atonement (Non quia nos digni, sed quia mitis eras), and the *victoria Christi in coelo* (Rector, et in summo tu caro nostra thronoes — the *caro-in-throno* topos of the ascended-and-glorified human nature of Christ, paradigm-Chalcedonian). Selnecker was among the most important Lutheran hymnodists of the second generation: his German hymns include *"Ach bleib bei uns, Herr Jesu Christ"* (1572, based on Nikolaus Selnecker's Latin verse *"Vespera iam venit"* in this very hymn), *"Lass mich dein sein und bleiben,"* and settings of the *Nunc dimittis* and the *Vater unser*. Cf. **W. Blankenburg in *Handbuch der deutschen evangelischen Kirchenmusik*** I/1 (Göttingen 1969) on Selnecker as hymnodist.

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §§1–3 (Definition, Law-vs-Gospel, three parts)

¹³⁶ **Ausonius, *Epigrammata* 12 (or 33 in the older numbering).** — The couplet *"Sum Dea, quae facti, non facti que, exigo poenas, / Nempe ut poeniteat, sic Metanoea vocor"* is from **Decimius Magnus Ausonius (c. 310-c. 395), *Epigrammata*** on the goddess *Metanoea* — a personification of the Greek *μετάνοια* as a Roman-mythological figure. The paradigm-Reformation transmission is via **Scaliger's *Ausonii Opera*** (Lyon 1575) and via **Erasmus's *Adagia*** for the *metanoia*-etymology entries. Selnecker's use here is a humanist-classical *aside* to a pastoral-theological definition — characteristic of the second-generation Wittenberg pedagogical style. Cf. **Green, *The Works of Ausonius*** (Oxford 1991) for the modern critical text.

¹³⁷ **The *μετάνοια-vs-μεταμέλεια* distinction.** — Selnecker's careful differentiation between *μετάνοια* (salutary repentance leading to conversion) and *μεταμέλεια* (remorse without conversion — the "Epimethean" retrospective sorrow) is the paradigm sixteenth-century Wittenberg exegetical framework. Cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci Praecipui Theologici* (1559) *De Poenitentia*** (CR 21:892ff. / MSA II/2:225ff.); **Chemnitz, *Examen Concilii Tridentini* Pars II *De Poenitentia*** (Preus tr. 1978, II:588ff.) — the paradigm Concord-generation anti-Trent handbook on penitence. The Judas-*μεταμέλεια*-not-*μετάνοια* distinction is drawn from Matt. 27:3 *μεταμεληθεὶς ἀπέστρεψεν* — the paradigm New Testament *sedes* for the deadly-remorse-without-faith framework. The Hebrew *Shob / Teshuvah / Nicham* triad is the paradigm Wittenberg-Hebraist etymology, drawn from **Sebastian Münster's *Hebraica Biblia*** (Basel 1534-1535) and **Forster's *Dictionarium Hebraicum novum*** (Basel 1557).

¹³⁸ **The Peter-vs-Judas paradigm.** — The distinction between Peter's *penitence unto salvation* (Luke 22:62 *ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσε πικρῶς*) and Judas' *remorse unto damnation* (Matt. 27:3-5 *μεταμεληθεὶς... ἀπελθὼν ἀπήγξατο*) is the paradigm Wittenberg pastoral-typological *sedes* for the doctrine of penitence. Cf. **Luther, *Kirchenpostille*** on Maundy Thursday and Passiontide (WA 10/I.2:143ff.); **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Poenitentia*** (CR 21:895ff.). Selnecker's own **hymn *"O Herre Gott, mein Sünd sind groß"*** (1572) works out the Peter-typology in vernacular verse. The *"drops of tears imprinting furrows upon Peter's cheeks"* topos is a paradigm medieval-hagiographic locus (via **Legenda aurea**) which the Wittenberg homiletic tradition retained. Cf. also **FC SD III. 22-31** (*BSLK* 923f. / *Kolb-Wengert* 564-565) which — although its principal focus is justification — echoes the Peter-Judas paradigm.

¹³⁹ **Luther on *poenitentia ex Lege dimidium poenitentia*.** — The Lutheran dictum *"Die Buße aus dem Gesetz ist eine halbe Buße"* traces to **Luther, *De poenitentia*** (WA 1:319-324) — the 1518 *Sermo de poenitentia* — and to the **1519 *Sermo de sacramento poenitentiae*** (WA 2:709-723 / *LW* 35:9-22). The paradigm-Reformation systematisation is in the *Ninety-Five Theses* Theses 1-4: *"Dominus et magister noster Iesus Christus, dicendo 'poenitentiam agite' etc., omnem vitam fidelium poenitentiam esse voluit."* Cf. **Luther, *Große Katechismus* — Beichte** (*BSLK* 725ff. / *Kolb-Wengert* 476ff.) for the mature Lutheran two-part penitence framework (which the Formula of Concord Article V — *De Lege et Evangelio* — codifies). The three German proverbs Selnecker cites (*Wol gebeicht ist halb gebusset*, *Gnad geht für Recht*, *Nimmer thun ist die beste Buße*) are paradigm second-generation Wittenberg vernacular-pedagogical formulations transmitting the Lutheran doctrine of penitence to children.

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §§4–6 (Causes to penitence · God's forewarnings · vera ratio + anti-despair)

¹⁴⁰ **Pseudo-Berosus and the Noahite flood-prediction.** — Selnecker's Berosus-source is the pseudo-antique **Berosus the Babylonian** of the Italian Dominican **Annio da Viterbo (Giovanni Nanni, 1432-1502)**, *Commentaria super opera diversorum auctorum de antiquitatibus loquentium* (Rome 1498). Annio's *Berosus* is a Renaissance-humanist forgery which claims to preserve genuine Chaldean historical material — including the Noahite 78-year building of the ark, the sending of Noah's sons to various parts of the world, and their inscription of the future calamities on stones. Widely circulated in the 16th century and treated as authentic by many Reformation-era authors (though scholarship later exposed the forgery — cf. **Grafton, *Forgers and Critics*** [Princeton 1990], Ch. 3). Selnecker's use here transmits the common Wittenberg reliance on pseudo-Berosus for antediluvian chronology. The 6 April eclipse: Selnecker's *Institutio* was in the 1579 edition; the specific "6 April" solar eclipse was likely the partial eclipse observable in central Europe on 6 April 1568 or a later projection — a *παράδειγμα* for the discussion.

¹⁴¹ **Jerome on divine clemency.** — *"Divinitatis natura est clemens et pia, magisque ad indulgentiam quàm ad vindictam prona"* — from **Jerome, *Commentarium in Prophetam Ionam* 3.4** (PL 25:1140f. / CCSL 76:405ff.), on Jon. 3:4 — Nineveh's repentance. This is the paradigm-Hieronymian formulation of the *voluntas antecedens salvifica* framework, widely cited in Reformation-era Lutheran discussions of the mercy-vs-wrath dialectic in the Old Testament. Cf. **Ambrose, *De poenitentia* II.6** (PL 16:496ff.) for the parallel Ambrosian *clementia divina* formulation.

¹⁴² **Chrysostom on divine punishment as mercy.** — *"Deus gaudet non de suo lucro, sed de nostra salute"* and *"Deus cùm poenas infert, facit hoc ineffabili clementia"* — paraphrases of Chrysostomean material at **John Chrysostom, *Homiliae in Matthaeum* 22 & 26** (PG 57:302ff., 331ff.) and at **Chrysostom, *De Statuis Homilia* 5** (PG 49:69-76) — the paradigm Chrysostomean *pater-non-tyrannus* framework, drawn from the 386-Antioch homilies delivered during the Riot of the Statues. **Clement of Alexandria on wrath as handmaid of goodness** — from **Clement, *Paedagogus* I.8** (PG 8:326-343 / SC 70:222ff.) on divine paideutic-wrath: *"ἐπὶ σωτηρίᾳ μὲν ἡ τιμωρία, εἰς ἐπανόρθωσιν δὲ ἡ ἐπιτίμησις"* — the paradigm Clementine *παιδεία*-framework for divine punishment.

¹⁴³ **Augustine to Macedonius and Gregory the Great on providence-vs-future-judgment.** — Augustine's letter *ad Macedonium* is **Ep. 153.3.6** (PL 33:653-665 / CSEL 44:397-425): *"Multa Deus in hoc saeculo punit, ne divina providentia non esse credatur; et multa servat ultimo examini, ut futurum iudicium commendetur."* The Gregorian parallel is at **Gregory the Great, *Moralia in Iob* XX.34-36** (PL 76:171-176 / CCSL 143A:1042ff.) — the paradigm-Gregorian *cur mala boni patiantur, cur bona mali habeant* framework, widely cited in the Reformation-era Lutheran theodicy tradition.

¹⁴⁴ **Gregory the Great, *Moralia in Iob* and Luther on Genesis 9.** — The *Moralia* citation is at **Gregory, *Moralia in Iob* IX.15-20** (PL 75:876-880 / CCSL 143:472ff.) on the *toleratio malorum* paradigm. Luther's Genesis 9 passage is at **Luther, *Enarrationes in Genesin* on Gen. 9:20-27** (WA 42:388ff. / *LW* 2:167ff.) — Luther's mature exposition of the *dilatio-poenae* framework in the doctrine of divine providence and the schooling of the Church through tribulation. This is one of Luther's most fully-developed treatments of the *Anfechtung*-as-schooling theme, which Selnecker transmits.

¹⁴⁵ **Gregory of Nazianzus — quatrain on divine gentleness.** — The four-line iambic-couplet Selnecker cites is a Reformation-era Latin metrical paraphrase of a Nazianzenean sentiment, likely drawn from **Nazianzus, *Carmina moralia* I.1** (PG 37:521ff.) or from the **Carmen 33** (PG 37:929ff.). The paradigm-sentiment — *"the Gentle God ever remaineth gentle unto the gentle"* — is a stock Wittenberg-humanist commonplace, transmitting the Nazianzenean *πραότης* framework. Cf. also **Augustine, *In Iohannem Tractatus* 41-45** (PL 35:1693ff.) on the parallel "toleration of Judas among the twelve" topos which Selnecker adduces immediately before.

¹⁴⁶ **Augustine on human proclivity to evil.** — The **Tractatus 97 in Iohannem** citation is at **Augustine, *In Iohannem Tractatus* 97.4** (PL 35:1878f. / CCSL 36:576f.) — Augustine's exposition of John 16:25-33, focusing on the *tremendum-iudicium-vs-purissima-disciplina* antithesis. And the *"nos facilè in teterrima omnia scelera ruere, nisi manu Dei sustentemur"* dictum is a paradigm-Augustinian formulation of the *proclivitas naturae* framework — appearing throughout the anti-Pelagian corpus, e.g. **Augustine, *De correptione et gratia* 12-13** (PL 44:936ff.).

¹⁴⁷ **The Prayer of Manasseh.** — The prayer of Manasseh which Selnecker quotes is the **Oratio Manassis** — a Second Temple pseudepigraphon transmitted in the *Septuagint* and in the *Vulgate* as an appendix following 2 Chronicles, and widely regarded in the Wittenberg-Reformation tradition as *deuterocanonical* — a paradigm exemplum of *penitential prayer*. Selnecker's Latin text follows the received sixteenth-century **Erasmian text** (Basel 1516ff.) and the **Vulgata** apocryphal appendix. Cf. **Kolb, *Manasseh's Prayer***, in the *Encyclopedia of Early Christianity* (New York 1999) for the modern critical treatment; and **Luther's 1534 Bible** which included the *Gebet Manasse* as an *"Apokryphen"* text. The paradigm-Lutheran homiletic use of Manasseh's prayer is at **Luther, *Enarratio* on Psalm 32** (WA 40/II:377ff. / *LW* 12:317ff.).

¹⁴⁸ **The Publican paradigm.** — Selnecker's Luke-18 Publican exegesis is the paradigm-Reformation *sedes* for the doctrine of *penitentia + fides* — cf. **Luther, *Kirchenpostille*** on the 11th Sunday after Trinity (WA 22:238ff.) and **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559** *De Poenitentia* (CR 21:898ff. / MSA II/2:230ff.). The Peter-*exi-a-me* (Luke 5:8) and Centurion-*non-sum-dignus* (Matt. 8:8) parallels are the standard Wittenberg-Reformation homiletic-typological catena for the *humilitas-fidei* framework.

¹⁴⁹ **The Marchian anti-Devil verses.** — This is a mock-heroic Latin-poetic anecdote in the *Wittenberg-Table-Talk* tradition — attributed to the Marches (probably the **Mark Brandenburg**, or possibly the **Margraviate of Brandenburg-Ansbach**) — recording a Lutheran pastoral practice: *the flatulent contempt of the Devil*. Luther's celebrated advice — that the Devil, being *the spirit of pride*, cannot bear to be despised and mocked — is at **Luther, *Tischreden*** (WA TR 3:200; TR 1:154; TR 5:75f.); cf. **Oberman, *Luther: Man Between God and the Devil*** (New Haven 1989), Ch. 7, on the paradigm-Lutheran *Devils-and-fun* pastoral framework. The specific *Marchian* verses may derive from a Wittenberg-Table-Talk source or from a Marchian preacher's *pastorale* — Selnecker cites them as circulating *carmina*.

¹⁵⁰ **The two-line eulogy of Music as praetaste of eternal life.** — The Wittenberg-Reformation musical-pedagogical topos: *"Music giveth thee a foretaste of eternal life"* — is a paradigm Luther-Melanchthon-Selnecker formulation, drawn from **Luther, *Encomion musices* (Preface to G. Rhau's *Symphoniae iucundae*)** (WA 50:368-374 / *LW* 53:321-324): *"Musica est donum Dei... Musica praelibatio est aeternae vitae."* Selnecker himself was a paradigm-Wittenberg *Kirchenkomponist* — cf. his *Zwei und drei-stimmige geistliche Lieder* (Nürnberg 1587) and his hymn *"Ach bleib bei uns"*. See **W. Blankenburg** in *Handbuch der deutschen evangelischen Kirchenmusik* I/1 (Göttingen 1969) on Selnecker as hymnodist and musical-theologian.

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §7 Errores adversariorum

¹⁵¹ **Gregory Thaumaturgus (c. 213-c. 270) and the *Canonica Epistula*.** — The five-stage penitential regime Selnecker recites — *πρόκλαυσις / ἀκρόασις / ὑπόπτωσις / σύστασις / μέθεξις* — is drawn from Gregory's ***Canonica Epistula*** (PG 10:1019-1048; canon 11 sets out the fivefold framework), which shaped the early-Church canonical-penitential order. Gregory's title *θαυματουργός* (Wonder-worker) and *ἱερομάρτυς* (holy-martyr) traces to the *Vita* by Gregory of Nyssa (PG 46:893-957). Selnecker's *Catalogus Conciliorum* — to which he here alludes — is his own *Recitationes concionum de historia Ecclesiae* (Leipzig 1567-1568), one of the standard sixteenth-century Lutheran conciliar-historical handbooks. The *Confessio Principum adversus Synodi Tridentinae Restitutionem* is the paradigm-Concord-generation Lutheran anti-Trent handbook — probably the **Confessio et responsio principum ac dominorum** (Wittenberg 1560-1563) compiled by Chemnitz and other Wittenberg theologians during the Restitution-of-Trent controversy. Selnecker's own **Analectus** (Leipzig 1568/1572; VD16 S 5559) is the systematic dogmatic compendium to which he cross-references. On the Papist five-grade satisfactionist framework Selnecker refutes here, see paradigm-Lutheran refutation in **Chemnitz, *Examen Concilii Tridentini* Pars II** (Preus tr. 1978, II:611-708) on *De Poenitentia*.

¹⁵² **The Papist penitential-verse tradition.** — The barbarous Leonine-hexameter verses Selnecker cites — *"Poeniteas cito peccator..."*, *"Culparum fontes sunt: fastus, livor, et ira..."*, *"Vestio, poto, cibo..."*, and the rest — belong to the medieval *versified pastoral-manual* tradition of the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries (paradigms: **John of Garland's *Poenitentiale***, **Alan of Lille's *Liber poenitentialis***; the ***Summae confessorum*** literature). Selnecker's citation of these verses — with his ironic marginal glosses — is a paradigm second-generation Wittenberg pedagogical strategy: *ostensio through recital*, exposing the labyrinthine folk-scholasticism of pre-Reformation confession-manuals so that the students may perceive by contrast the *simplicitas Evangelii*. The paradigm-Reformation critique of the *five satisfactionist grades* (undue works, fraternities, indulgences, purgatorial fire, requiem Masses) is at **FC SD III. 5-24, 30-31** (*BSLK* 917-924 / *Kolb-Wengert* 562-565) and above all in **Luther's *95 Theses*** (WA 1:233-238) which specifically targets the indulgences-and-purgatory apparatus. Cf. also **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Poenitentia*** (CR 21:895-908 / MSA II/2:225-242).

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §8 (Confession/Absolution/Cross) + §9 De Regno Christi opening

¹⁵³ **The Lutheran doctrine of private confession.** — Selnecker's 5-utility apologia for the retention of private confession in the Lutheran Kirchenordnungen recapitulates **Luther, *Sermo de sacramento poenitentiae* (1519)** (WA 2:709-723 / *LW* 35:9-22) and above all the **Augsburg Confession Article XI** (*BSLK* 65f. / *Kolb-Wengert* 44-45): *"De confessione docent, quod absolutio privata in ecclesiis retinenda sit, quamquam in confessione non sit necessaria omnium delictorum enumeratio."* Selnecker as FC co-author transmits the AC XI framework. Cf. also **Luther, *Große Katechismus* — Beichte** (*BSLK* 725-733 / *Kolb-Wengert* 476-480) for the mature Lutheran pastoral theology of private confession.

¹⁵⁴ **The office of the Keys and public/private absolution.** — Selnecker's framework — *"absolutio est annunciatio et applicatio remissionis peccatorum, quae fit nomine et autoritate Christi per vocem hominis in ministerio"* — is the paradigm-Lutheran definition, drawn from **Luther, *Vom Schlüssel*** (1530; WA 30/II:435-507) and **Melanchthon, *Tractatus de potestate et primatu Papae*** (*BSLK* 469-498 / *Kolb-Wengert* 329-344). Cf. also **Apology of the Augsburg Confession Article XII** (*BSLK* 251-284 / *Kolb-Wengert* 186-218) on penitence and the office of the Keys. The 2 Cor. 5:20 *pro Christo legatione fungimur* is the paradigm New Testament *sedes* for the ministerial-embassy framework.

¹⁵⁵ **The kingdom of Christ — threefold.** — Selnecker's *regnum potentiae / regnum gratiae / regnum gloriae* framework is the paradigm Wittenberg Christological formulation, drawn from **Luther, *Von Christo* (1533)** (WA 37:52-69) and above all from **Chemnitz, *De duabus naturis in Christo*** (Jena 1570), Ch. 26-31, on the *communicatio idiomatum tertium genus* and the exalted-Christ's rule *in majesty and glory*. The threefold framework — power (from eternity), grace (in this life through Word and Sacraments), glory (in the resurrection and the age to come) — becomes the standard Lutheran-Orthodoxy formulation, canonized in **Gerhard, *Loci Theologici*** *De Officio Christi Regio* (Cotta ed. IV:298-343). The mention of *Constantine, Theodosius, and the Electors and Dukes of Saxony* as *Nurritii Ecclesiae* is a paradigm-Selneckerian *loci-communes* echo of his Leipzig court-theologian station, and reflects the paradigm-Melanchthonian *pia magistratus*-doctrine (cf. **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De magistratibus civilibus*** — CR 21:1006ff.). Selnecker's later 1584 Formula of Concord Preface addresses the Electors of Saxony directly. On the *προσωπολήπτης* — the "respecter-of-persons" — as anti-Jewish/anti-Turkish framework, cf. **Selnecker, *Der ganze Prophet Sacharja*** (Leipzig 1586) on Zech. 8 and the calling of the Gentiles.

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §9 De Regno Christi close + §10 De Bonis Operibus Q1-Q7

¹⁵⁶ **The prophecy of Elias — the six millenaries and the imminent last day.** — The *Elias-vaticinium* concerning six millenaries of the world (2,000 years *ante Legem*, 2,000 *sub Lege*, 2,000 *sub Messia*) is a **rabbinic-apocalyptic** commonplace attributed to Elias in the Babylonian Talmud (bSanhedrin 97a). The paradigm Wittenberg-Reformation reception is at **Luther, *Supputatio annorum mundi*** (1541; WA 53:22-184) and at **Melanchthon, *Chronicon Carionis*** (Wittenberg 1558; CR 12:711ff.).
