Selnecker was Melanchthon's student and adopted the Elias-6000-year framework as an eschatological-imminent-parousia argument — reflecting Reformation-era chiliastic apprehension. See also **Barnes, *Prophecy and Gnosis: Apocalypticism in the Wake of the Lutheran Reformation*** (Stanford 1988).

¹⁵⁷ **The Melanchthon *"non utimur his verbis"* dictum.** — From **Melanchthon, *Loci Praecipui Theologici* (1559) *De bonis operibus*** (CR 21:775 / MSA II/2:139): *"Non utimur autem his verbis 'bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem,' quia per additionem 'ad salutem' intelligitur meritum."* This is the paradigm-Wittenberg resolution of the **Major-Amsdorf controversy** (1552-1560): Georg Major had said *"bona opera sunt necessaria ad salutem"*; Nikolaus von Amsdorf countered *"bona opera perniciosa sunt ad salutem"*; both formulations rejected in **FC SD IV** (*BSLK* 940-951 / *Kolb-Wengert* 574-581). Selnecker as FC IV co-author preserves the Melanchthonian formulation verbatim. The reference to **Brenz** is **Johannes Brenz** (1499-1570), the paradigm South German Lutheran and Selnecker's colleague at Tübingen — cf. **Brenz, *Confessio Wirtembergica*** (1552).

¹⁵⁸ **Bernard on merit as *via regni non causa regnandi*.** — From **Bernard of Clairvaux, *De gratia et libero arbitrio*** 14 (PL 182:1024): *"Non enim propter merita nostra, sed propter Dei misericordiam accepimus tam magnam gratiam; nostra merita sunt via regni, non causa regnandi."* One of the paradigm Bernardine formulations in the Reformation-received anti-Pelagian tradition. Cf. also **Bernard, *Sermones in Cantica* 68.6** (PL 183:1112): *"Sufficit ad meritum scire quod non sufficit meritum"* — cited at note ¹³² above.

¹⁵⁹ **Luther on averting God's eyes from our virtues.** — *"Nisi Deus oculos suos averterit non tantum a peccatis, sed et a virtutibus nostris, non salvabimur"* — a paradigm-Lutheran formulation appearing in **Luther, *Enarrationes in Genesin* on Gen. 22** (WA 43:239f. / *LW* 4:145): even the *iustitia iustificati* is unclean before the tribunal of God — a foundational-Lutheran *simul iustus et peccator* formulation. Cf. also **Luther, *Rationis Latomianae confutatio* (Antilatomus)** (WA 8:107f. / *LW* 32:224f.) for the same *virtutum-nostrarum-oculos-avertit* framework, and **FC SD III. 27-28** (*BSLK* 924 / *Kolb-Wengert* 565) which canonises the doctrine.

¹⁶⁰ **The Gregory-and-Trajan legend, and the anti-purgatorial polemic.** — The medieval *Gregory-freeing-Trajan* legend — that Pope Gregory the Great by his prayers and merits liberated the emperor Trajan from hell — is a paradigm **hagiographic-purgatorial fable** transmitted through **Paul the Deacon's *Vita Gregorii*** (PL 75:41-59) and reproduced widely in the medieval hagiographic tradition (e.g. **Legenda Aurea** on Gregory). The paradigm-Lutheran anti-purgatorial critique is above all at **Luther's 95 Theses** (WA 1:233-238) and at **Chemnitz, *Examen Concilii Tridentini* Pars II *De Purgatorio*** (Preus tr. 1978, II:451-570). Selnecker's dismissal of *"Trajan-Gregory"* as a foundational-fable of purgatorial superstition is the paradigm-Reformation *ostensio-per-ridiculum* rhetoric.

¹⁶¹ **Selnecker's 5 Pelagian arguments rebutted + Noah/Hezekiah "perfect" exegesis.** — Selnecker's rebuttal of the 5 classical Pelagian syllogisms (Rom. 2 lex-naturalis + Deut. 30 mandatum-non-supra + Matt. 19 serva-mandata + Ps. 7 iudica-me-secundum-iustitiam + Gen. 6 Noe-iustus-perfectus) recapitulates **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Peccato Originali*** (CR 21:697ff.) and **Apology of the Augsburg Confession IV.6-27** (*BSLK* 159-165 / *Kolb-Wengert* 120-124). The two-fold *iustitia personalis* vs *iustitia causae/officii* distinction is the paradigm Melanchthonian framework for reconciling David's Ps. 7 imprecation with sola-gratia. The *Thom* Hebrew "perfect" exegesis draws on **Forster's *Dictionarium Hebraicum*** (see note ¹⁰⁰), and on **Luther's *In Genesin*** on Gen. 6:9 (WA 42:305ff. / *LW* 2:56ff.) — the *simplex-in-doctrina-integer-in-conscientia* framework. The Prosper triad and Luther's *velle-esse-iustum-summa-est-iustitia* are Reformation-era commonplaces transmitting the *simul iustus et peccator* framework.

## From Locus II *De Poenitentia* — §10 Q11 close + Household Table + De Conscientia + §11 De Libero Arbitrio

¹⁶² **Luther on Genesis 2 and 13 — passive potency in divine matters, liberty in externals.** — Selnecker's *categorical response* quoting Luther on Gen. 2 is drawn from **Luther, *Enarrationes in Genesin* on Gen. 2:19-20** (WA 42:87-90 / *LW* 1:114-119), where Luther develops the paradigm *"in his quae sunt supra nos, mera potentia passiva"* framework. The Gen. 13 material is at **WA 42:497f. / *LW* 2:334**. The paradigm-Lutheran doctrine of the *passive-active* distinction — free will active in *inferioribus* (natural/political/economic actions) but merely passive in *superioribus* (spiritual/divine actions unto God) — is the foundational framework of **De servo arbitrio (1525)** (WA 18:600-787 / *LW* 33) — the paradigm-Lutheran anti-Erasmian treatise. Cf. **FC SD II** (*BSLK* 866-912 / *Kolb-Wengert* 543-562) which codifies the Lutheran framework — Selnecker was FC II co-author.

¹⁶³ **Luther on Genesis 12 — Abraham as *auditor Dei vocantis*.** — The extended Abraham-Luther citation is from **Luther, *Enarrationes in Genesin* on Gen. 12:1-3** (WA 42:436-450 / *LW* 2:243-267). This is the paradigm-Lutheran *sola-gratia* Abraham-exegesis, which Selnecker as second-generation Wittenberg student inherits and cites verbatim. The *"materia mere passiva quam divina maiestas per verbum apprehendit et formavit in Patriarcham"* is the paradigm-Lutheran *"nihil ex se, omnia ex Deo"* framework.

¹⁶⁴ **The synergist controversy and FC II resolution.** — Selnecker's careful handling of the *synergon* — the human-will-cooperating-with-Spirit-in-conversion — is the Concord-generation Lutheran resolution of the **Synergism Controversy** (1553-1580) between the strict-Lutherans (Amsdorf, Flacius) and the Melanchthonian synergists (Strigel, Pfeffinger). Cf. **FC SD II. 44-90** (*BSLK* 890-912 / *Kolb-Wengert* 552-562), which affirms the *servile-will* framework of Luther's *De servo arbitrio* against Manichaeism (which makes man a stone) while resisting synergism (which makes man a co-cause). Selnecker's *"non contumaciter repugnans + Spiritu movente cooperans"* is the paradigm FC II compromise-language.

¹⁶⁵ **The 3-causes framework and Clement of Alexandria on synergy.** — The paradigm Lutheran-Orthodoxy *tres causae rectae actionis* — Word of God + Holy Spirit + human will regenerate not resisting — is a paradigm-Wittenberg formulation used in the FC II resolution. The Clement of Alexandria citation is from **Clement, *Stromata* I.20** (PG 8:809f. / SC 30:120ff.) on the *συνεργός* framework. The Pauline *"θεοῦ γὰρ ἐσμὲν συνεργοί"* is at 1 Cor. 3:9 — the paradigm New Testament *sedes* for the *cooperator-Dei* framework. The **Bernard "non fidei sed perfidiae"** dictum is at **Bernard, *De diligendo Deo*** and **Sermones in Cantica** — a paradigm Bernardine formulation transmitted through the Reformation-era anti-securitas tradition.

## From Locus III *De Libertate Christiana* + De Praedestinatione (Theses I-XXV)

¹⁶⁶ **Christian Liberty — the Anabaptist deviation and Luther's Galatians framework.** — Selnecker's polemic against those who abused Christian liberty for *carnal licence, plundering of ecclesiastical goods, polygamy, and Decalogue-contempt* targets the **Anabaptists** (especially the Münster Rebellion of 1534-35 under Jan van Leiden) and the later **Antinomian-libertine** developments of the Radical Reformation. The paradigm-Lutheran framework of the *four grades of Christian liberty* — *Gratia + Donum per Gratiam + Liberatio a caeremonijs + Liberatio a traditionibus humanis* — traces to **Luther, *In Epistolam ad Galatas Commentarius (1535)*** (WA 40/I:640-702 / *LW* 26:428-461) on Gal. 5. Cf. also **Melanchthon, *Loci* 1559 *De Libertate Christiana*** (CR 21:990-1006 / MSA II/2:395-411). The four-grade scheme is codified in **FC SD X *De Adiaphoris*** (*BSLK* 1053-1063 / *Kolb-Wengert* 635-640), which Selnecker co-authored.

## §23. The four grades of necessity — first objection to the Gospel of gratuitous justification rebutted.

We are not to institute in this place the entire doctrine of predestination, but the younger sort ought only to be admonished that piously and soberly according to the norm of the doctrine of the Gospel they should both feel and speak concerning predestination, and accustom themselves not to speculations and inquiries into hidden mysteries but to hearing and considering the voice of the Son of God, according to that saying: *My sheep hear my voice.* Likewise: *This is my beloved Son, hear ye him.* And: *Come unto me, all ye.*

Yet in passing let the studious know that there are, in the main, **four** things which are commonly opposed to the true doctrine of God's *εὐδοκία* and good pleasure revealed toward us.

**The first is:** NECESSITY. *What God foresees must necessarily come to pass, because the foreknowledge of God is as immutably of the essence of God as are His justice, wisdom, and other virtues, which are not accidents in God. From eternity God foresees who are going to perish and who are going to return to God. Therefore those things happen necessarily just as they have been foreseen by God — otherwise the foresight of God would be deceived.*

The true response is this: There is a great distinction between those appellations which belong to God absolutely without any respect to creatures — as *wisdom, justice, goodness, omnipotence*, and the like (for such is God in His essence from eternity unto eternity, even if there had never been any creature) — and those appellations which stand *relatively* to creatures — as the foreknowledge of those things which shall be in creatures, and the like — which have as it were a certain accidentary relation to creatures. This distinction is to be held so that we may know that things predicated *absolutely* of God and things predicated *relatively* of God have themselves in a differing mode. And although no absolute accident falls into God, yet in Him there are many relations, whose names — although they are drawn from the nature of God — yet do not describe unto us the *nature or essence of God, such as He simply is*, but manifest a certain action of the divine nature which acts something into creatures either future or present.

Next, this distinction being considered, this also is to be held: God does indeed foresee all things universally and most exactly, and hath all things from eternity known and perspicuous to Himself, but yet He knoweth and determineth things which depend simply from His own will (as *creation, justification, sanctification, and the resurrection of men*) in a far other manner than He foresees and determines things which depend upon the *liberty and will of man*, who often is able and accustomed to act many things contrary to the will of God.

This distinction is to be held that we may avoid the Stoic delirium of God as if He were the author of sin. God foresees many things which certainly He wills not — the fall of our first parents, of Cain, of Saul, of Judas, and the rest. Afterward it must be known that by the divine foresight no necessity of sinning or of perishing is at all conveyed. For (that I may use the words of Augustine) *no one is compelled by his memory to do things which are to come; and just as a man remembers certain things which he doth, and yet doth not do all things which he remembers, so God foreknoweth all things whereof He is Himself the author, and yet is not the author of all things which He foreknoweth. And of those things whereof He is not the evil author, He is the just judge and avenger.* ¹⁰³

And Chrysostom on 1 Corinthians 11 (*It is meet that heresies be*) saith: *"Christ, saying, 'It must needs be that scandals come'* (Matt. 18) *neither taketh away the liberty of will, nor imposeth necessity or violence upon life, but hath predicted what without doubt was going to come to pass because of the depraved mind of men — which indeed was going to come to pass not because of the prediction, but because of the will of those who could not be cured. For not because He predicted these things did these things come to pass, but because they were certainly future, therefore He predicted them. For if scandals were of necessity, and not of the will of those who move them, superfluous would be that which He said: 'Woe to that man through whom the scandal cometh.'"* ¹⁰⁴

At last it must be known that, as concerns the word *necessity* (with which the sincere doctors of the Church sometimes use, saying that all things happen necessarily which God hath foreseen), we must diligently attend *what and how it is said, in what respect, and with what conscience it may be admitted, approved, or disproved*. For many with their rigid and absurd — nay, oftentimes blasphemous — locutions differ in nothing from the Stoic Fate and from the reproaches which arise thence against God, when they deny and reject all divine permission, all contingency in all things, and the *necessity of consequence*, without any distinction, and both concerning good and evil actions and events have nothing else in their mouth than: *God so wills*. Many from a lofty, free, and great spirit rise up with lofty and magnificent locutions and prostrate their adversaries who detract too much from the grace and efficacy of God and ascribe too much to free will — as sometimes Augustine and Luther soared up more loftily like an eagle, with certain phrases sublimely spiritual and true, but yet not to be rightly and piously understood except in their proper place and respect — and truly such, that they themselves, apart from context and the engagement with adversaries to be prostrated with such lightning-bolts, would not simply and absolutely have used, and which they themselves also explained and limited in others of their writings, especially when speech was to be directed to weaker persons unto whom to receive or hear such sublime things without offense was not granted.

But many, in the manner of monkeys, while they neglect the royal and safe way and try to put on the person of the heroes and to imitate their grandiloquence and majesty, compose mere labyrinths of questions and monstrous opinions, and entangle themselves and others with inextricable knots — without judgment or distinction seeking the deep and the arcane, and though patient of another's Phaethon's precipice, they at last are themselves melted in the sun's blaze. Such are today those who from Augustine and Luther affirm that God foreknoweth nothing contingently in general, but foresees, proposes, and does all things in unalterable, inevitable, and infallible necessity — and thence, contrary to the mind of those doctors, conclude that God from eternity has drawn to His Son a certain number of men whom He must Himself save, all the rest being ordained and destined to eternal ruin — whatsoever indeed they might will, believe, and do — in such wise that those once brought cannot but be saved, howsoever they may transgress, and those once rejected cannot but be damned, whether they live rightly or wickedly. ¹⁰⁵

That therefore we may be able to judge concerning these things, first let us know and attend concerning the word *necessity* that in the ecclesiastical writers there is commonly found a *twofold* necessity: namely the **absolute** and the **conditional**. The former they call that which hath place in those things which depend simply from the will of God, as *creation, justification, gathering, calling, sanctification, and the preservation of the Church, and the resurrection of the dead, the sending of the Son into flesh, the last judgment, the punishment of the impious, the joy and the eternal salvation of believers*. This will of God is *immutable*, according to that of Rom. 9: *Who resisteth His will?* And Isa. 46: *My counsel shall stand, and my whole will shall be done.*

**Conditional necessity** is that which hath place in those things which God Himself proposed with a condition, and which He wills to be perfected conditionally either by reason of His mercy or of His just judgment — as when to Jonah 3 and 4 to the Ninevites subversion is denounced, together with the condition included: namely, that the ruin is prepared upon this condition, if they do not repent; but if they do repent, there remaineth hope of salvation. King Hezekiah (Isa. 38) is bidden to commit his household to someone, because he is about to die. But Isaiah, after the King's penitence, brings word to him of the prolongation of life to fifteen years. So let us understand that of 1 Tim. 2: *God will have all men to be saved* — namely, by the will of His mercy patefacted in the Gospel, this condition only being added, that they hear the Son, believe in Him, and obey Him. Which if it be not done, there remaineth the will of just judgment, which is: *that every one who believeth not in the Son should be rejected and damned*. Those therefore who believe and are saved do this by the will and efficacy of God, which is the will of mercy. But those who do not believe and perish do this by their own free will, and yet perish by the will of God, which is the will of justice or of just judgment. For God willeth the believers to be saved, and the unbelievers to be damned.

An illustrious example of this condition is that of Gen. 20, where God saith to King Abimelech: *Thou shalt die because of the woman whom thou hast taken.* But when the King excused himself, again God saith: *Restore his wife unto Abraham, and he shall pray for thee — because he is a Prophet — that thou mayest live: if not, know that thou shalt surely die, thou and all that is thine.* And hither belong those of Exod. 7, 8, 9: *Pharaoh set not his heart to it, he hardened his heart, and hearkened not unto them.* For the condition is subjoined — that if he had heard Moses and Aaron, he would not have fallen into the just judgment of God. Isa. 10: *Assur regarded not the judgment of God, but he stirred up his own heart to do hurt.* Isa. 50: *The Lord hath opened mine ear, and I was not rebellious, neither turned away backward.* John 1: *As many as received Him, He gave power to become the sons of God, namely to them that believed on His name.* John 7: *If any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine.* Matt. 23: *How often would I have gathered thy children together — and thou wouldst not!*

Although we do not disapprove this distinction of necessity (as they call it in general) into the *absolute* and the *conditional*, yet — because there are truly several grades of things necessary, and that we may dexterously and rightly feel and speak distinctly and without ambiguity of each and every thing which is said necessarily to come to pass, and lest we confuse propositions or phrases concerning God, creatures, things, actions, and events into a single chaos (as many are wont) — let us hold the customary **four grades of necessity**. Of which:

**The first** properly claims for itself the name of *absolute necessity* — which indeed the ecclesiastical writers have called the *necessity of consequence* and the *simple necessity* — and which hath place in propositions concerning the essence and virtues of God: as, *God is good, and doth well and rightly, and willeth not, approveth not, nor aideth sin*. These are true necessarily — that is, the contradiction is simply impossible and false.

**The second grade** is that of the necessity of *definitions and demonstrations*, or of principles theoretical and practical, and of the true consequence out of them, or of conclusions. This grade hath place in propositions concerning the nature or the rational creature and its notices and virtues, as: *Man understandeth the distinction between the honest and the shameful, divinely implanted in the mind. Man ought to obey God in doing honest things and shunning turpitude.* These are true necessarily, because both God so hath framed man, and the opposite hath the implication of contradiction — as, *if man do not honest things and shun turpitude, he is not worthy of the name of man, and cannot please God.*

To this grade of necessity we can rightly refer those examples which just before we said were included under conditional necessity — not that those propositions be known by nature (which certainly outside of the arts are patefacted only in the sole Word of God), but that this is the necessity of *definition and demonstration in the Word of God* and the *unmoved rule and norm of the will of God* — that man, who after the Fall is by nature the son of wrath, believe in the Son of God and be saved. Now if the opposite be given, there is implication of contradiction — as, *if he believe not in the Son, he is not saved. And if he be not saved, he believeth not in the Son.* This is the *unmoved and true Evangelical necessity of definition and demonstration*, out of which a necessary conclusion is builded up: *He that believeth in the Son hath eternal life. I believe in the Son. Therefore I have eternal life.* Likewise: *He who promiseth, oweth the promise. Thou, God, hast promised to me life and salvation because of the Son. Therefore Thou owest it to me.* This consequence is *unmoved* — not that God oweth to thee or to me anything by absolute necessity, but that He oweth by *necessity of Evangelical definition and demonstration, or of the promise*, whereby (that I may use the words of Augustine) *by promise, by Scripture, and by the sending of the Son, He made Himself our debtor*. ¹⁰⁶ And this force is grateful unto God, saith Tertullian: *namely to demand the debt with true faith in the Son*. ¹⁰⁷ And as this is unmoved — *God willeth not sin nor our destruction* — so this also is unmoved: *The believer in the Son is saved.*

Under this second grade therefore we include the norm and the conclusions of the *Law of nature, of the Decalogue*, and — in its proper place separately — of the *Gospel*, which hath its own peculiar definitions, demonstrations, and conclusions — *graphical, not merely grammatical, καὶ ἐννοίας θείας, οὐ κοινάς* [and divine notions, not common ones]. And although there is a distinction between those propositions and locutions which by their own nature refer to the *second* grade of necessity (as are all the definitions of the virtues and the *legal sentences* — which indeed are the eternal and unmoved wisdom and the rule of justice in God, patefacted also to men and implanted in them — as: *chastity is a virtue; one ought to live honestly, etc.*; hither we also refer that of the rhetoricians which they call the *necessary of deliberation*, not with regard to the outcome of the deliberation but with regard to a right judgment) — and afterward between locutions and propositions *Evangelical* (as concerning the sending of the Son into flesh, the remission of sins, the resurrection of the dead), which by reason of their origin properly refer to the *fourth* grade of necessity, namely of consequence — because man ought to have and could have not fallen into sin and death, which if he had not done, there would have been no need of the sending of the Son and of the other things which are proper to the Gospel — yet now, since it has thus fallen out that after the man is fallen, the Son has been sent into flesh, and God has decreed all those things which are proposed in the Gospel, by reason of the event and of a more copious and true consolation — we rightly refer the Evangelical propositions to the *second* grade of necessity, both that the will of God may now be manifested as unmoved in this — *that the believer in the Son be saved, that the unbeliever be damned* — and also that our faith may be certain and firm. For it is as true, certain, and unmoved that *the believer in the Son is saved*, and likewise *the resurrection of all the dead shall be*, as it is true that God is, or that twice four is eight. For that is the *Evangelical definition, demonstration, and promise* — not legal, not natural — but brought forth and patefacted out of the bosom of the eternal Father through the Son, and as certain as are all natural and legal notices — yea, as certain as absolute necessity itself.

**The third grade** of necessity is that of *naturally acting* things, which differ from *voluntarily acting* things (as regards their actions) in three modes:

1. **By subject** — for effects in naturals arise from *matter, form or nature, and temperament* — as fire heateth necessarily by *physical necessity*, because such is its nature.
2. **By mode of acting** — for naturals cannot but act when they are entire and have their congruent and *σύμμετρον* object — as fire burns fit and applied matter, by physical necessity; the Sun liquefies wax and hardens clay, by physical necessity.
3. **By constancy of action** — for nature acteth in one and the same mode — as fire always heats and dries.

But *voluntary* things arise from a thinking, rational, and free potency, and are able to act, or not to act, nor to act always in one and the same mode. But concerning these things which properly pertain to causes and effects, in their proper place a fuller discourse is had. Here only they are repeated so that the ordered mode of acting in the natural causes may be shown — how that, if not interrupted by God, those causes cannot act otherwise. Fire necessarily burns, by physical necessity. But in the Babylonian furnace the three Israelites are divinely preserved, the natural force of fire being repressed (Dan. 3). The Sun necessarily moves, by physical necessity. But God can stay the Sun (as Josh. 10). *For our God is in the heavens; He hath done whatsoever He hath pleased* (Ps. 115).

Hence it is customarily said:

> *Fata movere Deus, tollere fata potest.*
> — *God can move the fates, God can take away the fates.*

And:

> *Non plus fata tamen, quàm pia vota valent.*
> — *Yet the fates avail no more than pious prayers.*

Likewise:

> *Non Deus est numen Parcarum carcere clausum,*
> *Quale putabatur Stoicus esse Deus.*
> *Ipse potest Solis cursus inhibere volantes,*
> *Ipse velut scopulos flumina stare iubet.*
>
> — *God is not a divinity shut up in the prison of the Fates, as the Stoic supposed God to be. He can Himself stay the flying courses of the Sun; He commandeth the rivers to stand like rocks.* ¹⁰⁸

And as regardeth each of us singly, let us ever hold that of Psalm 31: *Bǝyādechā ʿittotai* — *In Thy hand, O Lord, are my* καιροί — that is, my fates, times, occasions, lots, circumstances, events, accidents, and both my life and my death. Likewise, *the very hairs of your head are all numbered* (Matt. 10).

Let us therefore beg of God that He Himself by His own liberty rule us and moderate the *secondary causes*, unto which He is by no means bound (as the Stoics impudently feigned) and which are by no means immutable, but are subject to the will, nod, mandate, and ordination of God, and execute what He commandeth — as Sirach beautifully discourseth (Ch. 40), and in the Book of Wisdom (Ch. 19) it is written: *Every creature in its own nature is so conditioned and framed that it may serve Thy precepts.*

**The fourth grade** of necessity is called *of consequence*, and consisteth in mutable things which needed not to be nor to have been done, and yet, being once done, cannot be undone — that is, when either by reason of preceding causes an effect certainly followeth, though the beginning and the things which follow are by their own nature contingent — as the Egyptians were led by a worthy necessity to this end, that they should perish suffocated (Wisd. 19), namely by *necessity of consequence*, because their sins ceased not, therefore it was needful that they be atrociously punished. Or when by reason of a dialectical connection something certainly followeth, which yet by its own nature is contingent — as, *A raven has been wounded by Ajax; therefore it must be extinguished.* Or when in contingents contradictories cannot both be true at once — as, *Pompey fled the field. Therefore it is impossible that he did not flee* — namely, because he fled. For what has been done cannot be rendered undone, even though it were not necessary that it be done. Or when God decreeth something in a matter which was not necessary to come to pass, but which being done, the decree of God must remain immoveable — as the fall of man was by no means necessary, but now that man has fallen by his free will, obeying the Devil, God from His immense goodness made the decree of the sending of the Son in the flesh for the redemption of the human race. By reason of origin and cause, therefore, that decree of the sending of the Son and of the resurrection of the dead is necessary by *necessity of consequence*, though the same decree of God (who from eternity knoweth and foreseeth all things) is likewise *eternal* — how it be so, we cannot scrutinize, but reserve to the eternal Academy. Certainly God willed not the fall either of angels or of men, and is not the author or approver or aider of sin; but when sin was committed, from His immense goodness He applied a remedy, decreeing that the Son should become a victim, *μεσίτης καὶ ἱκέτης* — the *Mediator and Suppliant* — for the human race. This decree, by reason of the cause for which it was made, is necessarily true by *necessity of consequence*; but by reason of the effect, because it is now unmoved and it is the immutable will of God that the believer in the Son may have eternal life, and the unbeliever may not have it — it can rightly also be called necessary by *necessity of definition and demonstration*, not legal nor philosophical but Evangelical, as before it was said.

These things concerning necessity had necessarily to be said. If any man say these are drawn from Philosophy — as concerning words and terms (for as concerning the matter itself, those things are contained in the sacred letters in the same mode) — let him know that: *τὸ καλὸν ὅπε ἄνποθ᾿ ὑρεθείη, τῆς ἀληθείας ἴδιόν ἐστί* — *the good, wheresoever it be found, is proper to the truth*. For Philosophy is brought in as an handmaid ministering to her mistress; this is grateful unto God.

Now I will only add this concerning the foresight of God: that it is to be received with a twofold respect. For God foreseeth and ordaineth and determineth certain things which depend upon His own will: these are certain, unmoved, and infallibly necessary — whether you shall call them the necessity of consequence, or of definition patefacted, or of pre-ordination. But certain things He foreseeth conditionally, which depend upon the will of rational creatures — as God foresaw the fall of angels and of men, which yet He willed not to be, but foresaw it conditionally: *that if they should fall, they should be subjected to punishments; but if they should persevere in their obedience, they should have God ever present to them and propitious*. Neither piously therefore, nor rightly, is it said that the foresight of God would be deceived if all things did not come to pass necessarily. For He Himself testifieth that He foreseeth the sins of men conditionally — as if He indulges them, He appointeth a limit *how and how far, yea also wherefore* He will bear them. But let these things suffice concerning the first objection, which show that it is most false, if any man say that all things come to pass necessarily, and that the wills of men both for designing vices and crimes, and for designing virtues and rightly-done deeds, are constrained and impelled by God even unwilling and struggling.

## §24. The second, third, and fourth objections rebutted.

**The second thing objected is Faith itself.** *Faith is the gift of God. Therefore since we cannot believe unless God Himself hath given it to us, in vain do we labour in hearing, willing, striving, etc.*

**I answer:** When it is said that *faith is the gift of God*, the dignity and merit and efficacy of our own powers is excluded — not the rapture or afflatus is confirmed, much less is apprehension excluded, nor is it denied that faith is the *instrument* by which we ought to receive the good things offered. For the order of the divine efficacy remaineth thus: *Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing through the Word.* It is needful therefore that thou hear the Word, and by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit assent and believe it, and not expect other draws, but embrace the grace offered — and pray that faith be in thee increased and confirmed. Nor canst thou in aught attribute or ascribe anything unto thyself, even though thou knowest that thou oughtest and canst hear the Word, and, the Holy Spirit moving thee, assent and believe. *For what hast thou which thou didst not receive?* What physician glorieth of that which he receiveth, as if it could not have been given unless he had received it? *Far be it that there be, or be called, a good will which glorieth in others or in itself, and not in the Lord*, saith Augustine. ¹⁰⁹

**The third is this:** *If God willed that I should believe and be saved, this would come to pass. If He willed that I should not sin and perish, this also would come to pass. If He willed the nations who now lack the true knowledge of God and the doctrine of the Gospel to be converted and saved, certainly they would be saved. For who resisteth His will?*

**I answer:** The Word of God showeth us the will of God in a twofold respect. For His will is either of *mercy* or of *justice*. Of mercy — *that thou believe in the Son*. Of justice and judgment — *that unbelieving thou perish*. Neither will can be resisted. For he who believeth in the Son is saved, according to the unmoved will of God out of the mere mercy of God. He who believeth not perisheth by his own fault, according to the unmoved will of God out of the just judgment of God. He therefore who believeth cannot refer aught acceptably to himself, because that whole matter — the true faith and the salvation — is the mercy of God, which the believer receiveth. He who believeth not cannot blame God, but must accuse himself and confess that he is rejected and damned for his own unbelief by the just judgment of God. As to what pertaineth to the Gentiles: let us know that the fault is not of God but of men, who hear not the Church, nor inquire after the Son of God, and labour with an affected ignorance which cannot be excused.

**The fourth is:** *The event and experience testify that there is* particularity. *Therefore we cannot be certain of our salvation.*

**I answer:** With all our might in the Church of Christ the *universal promise* is to be held and defended — that God by His *εὐδοκία* willeth all men to be saved — namely, upon that condition which He Himself hath proposed. And that God by His will (which is the universal will of mercy) willeth no man to be excluded, these perspicuous grounds testify: ¹¹⁰

1. Because He Himself made man not for destruction, but for salvation.
2. Because He willeth the human race to be restored through the Son.
3. Because He so loved the human race that He gave the Son, that through Him every one who believeth might be saved.
4. Because He gave the promise unto the first parents, who then stood in the place of the whole human race.
5. Because the promise of grace is always universal, *in all and upon all*.
6. Because as the discourse of penitence and of the Law is universal, so also is that of the remission of sins — according to that saying: *He hath concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy upon all.*
7. Because He Himself sweareth: *As I live, I will not the death of a sinner.*
8. Because He is just and true, loving and keeping His promises.
9. Because His mandate is universal — *that we hear the Son*.
10. Because also the mandate of Christ is universal — that in all the earth all the Gentiles be taught. And so said His disciples, who manifestly and *ἐμφατικώτατος* [most emphatically] say: *μαθητεύσατε πάντα τὰ ἔθνη*  ¹¹¹ — *Make disciples of all nations*.
11. Because Christ often lamenteth the unbelief of the Jews, and God prayeth for His people and beseecheth as it were their obedience: Deut. 5: *O that they had a heart to fear me and to keep my commandments.* Likewise: *How oft would I have gathered thee!* (Matt. 23) His tears and *σπλάγχνα* or commiserations, full of groans, certainly admit no particularity as regardeth the good pleasure of God.
12. Because it is certain that God is not *προσωπολήπτης*, nor are there in Him contradictory wills, nor doth He will either our sin or our destruction. But that many perish is by the fault of men, not by another will of God, save only that of justice. And this very particularity — which seemeth to be *a posteriori* — men themselves cause by their own unbelief and affected ignorance against the express will of the mercy of God.

## §25. On the fruits of faith and of righteousness.

By the name **fruits of righteousness** we call all the connected internal and external testimonies of righteousness: *regeneration, eternal peace with God, joy in God, consolation, newness of life or new obedience, and all good works, of which the root is faith*, as Ambrose speaketh. ¹¹² And although that newness or health in the regenerate (kindled by the Holy Spirit) is not perfect and absolute in this life — and there is none who can satisfy the Law perfectly — yet the incepted obedience is pleasing unto God through and because of the Son. For the grace of God bestoweth in this life the zeal for keeping the precepts, and the same grace pardoneth if in those precepts any thing be kept less well, saith Augustine to Boniface, Bk. 3 Ch. 7. And in *Retractationes* Bk. 1 Ch. 19: *All the mandates of God are reputed as done, when whatsoever is not done, is pardoned*. ¹¹³ And piously said by D. Snepfius of pious memory: *Just as unto a good and* φιλόστοργος *father the toil and obedience of the little son bringing him something at the father's bidding — playing with the little son with great effort proportionate to his own strength but insufficient and unequal — is pleasing, so unto God our Father is pleasing our imperfect newness, since we are sons of God and are led by the Spirit of God; and whatever is not done in us which yet ought to be done, is pardoned for the sake of Christ, and thus we are called perfect by imputation and invocation.* ¹¹⁴

For first, faith in Christ receiveth, hath, and possesseth by *imputation* the most complete and most perfect fulfilment of the Law unto righteousness and unto salvation. Next, the Holy Spirit reneweth the hearts of the believers, charity being kindled, that they may begin to do the Law. Afterward, whatsoever in that incepted obedience is imperfect and unclean because of the flesh is not imputed unto the believers for the sake of Christ, but is covered.

But it is asked whence the fruits of righteousness are to be taken, and by what rule they are to be instituted — of the Law or of the Gospel? This question is easily expedited if it be considered that the Holy Spirit is given to us and dwelleth in us essentially and efficaciously for these principal causes:

**1.** That He may seal in us the promise of grace and the confidence of the Evangelical promise. For He is the *ἀρραβών* and pledge which the Bridegroom Son of God giveth to us as unto His bride, and He maketh us certain of the truth of the promises, of the righteousness, and of eternal life.

**2.** Next, the Holy Spirit is given, that He may renew us, illuminate the mind with the true knowledge of God, regenerate the will and bend it unto spontaneous obedience, move the heart, and imbue it with pious, placid, and chaste affections — with *fear of God, desire of life and of salvation, groans, contrition, sorrow because of sin, confidence in Christ, consolation and joy, hope of deliverance*, and *love also toward the neighbour, or works of charity*.

**3.** Afterward He is given to rule us in all our external life, that we may do the works of our vocation, live piously and honestly, offend no one through our own fault, give no scandals unto the weaker, willingly serve others and do them good.

These three offices the Holy Spirit performeth in us unto this end: that we may at last again be conformed unto God and His will (which is expressed in the Law); or that the image of God may be restored in us, and perfect obedience congruent with the Law. But the Holy Spirit performeth the first office according to the promise of the Gospel, because He is the pledge of our inheritance, which we have promised in the Gospel. He performeth the second office by a certain conduct and transition from the doctrine of the Gospel unto the rule and prescription of the Law which requireth the inward purity of the mind, will, heart, and of all the affections of man, and their full conformity — and simultaneously in this very conduct He showeth to us and holdeth forth the Son of God crucified, whom we ought to behold as often as we see how much is lacking to our mind, will, heart, and to our whole substance, soul, body, and to all our powers. For because of the Son — who hath perfectly fulfilled the Law both for us and on account of us — the Father pardoneth and remitteth unto us the whole of what is wanting to us. And rightly it is said: *Faith bringeth us who are gone forth from the Law back unto conformity with the Law — not as unto a merit of salvation, but as unto an index showing how much is wanting to us (which we ought elsewhere to seek, namely in the Son of God), and as unto a norm of the life to be rightly performed*.

The third office the Holy Spirit performeth through the third use of the Law, as we customarily speak. For there is (that we may briefly repeat this) a **threefold use of the Law**:

- **The first**, to guide discipline, without which men can neither be taught concerning God nor be vivified by the Son of God.
- **The second**, to accuse and condemn sin, and to terrify the conscience.
- **The third use** (whereof we here speak) is to teach *what worships please God*. For God willeth our faith and works to be conspicuous and ruled according to the norm of His Word — according to that saying, *Thy Word is a lamp unto my feet*. And He willeth us not to choose or do works which we ourselves feign, as the Monks and hypocrites do. For it is written in Deut. 12: *Let not each man do what seemeth right in his own eyes, but whatsoever I command, this shall ye observe to do unto the Lord — thou shalt neither add anything unto it, nor take anything from it*. And Num. 15: *Let them not follow their own imaginations or their own eyes, after which they go a-whoring, but let them be mindful of the mandates of God, and do them, and they shall be holy unto their God*. Likewise, Ezek. 20: *Walk in my precepts*.

By these testimonies we are convinced that God willeth the regenerate to be exercised in obedience in the works prescribed in the Law of God (which customarily is named the *Decalogue*), and to repudiate all *ἐθελοθρησκείας* or *elective worships* — which must be held against the Monks and against the new Pontifical parties. *In vain do they worship me by the mandates of men*, saith Christ from Isa. 29 (Matt. 15). And in Isa. 1 God saith: *Who hath required this at your hands?* For this cause Paul, when in the Epistle to the Romans and to the Galatians he had delivered the doctrine of the righteousness of justifying faith, and now would speak of the fruits of faith or of good works, nameth **the Law** — in which what is the *good, pleasing, and perfect will of God* (as himself saith, Rom. 12) is to be seen — and therefore almost verbatim reciteth the precepts of the Decalogue in Rom. 13. And unto the Gal. 5 he saith that *charity*, which is the root and sum of good works, is nothing else than the *plenitude of the Law* and the *sum of the mandate* (1 Tim. 1). And to the Eph. 2 he saith: *God hath prepared works, in which they should walk who in Christ Jesus are created for good works*. These evident testimonies must diligently be held against the fanatics who today disapprove the third use of the Law ¹¹⁵ — whereas Christ Himself saith that He came not to loose but to fulfil the Law: which this faithful Redeemer both did perform by His own obedience and by the derivation of the penalty upon Himself, and doth still perform even to the consummation of the age by the restitution of righteousness and of eternal life in us and simultaneously by the inception of obedience, and shall perform unto all eternity by the consummated confirmation of the precepts of the Law and by perfect obedience toward the Law, when we shall be free from every sin and stain.

Of this doctrine of the justification of man before God we have discoursed briefly (indeed not according to the dignity of so great a doctrine), yet with good faith we have explained the things necessary unto the capacity of those learning. If anything hath been said less properly, less ornately, or less accurately, let all that be imputed unto my infancy. If anything hath been said properly, rightly, in order, perspicuously, and with fruit unto the disciples, let all that be referred unto the mercy of God, whom we serve in our calling and to whom we accommodate our tongue and our hand.

## §26. Recapitulatio — the Summary Theses on the Justification of Man before God (Capita I–XLIV)

Now by way of a *coronis* we shall add the *heads and theses* of the sum of the doctrine of the justification of man before God, and of the fruits of faith or of good works — as it were an *ἀνακεφαλαίωσις* of all things which have hitherto been said — so that the studious may have (as we have set before them at Leipzig) certain *themes* wherein they may exercise their doctrine and piety.

**I.** Most rightly hath it been said, both by Luther and by others: *So long as the article of justification standeth and is safe, our true doctrine, faith, and religion stand and remain safe.* ¹¹⁶

**II.** Since therefore in our Churches and schools, as other articles of Christian doctrine, so also this article — comprehending the doctrine of the justification of man before God — hath been rightly, orderly, and perspicuously illustrated and explained by the ministry and the voice of the doctors: for which benefit we ought to give thanks unto the eternal and merciful God, both in this and in the eternal life; we, who are the disciples of those doctors, and yet do hear, teach, learn, and hold the sound doctrine, ought to be more diligent and more alacritous in guarding the truth — both in the other heads of Christian doctrine, and above all in this doctrine of Justification and of its effects, which we call *good works*.

**III.** That we may briefly and compendiously serve the studious and pious youth in this matter, we shall include the sum of this doctrine of the Justification of man before God, and then of good works, under these Heads, of which — in true invocation of God and in fear — we shall speak orderly what things are both true and *οὐ μόνον παισίν, ἀλλὰ πᾶσι χρήσιμα* [profitable not only unto children, but unto all] and necessary — namely:

1. Of the word *Iustificare* and *Iustitia*.
2. Of the signification of the word *Grace* and *Gift*.
3. Of the signification of the word *Faith*.
4. Of the exclusive particles, and of their force, especially when it is said, *That we are justified by Faith Alone*.
5. What is the righteousness of faith, or of the Gospel.
6. Of the causes of Justification, and of the causes of Faith.
7. Of Imputation.

Then we shall speak:

1. Of regeneration — whether it be any part of our righteousness whereby we stand before God.
2. Of good works — that by the works of the Mosaic Law no man is justified.
3. What are named *good works*, and what works are to be done; how they may be done; how they please God; and of the necessity of good works, and of the distinction of sins.
4. Of the errors and principal arguments of the Papists ascribing unto good works the merit of righteousness and of salvation; and of the others who have taught that good works give access unto the apprehension of grace.
5. Against the Papist *doubting*.

### Of the First — the word *Iustificare* and *Iustitia*.

**IV.** The use of the word *Iustificare* and *Iustitia* is considered in a threefold respect: either *general* (which use is nearly the same in all languages), or *special* (which is proper to the doctrine of the Law), or *peculiar* (which pertaineth to the doctrine of the Gospel).

**V.** For the word *Iustificare* customarily in nearly all tongues signifieth: *to judge someone and either to excuse or to approve his cause (whether good or bad) — either publicly, as in the forum, or privately; whether by right judgment, or out of favouritism and compassion, or by some other reasoning and persuasion* — as, Luke 10, *wishing to justify himself*; Job 32, *Elihu was angered when Job justified his soul before God*; Ps. 51, *Thou art justified in Thy words* — that is, Thou art praised, that Thou alone art just and keepest Thy words or promises; Matt. 11, *Wisdom is justified of her sons* — that is, in such great security of men, yet God hath His own sons and elect, who *justify* wisdom — that is, approve, and worship it religiously. Though there are many who interpret the same words in Matthew and Luke *by antiphrasis* — that is, by the reverse — with the sense: *"They who ought as sons to obey and to submit unto wisdom, they reprove wisdom as if wiser and as her masters."* For often disciples wish to seem more excellent than their masters, and sons than their parents. The Germans use a similar phrase — *rechtfertigen* — that is, *meistern, überklügen, straffen* [to master, over-outwit, chastise]; and *iustificatores* they call *die Meisterklüglinge*, snub-nosed reformers and glossers.

**VI.** Next in the doctrine of the Law, *to be justified* is *to be pleasing unto God and to be saved because of perfect, pure, and perpetual obedience — or of love toward God and neighbour — and thus to be able to stand before the judgment of God, and to be in every part innocent*. For under the appellation *righteousness* is understood the highest purity and integrity, according to the grade of human nature, which he must needs bring into the sight of God who willeth to be a partaker of eternal life.

**VII.** From this legal signification of the word *Iustificare*, the Philosophical doctrine — which is named *διανοητική* or *moral*, and is a particle of the Divine Law — hath borrowed its own universal *iustitia*, which is (or rather ought to be) *obedience toward all laws* — that is, congruence with the Law — that is, as they otherwise call it, *virtue*. As in the verse:

> *ἐν τε δικαιοσύνῃ συλλήβδην πᾶσ᾿ ἀρετ᾿ ὅτι.*
> *Iustitia in sese virtutes continet omnes.*
> — *Righteousness in itself containeth all the virtues.* ¹¹⁷

And Aristotle calleth *iustitia* the right use of all the virtues.

**VIII.** Hence also arise other usages of the word *iustitia*, whereof in their proper place discourse must be had — when in ordered fashion is to be expounded that concerning *iustitia particularis* (which giveth unto each his own, as the *iurisconsulti* speak out of Simonides), likewise of *iustitia commutativa* and *distributiva* — the one accommodated to *geometric*, the other to *arithmetic* proportion.

**IX.** But this must not be omitted: that in the Philosophical doctrine, *to be justified*, or *to be made just*, and *to be just*, is so far preached as obedience toward the laws, and love and observance of discipline and honesty, cometh into the eyes of men who rightly judge — as when we say that Aristides, Pericles, Socrates, Cicero, and others like unto them were *just and innocent*. But the divine Law examineth and judgeth not only outward actions but also internal motions.

**X.** Other more special significations we now omit — as, that *to justify* signifieth *to administer justice, and to affect the guilty with due punishment* (which is the office of distributive justice), as Absalom saith 2 Sam. 15: *I would justify a man that hath a judicial cause* — that is, I would administer justice. Likewise, that *to be justified* sometimes signifieth *to progress in righteousness*, as Apoc. 22: *He that is just, let him be justified still* — that is, unto whom it is given both to will and to do, he ought daily to stir up the gift of God in himself, that he may increase more and more in zeal for piety and innocence. Likewise: *to have a good cause, and out of a good cause a good conscience*, as often is said in the Psalms.

**XI.** Afterward in the doctrine of the Gospel — as we have said — there is a peculiar use of the word *Iustificare*, drawn indeed from the Hebrews and Greeks, who in the forum have used the voice *Hizdiq* and *δικαιοῦν* (as also appeareth from Herodotus) in this signification: that they who are brought unto judgment are absolved from the guilt of sin and of damnation, and declared *guiltless* and pronounced *just*. But it is accommodated to the peculiar business of man the utter sinner standing before the tribunal and the judgment of God, and who is by most just causes of damnation guilty, and yet hath obtained pardon and absolution by the intercession and merit of the Son of God.

**XII.** *To justify* signifieth therefore, in the doctrine of the Gospel: *to absolve from sins, to condone them, and to receive the sinner into grace; to liberate, and having absolved him from the guilt to hold him for just; to think him just, to hold him just and to pronounce him such, because of the intercession and satisfaction of the Son, apprehended by faith and applied.* For *to justify* and *to condemn* are opposed, as with the Hebrews *Hizdiq* and *Hirshia*, according to that Pauline word, Rom. 8: *It is God who justifieth: who is he that condemneth?* — For Paul alludeth to that of Isa. 10: *The Lord will help me: who is he that shall condemn me?* And Rom. 5: *As through the lapse or offence of one, death or guilt came into all men unto condemnation: so through the righteousness of one, the benefit hath redounded upon all men unto the justification of life* — that is, that we may not perish in death or be damned.

**XIII.** *Justification* the Gospel therefore nameth *absolution from sins, and the gratuitous imputation of righteousness — that is, the innocence and obedience of the Son of God — or the remission of sins, reconciliation with God, and gratuitous acceptation of us before God*: as, the Publican went down to his house justified — that is, absolved from sins and having received also imputed righteousness. And the voice *Iustificationis* is in the category of *Relation*, and hath its foundation in God Himself justifying and saving us because of Christ, and its terminus in the believing person. The *relation* is the application of the divine mercy and of the benefits of Christ unto the believing person.

**XIV.** Of this justification Paul speaketh eloquently in his Epistles — especially unto the Romans and Galatians, which two Epistles truly are the *sedes* of the solid doctrine of the justification of man before God. For here saith Paul, Rom. 5: *We are justified in His blood*. And: *We are reconciled to God by the death of His Son*. And again: *Through the obedience of one many are justified*. Rom. 4: *Unto him that worketh not, but believeth in Him that justifieth the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness*.

**XV.** Here the word and the matter of Justification plainly taketh away every dignity of all works of the Law, and of all our qualities and virtues in us — since we cannot have the *iustitia legis*, according to that of Paul, Rom. 8: *What was impossible unto the Law, because it was weakened by the flesh, that God did, showing us the Son of God, whose obedience and righteousness is imputed unto us, and in whom we are made perfect and consummated* (Col. 2).

**XVI.** This also must be indicated: the word *iustitia* often signifieth the *renovation* in man — or (as Paul speaketh) the *law of the mind* to which the *law of the members* resisteth, and the *incepted obedience* which the pious in this life begin to perform, and which we customarily name *peace with God and good conscience* and *the fruit or effect of the justice of faith* — whereby alone we stand before God, but which is always conjoined with the presence of God, the donation of the Holy Spirit, the new light in the justified, regeneration from God, purification of the hearts, consolation, peace, good conscience, and the inception of new and eternal life, wisdom and glory, or new obedience — as below shall be said. For *to be justified* often is *to be declared just* — that he indeed is just who doth righteousness — as by James we are said to be justified by works, that is, to be declared just; but contrary Paul testifieth that no man is justified by works — that is, held just and absolved as by nature or by his own virtues entire and *ἀνέγκλητος* [unimpeachable] before God. 1 Tim. 3: *God was justified in the Spirit* — that is, was acknowledged the true God, and affected with due honour, and declared *entire, perfect, and powerful*. But of the word *iustitia*, so much as seemeth requisite for our discourse, let this suffice.

### Of the Second, namely of the words *Gratia* and *Donum*.

**XVII.** The word *Grace*, which Paul useth in the doctrine of the justification of man before God, signifieth without all doubt the *benevolence and favour whereby God — men not meriting any such thing — of his own accord embraceth them, receiveth them, absolveth them, and giveth unto them the righteousness of His Son*: according to that saying — *By grace, or freely, we obtain remission, or are justified*. For these are synonyms: *the favour of God, grace, benevolence, φιλανθρωπία, εὐδοκία, mercy, goodness, gratuitous acceptation, benignity, the charity of God or His love toward us, adoption, reconciliation, gratuitous remission of sins for the sake of the Son, given unto believers.*

**XVIII.** But this signification of the word *grace* — and of the other words which are equipollent unto it — showeth that there is in us no cause or merit at all, whereby we may be justified before God unto life eternal, nor doth aught cleave to us; but rather God findeth in us very many, yea infinite causes for which He might justly damn us — but out of mere goodness and mercy, though unworthy and having merited far otherwise, we are received into grace because of the Son and accepted unto life eternal, according to that of Eph. 2: *By grace ye are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast.*

**XIX.** Often also we read the word *Grace* used for that *gift* whereby God from time to time adorneth the man whom He hath already deigned to favour or grace and mercy because of the Son — which gift is that of the Holy Spirit and the donation of eternal life, of the new and eternal righteousness and life which is here incepted and afterward is perfected. For *unto every one of us grace is given*, saith Paul (Eph. 4), *according to the measure of the donation of Christ* — that is, by a geometrical analogy, which distributeth to each what is congruous to his vocation.

**XX.** That Paul might expressly in the article of Justification show what he meant by *Grace*, he set forth two appellations — *Gratiam* and *donum per gratiam* — where by *Grace* he named nothing else than *the mercy of God promised through Christ, or the remission of sins, or gratuitous acceptation* (Rom. 5). And by *Gift* he called *the donation of the Holy Spirit, and the new virtues stirred up by the Holy Spirit, the true light, the true knowledge of God, the true and eternal righteousness and life which is here incepted but afterward is perfected* — as also John saith: *The Law was given by Moses; grace and truth was made through Jesus Christ.* And although we are not ignorant of the interpretations of others upon this Pauline locus which we adduce concerning *grace* and *gift* — especially of those who take *χάρις* concerning the *redemption and the liberality of the propitious God*, but *δωρεά* concerning *the very justification of man* and the *treasure which is given unto him* — nevertheless we retain now the true sentence which we have learned, and which no man can disapprove, and which by faith is analogous through all things — although we also do not reject the sentence and the explanation of the others, which here also we have appended, especially since it optimally agreeth with the context of the Pauline discourse. But this in passing.

**XXI.** Nevertheless we openly confess that unto Grace — which is the *gratuitous remission of sins*, or *mercy promised for the sake of Christ* — there is added the *donation of the Holy Spirit*, and we conjoin them in an individual nexus with the *χάρισματι δώρημα*, or (that we may speak more specially) with the *χάριτι δωρεὰν ἐν χάριτι* — that is, the donation of the Holy Spirit and the *fruits of faith*: invocation, hope, patience, charity, and good works, which are not the *causes* but the *effects* of our righteousness before God — and he who hath them not, falsely and in vain boasteth that he hath the *cause* of these gifts, that is, grace and faith. And with clear voice we damn the error of Pelagius, who — about the year of Christ 400 being convicted that men are called, justified, and received by the grace of God — feigned that men who are now justified by grace either general or special (for so he was accustomed to sport, agitating the orthodox) can institute a pious and irreproachable life, fulfil the Law, and obtain eternal life *by their own free will and by the powers of human choice* — nor is there need of *special grace* or of the donation of the Holy Spirit. ¹¹⁸

**XXII.** For this cause the ancients — to damn the raving of Pelagius — rightly studied to explain the word *grace*, and delivered perspicuous distinctions between *general* and *special* grace; and this they divided into first and second — that is (that we may speak with Paul) into *χάρις καὶ δωρεά*, *grace* and *gift*; or into *preventing, preparing, liberating, and operating* grace, and *subsequent, cooperating, and assisting* grace — as from Augustine and others it is manifest. ¹¹⁹

**XXIII.** And although both — *Grace* and *Gift* — are the benefit of the Son of God, for whose sake we are reconciled unto God and endowed with the Holy Spirit (for so Paul named it, *τὴν περισσείαν τῆς χάριτος καὶ τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς δικαιοσύνης* — the *redundance* of grace and of the gift of righteousness) — yet when the Scripture saith that *we are justified and saved by grace*, it understandeth that Grace which is distinguished from the Gift — that is, it doth not understand the donation of the Holy Spirit, or newness, or fruits, good works, or anything cleaving inwardly to us, nor charity nor other virtues, but the *mercy of God and the gratuitous acceptation* which is made because of the Son — or gratuitous benevolence, reconciliation, and imputation. According to that of Paul, Rom. 4: *Unto him that worketh, the reward is not imputed of grace, but of debt; but unto him that worketh not — that is, who bringeth no work whose reward he might demand, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly — that is, resteth on the gratuitous promise of God — his faith is imputed unto him for righteousness* — that is, he is pronounced just in Christ, having the righteousness of Christ imputed unto him. And again: *Therefore of faith, according to grace, that the promise may be firm* — that is, that there may be a certain reconciliation without doubting, not hanging on the condition of our dignity. And Rom. 5: *Where sin abounded, grace superabounded* — that is, the gratuitous imputation of the righteousness of Christ.

### Of the Third — the word of *Faith*.

**XXIV.** The word *faith* is variously used. But we do not now institute to speak of all its significations — but only, of that faith by which Paul affirmeth we are justified before God, we shall add a few things. For there are those who interpret faith as the obedience whereby it cometh to pass that men live according to the prescript of God's will, as they promised in baptism — as by Cicero *fides* is defined *the constancy and truth of things said and agreed*. But that Paul is not speaking of this faith, that alone showeth manifestly, that everywhere he opposeth faith to works. No quality inhering in us, therefore, or infused, can have place in the signification of the faith by which Paul showeth we are justified before God.

**XXV.** Others define faith as *notitia*, and assent, whereby we believe true whatsoever is written in the Old and New Testament — as it is reported of Thomas Aquinas that in the agony of life he received the Bible and said: *I believe whatsoever is written in this book.* Hence many teach that it sufficeth if in general men believe what the Church proposeth as to be believed — and they trouble themselves not with expounding singulars, or rightly accommodating them, and transferring them unto use where this ought to be done. But that Paul is not at all speaking of this faith, this also showeth: that James testifieth that even the demons have this *implicit and historical faith*, and therefore *tremble*; but Paul affirmeth by testimony of all the pious that those justified by faith *have peace with God*. And he citeth from the prophet Habakkuk the saying: *The just shall live by his faith*, where the Hebrew word *Emūnah* is placed — which signifieth not only *constancy* and *virtue observing what was promised*, but also often *confidence in the mercy promised for the sake of Christ*.

**XXVI.** We define therefore *faith*, of which here question is made, to be *the true and firm assent whereby we assent to every word of God delivered unto us, and in this to the promise of grace promised for the sake of the Son of God concerning the remission of sins and reconciliation; and the firm and constant confidence of the soul resting in God because of the Mediator — whereby every one of the faithful is certain with himself that the Word of God in general is not only true and firm and (above all) that the promises of God concerning gratuitous reconciliation through Christ are true — but also believeth that these promises pertain properly and peculiarly unto himself, so that this universal promise of eternal life acquired through the blood of Christ unto all believers, each one embraceth and applieth unto himself, and in true fears he is uplifted, and feeleth life and joy in God, and approacheth Him, and invoketh Him, His mercy and His presence being acknowledged* — according to that: *Being justified by faith we have peace*. Likewise: *Every one that believeth on Him shall not be confounded.*

**XXVII.** When therefore Paul saith *We are justified by faith*, he comprehendeth in the thinking potency both *notitia* and *assent*; and in the will, *confidence*. Hence rightly we say that *faith is apprehensive and quietative*. For notices form images and behold the object; but confidence in the heart and the will is the *motion* whereby we rest in the apprehended object. And hence it comes that we rightly call justifying faith the *organ or instrument only* — and that indeed freely given unto us — by which, as by a hand, we apprehend and apply unto ourselves Christ our righteousness, perfection, and integrity; certainly setting: that because of the obedience, satisfaction, and merit of the Son of God, we are in grace, and have the remission of sins, are justified and saved unto eternity, and are truly just in Christ, His righteousness being imputed unto us, beloved in the Beloved.

**XXVIII.** That we may know the faith of which we speak to be *notitia*, *assent*, and *certain and infallible confidence*, this must be considered: of justifying faith there is one *true, certain, firm, unmoved, peculiar, principal, and proper object* — which is the *divine promise of the Gospel, proper concerning the gratuitous mercy of God, remitting sins because of the Son the Mediator, adopting and accepting us as sons of believers unto eternal life*. Into this object faith looketh principally when it wills to receive the remission of sins, reconciliation, and adoption, and to make man certain that he is in the grace of God, son and heir of God, and coheir of Christ.

**XXIX.** Although faith also hath other objects — namely all those things which are divinely patefacted in the Word of God, as in Hebrews 11 the objects of faith are described in multiplicity — external namely in general, about which *general faith* is exercised, and which even they can have who often are without *justifying faith*, and *do not look upon the principal object of true faith which after the Apostolic mode we name justifying* — as there it is written: *By faith they passed through the Red Sea*; and yet in all these the Lord was not well pleased, as Paul testifieth 1 Cor. 10; and the ten lepers (Luke 17) apprehended by *general* faith the external object of healing; and yet only one of them had *justifying* faith. Nevertheless it is certain that of faith not in general but in species considered — that is, of justifying faith — there is only one object: the promise namely of the gratuitous mercy promised because of the Son the Mediator, for whose sake God is placated toward us, reconciled, and propitious. Wherefore Paul saith: *Therefore of faith freely, that the promise may be firm.* And this maketh this one object of justifying faith so that afterward the exercise of faith may be firm and stable even concerning other objects — as Paul saith 2 Cor. 1: *Whatsoever promises of God there are, they are yea and Amen in Christ unto the glory of God through us* — that is, the fulfilment of the promises concerning whatsoever objects or things is certain, when by faith in Christ we are reconciled with God — as Abraham is certain concerning his posterity according to the promise, since he knew he had God placated and propitious through and for the sake of the Son. Hence we say: *With faith in Christ shining ahead, all things are safe.* And although often the external objects be wholly absent, yet faith looketh upon the proper and principal object, which is the promise of the gratuitous mercy of God because of Christ the Mediator — as the thief on the cross, destitute of external objects, apprehendeth the Son of God by faith; and Job saying: *Even if the Lord slay me, shall I not hope in Him?* — that is, though I be destitute of every external object and prop, of every human means in my whole life, yet fixed is my hope in the Lord my Saviour. And Asaph saith (Ps. 72): *Though my flesh and heart fail me, yet Thou, God, art the portion of my heart, etc.*

**XXX.** That we may render somewhat plainer what we have said, two things are set before us to be considered in the sacred letters — of which the first is the *definition and description of faith*, and the other, *how Paul understandeth faith* — namely *correlatively* — when he affirmeth that we are justified through it.

**XXXI.** An illustrious appellation and description of faith is extant in Isa. 26, where faith is named *Yēṣer sāmūch* — that is, *sustained or upheld thought*. The words are these: *Open ye the gates* (that is, the ministry) *and there shall enter in a just nation keeping faith, which is Yēṣer sāmūch, firm thought — that thou mayest keep peace, peace I say, because in thee we hope*. And out of these words Paul without doubt hath builded the foundation of our doctrine and consolation, when he saith: *Being justified by faith, we have peace with God.* And in few words Isaiah hath comprehended great things. He saith that faith is *Yēṣer* — that is, *a gift of God, or a new πλάσμα καὶ ποίημα of the Holy Spirit* — opposed to that old thought of which is written Gen. 6 and 8: *Yēṣer* or *πλάσμα* or *figment of the human heart is evil at all times from its youth*. For by faith the hearts are purified. Next, he saith faith is *Sāmūch* — that is, *upheld from above by God, confirmed and preserved in the minds and hearts of the pious, that in wrestling and trepidation it may not succumb, but may be and remain firm, even if it may seem to us to be infirm*. For *Sāmach* is *to sustain, lest we fall or perish* — as *Sāmach* is named in Scripture God Himself, our sustainer. And *to sustain the hands over one* is *to lay hands on one, and to consecrate or destine him, both unto the public function of the ecclesiastical ministry and unto receiving and retaining the gifts of the Holy Spirit*. For thus God, *Sāmach*, sustaineth us daily with His hand, confirmeth, uplifteth, and preserveth us, that with David we can say: *My heart is sustained; I shall not fear*. Afterward faith is named *Sāmūch* by Isaiah also because it leaneth upon the Word and promise of God, and hath itself *correlatively* to the promise. For faith by its own virtue and dignity could plainly not stand, unless it had this object and this staff on which to lean, and this invincible wall wherein it may ever remain safe. Lastly, faith is *unmoved thought* — that is, it is not only *notitia* or fleshly assent, but is *πληροφορία*, that is, *certain confidence and application* — whereby we accept as with a begging hand the gift and benefit offered and given by God, and now certainly determine it to be ours, without doubting; which doubting though we feel in our flesh, we yet repress and overcome by two chief modes — considering namely (from the object of faith which it apprehendeth, and not from the quantity or quality of faith) that concerning faith itself and its force and power we must judge. For an *absolute idea* of faith is not required, nor is faith estimated from its firmness or perfection; but faith, though languid, ought from the object which it apprehendeth to seek a *certain and firm consolation*; further, we ought to pray with that father, Mark 9: *Lord I believe, help my unbelief*. Luke 19: *Increase our faith.* ¹²⁰

**XXXII.** The Epistle to the Hebrews Ch. 11 defineth faith in this mode: *πίστις ἐλπιζομένων ὑπόστασις, πραγμάτων ἔλεγχος οὐ βλεπομένων* — that is, *Faith is the hypostasis of things hoped for, and the elenchus of things not appearing*. But *hypostasis* signifieth *expectation, or expecting confidence, constant and firm* which maketh those things not yet seen to stand, and firmly applieth to itself the promise — as the Greek Scholiast rightly expounded: *πίστις ἐστὶν αὐτὴ ἡ ὑπόστασις καὶ οὐσία τῶν ἐλπιζομένων πραγμάτων. Ἐπειδὴ γὰρ τὰ ἐν ἐλπίσιν ἀνυπόστατα ὄντα, ὡς τέως μὴ παρόντα, ἡ πίστις οὐσία τίς αὐτῶν καὶ ἡ ὑπόστασις γίνεται, εἶναι αὐτὰ καὶ παρεῖναι τρόπον τινὰ παρασκευάζουσα, διὰ τὸ πιστεύειν εἶναι. Ἔστι δὲ ἡ πίστις ἔλεγχος καὶ ἀπόδειξις τῶν οὐ βλεπομένων. Ἀποδείκνυσι δὲ ὁρατὰ τὰ ἀόρατα ἡ πίστις· πῶς; τῷ νῷ καὶ ταῖς ἐλπίσιν ὁρῶσα τὰ μὴ φαινόμενα.* ¹²¹ — That is: *Faith is the very substance and essence of things which are hoped for. For since those things which are in hope do not yet exist, and therefore are void of essence, faith is as it were a substance and essence of them, in that in some manner it causeth them to exist and to be present, in that it believeth they exist. But faith is also the argument and demonstration of things which are not seen: for it demonstrateth those things which are not seen, that they may be seen. How? By the mind and by hope beholding the things not appearing.*

Thus he — with whom the Syriac interpretation beautifully agreeth, which is thus: *Faith is the persuasion or confidence of those things which are in hope, as if they were in effect to the believers* (that is, which so maketh men certain of that which they hope, as if it were now completed and by effect performed) *and it is the manifestation or evidence of things not seen* (that is, of things which are not beheld). And there is extant the appellation *τῆς ὑποστάσεως* concerning faith in the Book of Wisdom Ch. 16, where it is written: *Thy Hypostasis showeth how sweet Thou art* — that is, faith in Thee, or confidence in Thy promises, maketh every one certain of Thy sweetness, mercy, and goodness. And Paul sometimes speaketh so, as 2 Cor. 9 and 11: *ὑπόστασις καυχήσεως*, *confident and unmoved boasting*. For the word *ὑποστάσεως* comprehendeth both in the definition of faith — namely *notitia* or firm representation, and confidence in the mind — as the Germans also say: *sich etwas unterstehen* — *to subsist*, that is, not merely to attempt but with great confidence to undertake and to do something — as Polybius Book 6 writeth of Horatius, that the enemies feared more his *θράσος*, that is, confidence and animosity, than his *δύναμις* or strength and might. And the Epistle to the Hebrews Ch. 3 saith: *We are made partakers of Christ, if we hold the beginning of his hypostasis unshaken unto the end* — that is, *if we retain the faith, τὴν πίστιν δι᾿ ἧς ὑπέστημεν*, as Chrysostom saith — which faith is the beginning by which we are sustained in this life, that is, both is our primary and principal foundation on which we lean, and simultaneously is the beginning of eternal and consummate life and joy. Meanwhile the Epistle to the Hebrews calleth *ἔλεγχος* firm and unmoved proof and conviction — or (that I may speak more clearly) *the utmost certitude and conclusion*, confirmed by the Word, the promise, examples, testimonies, and internal motions, and by infinite arguments — such certainly as is that of things apprehended by the eyes, hands, and all the senses. Let me add also this: *the things which are hoped for* are referred to future things — namely the help of God in all adversities, the resurrection of the body, the last judgment, the eternal life and joy; but the *things not seen* are referred to all things which either have been done, or truly exist, and yet cannot be seen by us — as is the whole divine essence, the doctrine concerning creation, angels, the fall, the whole history of Christ and His satisfaction for our sins, and so forth.

**XXXIII.** Hither also pertaineth that the Sacred Letters call faith *πεποίθησιν, παρρησίαν, πληροφορίαν* — all which agree with the prior descriptions, and are to be opposed to the Papist figment concerning doubting, and take away the Academic *ἐποχή* [suspension], and instruct tender minds and consciences to grow in faith. *τί γὰρ ἴδιον τῆς πίστεως*, saith Basil, *ἡ ἀδιάκριτος πληροφορία τῆς ἀληθείας τῶν θεοπνεύστων ῥημάτων, οὐδενὶ λογισμῷ, οὔτε φυσικῆς ἀνάγκης εἰσαγομένῳ, οὔτε πρὸς εὐσέβειαν σχηματισμένῳ διασαλλομένη* — *For what is proper to faith? The indiscriminate fullness of assurance of the truth of the God-breathed sayings, disturbed by no reasoning — neither one brought in by natural necessity, nor one figured for the sake of piety.* ¹²²

**XXXIV.** This also is to be added: tender consciences, which lament the imbecility of their own faith and think themselves not sufficiently instructed with that *πληροφορία*, must be admonished that we are not always to judge concerning the truth of faith from feeling, but from the Word of God — which showeth that *the virtue of the Lord is perfected in infirmity* — and testifieth that faith is not always firm in one and the same mode, but sometimes courageous and sometimes weak and like a smoking flax — and teacheth also that the dignity of faith is estimated not from the quantity or quality of itself, but from the object which without error it apprehendeth. And at last it biddeth us to pray, that our faith may be confirmed and grow. For this prayer is an evident testimony of the presence of faith.
