**XXXV.** I have spoken of the definition of faith. Now, how Paul understandeth the faith by which we are justified, is briefly to be subjoined — namely *correlatively* (as customarily we speak), that is: *faith looketh upon and apprehendeth the promise*, as Paul distinctly saith, Rom. 4: *Therefore of faith freely, that the promise may be firm.* Faith therefore signifieth *the confidence of the mercy promised because of Christ the Mediator, and not because of human virtues*. And this sentence can easily be understood and judged by all pious minds in the true exercises of penitence, in daily invocation — which certainly cannot be done unless faith look upon the Mediator through whom we may be heard, as David saith: *Save me for Thy mercy's sake.* And Daniel: *Hear us, O Lord, not according to our righteousness, but according to Thy mercy for the Lord's sake.* And Augustine speaketh thus: *the certainty of the whole confidence is placed in the precious blood of Christ.* ¹²³ And these things commemorated concerning faith may suffice for now — which kindle a light upon all things remaining to be said concerning justification.

### Of the Fourth — the exclusive particles: *Freely, Alone.*

**XXXVI.** Not only doth Paul affirm that we are justified *by faith*, but for a dilucid declaration of his sentence — and to remove the occasions of all corruptions which may be devised concerning Faith as if it were a quality and work of ours, or *a fide formata* as the adversaries speak — he useth many exclusive particles: namely, that we are justified *freely, of grace, according to mercy, from the promise, not by the Law, not through the Law, without the Law, without works, not according to works, not from works, not from ourselves, boasting being excluded — through faith.* Gal. 2: *We know that a man is not justified by the works of the Law, but through the faith of Jesus Christ, ἐὰν μὴ διὰ πίστεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ* — that is, *ἀλλὰ* — in the Hebraic mode *Kīm*, as in the first Psalm: *But in the Law of the Lord is his will*. Likewise: *by Faith Alone* — as the purer Church at all times hath spoken, as from the writings of Basil, Nazianzus, Origen also, Ambrose, Augustine, Athanasius, Hilary, and others it is manifestly established, and as David also speaketh Ps. 71: *I walk in the might of the Lord, the Lord — I preach Thy righteousness alone* — that is, not mine, not that of the Law or of works, but that Thy righteousness which I apprehend by faith imputed unto me. And the Son of God saith: *μόνον πίστευε* — *only believe* (Luke 8). ¹²⁴

**XXXVII.** By these exclusives are eloquently taken away all merits — whether ceremonial, or forensic, or moral — and there is taken away from man the justification unto eternal life: first, as hath been said, from the whole *Law* in this life, and from all human qualities, powers, habits, actions, zeal, and works; second, from *Pharisaic* righteousness instituted according to the Law of God, and from external discipline of reason and from all elective worships; third, not only from all virtues *preceding* regeneration, but also from the *good works of the regenerate*, or from the spiritual newness and obedience divinely kindled in regeneration — yea, even from *faith itself*, whereby the hearts are quickened, as far namely as the quality or dignity of faith is regarded (for imperfect is that newness, as below shall be said). And faith perpetually ought to look upon the merit of the Son of God alone, for whose sake alone we are received and perpetually please, even though there be many excellent virtues and divine actions incepted in us, the Holy Spirit having been received.

**XXXVIII.** Piously, rightly, and gravely four great and necessary causes are recited in our Churches and Schools which show that the exclusive particles — *Freely, without the Law, not from works, without works, not from ourselves, by Faith Alone, etc.* — must be retained, defended, and illustrated.

**The first cause** is: that the benefit of the Son of God may be beheld, and unto this Mediator may be attributed due and proper honour — since He alone is our Redeemer, Justifier, Mediator, and Saviour, and His obedience alone is *ἀντίλυτρον* for the sins of men, as John testifieth: *Behold the Lamb of God, that taketh away the sins of the world.* And Paul nameth Christ *ἱλαστήριον* or *Kappōreth* — the mercy-seat of the ark, wherewith our sins are covered (Rom. 3), and God is placated through the remission of all sins — both of those which in the human race have ever been done, and those which are being committed, or shall thenceforth be committed even unto the end of the world. For Paul joineth the past (naming *προγεγονότα ἁμαρτήματα*), and the present (saying, *for the declaring of righteousness ἐν τῷ νῦν καιρῷ, in the present time*), and the future (saying, *ὁ θεὸς δικαιώσει, God shall justify Jews and Gentiles through faith*) in ordered wise, that he may show that the price and merit for all the sins of all men at all times is the sole obedience of the Son of God.

**The second cause** is: that in the exercises of penitence and in great fears, minds may have *certain and firm consolation*, sought not from the Law or from natural reason, nor from our dignity or merits, contrition, love, and other virtues, but from *the promise of mercy which the Son of God hath brought from the bosom of the eternal Father* — teaching us that God truly is willing to receive us and hear us because of the Son. And utterly uncertain and vain would remission and reconciliation be, if it depended upon the condition of our dignity or were given because of our works — which, seeing they are so slender and imperfect, whether they might suffice, no one could ever determine. As for this cause the Monks — imagining an uncertitude — taught that one ought ever to doubt concerning grace: since certainly that is the extreme blasphemy, to despise the voice which sounded from heaven — *Hear ye Him* — and to God promising not to render the praise of veracity, according to that of 1 John 5: *He that believeth not God, maketh Him a liar.*

**The third cause** is: that *true invocation* may be able to be performed, in which faith may shine forth beholding the Son of God the Mediator, and setting that our prayers are received because of that High Priest — as it is written: *Through Him we have access unto God.* And: *Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, He will give it you.* And Daniel prayeth: *Hear us, O Lord, for the Lord's sake.*

**The fourth**: that there may be an illustrious distinction of Law and Gospel. For the Law hath no gratuitous promises but *conditional*, as it is said: *He who doth these things shall live in them.* But the Gospel offereth freely the benefits of the Son of God and excludeth the condition of our own merit and the confidence of our own dignity.

**XXXIX.** But this also must be known: that by the exclusive particles — *Freely, Alone*, etc. — is by no means excluded contrition in those who are converted, or the other virtues, so as not to follow. Nay, Paul willeth these as testimonies and fruits of righteousness to follow. But there is excluded the *condition of our merit or dignity*, and is denied that *contrition and our virtues are the causes of reconciliation*; and is shown that the *one and only cause* is the merit of Christ the Mediator, so that the sentence be: *By faith, freely for the sake of the Son of God, we receive reconciliation — not for the sake of our dignity*. And for this reason we rightly say: *We are justified before God by Faith Alone; and yet faith is never alone; and with faith, in an individual nexus we conjoin confidence, hope, patience, invocation, charity, and good works — not as causes but as effects of the righteousness of that faith*, which he who hath not, falsely and in vain boasteth that he hath the cause of those virtues — namely faith. Nor is it thence to follow that works concur with faith in justification, as the Sophists falsely think — since Paul expressly saith: *We gather or conclude that a man is justified by faith without the works of the Law*. Likewise Rom. 11: *If by grace, then no more of works; otherwise grace is no more grace. But if it be of works, it is no more grace; otherwise work is no more work.* This antithesis of works and of faith taketh away every sophistical *iustitia partim gratiae sive fidei, partim operibus tribuenda*, which although they must follow and be present (in such wise that faith is not true faith unless it have with itself these most beauteous virtues — love, patience, and invocation) — yet are not the cause or merit of reconciliation, nor do they enter into the act of justification, but are companions, handmaids, and ministers of faith — by which alone we are justified and obtain the grace of God, as it is written 1 John 2: *By this we know that we know Him — namely by faith — if we keep His commandments* — that is, good works do not commend us to God, but we, being inserted [into Christ] and by this (namely because Christ is the propitiation for our sins and for those of the whole world) *freely justified and already having attained salvation in Christ*, obtain the fruits. And immediately John addeth: *He that saith, I know Him* (he speaketh of the cognition of faith) *and keepeth not His commandments, is a liar, and the truth is not in him* — that is, gratuitous justification from the one faith in Christ by no means excludeth good works as its fruits, but openeth the fountain of good works, and showeth what and how they can be done and please, and testifieth that *good works follow the man justified and saved, and do not precede the man to be justified* (that we may speak with Augustine), and that unless they follow (without interval of time) they certainly indicate that they who by mouth alone and profession boast of faith are not yet justified — and in reality they have and exhibit none, not invoking God, impatient overmuch in the cross, and living and persevering in sins against conscience. And this is the cause that Paul (Eph. 2) with clear voice pronounceth that *we are justified by Faith Alone, and yet faith is not alone* — saying of the former: *By grace ye are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest any man should boast.* And of the latter: *For we are His workmanship* (Paul speaketh of grace, not of nature), *created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared that in them we should walk.* And Gal. 5: *Neither circumcision availeth aught, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love.* For thus is *living and true faith* distinguished from *dead and adulterine faith* — and yet charity is not conjoined with faith as *συναίτιον* [co-cause] of justification, as from what hath hitherto been said sufficiently is clear.

**XL.** We therefore flee the voices of certain persons who clamour that *good works are hurtful unto salvation and unto justifying faith, if they be present*. And: *God careth not for works*. Likewise: *Faith is sometimes and for some time without works*. Likewise: *the third use of the Law is either nothing, or is a diabolical phantasm*. Now let us hear the words of D. Luther, whereby he affirmeth that it cannot come to pass that true faith be in any who doth not assiduously operate — no otherwise than it is impossible for a pyre to be kindled which shineth not. *It is impossible*, saith he, *that faith without intermission not operate good. And it is impossible that works can be separated from faith, as it is impossible that burning and shining be separated from fire.* ¹²⁵ And rightly it is said that good works and faith by reason and order can be distinguished, but by time from each other cannot be separated. Wherefore also Paul saith: *Wage a good warfare, having faith and a good conscience.* Yet we reprobate and damn the opinions of all who so conjoin works with faith that they imagine those to concur in the very justification, as some merit and cause, or *συναίτιον*.

**XLI.** From what things therefore have been said, must be built up the *Definition of the Righteousness of Faith* — namely, that it is *the absolution from sin and from guilt, the acceptation and reconciliation of the converted sinner*, which is made through faith in Christ dead for us and raised from the dead — or *the remission of sins, the imputation of the righteousness or obedience of Christ, the gratuitous redemption and liberation from sin, from eternal death, from the wrath of God, from the malediction of the Law, from the tyranny of the Devil, and from damnation* — which liberation cometh unto us out of the sole mercy of God, freely, for the sake of the Son, without the works of the Law and without human merits — and is *the adoption of the believers as sons and heirs of God and coheirs of Christ unto life, joy, and eternal salvation*.

**XLII.** The praise of this righteousness is wholly and *in solidum* to be attributed unto Christ, which is imputed unto us freely through faith, that the firm word of David may stand: *In Thy sight shall no man living be justified.* And that of Paul, Gal. 2: *If righteousness be by the Law, then Christ died in vain.* And Rom. 4: *If Abraham were justified by works, he hath whereof to glory, but not before God.* Likewise 1 Cor. 4: *I know nothing by myself, yet am I not hereby justified.* And Rom. 3 he saith distinctly: *By the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified in the sight of God — for by the Law is the knowledge of sin. But now without the Law the righteousness of God is manifested, being witnessed by the Law and the Prophets — even the righteousness of God through the faith of Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all them that believe. For there is no difference — for all have sinned, and are destitute of the glory of God* (that is, of eternal life), *being justified freely by His grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth to be a propitiation through faith in His blood, to declare His righteousness, for the remission of former sins, etc.*

**XLIII.** This righteousness God offereth through the Gospel *under the condition of faith as of an instrument* — which through the Spirit of Christ He Himself giveth; therefore Paul and others sometimes call it *the righteousness of God*, sometimes *of the Gospel*, sometimes *of faith*. And that we may add this concerning the word: it is certain (as Augustine, Luther, and others often have noted) that the *righteousness of God* in the article of justification signifieth not that righteousness whereby God is essentially just, but that which availeth before God, or by which we stand and lean in the judgment of God, and which God bestoweth upon man the sinner to be justified — absolving him, and pronouncing him just because of the Mediator Christ apprehended by faith. As it is written: *The righteousness of God through the Gospel is unfolded or exhibited from faith to faith* — that is, by the faith which daily receiveth increment. ¹²⁶ And this is named the *righteousness of God* because it is the gratuitous gift of God — and that indeed by imputation; and because in bestowing this God showeth Himself just, faithful, and truthful; and because this righteousness is opposed to the righteousness of men (which is from works, and by which no man is justified); and finally because by this one righteousness we stand before God.

**XLIV.** The condition of faith the Gospel setteth forth, not as the Law offereth blessing (with the added condition of works — for so both the Law and the Gospel would offer not life but death, since we cannot by ourselves rightly do anything or truly believe), but by an altogether different reasoning. For the Law demandeth works and deeds and yet cannot supply the faculty of doing. But the Gospel freely offereth and giveth the benefits of Christ, and yet willeth us to receive them, and through the Spirit of Christ also giveth us the faculty of believing and of receiving the benefits offered — as it is written, Phil. 2: *It is God that worketh in you both to will and to do of His good pleasure.*

### Of the Sixth — the causes of justification and of faith.

**XLV.** Since therefore what the *iustitia Evangelii* is hath been shown, it behoveth us to inquire into the *causes of justification*. For since the righteousness of faith is not a simple form or quality but a certain wondrous action or relation, it cometh to pass that on account of many causes, things, or forms concurring in the same action (as is customarily done in relations) with necessary nexus and coherence, our righteousness is called now *the grace of God*, now *the obedience of the Son*, now *imputation*, now *faith* — and yet these appellations, though diverse as they seem, always signify the same thing, and each singly comprehendeth the whole action.

**XLVI.** The **efficient cause** therefore is *God*, or the whole Trinity. Whence we say: *God justifieth us — namely as efficient cause.* Likewise the *favour and mercy of God*, or the *φιλανθρωπία* of God, and love toward the human race, or the *grace promised and offered unto the whole human race*. For all these we refer unto the efficient cause.

**XLVII.** The **impulsive cause** is *the love of the Son of God toward the human race, His intercession for the human race, His humble supplication, His obedience, His satisfaction or merit, His redemption, the fulfilment of the Law performed by Christ* — or *some part of all these, namely His humiliation, incarnation, passion, crucifixion, death, blood, wounds, resurrection, and the journey of Christ unto the Father*. This impulsive cause (which can also comprehend the favour and grace of God — for we do not contend concerning title and appellation, provided that the matter be plain and true) others call the *material cause* and the *cause on account of which* — as we ourselves have done elsewhere — since there is no other, so to speak, *materia* of our justification and salvation than the obedience of Christ himself. Yet the appellation *impulsive cause* pleaseth us more, which can be used without ambiguity or perplexity. Rightly also is set down the *external, remote, and προκαταρκτική* impulsive [cause] — namely *the misery of the human race*, according to that of Rom. 5: *When we were yet weak, Christ died.*

**XLVIII.** There is no **form** in us or in our own powers. Nor can we call *vivification, regeneration, charity inhering or infused in us, or the habit elicited through charity* (as the Pontificials speak), nor *newness of life or dignity of any kind, or new obedience, or our works and merits*, the *form* of our justice. And that whole figment which is brought forth concerning *fides formata* is vain. For our true righteousness is *alien, outside of us* — that is, its positive and singular foundation lieth *not in us or in our powers and qualities but in Christ*, whose obedience is imputed unto us who believe in Him. Wherefore the **formal cause** of our righteousness is *the gratuitous remission of sins* (or expiation, whereby our sins are not imputed unto us), the *imputation of the obedience, innocence, and righteousness of Christ*, reconciliation with God, adoption as sons and heirs of God — with which is always conjoined peace with God and *confidence resting in the promise of God and in the merit of the Son*.

**XLIX.** The **instrumental cause**, or means, as far as respecteth God, are *the Gospel and the Sacraments*. But as respecteth us it is *Faith*, whereby we receive the benefits of the Son of God offered and given. For faith alone is the organ in this world of our conjunction with Christ. But the causes of faith are three:

1. *The doctrine of the Gospel heard*, which is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth.
2. *The Holy Spirit* efficacious through the Word of the Gospel. For this is the work of God, saith Christ, that ye believe on Him whom He hath sent. And Paul calleth faith the gift of God.
3. By reason of the subject and of the order prescribed and instituted by God Himself, there is added *the very will of man*, which the Holy Spirit through the Word draweth, bendeth, reformeth, and endoweth with faith. For we ought not to be and remain *stocks, trunks, and stones*, but the Word having been heard and the Holy Spirit acting, we now well will — not because the Holy Spirit only aided the imbecility of our will, but because He made the ill-willing will out of the bad into a good one, and that freely, according to that: *God worketh that ye may both will and do.* For when the Word hath been heard, and by this the Holy Spirit acting, the will can no longer be idle — not for evil (as it is in a man not yet regenerate, and therefore too busy for destruction), but for good.

**L.** That in the conversion of man an assent is required, and the man not compelled contrary to all his own will, but hearing from the Father and learning (as the Son of God Himself speaketh, John 6) — and willing to be converted — this all sound and pious persons testify. And yet we say that when the man wills and assents, this happeneth not by the force or dignity of *liberum arbitrium*, but by the grace and efficacy of God, who in this mode is efficacious through the Word and the voice of the Gospel, and not otherwise. And ingenuously we confess that unless the will received the gift of faith (which is notice, assent, and confidence) from God, it were itself worth nothing or of no avail. Yet faith or assent is not impressed upon the will as an image is impressed upon wax, or as oil is poured into a jar, or a liquor into empty vessels — but God giveth *this willing of the will*, and that assent. He giveth it not to wax but to a man; nor doth He create a new *substance of the will*, but through the Holy Spirit He offereth unto the mind and will of man the Word heard (whose soul He himself is), illuminateth the mind, bendeth and moveth the will — and so converteth the whole man, that from the *old*, such as he is according to natural depravation, there may be made a *new man* according to the promise and exhibition of grace.

**LI.** Deservedly therefore we shun those voices which triflingly say that man in justification and in receiving the gift of faith — nay, in the whole conversion — is not only a *stock and trunk* to bear all things, but even after the change is *repugnant, hostile, and adverse*; and that the Holy Spirit is given not only unto those repugnant, but unto those exercising in the very conversion the extreme and most bitter enmities with God, unwilling and holding God for folly. Likewise, that man is *violently constrained* unto conversion. Likewise, that the will of man in conversion cannot even *be stirred* by grace to perform anything. Likewise, that assent is impressed upon the will by God, but not created, and the rest. Let us flee these ravings, and with all our hearts pray the Son of God our Lord Jesus Christ that He Himself be the assertor of His own simplicity, rectitude, and truth, and repress the furors and the madness of the devils and of evil men who befoul the truth with horrid opinions.

**LII.** Concerning the **final cause** of justification it is established that this is *the glorification of the name of God, and the eternal life and salvation of the believers, and the destruction of sin, of death, and of the whole kingdom of Satan.* And unto these also we subjoin *all the effects of the righteousness of faith* — as are the donation of the Holy Spirit, the inhabitation of God in us, *renovation, new light or illumination, peace of conscience, joy, consolation, invocation, confession, thanksgiving, patience, love of God and neighbour, newness of life* — or new and incepted obedience, or all good works, whose root and mother is faith. Of the *adjacent things* — which are the offices of the justified and the obligation to obedience — and of the *cognate things* — predestination, calling, and glorification — likewise of the *repugnant things* — that is, errors in the foundation, corruptions of doctrine, sins against conscience, condemnation, and eternal punishments — otherwhere it shall be spoken.

### Of the Seventh — namely of Imputation.

**LIII.** Since hitherto often *imputation* hath been mentioned, it is worth the while also to inquire into the proper signification of this word in the article or doctrine of Justification. Now we apprehend in the sacred letters that the voice of *Imputation* is used in a twofold signification. The **prior signification** — in the category of Relation (that we may speak scholastically and perspicuously) — hath its foundation in a *certain quality in those unto whom the imputation is made*, and hath its terminus in either *reward or recompense*, or *penalty and guilt*. And the *relation* between these two is the imputation itself, either unto reward or unto guilt. So we say that *iniquity is imputed to someone*. And of Phinehas it is written Ps. 106 that his deed of killing the fornicator was *imputed to him for righteousness* — that is, was accepted by God for a just work and manifoldly recompensed in his seed and posterity. And Paul retaineth this signification also, Rom. 4: *Unto him that worketh, the reward is imputed, not of grace but of debt.*

The **posterior signification** — in the same category — hath its foundation not in a *quality inhering in those to whom the imputation is made*, but in another; and hath its terminus in the *person* to whom the imputation is made, either unto good or unto evil. But the *relation* is the *thought, will, or decree of him who imputeth* — as when Paul saith unto Philemon: *If Onesimus hath hurt thee anything, or oweth aught, put that on my account: I will repay it.*

**LIV.** Now therefore it is asked in which signification the word *Imputation* is received in the doctrine of Justification of man before God — whether that *real* prior signification of an *inhering righteousness or infused charity*, or the *rational* one of *the imputation from the mercy of God imputing unto us an alien righteousness*, not inhering in us, nor consisting in our works. But Paul himself hath responded in clear words, Rom. 4, saying: *Unto him that worketh not, but believeth in Him that justifieth the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness — not of debt, but of grace.* Paul also affirmeth that Abraham is not justified before God by that imputation of righteousness which is done *according to debt* — that is, which hath its foundation in the very one to whom the imputation is made, as if it were done because of works. For *unto him that worketh, the reward is not imputed of grace but of debt.*

**LV.** We define *imputation* in this mode: *Imputation is the will, εὐδοκία, or action of God, whereby that which we are not, and that which we neither have nor have done, out of ineffable love and mercy toward us God judgeth, thinketh, decreeth, and pronounceth us to be, to have, and to have done — because His Son, in whom we believe, is that whole thing for us, in our name and place, in solidum, and hath it and hath done it.* And contrariwise, *non-imputation is a gratuitous action of God, whereby God pronounceth us not to be, nor to have, nor to have done that which by nature after the first fall we truly are — namely, impious and to be damned, sons of wrath, enemies of God, guilty of death and of eternal punishments — because His Son, in whom we believe, hath drawn that whole thing into Himself, and by His obedience hath expiated it, and hath satisfied for us.*

**LVI.** Rightly therefore and piously we say that ours and Christ's *imputation is commutative*. For unto Christ are imputed our sins, which He as the *ἄμωμος καὶ ἄσπιλος, ἅγιος καὶ ἀνέγκλητος* Lamb neither hath nor did. But unto us is imputed the righteousness of Christ, and all His obedience — which by faith alone we receive as imputed unto us, *as though the whole were ours and had been performed by us* — so that we can be accused of no crime whatsoever, but be pronounced *ἅγιοι καὶ ἀνέγκλητοι* — holy and blameless.

**LVII.** This reasoning of imputation is therefore more diligently to be pondered, that we may take away from our minds the *imagination of infusion or of an inhering natural quality or righteousness*. Which if it were to have place, it would also be necessary to determine that our sins are so imputed unto Christ that He is feigned to be made partaker of them, conscious of them, and guilty of them by His nature and in reality — which to say is blasphemous, contumelious, and false.

**LVIII.** But whereas certain object that *righteousness is a positive thing* — since nothing can have the force of justifying unless it be something positive — and that *imputation is not a positive thing*: the response is easy and true. Of the *legal righteousness* and of the righteousness of our works, it is true — this must be a positive thing, a quality or virtue in us. But here question is made of the *righteousness of the person before God*, or of the *acceptation and gratuitous reconciliation*, which is the remission of sins and the imputation of righteousness because of the Mediator. This imputation we say is not a *privative thing*, nor destitute of a certain and firm foundation. For God Himself most severely reprehendeth an imputation lacking foundation, as Isa. 5: *Woe unto those who call evil good and good evil*. Likewise: *To justify the wicked is an abomination unto God*. But the solid, firm, unmoved, and august *foundation* of the imputation of the righteousness of the Son of God — which is imputed unto us without our works — is a positive thing, namely the *obedience and satisfaction of the Son of God*, as Paul expressly testifieth Rom. 4: *It is imputed unto us who believe on Him who raised up Jesus our Lord from the dead, who was delivered for our offences and raised for our justification* — that is, that He might atone for and expiate our sins, and that He might give His righteousness unto us. For Paul diligently declares the end in that Pauline locus.

**LIX.** By this same reasoning we say that *faith is imputed unto us for righteousness* — namely, not because of the dignity of the work, but because faith apprehendeth in the promise of the Gospel the merit of Christ.

**LX.** We say also that our *righteousness is passive* — namely in the same mode and not otherwise — that is, *the righteousness of the Son of God is imputed unto us*, in the order which God Himself hath instituted in His Word. That *the imputed righteousness* (that we may retain Paul's words) and *the passive righteousness* (as Luther hath spoken) are the same, and hold themselves in the same mode, is certain. For neither Paul nor Luther nor other pious and orthodox doctors of the sincere Church of Christ dreamed anything of *violence and coaction against and beyond our will*. And though these often instituted just complaints of the impotence and imbecility of the human will, and by this reason also said that the will *hath itself passively*, yet they did not feign *raptures and enthusiasms*. And let me add also this which I heard from my preceptors: When D. Luther had read in Paul *the righteousness of God is revealed*, he at first thought the *active* righteousness of God was understood — whereby God is just and judgeth others according to works — and therefore for a long time he carried with him in his conscience terror of the divine wrath against the sins of men. But afterward by the diligent consideration of the context he perceived his error, and observed that the *passive* righteousness of God is to be understood — namely of the righteousness whereby God receiveth us and pronounceth us just because of the Mediator. And Luther was accustomed to say that, when he had recognised that signification, he had as it were a *new and divinely kindled light in Paul* — and in the whole of Scripture dexterously to be understood. ¹²⁷

**LXI.** Some object that it very ill befitteth the nature of God to *absolve the unjust and pronounce them just* — this on the ground that Paul himself expoundeth the word *δικαιοῦν* by *δίκαιον καθίστασθαι, to be constituted just* — Rom. 5, when he saith *διὰ τῆς ὑπακοῆς τοῦ ἑνὸς δίκαιοι κατασταθήσονται οἱ πολλοί* — *through the obedience of one, many shall be constituted just* (that is, more than one — for he opposes *many* to *one*, not to *few* or *all*). But the true response to this objection is: *we are justified by faith, the righteousness of Christ namely being imputed unto us*; and therefore, although in ourselves we are unjust, yet in Christ we are absolved as truly just, and our sins remitted we are made coheirs of Christ — as Paul saith, God hath made us *τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ ἐχαρίτωσεν* (Eph. 1) — accepted in the Beloved. But as concerns the *new obedience*, or (as they call it) the *inhering righteousness*, that certainly is not the *cause*, but a *witness* of that righteousness by whose imputation we are saved.

**LXII.** It hath been asked (that we may also add this) concerning that form: *We are just — that is, accepted of God — by imputation and by inception*. Where by certain doctors of the Church it is not said that we are justified before God by both modes, partly by imputation and partly by inception (for this is by no means true, nor by any rightly sentient and believing person ever thought, said, or written) — but it is said that we are accepted of God by imputation and by inception — that is, both *reconciled unto Him by the sole imputation of the righteousness of Christ alone*, and *that our obedience pleaseth Him because of the Son*, as if we were plainly *ἄμωμοι καὶ ἀνέγκλητοι* (Col. 1) — though that obedience itself is imperfect, defiled in many modes, and is only *inception* in this life. For the word *iustitia* is received in that form of speech *universally*, or in general concerning the whole business of saving man — that is, concerning grace and gift, or concerning the whole benefit of Christ, cause and effect, concerning person and works, concerning reconciliation and the donation of the Holy Spirit. And there was use of this form of speech hitherto in some places outside of controversy, especially when it had to be said how far we are perfect and inculpable in this life, and accepted of God — namely by *imputation* because of the Son in whom we believe, and by *inception* of the new life (whose author and leader in us is the Holy Spirit, of whom we have the firstfruits) — even if in us there be yet many stains and manifold and foul deformities. And nothing else did our preceptors and others who used that form wish to say than this: *the person pleasing, the obedience or good work pleaseth; but the person pleaseth God unto whom the righteousness of Christ hath been imputed; and therefore also unto God the good works of that same person are pleasing, which yet in this life are not perfect or pure.* But because of the ambiguity and danger, we ought to shun this proposition: *We are just before God by imputation and by inception.*

**LXIII.** Some have called *righteousness* God Himself impelling us unto just deeds and clothing us with His *essential* righteousness. By this reasoning they seemed to confound God with His effects in us, and to exclude the obedience of Christ imputed unto us, and to confound also without distinction this imputed righteousness with the righteousness *incepted in us*, and *justification with sanctification*. Therefore that it might be shown that we lean upon the one imputed righteousness of Christ — and also in the *renewal of the Spirit*, which is the effect of our justification before God, though excellent, is yet only *inception and firstfruits* in this life, by which we cannot stand before the tribunal of God, whatsoever indeed and how magnificently may be said of *essential righteousness* — and yet that God is well pleased also with this inception and these firstfruits of the Spirit, which we offer in faith — some have therefore said that we are just, that is (for this interpretation was always added, lest our righteousness before God be confused with the righteousness of works), *accepted of God by imputation and by inception*. But since this very phrase hath now come into controversy — because some have drawn *inception* over unto good works as unto a *συναίτιον* of the justification of man, and confounded cause and effect (or the fruits of faith) with faith itself, as also the Jesuits take this phrase in the same sense and approve it, and understand faith as *charity-formed* — therefore, to avert the peril into which through equivocations we most easily fall, this phrase hath begun to be used more cautiously — yea, rather rightly to be wholly omitted — not however with any accusation of those who without deceit have used it rightly.

**LXIV.** We reject moreover the speculations and new opinions of those who feign that *we are just before God not by the actual righteousness of Christ, whereby He fulfilled the Law by His own obedience and innocence, but only by the passive righteousness of Christ, whereby He sustained passion, crucifixion, and death*. For these say that Christ, as man, performed the works of the Law for his own personal salvation and not for others, and that no one can perform the offices of piety in the place and name of others. Likewise they say that God is accused of tyranny if He simultaneously requireth both the *active* and the *passive* righteousness of Christ His Son for us, since the Law obligateth either unto obedience or unto punishment, and doth not obligate unto both simultaneously — therefore they imagine that Christ's *passive* obedience alone is imputed unto us, not the *active*.

But the response is not difficult, but plain, and by the benefit of God well-known unto boys rightly instructed. Namely: (1) Christ could not have sustained His passion and infringed and abolished the malediction of the Law unless He had by nature been God, just, perfect, innocent, and *ἀναμάρτητος*; nor would His *passive* righteousness have profited us anything, unless the *active* righteousness had been in Him in all numbers and parts, and *in solidum* most absolute and most perfect. (2) But Christ had that (as they call it) *active righteousness* not for the sake of His own person, or of private utility and salvation — since He could not but be, or be born, or live as *ἀναμάρτητος καὶ ἄμωμος, ἄσπιλος καὶ ἀνέγκλητος* — but for our use and commodity, we who believe in Him. As testify the faith and consolation of all the pious and rightly believing, kindled in their souls by the Holy Spirit and founded on the Word of God, which expressly nameth Christ *τέλος νόμου εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι* (Rom. 10), where the word *τέλος* signifieth both *consummation* and *perfection*, or *entire satisfaction, and both active and passive obedience*. For we are justified through Him who fulfilled the Law for us, made unto us of God *wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption* (1 Cor. 1). And Paul (Rom. 5) in the comparison of the offence or disobedience of Adam and the obedience of the Son of God — as by the disobedience of one he nameth not only the punishment, exile, and ejection from Paradise and the calamities which followed upon the fall of the first parents in the human race, but also *the very action and transgression, the fault and the violation of the divine mandate* — so also he nameth by the obedience of the one (whereby we are justified) not only the *passion and death*, but *innocence, integrity, action, and fulfilment of the Law* performed by Christ. And unless Paul be so understood, not only this comparison of Adam and Christ, or of *παρακοή and ὑπακοή*, plainly enervated and mutilated falleth to pieces; but also the whole doctrine of the justification of man before God is corrupted in many ways, and faith in Christ is diminished, and true and full consolation is taken from us, and again the opinion of our own dignity and virtue, or of inhering righteousness, is recalled from the shades, and doubting is confirmed in the minds of many, and the merit of Christ is extenuated — which now only in passing we may indicate, but which otherwhere we have determined more copiously to examine. (3) As to what pertaineth to the rule — *the Law obligateth either to obedience or to punishment* — this availeth in the political judgments of men and in the common life, and is not to be wrested unto sufficient reason why the Son of God for the sins of men did with His own *active and passive* obedience — or with the entire fulfilment of the whole Law — pay the debt, that there might be *περισσεία τῆς χάριτος*, superabounding grace, more copious and stronger than every sin, and that consciences terrified with their own unworthiness might have firm consolation and a sufficient satisfaction on every side in Christ. Nor for this is God accused of tyranny, but pious minds acknowledge the magnitude of the wrath of God, the atrocity of sin, the severity of justice, and the immense love of the Son of God toward us, and seek and find all their sufficiency in Christ, who fulfilled the Law *εἰς δικαιοσύνην παντὶ τῷ πιστεύοντι* — actively and passively — and give thanks to God for this salutary doctrine, and pray Him for the increase of their faith. ¹²⁸

**LXV.** These things then thus far having been commemorated concerning the justification of man before God — from which by certain [proofs] it is established that the *justifying righteousness* is nowhere else to be placed or sought than in the most perfect obedience of Christ — now unto the other part of our theses (which at the beginning we constituted) we shall add a brief admonition.

### I. On Renovation.

**LXVI.** *Vivification or renovation is no cause*, either total or partial, of *justifying righteousness*, but is the *effect, fruit, end, or consequence* of that righteousness — and yet is a part, beginning, earnest, and firstfruits of the future life, and in this life is always imperfect, and is not equal in all, but in one is more illustrious and greater, in others less conspicuous. For the *gifts* are not equal. But *grace* is equal, the same, and one — and continuous in all and upon all. And rightly we say that *no man is vivified unless he be justified* — not by reason of any interval or of time, but by the order which God hath instituted between cause and effect.

### II. That from the works of the Mosaic Law no one is justified.

**LXVII.** That no one is justified from the works of the Mosaic Law, Paul and the whole of Sacred Scripture categorically testify: *In Thy sight shall no man living be justified. There is none that doeth good, no not one — that is, there is none.* Likewise: *When ye have done all, say, "We are unprofitable servants."* And: *By grace ye are saved, not of works.* Titus 3: *Not by works which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us.* 2 Tim. 1: *Not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus.* And worthy of consideration is Bernard's word: *"It is needful first of all to believe that thou canst have no remission of sins except through the indulgence of God; then that thou canst have no good work, unless He also hath given this; last, that thou canst merit eternal life by no works unless it also be given freely."* ¹²⁹

**LXVIII.** Frigid and vain is the commentary of those who by the name of *Law and works* in Paul understand *only ceremonies*, and who will not that we are justified through Mosaic ceremonies, but think we are made just through the moral works. For that Paul understandeth not only ceremonies but the *works of the Decalogue*, this whole disputation of Rom. 2 showeth: *Thou that preachest a man should not steal, dost thou steal? Thou that sayest a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege? Thou that gloriest in the Law, through breaking the Law dishonourest thou God?* And Rom. 3 expressly saith: *By the works of the Law shall no flesh be justified in the sight of God — for by the Law is the knowledge of sin* (by ceremonies certainly there is no knowledge of sin). *But now without the Law* (which is not opposed to ceremonies, but to the righteousness of men, or to that which is by works, whereof David testifieth that no man is justified by them, since not even the father who believed in Abraham can glory of them before God, Rom. 4) *the righteousness of God is manifested, being witnessed by the Law* (of Moses) *and the Prophets — the righteousness, I say, of God through the faith of Jesus Christ, unto all and upon all them that believe, etc.* And Gal. 3: *Whosoever are of the works of the Law are under a curse. For it is written: "Cursed is every one that continueth not in all things which are written in the book of the Law, to do them." But that no man is justified by the Law in the sight of God is evident, for "The just shall live by faith." And the Law is not of faith — but "the man that doeth them shall live in them."*

**LXIX.** Rightly therefore *λογιζόμεθα* — that is, by a certain and infallible reckoning we gather and conclude — that *no man is justified before God by his own works, whether preceding, present, or subsequent, and that there are no preparatory works, or works following after faith, whereby we could stand in the sight of God*. And it is certain that *works of preparation* or *foreseen merits* (which some feign) can in no wise be reconciled with grace, since it is written Rom. 4: *Unto him that worketh, the reward is not imputed or numbered of grace but of debt.* And Rom. 3: *We are justified freely by His grace through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus.* And that which is alleged from Cornelius (Acts 10) by the Sophists — as if Cornelius by preparatory works and the force and efficacy of his *free will*, through his own religion, devotion, prayers, alms, and other virtues, before he believed in Christ, could apply himself as *worthy and prepared* unto the grace of God — is unworthy of refutation. Certainly *without faith no man can please God* (Heb. 11). And Cornelius, not only before he was baptised, but also before he certainly knew that the person of Jesus was the true Messiah, yet truly was *faithful and religious* — just as all those who believed in Christ to come. No man certainly can bring forth good fruits without faith.

### III. On the necessity of good works, and on the distinction of sins.

**LXX.–LXXIV.** [OCR page-break at pp. 182→183 of the 1579 imprint loses the numbered headers §§ LXX–LXXIV; the underlying content — reasons for the *necessity* of good works — is preserved in the surviving OCR text on the following page.] Wherefore, since good works are necessary — namely by the *grades of necessity* which above we recited — they are necessary also by the *necessity of divine mandate* (God commanding us to walk in His precepts); by the *necessity of the covenant of the new obedience* into which we are received in Baptism; by the *necessity of the fruit and witness of faith*, whereby faith is proved to be living and not dead; by the *necessity of avoiding punishments* (Ps. 39: *Thou dost correct men for their iniquities*); and by the *necessity of retaining faith and the Holy Spirit* which by grave sins against conscience are lost. And diligently also is the *dignity of works* to be considered, which Paul expresseth in these words, 1 Tim. 4: *Piety hath the promises of the present life and of that which is to come.*

**LXXV.** We do *not* say that good works are *necessary unto salvation*, because by this addition *"unto salvation"* is understood *merit*; and this phrase (which yet many pious and orthodox men outside of controversy have often used in a sound sense) is snatched as a *μῆλον ἔριδος* [apple of discord] to inflame public dissensions, to bear reproaches, and to establish Pelagian and Pontifical errors. But we say that *good works are necessary according to the grades of necessity which we have recited — and indeed necessary unto testifying and declaring salvation*. For many things are necessary unto something in their order and mode, which yet are not the *cause*. Some are necessary under the name of *cause* unto *obtaining* [salvation]; some then unto *apprehending* it; some unto *confirming* it; some (as are the good works of the justified) unto *testifying* it — necessarily. ¹³⁰

**LXXVI.** But to say absolutely that *good works are pernicious unto salvation* is pernicious — especially in a Church rightly instituted, in which good works are called the fruits of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of faith (Eph. 5). And it is certain that if the works are good, they are not pernicious; but if they are pernicious, they are not good — much less the fruits of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of faith. For we speak of the works of the *justified and regenerate*. Though it be added that *if confidence be placed in them* — as if we would be justified and stand before God by works — *they become pernicious* (as Luther in the context of his discourse truly so spoke) — yet the absurdity of the locution is manifest from this: that in the Church of Christ *good works pleasing God* are preached — not concerning Pharisees, hypocrites, and boasters of works, but concerning the justified and regenerate — who certainly do not place their confidence in works, but in the precious blood of Christ.

**LXXVII.** But whereas Paul saith Phil. 3: *Those things which were gain to me* (whilst still I was among the Pharisees and boasters of works) *those I have counted loss for Christ. Yea doubtless I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, for whom I have suffered the loss of all things and count them but dung, that I may win Christ and be found in Him — not having mine own righteousness which is of the Law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith, etc.* — Paul understandeth first *his Pharisaic works, which he had performed before he was converted unto Christ*; then he understandeth also *all works in general and in species outside of Christ*; afterward from the comparison of the righteousness of faith diametrically opposed to the righteousness of men, he casteth away from himself very far every confidence in works, and glorieth in the sole righteousness of Christ imputed unto him — as also Isaiah nameth *all our righteousnesses* as *imperfect, unclean, a defiled cloth, which before the tribunal of God the eyes of all abhor* — the comparison namely being instituted with the righteousness of the Son of God — as Augustine's celebrated dictum also testifieth: *"Human righteousness, compared with divine righteousness, is unrighteousness — because even a candle in darkness is beheld to shine, but placed in the rays of the Sun is darkened."* ¹³¹

**LXXVIII.** Let us consider Paul's grave sentence, Eph. 2: *We are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God hath prepared that we should walk in them.* And Phil. 2: *With fear and trembling work out your own salvation, κατεργάζεσθε.* For although we are saved freely in Christ alone apprehended by faith, and salvation is given us freely, yet by a certain way we come unto it — namely by traversing the course of an innocent and integrous life, when we contend by the way of righteousness unto salvation, led by the Spirit of the Son of God — through whom being justified we ought to walk in good works, and thus complete our salvation freely obtained for us and given. For the promised salvation, or eternal life, is given unto no one who *liveth in sins against conscience and finally persevereth*.

**LXXIX.** But as concerns the *distinction of sins*: it is established that all sins in the *non-regenerate* are *mortal*, according to that: *He that believeth not, the wrath of God abideth on him*. But in the regenerate there are, cleave to, and remain *serving sins* (or non-reigning, or venial) — as are *original evil, many defects, evil inclinations, evil affections, doubts, etc.* — which the regenerate resist with assiduous strife. But in the regenerate there are not *dominating sins*, or sins against conscience, or errors, or lapses. And when the saints fall into these, they are no longer *saints*, but lose faith and the Holy Spirit, and rush into eternal ruin unless they be converted — as David falling into homicide and adultery.

### IV. On the errors of the adversaries.

**LXXX.** The doctrine of justification and of good works being expounded, the errors and corruptions of the adversaries can easily be refuted — which arise either from words not understood — *Iustitia, Fides, Imputatio, Gratia* — as their use is in the doctrine of the Gospel; or from the *confusion of the doctrines of Law and Gospel*; likewise from the *confusion of cause and effect*; or from certain ill-wrested passages of Sacred Scripture, especially those which speak of *rewards and remunerations of good works*, when yet it is manifest that in Scripture the name of *reward* is received *consecutively, for recompense, and indeed for a constituted reward — but that reward gratuitous*. But the voice of *merit* used concerning our works is nowhere extant in the sacred letters.

**LXXXI.** Now we shall assign certain passages which are ineptly wrested to establish the righteousness of works before God.

**Sirach 16:** *"All mercy shall make a place for every man, according to the merit of his works."* — **I answer:** the Latin versicle hath been depraved. For it readeth: *πάσῃ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ποίησον τόπον, ἕκαστος γὰρ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ εὑρήσει* — that is, *offer a place to every good deed; for each one shall find according to his own works*.

Such is that of Heb. 13: *"Of beneficence and communication (κοινωνίας, as also Rom. 15: κοινωνίαν τινὰ ποιήσασθαι) be not forgetful — for with such hosts God is merited."* Here in the Greek there is *ἀρέσκεται* — that is, *He is delighted*. For it is *impossible without faith to please God ἀρεστῆσαι* (Heb. 11). Our sacrifices therefore — namely thanksgiving and beneficence — if they should be pleasing to God, must be the good fruits of a good tree.

But that the holy Fathers have sometimes used the word *merit* — they have done this from vulgar custom and *καταχρήσει*, confounding the words of *merit* and *reward*. But most rightly saith Augustine: *"God crowneth His own gifts in us, not our merits."* And: *"Let no one attribute the grace which God hath handed unto him — to the merits of his own works, or to the merits of his own prayers, or to the merits of his own faith."* And Bernard's word is most worthy of consideration: *"It sufficeth unto merit to know that no merit sufficeth."* Wherefore the Pontifical commentary about the *merit of congruity and of condignity* plainly collapseth. ¹³²

Often is read in the Scriptures: *"Unto each shall be rendered according to his works"* (Ps. 62, Prov. 24, Matt. 16, Rom. 2, 1 Cor. 3, Gal. 6, Apoc. 22). But this phrase is used sometimes *legally*, sometimes *Evangelically*. As in Ps. 62: *Unto Thee, O Lord, is mercy, for Thou renderest unto each according to his works* — that is, *Thou savest the believers freely, and subjectest the unbelieving unto eternal punishments*. And Rom. 2 there is described *faith as cause; good works as effect; eternal life as reward or wage, given freely indeed, and yet recompensing the obedience, cross, and labour of the believers*. For the words sound thus: *God will render to every man according to his works — namely the glory of good work, honour, and immortality* — to those, namely, who *καθ᾿ ὑπομονὴν ζητοῦσι ζωὴν αἰώνιον* — that is, who patiently seek eternal life; which cannot come to pass in any other way except through faith.

**Another. Ps. 106:** *"Phinehas stood up, etc. and it was imputed to him unto righteousness."* — See position 53 above.

**Prov. 17:** *"He who justifieth the wicked is an abomination before God."* — Here Solomon speaketh of *the absolution whereby impiety is disguised and excused before men*, and not of the gratuitous justification of man before God.

**Matt. 12:** *"By thy words thou shalt be justified, and by thy words thou shalt be condemned."* — Here Christ speaketh of *fruits*, as the preceding words testify: *How can ye speak good things, being evil? Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.* He saith therefore: *By thy words thou shalt be justified* — that is, *thou shalt be declared just, being previously made just*. For one thing is *to be made just*, another *to be declared just*. And so at Apoc. 22 the *δικαιώματα τῶν ἁγίων*, the *righteousnesses of the saints*, are those good works which are the testimonies of living faith.

**James 2:** *"By works a man is justified, and not by faith only."* — James speaketh not of the thing itself and of its causes (as Paul), but of the *declaration and approbation* of the thing. *He is justified* — that is, *is proved to be just, and from the effects is understood and declared to be justified*. Faith also James understandeth as *dead and vain*, of which the careless boast — not the *living* and *true* faith. And as the faith of the Church which invocateth God, and the faith of the Devil which fleeth God, differ, so the faith of which Paul speaketh, and the faith of which James discourseth, differ. What also the ancients determined concerning the whole Epistle of James, from Eusebius and Jerome is well established: many of whom called it *spurious and adulterine*, and Jerome saith it was *decorated with the name of James but written by another, and not received among the Scriptures, but only reckoned in*. It is certain however that James saith not that *we merit grace by good works*, but he speaketh of works *as of effects*, which show that faith is not *idle or dead, or only notitia* (such as the demons also have) or *bare profession* — but is *living and efficacious*, as Paul saith: *Faith working through charity*.

**Jer. 35:** *the works of the Rechabites are preached, and adorned with many promises*. The whole chapter of Jeremiah is a comparison between *the obedience which the Rechabites performed unto their father, and the obedience of the people unto the mandates of God*; and the Rechabites are preferred to the Jewish people, and nothing else is said than this: *the obedience of children toward parents is worthy of praise, and by many benefits and rewards in this life (for the promises made unto the Rechabites extend so far) is recompensed — how much more therefore obedience toward God.*

**Luke 7:** *"Her many sins are remitted her, for she loved much: unto whom little is remitted, the same loveth little."* — In these words is not shown the *cause* of the remission of sins, but rather from the consequent is gathered the antecedent. For *God first loved us when we were yet sinners*. And the order and context of the history showeth how the words of absolution of Christ are to be received. For Christ denieth that this woman — whom the Pharisee had with himself accused — was any longer a *manifest sinner*, since the sins of her prior life have been remitted her — which she herself proveth by this, that she followeth the remission of sins, namely by charity which she publicly testifieth.

**Daniel 4:** *"Redeem thy sins by alms."* **Tobit 4:** *"Alms delivereth from all sin and death."* — These and similar sentences speak only of *believers*. Therefore *thetic* sentences of this kind must be transferred unto their own *hypotheses*. And this is a customary *metonymy* whereby unto the *effect* is attributed what is proper to the *cause*.

**Luke 6:** *"Forgive, and it shall be forgiven unto you"* — that is, *use ye among yourselves Christian charity and equity in bearing and forgiving injuries*, as Joseph forgave his brothers, yea most excellently interpreted the matter, saying: *"Ye did not send me hither, but God."*

**Matt. 19:** *"If thou wilt enter into life, keep the commandments."* — This is the voice of the Law, to be interpreted according to the voice of the Gospel — or the *ταμιεία* [distinction] which the Gospel addeth.

**1 Cor. 13:** *"Though I have all faith, so that I could remove mountains, and have not charity, I am nothing."* — Paul is speaking properly of *the faith of miracle-workers*, or of *historical faith*; but he is not speaking of *justifying faith*, which by its nature can never be sundered from charity — as light from fire cannot be sundered — unless it be done *by hypothesis*, that is, by cogitation.

**Ibidem.** *"The greatest virtue among faith, hope, and charity is charity."* — Namely, not with respect to our justification in this life, but with respect to duration. Faith and hope shall cease; charity in all eternity shall burn — and even in this life is more conspicuous than faith and hope, which converse only with God, since love in the human society multipliciter poureth forth itself, and hath infinite offices.

**Col. 3:** *"Charity is the bond of perfection."* — Namely, in the whole body of the Church. For charity toward the neighbour is the *coupling and conjunction of many members of the Church among themselves*. Paul speaketh not of the personal perfection of individuals.

**1 Pet. 4:** *"Charity covereth a multitude of sins."* — Peter speaketh of *the condoning of the offences of others*, that we may cover the offences of others and repress the desire of vengeance.

**1 John 3:** *"He that loveth not, abideth in death."* — John speaketh of *love as effect and fruit of faith by which we are justified*. Chrysostom's sentence let me here inscribe: *οὐδὲν ὄφελος ἀγάπης πίστεως χωρίς, μᾶλλον δὲ οὐδ᾿ ἂν γένοιτο ἀγάπη ἡ ἑτέρα* — *"There is no profit in love without faith; nay rather the other cannot even exist without faith."* ¹³³

These passages, wrested to unstable the righteousness of faith, we have thought good to adduce in passing that the studious may be exercised.

**LXXXII.** The *boldness* of some is also to be disapproved who say that *good works give access unto the apprehension of grace*. For we have access and approach only through Christ, whom we apprehend by faith.

### Against the Papist *Doubting*.

**LXXXIII.** It is also to be lamented that the Monks and Pontificials were smitten with such blindness, that when they saw their own works to be *imperfect and insufficient* — such as they could not lean upon in the sight of and before the tribunal of God — they should have introduced *doubting* concerning the grace of God. This doubt is *diametrically repugnant and contradictory* unto the will and mandate of God commanding us to hear the Son, and it *extenuates and enervates* the merit of the Son of God, and *despoils* the Holy Spirit of His own virtue and efficacy, and *utterly destroyeth the minds of men*, and by a diabolical fury and satanic malice most maliciously casteth them into desperation and damnation. For we have the promises of the Son of God. We know what is the nature of faith. We know that the Holy Spirit is the *ἀρραβών*. We hear the doctrine of the Gospel. We have the true use of the Sacraments, which are the seals of faith. We know the distinction of Law and Gospel. We have exercises of penitence. We invoke God. We have peace with God, and are the Lord's — whether we live or whether we die. All these things testify — and openly pronounce — that *doubting concerning the grace of God is blasphemous and contumelious against God, against the Son of God, against the Holy Spirit, and against all Angels and blessed and believing men*. ¹³⁴

**LXXXIV.** The Pontificials object the saying of Solomon (Eccl. 9): *"Man knoweth not whether he be worthy of love or hatred."* — But this pertaineth not to the matter, since it speaketh of *external cases and events* and admonisheth that from these one is not to judge concerning the love or hatred of God toward us, since often *good things happen unto the evil and evil unto the good* in this life. Likewise, Sirach: *"Be not secure concerning a propitiated sin"* — where doctrine and paranesis is delivered concerning *not accumulating sins without penitence*, and confidence in sacrifices and *opus operatum* is reproved. Likewise the particles *Mi yodea* which are extant 2 Sam. 12, Joel 2, Jonah 3 — *"Let every one repent: who knoweth if perchance the Lord may turn, and pardon?"* — are not particles of a *doubting soul*, but of a *hoping* one, casting itself and all its affairs upon the mercy of God, and committing itself in bodily calamities to the divine will and protection, and asking of God help and deliverance. Other things which they object, I now pass over, since easily from what we have discoursed in the doctrine of justification they can be refuted.

### Closing Prayer and Christ-hymn against Heretics.

**LXXXV.** But I beseech the Son of God our Lord Jesus Christ, that He sanctify us all in His truth — that is, in His Word — and preserve us unto the glory and praise of His name, and unto our salvation and that of many. Unto Him with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the eternal, true, omnipotent, propitious, one and only God, be praise, honour, majesty, glory, and grace unto all eternity. Amen.

>

>

> O harbour, and Captain, and Head of Thy host.
>
> For us Thou didst shed Thy holy blood, O Christ,
> Not because we were worthy, but because Thou wast merciful.
> Made man a victim, now Thou governest all things supreme,
> Ruler — and in the highest throne Thou clothest our flesh.
>
> Look upon us; hear the groans and vows of the pious;
> Preserve the deep lights of Thy doctrine.
> Resist heretics, Satan, the world, and the furies;
> And be Thy glory great by Thy great hand.
>
> Christ God, be present unto us in the dregs of the world:
> Without Thee no quiet, without Thee no salvation. ¹³⁵
