## §10. DE BONIS OPERIBUS — On Good Works.

Now that we have discoursed concerning justification, penitence, and the kingdom of Christ, there must be added the doctrine of good works. And although out of what has been said this can be understood, yet separately in a few words it must be touched, that certain things may more perspicuously be expounded than could be done above.

He who wisheth to live in the kingdom of Christ, it behoveth him as a servant to know *what worships he ought to render unto his Lord*; that he so bear himself, lest by his own contumacy and improbity being conquered he be cast down from the kingdom of Christ. But of the doctrine of the worship of God, below in the explication of the Decalogue we shall speak. Now the general doctrine of good works I shall append — comprehended in these questions:

1. What works are to be taught and to be done.
2. How they may be done, and what things are required to the reasoning of a good work.
3. How they please God.
4. For what causes are they to be done, and why are promises added to good works.
5. What is the distinction of sins.
6. Of the words *merces* (reward) and *meritum* (merit).
7. That from works no man is justified before God — and why by works no man can be justified.
8. Whether and how far men before and after conversion can obey the Law of God.
9. Refutation of the arguments which the Pelagians and Pontificials advance concerning the *possibility* of the precepts of the divine Law.
10. What is the reasoning of the works of charity.
11. Of the calling of all Christians and of each one, and of the good conscience.

### Q1 — What works are to be done?

The response is extant Ezek. 20: *Walk ye in my precepts, saith the Lord.* And Ps. 119: *Thy Word is a lamp unto my feet.* Likewise: *In vain do they worship me by the mandates of men.* For by no means does the human mind in this corruption of nature understand what either pleaseth or displeaseth God. It must therefore be thought that *only that pleaseth God which He Himself, as the Lord our God and the sole Legislator, hath prescribed unto us in the Word of the Law and of the Gospel*. And this true and perpetual rule remaineth in the Church: **No works are to be reckoned good unless those which are commanded by God.** All fictitious worships therefore, all monastic vows destitute of the Word of God, *ἐθελοθρησκείαι*, and works which they call *of supererogation*, are of no moment, but are plainly rejected by God as *idolatrous and useless*, without exception — according to the evident demonstration: *In vain do they worship me by the mandates of men.* Likewise, *Nothing pleaseth God without faith*. But faith resteth upon the Word, mandate, and promise of God.

### Q2 — How can good works be done?

The response is extant Heb. 11: *Without faith it is impossible to please God.* Likewise: *Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.* And Christ saith: *Without me ye can do nothing.* Rightly then and piously is it said that unto the reasoning of a good work **five things** are required:

1. **The precept.**
2. **The Spirit of Christ.**
3. **Faith.**
4. **A true end.**
5. **Grace.**

Without these, a work done by man can in no way be called *good* before God. The **precept** is beheld in these four things:

- In our *condition* — for we are servants and debtors.
- In the *mandate* — Ezek. 20.
- In the *prohibition* — Deut. 12: *Ye shall not do what seemeth right in your own eyes.*
- In the *reason of divine worship*, which is: that the work which ought to please must be *commanded in the Word of God*. For every *ἐθελοθρησκεία* is damned (Col. 2).

Of the **Spirit of Christ** it is written, Rom. 8: *As many as are led by the Spirit of God, they are sons of God. But if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is not His.*

Of **faith** is extant the saying already often cited: *Impossible it is to please God without faith.* And: *Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.* For there can be no love or obedience unless first mercy and reconciliation have been apprehended by faith because of the Mediator.

Of the **end** it is written, 1 Cor. 10: *Do all things unto the glory of God.* 1 Cor. 14: *unto the edification of the Church.*

Of **grace** it is written, Ps. 32: *Blessed are those whose iniquities are remitted and whose sins are covered.* And Rom. 8: *There is now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.* For although the man justified by faith doth not perform perfect obedience to the Law, and hath only the firstfruits of the Spirit in this life, yet (as a little below shall be said) *his works please God — and what is in them of sin, grace covereth with the covering of the obedience of Christ*.

**On the works and virtues of the Gentiles**, when asked: it is certain that by the judgment of understanding reason (which perceiveth the distinction of things honest and shameful) and by the counsel of conscience the study of discipline hath cultivated these, and that they have had honest external morals — and often too were pre-eminent in heroic motions — as a testimony:

1. That God preserveth in human nature the judgment of reason and the distinction of honest and shameful things.
2. That discipline is necessary in the human race.
3. That God willeth human society to grow with virtue, and that those who neglect virtue and draw punishments upon themselves are *inexcusable*.
4. That God willeth the citizens of His Church to be *studious and doers of the obedience of the Law with such great diligence* that, beholding the virtues of the Gentiles, they may know they ought to surpass them by their own piety — and are therefore endowed with the Holy Spirit that they may leave the Gentiles behind them at a long interval.

### Q3 — How good works please God.

The response is extant 1 Pet. 2: *Offer spiritual sacrifices accepted of God through Christ.* Named as *spiritual sacrifices* are: the *contrite spirit*, the *sacrifice of righteousness*, the *sacrifice of praise* or *the calves of the lips confessing the name of God*, the *hosts of beneficence and communion* in which God is delighted, and the *rational host of our own bodies* — and finally *all our obedience which God requireth of us*. And this rule is to be held: **The person pleasing, the work pleaseth. The person displeasing, the work displeaseth.** The person pleaseth if reconciled by faith and just for the sake of Christ freely — not for the dignity of the person. And although this same person justified by faith cannot yet satisfy the divine Law — according to that saying, *Even innocent before Thee, he is not innocent*; likewise, *For this shall every saint pray unto Thee: enter not into judgment with Thy servant*; *Unto Thee, O Lord, is righteousness; unto us confusion of face* — yet God demandeth the *incepted obedience*, and affirmeth that this pleaseth Him *by faith because of Christ*. Scipio's works please not, howsoever magnificent and splendid — because Scipio was not converted, though those works were honest. For the person not pleasing (not reconciled by faith in Christ), even a praiseworthy work of the judgment of human reason cannot please God. But David's warfare pleased God, because David by faith was reconciled and accepted by God.

### Q4 — Why good works are to be done, and why promises are added to good works.

Often it is asked, since good works neither justify nor save, why they should be done. First, let us know that good works are **simply necessary**, and let us not be so foolish, ungrateful, and contumacious as to deny that new obedience is necessary. For this is the eternal and unmoved sentence: *those who live in sins against conscience — as long as they persevere in them — are not in the grace of God, nor can be saved unless they be converted.* For we speak of the obedience *which followeth conversion or regeneration*. Truly horrid it is to hear said in the Church of Christ that good works are not a debt or are not necessary. Two arguments of those who deny the necessity of works are chief:

**Argument 1:** *Obedience ought to be spontaneous and free. Therefore it is not a debt.* — **Response** to the antecedent: If obedience ought to be spontaneous, therefore it *is* a debt, *because it ought to be spontaneous*. Further, to be *spontaneous or free* is not opposed to *debt or necessary*. For even *spontaneous obedience is commanded and is necessary* — as *Christian liberty*, although it is liberty, is yet necessary. Obedience must be voluntary and spontaneous, and yet it is a mandate. Afterward, unto the voice of *debt* or of *necessity* by no means is understood *coaction*, or obedience extorted by fear (as some ineptly interpret) — but these two words, *debitum* and *necessarium*, signify *the divine and immutable order* whereby the rational creature is subject unto God the Creator and willingly obeyeth Him.

**Argument 2:** *Good works, if confidence be placed in them, as if they had a force of justifying and saving, are noxious unto salvation. Therefore they must not be said to be necessary.* — **Response:** *Necessary* and *noxious* are not at all opposed. And even if the antecedent — with the condition of confidence added — be plainly true, yet the divine order remaineth: that the rational creature render obedience to the Creator both *freely and necessarily*. And that voice *to be noxious* by no means can be attributed to good works *per se*, especially of the regenerate. For the justified and regenerate themselves know that they *cannot and ought not lean upon their own works*, even though they are bound to perform them. Further, good works in the justified and regenerate are *the fruits of righteousness through Christ*, and are done unto the glory and praise of God (Phil. 1), and are the fruits of the Holy Spirit (Gal. 5).

These things concerning the words *necessary* and *debt* being indicated, why good works are to be done can easily be judged. And these are the **causes**:

1. **The necessity of the mandate**, which all rational creatures ought to obey.
2. **The necessity of debt** (Rom. 8).
3. **The necessity of conversion or regeneration**, whose *formale* is the inception of new obedience.
4. **The necessity of not losing faith**, which — together with the Holy Spirit — is expelled by sins against conscience.
5. **The necessity of avoiding punishments.**
6. **The dignity of works**, as it is written 1 Tim. 4: *Piety hath the promises of the present life and of the life to come*; and Luke 14: *It shall be recompensed unto thee in the resurrection of the just.* For out of His immense goodness and grace — and not out of debt — God deigneth to compensate our works, though they proceed from faith and though they be imperfect and defiled with the filth of many sins, *with recompense, reward, and paternal retribution* — as a pious father approveth and rewardeth whatsoever kind of obedience of his son. But by this goodness of God the pious are not puffed up: they acknowledge their own unworthiness and admire and preach the mercy of the most clement Father in heaven — confessing that nothing is owed unto them for their due works: as at Matt. 25, the elect wish not to recognize the dignity of their own works, even though the Son of God Himself before the Angels and all men celebrateth them, but they say: *Lord, when saw we Thee hungering, thirsting, naked, and we fed, and gave drink, and clothed Thee?* And Apoc. 4: the elders cast their crowns before the throne and say: *Thou, O Lord our God, art worthy to receive glory and honour* — that is (as Daniel saith), *Unto Thee, O Lord, is righteousness; unto us confusion of face.* When therefore God promiseth *remuneration*, let us do two things: let us acknowledge the unworthiness and imperfection of our work; then, relying on the goodness of God — not on the dignity of the work — let us establish God as veracious in His promises.

As the **Pontificials** are to be damned who say that *by good works they merit eternal life* — against the saying of Paul, *The gift of God is eternal life* (Rom. 6) — so on the other side are to be rejected the sleights and opinions of the **Antinomians** who clamour that *new obedience is not necessary or a debt*, and that the *Law of God, customarily named the Decalogue*, is not to be preached in the Church of Christ. Now — that we may add this too — as concerneth the proposition *"good works are necessary unto salvation"*: though from the sentence of Brenz and of others rightly teaching, who have used it, it is sufficiently established that they wished by no means to attribute any merit of salvation and eternal life to works, but to speak of *the order of obedience and of the testimony whereby internal faith is proved* — yet we retain the words and sentence of D. Philip, who thus saith concerning that proposition: *"We do not use these words, 'Good works are necessary unto salvation,' because by this addition — 'unto salvation' — merit is understood."* ¹⁵⁷

The **causes** for which God hath added promises to good works are rightly recited as these **five (or six)**:

1. That they may be *testimonies of the providence of God*.
2. That they may be *testimonies that God will preserve the Church even in this life* — whence 1 Tim. 4: *Piety hath the promises of the present life and of that to come.*
3. Because God willeth *even bodily necessity to be an admonition unto faith, invocation, hope, thanksgiving* — and He wisheth these goods to be asked by faith and expected through patience.
4. That they may be *admonitions concerning the promise of grace*. For corporeal benefits are, unto the faithful, *seals of grace*.
5. Because God willeth *both to happen* — that the Church be subject to the cross, and yet in these very perils be preserved. Both are indicated Isa. 37: *Lord our God, save us from the hand of Sennacherib, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that Thou alone art Lord.*
6. To these five it pleaseth me to add a sixth: *a testimony that another and eternal life remaineth, in which freely there shall be the compensation of all the pious zeals, works, and labours*. For the world is ungrateful, and many things are done by the pious which the world acknowledgeth not — much less doth it adorn them with any gratitude — nay, often it is not worthy of the praise of compensation and gratitude offered. Many things therefore there are which God layeth aside and reserveth, gathereth and guardeth — to be produced and displayed and adorned *on the last day and in eternal life*, in which the Doctors shall shine as the splendour of the Sun and as the stars unto all eternity (Dan. 12).

### Q5 — What is the distinction of sins.

Always in the doctrine of good works these **three things** are to be regarded:

1. First it must be established that the *person is reconciled by faith and freely just for the sake of Christ, not for the dignity of the person*.
2. Second, it must be confessed that the *person even justified by faith cannot yet satisfy the divine Law*, but that sins remain even in the regenerate — which must be acknowledged and deplored. For always must it be said: *Remit unto us our debts. Who understandeth his offences? The just falleth seven times a day. Enter not into judgment with Thy servant. In Thy sight shall no living man be justified.*
3. Third, at the same time it must be established that *God demandeth also the incepted obedience, and that this pleaseth Him by faith for the sake of Christ — not for the dignity or perfection of the work*.

Since it is established that many sins remain in the regenerate, the question is asked of the *distinction of sins*. For those who rush into errors and crimes, and live in sins against conscience, *lose faith and the Holy Spirit*. Rightly therefore is the distinction thus delivered: **Sins are twofold.** Some are committed by those *knowing and willing, against conscience*. Those who do these entirely cast off faith, shake off the Holy Spirit, and become guilty of the wrath of God — and unless they do penitence, rush into eternal punishments. And hither are to be referred also those *who defect from the foundation* — that is, wrench away some article of faith and allow themselves to be deceived by trickeries — as Arius, Manes, Servetus, Karlstadt, and similar heretics. Of all these it is written, Gal. 5: *They that do such things shall not possess the kingdom of God.*

**Other sins are venial**, which are not committed against conscience — as *darkness of understanding, doubt, many vicious affections, sins of oblivion and omission, interior uncleanness*. Though these be horrid and atrocious evils because of which man by nature is *son of the wrath of God* (as Paul speaks), yet the saints know these are remitted them through and for the sake of the Son, and *they resist them* — nay, grieve as often as they feel the inordinate flames — as Paul crieth out: *O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death?* And they daily ask that their sins and interior uncleanness be remitted them for the sake of the Son the Mediator, and they study to retain *good conscience, warring the good warfare* — and certainly know that *faith and the Holy Spirit cannot stand with an evil intent against conscience*.

Let me add also this admonition: **Sinners are threefold**: (a) some who *indulge sins even against conscience* — as heretics, tyrants, Epicureans, criminals; (b) others *hypocrites, honest before the world, but before God impious because of confidence and arrogance*; (c) others *who do penitence* — as the Publican, David, Manasses, the thief, Paul, and all the converted in every age, whom Christ seeketh, calleth, receiveth, cares for, cherisheth, and healeth (Luke 15).

And there are **three errors** in the Church to be fled:

- **The first**: that those once converted *cannot henceforth shake off the Holy Spirit or be damned, whatever they do*.
- **The second**: that those once fallen *cannot be received back* (so said the Novatians and Cathars).
- **The third**: that we *cannot be certain of the grace of God and the remission of sins* — as the adversaries, uncertain of their own salvation, have taught.

To the **first error** let us oppose the examples of David, Solomon, Peter, and others who have both fallen, and by enormous sins lost the Holy Spirit and faith, and unless they had done penitence would have rushed into eternal punishments. Therefore David saith: *Restore unto me the joy of Thy salvation.* And Paul (1 Cor. 10): *Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.*

To the **second error** let us oppose the examples of the same men — of Adam, David, Manasses, Peter, the thief, and of countless others. For it is written: *As I live, I will not the death of a sinner, but that he be converted and live.* Apoc. 2: *Remember whence thou hast fallen, and do penitence, and do the first works.* Luke 15: *There is joy among the Angels over one sinner doing penitence.*

Now what is written in Heb. 6 — *"It is impossible for those who once have been enlightened, and have tasted also of the heavenly gift, and have been made partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted nevertheless the good Word of God and the virtues of the age to come, and have fallen away, again to be renewed unto penitence, since they crucify unto themselves again the Son of God"* — this is all to be received *of universal apostasy and of final impenitence and unbelief*, not of any special sin. For such cannot be renewed who crucify Christ afresh and hold Him for a mockery — that is, who no longer hearken unto the Gospel but despise it, nor study to retain the doctrine of the beginnings of piety, namely of Baptism and of penitence. For this is the sin *against the Holy Spirit* and *unto death*, which is not remitted, since it is *final unbelief and impenitence*. Likewise rightly is that of Heb. 10 to be understood: *"To us sinning voluntarily after the received knowledge of the truth, there is no longer left a host for sins"* — namely, no other beside the benefit of Christ. For it is the comparison of Law and Gospel. In the Law there were frequent expiations of uncleanness; in the Gospel new sacrifices are not to be feigned, but there is only *one host*. But of these things in passing.

To the **third error** let us oppose the whole doctrine of the justification of man before God — of faith and firm confidence, of the grace of God, of the promise, of the satisfaction and merit of the Son — of which above hath been said.

### Q6 — On the words *merces* (reward) and *meritum* (merit).

The word *merces* is used for the *compensation of an office or of a labour, owed as a debt* (Rom. 4): *Unto him that worketh, the reward is imputed, not according to grace, but of debt.* Of this signification here in the doctrine of good works — which are fruits of faith and pertain not to the *efficient causes* of justification but to its *effect* — we do not speak. For God oweth us nothing for our imperfect and slender works; and whatsoever He promiseth or requiteth, He doeth not out of any debt or *de condigno* (as in the following question we shall say more amply), but out of *paternal charity and gratuitous benignity*. The word *merces* therefore in the doctrine of good works signifieth *not a debt but plainly a gratuitous reward for some office or labour due*. This *merces* fighteth not with the *gratuitous donation of eternal life*. For both is the *inheritance gratuitous* — and simultaneously is *the compensation of the due labours of the sons*. And the father of the family promiseth his son or servant and giveth him something as a *not-owed prize* for a due labour. Rightly it is customarily said that *eternal life is called reward consecutively*, because though it fall out because of another cause (namely, because we are sons of God, beloved in the Beloved, made and refreshed by God), yet He compensateth out of *mere grace and unowed benignity* our due labours, afflictions, and good works. In vain, therefore, do the Scholastics dream up a mutual relation of *merit and reward*. Moreover Luke 6 nameth *χάριν* [grace] what Matt. 5 had called *μισθόν* [reward]: *"If ye love those who love you, what reward shall ye have?"* — Luke: *ποία ὑμῖν χάρις ἐστί, what grace shall be yours?*

Of the word **Meritum** we shall admonish a little below — which is *nowhere used in the sacred letters* for a certain work by which we merit anything from God, as also we have shown in the theses on justification above. Let us observe Bernard's saying: *"Our merits are the way of the kingdom, not the cause of reigning"* — that is, they are works pleasing to God which God requireth of the saints, but they are *not the cause of justification, or of salvation, or of eternal life*. ¹⁵⁸

### Q7 — That no man is justified by works before God; and why not.

The whole doctrine of the Gospel manifestly showeth that *all the spiritual goods which pertain to salvation and eternal glory depend upon the grace of God*, and are given unto us out of the sole good purpose of God through and for the sake of the Son, *without our works or merits*. For the *grace of God* and *works or merits of men* the Sacred Scripture taketh as *contraries and opposites* — as Rom. 11: *If by grace, then no more of works — since grace is no more grace. And on the other hand: if of works, then no more of grace — since work is no more work.* Eph. 2: *By grace ye are saved through faith, and that not of yourselves nor of works, lest any man should boast.* Titus 3: *Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He hath saved us — that, being justified by His grace, we may be made heirs.*

Now let us briefly examine and overturn the opinions of those who acceptably refer part of salvation unto our own merits.

**First Opinion.** *"Christ hath merited for us the first grace, without any merit of ours. But this first grace is the beginning of merit, the foundation and as it were the efficient cause — so that the good works which are afterward done by the man are not only pleasing and accepted of God, but are moreover meritorious, and are as it were the effects of the first grace. For the first grace is conferred without the works of the Law; but when the man is regenerated, his works — since they are fruits of the Holy Spirit, and His gift and operation (Eph. 5) — merit the glory of righteousness before God unto eternal life."*

**Response.** This is the chief contention of the Pontificials today — namely *that the newness which Paul himself Rom. 6 calleth righteousness, and which the Holy Spirit worketh in the believers, meriteth righteousness, life, and eternal salvation*. And though it be true that the man pleaseth God whom once He hath deigned with His grace, and that his good works are grateful to God and are recompensed by God with reward — yet God regardeth these not *because of themselves*. For as long as the person is not reconciled to God, so long the works cannot be accepted of God. But after the reconciliation of the person, works please God — not because *per se, for their own sake*, they are grateful to God, but because *the person is reconciled through and for the sake of Christ*. And yet the works even of a person reconciled and regenerate are by no means that thing whereby one could stand in the judgment of God so as not to be damned, and *because of which* God is placated and made propitious. For Paul (Rom. 4) of Abraham reconciled and regenerate — and adorned with many most excellent virtues — manifestly from Moses showeth *that Abraham was justified not by those good works which regenerate he himself did by faith, but simply justified by faith*, as these terms prove: *unto him that worketh not, but believeth in Him that justifieth the ungodly, faith is imputed for righteousness*. And: *If Abraham was justified by works, he may indeed have glory before men, but not before God.* And, lest anyone infer that Abraham is a singular person and that the universal rule of justification cannot be built from him, Paul calleth Abraham *the father of faith* and setteth him forth as a universal exemplar of true justification before God, saying: *Abraham is the father of all believers, both among the Jews and among the Gentiles* — that is (as himself speaketh), *in circumcision and in uncircumcision*. And again: *It is not written only for Abraham's sake that it was reputed unto him for righteousness, but also for our sake, unto whom it shall be reputed as we believe.*

Let this also be diligently considered by pious minds: if any man saith that Christ hath merited for us the first grace, but that we ourselves ought to merit some spiritual goods that follow it by our own works, that man plainly *separateth himself from Christ*, despiseth the grace of God and the dignity of the merit of Christ, and *not only conjoineth his own merits with the merit of Christ but also prefereth them, ascribing more virtue and efficacy to them than to Christ's merit*. Let us always consider the voice of the Son of God, Luke 17, which He said not to unbelievers or unprofitable servants but to His sanctified and regenerate disciples: *When ye have done all, say, We are unprofitable servants.* And Paul, Phil. 3, in the article of justification calleth his own works even after his regeneration *σκύβαλα, dung and detriments*. As at Isa. 64, *all our righteousnesses are said to be as a defiled cloth*. Whence Luther most gravely saith: *"Unless God avert His eyes not only from our sins but also from our virtues, we shall not be saved."* ¹⁵⁹

**Second Opinion.** *"We are justified by faith indeed — but by faith formed through charity, which God infuseth, and which is a righteousness inhering in us."*

**Response.** First we say that *faith is not alone or idle or dead*, but bringeth forth manifold fruits and hath most copious effects — *charity and many other virtues, or gifts of God inhering in us*. But these effects we deny to be the *cause of justification*. For **cause must be distinguished from effect**. The true cause of justification is: *first the impulsive*, namely the very obedience, satisfaction, or merit of Christ, or the very redemption, the fulfilment of the Law, the passion, death, blood, crucifixion, and resurrection of Christ. Then *the formal cause* is the very favour, or acceptation, or mercy of God remitting our sins and imputing unto us the righteousness or obedience of the Son. *The instrumental cause* is faith, or the confidence of the obedience of Christ, which the prophet Isaiah (53) nameth *scientia* and Paul nameth *sapientia*. What remaineth is *effect* — namely that a man henceforth is led by the Holy Spirit, liveth piously, and rendereth acceptable worships to God, and doth good to his neighbour.

Secondly, we inquire: on what may we lean, standing before the tribunal of God? In the whole doctrine of the Gospel we find that this prop is nothing other than *the merit of Christ*, for which the Father imputeth not unto believers their sins — and is not an *infusion of charity*, or any virtue inhering in us.

Thirdly, if *justifying faith* were understood of our quality or work in us, then also the *form of faith* which they establish as charity could obtain this praise — that it maketh us just. But the whole doctrine of the Gospel showeth that *we are justified before God without works*; but to *faith* is attributed the justification as unto an *instrumental cause*, whereby we apprehend the merit, satisfaction, and obedience of Christ.

Fourthly, *charity or inhering righteousness, or the new obedience which we have through the Holy Spirit* — although it lacketh not its own most ample commendations and certain and great rewards — yet since in this life it is imperfect because of the flesh, and yet many-modedly unclean, and is manifoldly contaminated (so that in the believers there is a perpetual strife of the flesh and the Spirit) — certainly this new obedience *cannot so stand in the judgment of God* that through and for its sake we could truly determine ourselves absolved from the sentence of damnation. For we have need before the tribunal of God of a *perfect and absolute righteousness*, which the Scripture showeth us to be *in the merit of Christ the Mediator*, provided only that we apprehend Him by faith — as it is written: *As many as received Him, unto them gave He power to be made sons of God, who believe on His name.*

**Third Opinion.** *"There is a distinction between* meritum de congruo *and* meritum de condigno. *The former is when a man of his own arbitrament doth things whereby it is fitting and just that God should be moved to do good in his turn — as even a Gentile can do good by his own powers and merit the grace and benefits of God. The latter — meritum de condigno — is when a man endowed with grace and the Holy Spirit meriteth by his works eternal life de condigno."*

**Response.** First, the studious must be admonished concerning the *word Merit* — that *it is nowhere extant in the sacred letters*. For what is brought forth from Sirach 16 is (as we have shown in the theses) to be rendered otherwise from the Greek: *πάσῃ ἐλεημοσύνῃ ποίησον τόπον, ἕκαστος γὰρ κατὰ τὰ ἔργα αὐτοῦ εὑρήσει* — *"Give a place to every beneficence; for each one according to his own works shall find."* And Heb. 13: *"With such hosts of beneficence God is merited"* — in the Greek is read *ἀρέσκεται ὁ θεός*, *God is delighted*. And that it be lawful (as the Pontificials think) to use the word *merit* with the same reasoning by which we use the word *reward* is plainly absurd. For great is the distinction: **merces** in general signifieth *what is given to any man after a work performed, whether much or little, and whether corresponding to the labour or not*, and often is used of *blessing and gratuitous benefit* — as Ps. 127: *The fruit of the womb is a reward from the Lord*; Gen. 15: *I shall be thy exceedingly great reward*. **Meritum**, on the other hand, *establisheth an equality between labour and reward*, and therefore is called by Paul *merces secundum debitum*. And this distinction is manifestly beheld in the parable, Matt. 20, where all who labour in the vineyard alike receive their reward — as much they who laboured least as those who laboured most. That the holy Fathers have often used the word *merit* — this they did by *vulgar usage καταχρηστικῶς [by abuse]*, and *confounded the words merit and reward* — not imagining that from that usage would afterward arise such gross errors concerning the dignity of human works as afterward arose.

Secondly, as concerneth **meritum de congruo** — by which profane persons imagine that an impious or Gentile man, when he giveth himself to good works, meriteth by his own diligence that God should benignly regard him — all this is prostrated by that one Pauline axiom, Rom. 14: *Whatsoever is not of faith is sin.* And Heb. 11: *Without faith it is impossible to please God.* Likewise Matt. 7: *A bad tree cannot bring forth good fruits.* For since even the works of the regenerate are not said to merit the grace of God *de congruo*, much less can the works of the non-regenerate do that.

Thirdly, as concerneth the **works of the Gentiles or unbelievers**: although these are in themselves good, insofar as they agree with the first creation and with the norm of the divine Law, yet they are so *wounded, polluted, and vitiated* that they become sins before God — by reason of the *old man* not yet reconciled to God, and still destitute of the Holy Spirit; and by reason of the *end*, since indeed all things which are undertaken and done are *not* referred unto the glory of the true God.

Fourthly, as concerneth **Cornelius** (Acts 10): he certainly had *faith in Christ*, and by faith came unto the works which pleased God. And Bede saith on that place: *"Not by virtues unto faith, but by faith are we brought unto virtues. For Cornelius — whose alms even before Baptism were praised by the Angel — came not by works unto faith, but by faith unto works."*

Fifthly, since from these things it is established that there is *no meritum de congruo*, it followeth also that there is *no meritum de condigno*. For Paul refuteth this fantasy in one saying, Rom. 6, where he calleth *eternal life a gift through Jesus Christ*. And let pious minds consider how great is the temerity, impiety, and ingratitude toward the merit of the Son of God, to say that unto us wretched sinners — who always ought to have in heart and mouth that word *"Remit unto us our debts"* — unto us, I say, by right and *de condigno* the celestial glory is owed: *we*, who are not sons of God by right and by nature, but who receive the inheritance *freely as adopted sons*. If we have merited anything *de condigno*, certainly we have merited *wrath, death, and damnation*, according to that saying: *The wages of sin is death* (Rom. 6). And Ps. 130: *If Thou, Lord, wilt mark iniquities, Lord, who shall stand?* Likewise Ps. 143: *Enter not into judgment with Thy servant; because in Thy sight no living one shall be justified.*

Together with this error concerning merit *de congruo* and *de condigno* there fall also the other contumelious portents of opinion against the Son of God and against the mandates of the divine Law — as are the *figments concerning the works of supererogation*; likewise concerning the *efficacy of the merits of a man in grace, as if he could merit spiritual goods not only for himself but also for others*; likewise concerning the *participation of merits* accommodated not only to the living but also to the dead who have departed from this life. These are unworthy of prolix refutation. Only for the sake of the younger ones we shall indicate:

**Works of supererogation** the Monks and Sacrificers named those which are *not commanded in the Decalogue but excogitated and chosen by men out of spontaneous will* — as it were superadded to the Law of God, and so holy and pleasing to God that they merit the remission of sins and eternal life. Such are *the monastic life, Franciscan poverty, Origenic chastity, abstinence from certain foods, sleeping on the ground, clothing and manner sordid and troublesome to the body, difficult pilgrimages*, and similar observations which they called *rules of the Orders*. All these are *Pharisaic and hypocritical*, and are prostrated by the one voice of the Son of God: *In vain do they worship me by the mandates of men* (Matt. 15). Likewise: *The kingdom of God cometh not with observation* (Luke 17). And what is it to condemn the Law as *imperfect*, if not this — as if something worthy could be *added* unto the Law of God? God Himself certainly is accused of negligence, as if He had omitted many notable works. Insolent arrogance is presumed. Others who do not such things are contemned, as if they were not so holy and pleasing unto God.

As concerneth the **efficacy of the merits of a man constituted in grace** and the argument that *the prayer of a pious man obtaineth healing and other gifts for those for whom it is made* (Matt. 9), and *prayer is a work; therefore some works can merit spiritual goods for others* — the response is: *The prayer of a pious man is not heard because of the quality or dignity of the one praying, but simply because of the benignity and mercy of Him who is invoked, and because of the excellence of Him in whose name the prayer is made, who Himself saith, "Whatsoever ye shall ask the Father in my name, He will give it you"* (John 15). *"Let no one say that the grace given him hath been handed unto him by the merits of his own prayers,"* saith Augustine. God heareth the prayer — not by reason of *opus operatum* or of merit — but by reason of *His own mandate and of His own promise*, that He wisheth *for the sake of His natural Son* clemently to hear the prayers of the adopted sons.

*The just liveth by his own faith* (Hab. 2). Rightly it is customarily said: *"The intercession of others profiteth not without the man's own conversion unto God"* — as the prayer of Jeremiah profited not king Zedekiah the hypocrite. And *another's faith* effecteth no more than the care of a faithful physician can in healing a sick man. The physician can communicate nothing of his own health to the sick, but strenuously plieth his work that the sick may recover. In the same reasoning *another's faith* urgeth with God that the sinner may be converted — as Monica prayed for her son Augustine still a Manichaean and heard from the Bishop: *"Go, for it is impossible that the son of so many tears should perish."* And the paralytic (Matt. 9) by no means lacked his own faith. From these things it can easily be concluded that *another's faith and works profit no man, unless he himself study to have his own faith and piety* — as Paul saith (Rom. 14): *Each of us shall render account to God for himself*. And Matt. 25: *Those virgins are turned away as foolish whose lamps lack their own oil.*

Since another's works profit not the living, *much less can they be accommodated to the dead*. For *from the shades there is no redemption*. And Jerome saith: *"So long as we are in the present age, we can aid you by counsels or by prayers; but when we shall come before the tribunal of Christ, neither Job nor Daniel nor Noah can pray for anyone, but each shall bear his own burden."* Diabolical, therefore, are the visions and apparitions of the dead asking intercession, whereby both idolatrous worships have been confirmed and the bellies of the Monks fattened — with the added most foul lies concerning purgatory and the liberation of souls from purgatory and infernal pains, as they feigned that Trajan the emperor was delivered thence by the merits of blessed Gregory. ¹⁶⁰

### Q7-b — Why no man is justified by works.

**The first reason** is the *efficient cause* — the reason of the glory of God and of our own humble and due confession. For good works, if any we do, are *not ours but of God working in us* — unto whom all good must be referred with acceptance. As John 15: *Without me ye can do nothing.* And 2 Cor. 3: *Our sufficiency is from God.* And 1 Cor. 4: *What hast thou which thou didst not receive? And if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory?* Likewise: *He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord* (1 Cor. 1). Phil. 2: *God worketh in us both to will and to do*. The Church chanteth: *Without Thy divinity nothing is in man, nothing innocent*. And the Son of God saith Luke 18: *No one is good but God* — that is, *God alone is the author, fountain, gushing-source, and giver of all good*:

> *Quod caelum, quod terra bonum, quod pontus et aër*
> *Possidet, à Domino, non aliunde, venit.*
> *Grata igitur mens est, quae se debere fatetur*
> *Quicquid habet, quicquid possidet, omne Deo.*

*(Whatever good the sky, the earth, the sea, and the air possess, cometh from the Lord, not elsewhere. Grateful therefore is the mind which confesseth to owe whatever it hath, whatever it possesseth, all unto God.)*

**The second reason** is placed in the *order*. Man can perform no work pleasing to God unless he first be reconciled to God by faith in Christ. For the work pleaseth not sooner than the person pleaseth; and the fruits are not called good before the tree be good (Matt. 7). Works therefore, since they follow faith and are its fruits or effects, cannot be the *cause* of justification.

**The third reason** is the *condition of our works*. For all good works — even of the regenerate — are on the part of man imperfect, and never fully answer the divine Law, but are hindered by manifold confusion of affections, and never *outweigh sins* — as the wrestling of the pious testifies, who daily say with Paul (Rom. 7): *The Law is spiritual, but I am carnal.* And Isa. 64: *All our righteousnesses are as an unclean cloth before God.* And Dan. 9: *Unto Thee, O Lord, is righteousness; unto us confusion of face.* Wherefore Christ teacheth us to say: *When we shall have done all that is commanded us, still we are unprofitable servants.* Likewise: *Enter not into judgment with Thy servant.* And Paul calleth his works *σκύβαλα* (Phil. 3), and evidently pronounceth that *we are not in this life perfect but have only the firstfruits of the Spirit* (Rom. 8) — in which, since even the theoretic is only *ἐκ μέρους* or *γνῶσις μερικὴ ἐν αἰνίγματι* (with respect to the future light and perfect cognition in eternal life), much more the *praxis* consisting in the exercise of good works is only *initiation* — or (as Paul speaketh) *ἀπαρχὴ ἐκ μέρους* (1 Cor. 13).

**The fourth reason** is instituted from the *collation of the benefits of God and of our works*. For the benefits of God, which daily — partly spiritual, partly corporeal — are freely conferred upon us, are more and greater than that we could merit the least part of them. What proportion can ever be established between our works and the benefits of God? — as Jacob the patriarch saith: *I am less, Lord, than all Thy mercies* (Gen. 32). And David (Ps. 116): *What shall I render unto the Lord for all His benefits toward me?* And it is certain that we are so bound by the innumerable benefits which we have first received from God — in creation, in the preservation of life, in vocation, redemption, and renovation — that we can require nothing back from God for our few, imperfect, and manifoldly contaminated works. Therefore Christ teacheth us, that after having performed all that has been commanded us, we acknowledge and confess that we are *unprofitable servants* or insufficient, because none of us feareth or loveth or believeth God, or satisfieth the Law, as much as we ought.

**The fifth reason** is gathered from *acceptation*. For that God accepteth our good works, He doth this not because of the works themselves or because of the dignity of us, but out of His own *spontaneous goodness*, whereby He also freely remunerateth all things — as 1 Pet. 2: *Our hosts are accepted of God through Jesus Christ.* For God is not by debt obligated unto us to render rewards for due works, since we are the servants of God (1 Cor. 6): *Ye are not your own — for ye have been bought at a price.*

**The sixth reason** is taken from *duration*. For righteousness, salvation, and eternal life shall be given to the believing man, and shall endure unto all eternity. But our works in this life are in many modes corrupted and cease to be. Wherefore it followeth that *by our transitory, imperfect, and evanescent works we cannot merit those things which are eternal*. For no one can give what he himself hath not. And only God, who is eternal, can give eternal life — which the sole Son of God meriteth for us. And since this temporal life which we now enjoy we have not obtained or merited by our own works (seeing that without our works and merits — nay, when we knew not, and when we were nothing — it was given us) — much less shall we be able to merit *eternal* life by our own works. Therefore is it written Eph. 2: *By grace ye are saved, not of works.* Titus 3: *Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to His mercy He saved us.* 2 Tim. 1: *Not according to our works, but according to His own purpose and grace, which was given us in Christ Jesus.* And Bernard illustriously saith: *"It is needful first of all to believe that thou canst have no remission of sins except through the indulgence of God; then that thou canst have no good work unless He hath given it; last, that thou canst merit eternal life by no works unless it also be given freely."* — But of this whole discourse of Bernard above in the locus of Justification of Man we have heard.

### Q8 — Whether and how far a man before and after conversion can obey the Law of God.

The response is plain. Since the Law of God requireth *integral, perfect, and perpetual obedience or conformity of human nature with the will of God*, and the human nature is horribly corrupted by original sin, it is established that *no man in this sad corruption of nature can integrally obey the divine Law* — as above in the locus of the Law of God has been said more copiously.

But *how far* a man can obey the Law, the response is also plain:

1. **First**, as concerneth *the faculty remaining in all men — namely, of ruling the locomotive [powers] and of moderating in some way the impetuses of the affections and of effecting external honest and just works* — a man can in some way perform *discipline*, or the *external works* which the Law demandeth, though many and great impediments intervene, as in the doctrine of *free will* we shall hear.

2. **Secondly**, as concerneth *integral obedience and true conversion*, a man of himself *can neither think, nor incept, much less prosecute and perfect anything*.

3. **Thirdly**, with the Holy Spirit dwelling in the regenerate and ruling and helping them, *obedience can be incepted*, pleasing to God for the sake of the Son — even though many things repugnant to the Law of God remain in the regenerate.

### Q9 — On the principal arguments of the Pelagians affirming that a man can satisfy the Law of God.

Above in the seventh question we have said certain things also pertaining to this question. And we remit the studious to the *Apology of the Augsburg Confession*, and to the *Loci* of Philip, where the arguments of the adversaries concerning the Law and Works are dilucidly and gravely refuted. Now let these be observed:

**I.** *"All natural things are possible to the nature whose they are. The Law is natural to man (Rom. 2). Therefore the Law is possible to man."* — **Answer:** The whole is true of *integral, not corrupted nature*. But how far the Law be natural to man — namely in some part, not integrally, not perfectly — has been said above in the distinction of Law and Gospel.

**II.** *Deut. 30: "The mandate is not above thee." 1 John 5: "The mandates of God are not grievous."* — **Answer:** Moses speaketh of the *knowledge of the Law*: the mandate is not hidden from thee but soundeth in thine ears — yea, in thy mind and conscience. But John speaketh of the *regenerate*, who are led by the Spirit of God and liberated from the execration of the Law.

**III.** *"If thou wilt enter into life, keep the mandates."* — Namely, according to the *interpretation of the Gospel*, which showeth Christ and by the Spirit of Christ giveth the believers to will and to perform, that some things may be pleasing to God. Such also is that: *If any man will keep my word*. For this is the discourse of the Gospel, not of the Law; and is a most sweet consolation for believers.

**IV.** *Ps. 7: "Judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness." Ps. 17: "According to the purity of my hands." Here David allegeth his own righteousness in the judgment of God. Therefore we can also stand by our own works before God.* — **Answer:** *Righteousness* is twofold: *one personal and private*, another *the righteousness of the cause, or of public office, or of good conscience*. **Personal righteousness** is that whereby a man is just before God — *not by his own virtues* (as David saith Ps. 143: *Enter not into judgment with Thy servant, for in Thy sight no living one shall be justified*) — but *out of the sole mercy and goodness of God imputing unto the believing man righteousness through and for the sake of the Son*. Of this righteousness David is *not* speaking, but of the *righteousness of good conscience in a just cause and in the office of vocation, or public ministry*; and he signifieth that in the matter of which he is accused he is guiltless of every fault, and by neither word nor deed hath violated Saul or others.

*"Hear my righteousness"* — namely, not the personal or private, but *the public [righteousness] of the public ministry*. *"My cause is just, because it is Thine. This is Thy business, not mine."* On the contrary, the cause of the enemies is not just, because they fall away from Thee and from Thy Word. They plead their own causes, not Thine — and desire the external appearance, applause, and worldly felicity — and hear and pronounce hypocrites and heretics as though they were just. But Thou, who alone canst judge the just, hear my righteousness and my prayer, which from the soul and from the humility of a true heart, in faith, I offer. These men with deceitful and lying lips invoke Thee — that is, they use their own righteousness and the merits of works, and seek not Thy glory, nor come unto Thee in faith in Thy Son.

Since the righteousness or just cause of the pious is for the most part damned before the human judgment, therefore there is need of an *appellation and provocation* from the face of the human judge unto God Himself, the supreme Judge, approver and defender of truth and innocence. Therefore David saith: *"Let my cause be judged by Thee Thyself"* — for the eyes of men see only depravity, and desire the appearance of wisdom and power, and are demented by the external mask. But Thou seest equity, and art not *προσωπολήπτης*, but a *just judge*: Thou art not moved by private affections of wrath or hatred; Thou hast not standing at Thy back ignorance; Thou judgest not from suspicions; Thou art not deceived by fraud and treachery; Thou believest not the delator; Thou admittest not calumnies (which things all unjust judges do); but Thou diligently ponderest the cause and considerest all circumstances; Thou art *καρδιογνώστης*, *searcher of hearts and reins*.

**V.** *Gen. 6: "Noah was just and perfect." Isa. 38: Hezekiah saith, "Remember, Lord, that I have walked before Thee with a perfect heart."* — **Answer:** In each place it is spoken of *faith and good conscience*, in which the life pleasing to God consisteth — even though yet many stains cleave to the saints, which Hezekiah also deploreth, saying: *"I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the tomb; I shall not see the Lord."* Likewise: *"Thou hast cast behind Thy back all my sins."* Of Noah it is written: *"He found grace before the Lord."* Then followeth: *"He was a just man and perfect."*

- **A just man** — namely, *by the faith of the promised seed accepted unto eternal life*. For so the Epistle to the Hebrews Ch. 11 interpreteth it: *He was made heir of the righteousness of faith*. And 2 Pet. 2 Noah is named the *herald of righteousness* — that is, of the *true doctrine of God, of sin, and of the righteousness of faith* and its propagator.
- **And perfect** — namely, *by faith and the fruits of faith*, blameless and excelling in piety, virtue, and wisdom all men of his age; *not contaminated with the worship of idols or with external crimes against the Law of God*. For *Thom* [the Hebrew word for *perfect*] signifieth not one having the highest degrees of all the virtues, being *ἀναμάρτητος καὶ τετράγωνος ἄναψόγος*, but properly one who *in doctrine and faith is upright and simple before God, and irreprehensible before the world, and hath a good conscience*. The Greeks rendered *ἀνέγκλητον καὶ ἄμωμον*, *inculpable both in doctrine and in life*. Paul sometimes rendered *simple*: *I will you to be simple concerning evil, wise concerning good* (Rom. 16). And Phil. 2: *Be ye simple sons of God, without reprehension, in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation, among whom ye shine as luminaries in the world.* Solomon saith that righteousness is the fountain of this perfection (Prov. 13): *Righteousness maintaineth the integrity of life.* For there cannot be integrity or simplicity of life without true faith. And, *Whatsoever is not of faith is sin*. Rightly also it is said that *perfection is to be understood of imputation and of inception*. For so all the saints are *perfect* — namely in Christ imputing unto us His righteousness and giving us His Holy Spirit. And hither pertain the celebrated sentences of Jerome: *"This alone is unto men perfection, if they shall know themselves to be imperfect."* And: *"This is the true wisdom of man — to know that he is imperfect."* And of Prosper:

> *Verus amor Christi, vera est custodia Legis.*
> *Vera fides Christi, vera est impletio Legis.*
> *Vera fides Christi, tota est perfectio vitae.*

*(True love of Christ is true observance of the Law. True faith of Christ is true fulfilment of the Law. True faith of Christ is the whole perfection of life.)*

And of Luther: *"To will to be just, is the highest righteousness."* But of these things now enough. ¹⁶¹

### Q10 — On the reasoning of the works of charity.

The **works of charity** are comprehended in the *second table of the Decalogue*, of which in the explication of the Decalogue we shall treat. Many causes ought to impel us to render them unto the neighbour — chief of all *the example of the Son of God Himself, who is merciful to all, and* σπλαγχνίζεται *[hath compassion]*. Let these causes be in the sight of the studious:

**I. Efficient cause:**
- *The mandate of God*, which all creatures ought to obey — Luke 6: *Be ye merciful*.
- *Faith*, which is dead and idle and an empty name unless it be efficacious through charity.
- *The Holy Spirit*.

**II. Object** — *the neighbour*, needing our counsel and help, who is our neighbour *both universally and peculiarly*, by reason of:
- Creation.
- Similitude.
- Common society and life.
- The mystical body — for *our Head is Christ*.
- Regeneration.
- Common calling unto the unity of the Spirit *in the bond of peace* (Eph. 4).
- Future glory.

**III. End — a fourfold end:**
- The glory of God.
- The alleviation of the indigent.
- Example and edification of others.
- Reward: *Whosoever shall have given unto one of these my least disciples in my name — even a cup of cold water — he shall not lose his reward.*

Honest is the saying: *"Man is neighbour to man."* For God hath created us, and all are conditioned unto the similitude of God, and we have all the same human nature, and live together in a common society. And by this reasoning of society, the neighbour is *common to us with all men in the world — Gentiles and Jews*. But *in the Church* the man is by a far tighter bond neighbour to man. For all who believe in Christ have put on Christ, and are His members, and He Himself is our Head; and we live from the same Spirit of Christ. We are also sons of God, having God as common Father; we are germane brothers, and more than uterine — called by the Word of God unto the *unity of the Spirit*, in the certain hope and infallible expectation of future and eternal immortality, glory and life, salvation and joy, of the society and conversation *in which for all eternity we shall unanimously celebrate God*.

Hither pertain notable sayings, which also show the *mode of aiding the neighbour and the distinction of the works owed to the neighbour*:

**Isa. 58** *(the true fast, which God chooses):* (1) Loose those whom thou hast unjustly bound; dismiss those whom thou oppressest. (2) Restore unto liberty those whom thou deceivest; break down various burdens. (3) Break thy bread unto the hungry, and lead the poor exiles into thy house. (4) *If thou shalt see the naked, thou shalt cover him, and thou shalt not despise thine own flesh.* Then shall thy light break forth like the dawn, and thy health shall grow speedily, and thy righteousness shall go before thee, and the glory of the Lord shall gather thee. Then thou shalt invoke, and the Lord shall hear; thou shalt cry, and He shall say: *Behold, I am here*. These promises of spiritual and corporeal rewards — than which nothing sweeter can be conceived — must diligently be considered and constantly inculcated in all — especially in Princes, Counsellors, nobles, merchants, and the opulent, who are wont to be *most sordid and most niggardly*, and in rendering beneficence to the ministry and to the poor overly fasting, and prefer to trust in their own coffer than in Christ.

**Job 6:** *"Judgment without mercy shall be his who hath not shown mercy."* **Prov. 14:** *"He lendeth unto the Lord who hath mercy on the poor."* **Prov. 21:** *"He that stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he shall himself in turn cry and shall not be heard."* **Prov. 5:** *"Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad, and rivers flow into the streets; but be thou lord of them, and the alien not with thee."* **Sirach 4:** *"Thou shalt bear thyself toward orphans as a father, and toward their mother as a father of the family; and thou shalt be a tender son of the Most High in his turn, and He shall embrace thee more sweetly than thy mother."* **Hos. 6, Matt. 9:** *"I will mercy and not sacrifice."* **Luke 6:** *"Be ye merciful, as your Father is merciful."* Behold the mandate and the example.

**Judge not** — namely, in the heart perversely concerning the neighbour.
**Condemn not** — in the mouth, by calumnies.
**Remit** — in counsel and in the very work.
**Give** — with a joyful and humble mind.

Added is the reward: *Ye shall not be judged; ye shall not be condemned; it shall be remitted unto you; it shall be given unto you.*

Let us also know that goods and wealth are given us for this end: that we may aid, promote, and nurture *religion and the glory of God, Churches and schools, teachers and disciples*; likewise that we may aid and adorn the Commonwealths; likewise that we may with a good conscience — God blessing our labours — serve ourselves and our own; likewise that we may take care of the poor, foster hospitals, sustain exiles. Of this beneficence — against prodigality and against avarice — we have said more copiously in the *Paedagogia*, expounding the seventh precept. Now therefore we shall be briefer, and hasten unto the eleventh question.

### Q11 — On the calling of each one.

The **true fruits of faith, righteousness, and of the Holy Spirit** — which are truly good works pleasing to God for the sake of Christ — chiefly are eminent in these:

- In the *invocation of the divine name*.
- In *the confession of true doctrine, and constancy*.
- In *patience in all calamities* — or in *hope*.
- In *beneficence*.
- In *chastity and temperance*.
- In *fidelity in the works of vocation*.

And piously a **twofold vocation** is recited — *common* and *personal*.

The **common vocation** is that by which all and each of us who are members and citizens of the Church of Christ have been called and separated by the Gospel out of the world, that we may be and be named *Christians* — that is, *spiritual Kings and priests, clothed with righteousness, glad in sanctity, and with perpetual praise celebrating God*, and offering unto Him pleasing hosts, of which above in the third question has been spoken. Unto this common vocation is required:

1. *True doctrine* — the knowledge and confession of Law and Gospel.
2. *The legitimate use of Baptism and of the Supper of the Lord.*
3. *Piety, and honesty of life and morals.*
4. *Constancy in the acknowledged truth and in piety* — that is, *the whole obedience which God demandeth of us*, or all the *sacrifices εὐχαριστικά* and *the whole Christian militia*, of which Paul saith: *I shall war a good warfare, having faith and good conscience.*

The **personal vocation** is *the legitimate function of some office proper to a certain person* — as vocation unto governing, teaching, learning, working. For rightly even the Gentiles said: *Not from the physician alone doth the Commonwealth stand, but from the physician and the farmer.* Therefore God hath instituted *certain orders and states* in the human race — the *Ecclesiastical, Political, and Economic* — as it is customarily said: *Thou pray suppliantly; thou protect; and thou labour.* And the Germans use a beautiful paronomasia: *Lehrestand / Wehrstand / Nährstand* [Teaching-order / Defending-order / Nourishing-order]. Of this personal vocation Paul saith 1 Cor. 7: *Let each remain in the calling wherein he was called.* Eph. 4: *Walk worthy of the calling wherewith ye were called, with all humility and meekness.* Rom. 13: *Let us walk honestly, as in the day.*

Many things are required unto the calling of each one rightly to be discharged:

1. **First**, the *mandate of God*, or an expressed Word by which the office is enjoined *at least in general* — pertaining to the preservation of the Churches and schools, or of political governance, or of the economy, or of common pious and honest society. For a pious mind must not undertake anything *without the mandate of God*.

2. **Secondly**, the vocation must be *legitimate and ordained* — not seized by force, not snatched by fraud, extorted, or slyly suborned or falsified. For those who intrude and thrust themselves in, and use various arts, and remove others that they themselves may succeed, never enjoy divine blessing.

3. **Thirdly**, let *faith and charity* be the rule of the actions in the vocation. For without faith nothing can please God.

4. **Fourthly**, let there be added *pious and holy care and solicitude*, without which no one can be reckoned among the sons of God — as it is written 1 Tim. 5: *If any man have not care of his own, and especially of them of his household, he hath denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.* Let there be in view the examples of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Daniel, Paul (who testifieth his solicitude for the Church at 2 Cor. 11, Col. 2, and 1 Thess. 2).

5. **Fifthly**, let there be added in all things the *invocation and imploration of divine help*. For *Except the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain who keepeth it*. Likewise: *Help us, we perish.* And: *Without me ye can do nothing.* No effort in vocation, without divine blessing, is successful. *ἐάν πόνον, ἐάν πόλεμον, ἀνατεῖ* — *Whether labour or war, without God's aid nought availeth.* Well known are the little verses:

> *θεοῦ διδόντος, οὐδὲν ἰσχύει φθόνος,*
> *ἀλλ᾿ οὐ διδόντος, οὐδὲν ἰσχύει πόνος.*

*(God giving, envy availeth nothing; God not giving, labour availeth nothing.)*

**Sixthly**, in the discharge of vocation let *πολυπραγμοσύνη* [meddling] be shunned — which is the extreme disgrace, and imprints even upon the best-done words and deeds of the best men a stain. *Let us do our own things* (as Paul saith) *and be not occupied with the business of others*. As each day hath its own cares, so each vocation hath its own proper business.

> *Fac tua, quae tua sunt, quae functio vera requirit,*
> *Committas unicae tera cuncta Deo.*

And:

> *Ni tibi sit commissa aliosque cura regendi,*
> *Si sapis, esse, quod es, cura sit una tibi.*

**Seventhly**, let every care tend principally to the *glory of God*, the *commodity of the Church of Christ*, and the *utility of the Commonwealth in which thou livest* — and (if it can be done with good conscience without detriment to the neighbour, by way of honest vocation) to the safety of one's own household: *If any man have not care of his household, he hath denied the faith*.

**Eighthly**, let there be *humility and subjection, and patience*, if any adversity befall in the vocation. *Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God*, saith Peter. And the Son of God willeth *that in patience we possess our souls*.

> *Sis patiens, si vis sapiens et sanctus haberi,*
> *Semina post fletus, gaudia messis habet.*

According to these things briefly delineated, each ought to institute his life, zeals, and morals in his vocation, always mindful of the Pauline saying: *I shall war a good warfare, having faith and good conscience.* Here might be instituted a catalogue of *all the orders in the human race — doctors, disciples, magistrate, subjects, spouses, parents, children, lords, servants*. But these singly are expounded in their proper place, especially in the narration of the Catechesis.

This one thing we shall add: that each ought to be incited to the works of his vocation not only by the causes already noted (the mandate of God, faith, and charity) but also *in species* by these:

1. **Good conscience**, and its tranquillity in all adversity.
2. **The presence of the Angels**, as it is written: *He hath given His Angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.*
3. **The Devil's hatred and indignation**, who can bear nothing less than a man's vocation being safe and sound — that is, when someone doeth in the fear and invocation of God what pertaineth to his office and shunneth enormous sins.
4. **Cheerfulness and alacrity, promptitude and preparation** for the migration from this life, or for the *agon* — which can never be difficult if it be prearmed by faith and good conscience.

### Sentences from Scripture for all Sanctified Orders and States.

Since concerning vocation something has now been said, unto which the studious may refer *the tablet of piety and morals* (called in the Catechism *the Household-Table*), we now shall add some elegant sentences from Scripture *for all the sanctified orders and states* — through which they, as by a certain proper lesson, are admonished of their office and duty.

**For Bishops, Parochial Ministers, and Preachers:** *A Bishop must be irreprehensible — husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, modest, hospitable, apt to teach, no wine-bibber, no striker, not greedy of filthy lucre, but equitable, averse to fighting, averse to avarice — one who ruleth his own house well, having children in subjection with all reverence, no novice* (1 Tim. 3, Titus 1).

**What auditors owe their Bishops:** *The Lord hath ordained that they who announce the Gospel should live of the Gospel* (1 Cor. 9). *Let him who is instructed in the Word communicate with the teacher in all good things* (Gal. 6). *Let the elders who rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially those who labour in the word and doctrine. For the Scripture saith: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. And the labourer is worthy of his hire* (1 Tim. 5). *Obey those set over you, and believe them; for they watch, as those who shall render account for your souls; and let them do this with joy and not with groaning — for this is not expedient for you* (Heb. 13).

**On Magistrates:** *Let every soul be subject to the higher powers. For there is no power but of God. And the powers that be are ordained of God. So whoever resisteth the power resisteth the ordinance of God. And they who resist shall receive judgment for themselves. For he beareth not the sword in vain — he is God's minister, an avenger of wrath upon him who doeth evil* (Rom. 13).

**What subjects owe their Magistrates:** *Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's* (Matt. 22, Mark 12, Luke 20). *Be ye subject of necessity, not only for wrath but also for conscience' sake. For this cause also ye pay tribute, for they are God's ministers. Render to all their dues: to whom tribute is due, tribute; to whom custom, custom; to whom honour, honour* (Rom. 13). *I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, and intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and all in high estate, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life with all piety and gravity* (1 Tim. 2). *Admonish them to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready unto every good work, to speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers* (Titus 2). *Be ye subject to every human creature for the Lord's sake — whether to the king as supreme, or to governors as sent by him* (1 Pet. 2).

**For Husbands:** *Ye husbands likewise, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the weaker vessel — the woman — as being heirs together of the grace of life, that your prayers be not hindered* (1 Pet. 3). *Husbands, love your wives, and be not bitter against them* (Col. 3).

**For Wives:** *Wives, be ye subject to your husbands as unto the Lord — even as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord — whose daughters ye are, as long as ye do well and are not terrified by any fear* (1 Pet. 3).

**For Parents:** *Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath, but bring them up in the discipline and correction of the Lord* (Eph. 6).

**For Children:** *Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. Honour thy father and thy mother — which is the first commandment with promise, that it may go well with thee and thou mayest be long-lived on earth* (Eph. 6).

**For Servants, Maids, Mercenaries, and others hired to labour:** *Servants, obey those who are your masters according to the flesh, in fear and trembling, with singleness of your heart, as to Christ; not with eye-service, as men-pleasers, but as servants of Christ, doing what God wills, from the soul, with good will, serving the Lord and not men — knowing that whatever good thing anyone doeth, this shall he receive from God, whether servant or free* (Eph. 6).

**For Fathers and Mothers of Families:** *And ye masters, do the same things toward them, giving up threats, knowing that also your Master is in heaven, and there is no respect of persons with Him* (Eph. 6).

**For Common Youth:** *Likewise, ye younger, be subject to the elder — yea, all of you be subject one to another. Have humility rooted in your souls, because God resisteth the proud but giveth grace to the humble. Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that He may exalt you in due time* (1 Pet. 5).

**For Widows:** *She who is truly a widow and desolate hopeth in God, and continueth in supplications and prayers night and day. But she who liveth in pleasures is dead while she liveth* (1 Tim. 5).

**For all in common:** *Love thy neighbour as thyself. In this word all the precepts are summarily comprehended* (Rom. 13). *Above all things, let there be made deprecations, supplications, intercessions, thanksgivings, for all* (1 Tim. 2).

### On Conscience.

Since, especially in the doctrine of the offices of vocation, mention is often made of good conscience, we shall subjoin a brief admonition concerning it, useful for boys.

**Conscience is the judgment of the mind, drawn from the law of honesty and piety, concerning a deed** — which judgment is accompanied and followed by either *sorrow or joy in the heart*. Hence customarily is said: **Conscience consisteth in a practical syllogism, and in a motion of the heart which followeth the syllogism**. The practical syllogism is built from a certain rule, and from a practical principle — or from the *συντήρησις* so-called, which pertaineth to the preservation of man — and from the accommodation of the deed to the rule. As Socrates when accused hath this *συντήρησις*: *Honest actions are worthy of praise.* Hence he builds the syllogism: *I have acted honestly. Therefore I am not to be blamed.* In the same mode, *κατ᾿ αὐτόθεσιν*, Oedipus ratiocinates: *Shameful deeds are at last punished. I have acted shamefully. Therefore I shall be punished.*

Hither pertain the sayings:

> *Conscia mens ut cuique sua est, ita concipit intra*
> *Pectora pro meritis spemque metumque suis.*

*(As each has his conscience, so within his breast he conceiveth hope and fear according to his merits.)*

> *Conscia mens scelerum poenas sub pectore nutrit.*

*(The mind conscious of crimes nurtureth punishments beneath its breast.)*

Juvenal: *"These the dire conscience of the deed hath stunned, and with mute lashing striketh — night and day they bear their own witness in their breast."*

The saying of Pythagoras: *"πάντων ἢ μάλιστα αἰσχύεο σαυτόν"* — *"Reverence thyself, above all!"* — *"Even if any man be most audacious, yet conscience maketh him most timid."*

These things concerning conscience can be said from the judgment of reason. Otherwise from Scripture one must discourse of conscience — namely, either *according to the Law of God*, or *according to the doctrine of the Gospel*. From the Law of God, or the Decalogue, is customarily disputed of conscience insofar as *obedience toward God and justice among men is either preserved or depraved*. Joseph cast into prison leans on the testimony of good conscience. David consoleth himself that he hath good conscience. Saul is tortured by evil conscience, contumacious against God — so Cain, Judas, and countless others.

But from the Gospel, conscience is drawn from *faith in the Son of God, glad and certain concerning reconciliation and the remission of sins through and for the sake of Christ* — so that a conscience terrified by the Law of God and prostrate revives here again, as David revived after committing homicide and adultery. *He that believeth in the Son hath life. I believe. Therefore I have eternal life.* So Manasseh, Peter, Paul, and all the pious uplift themselves. And the props of this conscience are four:

1. *The confidence of Christ* — as it is written: *Blessed are all who confide in Him.*
2. *A good purpose*, the will of sinning being cast off.
3. *Ardent desire henceforth to prove one's life to God by true worships.*
4. *Holy care in each one's vocation*, according to that: *Wage a good warfare, retaining faith and good conscience* (1 Tim. 1).

But it is asked what good conscience profiteth the Christians, and whether it be lawful to glory of it. The response is plain: **Good conscience** — which is a joyful motion of the heart because of a rightly-done deed and innocence — profiteth not indeed *unto justification before God*, since Paul manifestly saith (1 Cor. 4): *I know nothing by myself, but in this am I not justified* — but *unto internal testimony of charity and innocence, and unto tranquillity of soul, and unto joy*, as Paul saith (2 Cor. 1): *This is our boasting, the testimony of our conscience.* Each therefore can and ought to glory in his own innocence and in his rightly-done deeds — yet so that in this very glorying we refer all good unto God with acceptance, and ascribe and arrogate nothing to ourselves or to our own virtues, since it is written Jer. 9, 1 Cor. 1: *He that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord*; likewise 1 Cor. 4: *What hast thou which thou didst not receive?* Secondly, that we retain the foundation — *that the certitude and confidence of our salvation lieth in the sole mercy of God*. Thirdly, that we rest in the sole Author of all goods.

So David glorieth that he is innocent, and that Saul and others do him wrong — with God as witness; and that if he be guilty of the crimes of which he is accused, he is prompt for the punishments.

This glorying is a great consolation to the pious to whom wrong is done, and who are falsely delated, traduced, and afflicted — as any can affirm who has learned by experience. Men of the world, courtiers, and similar are not so affected by the care of preserving good conscience; therefore sin lieth at the door in them, until it riseth up — at whose awakening they tremble and often fall into despair. Very many examples we could bring forth.

And this is the truest rule: *The more pious a man is, the tenderer conscience he hath, and easily is affected by a scarcely-existing lapse. But the more secure a man is, the harder conscience he hath, and by even great sins is not wont to be affected.*

Hitherto we have discoursed of good works in general. Now, imposing an end on this doctrine, we pray God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, that by His Holy Spirit He may rule, govern, keep, and retain us — born and reborn unto good works — that we may not rush into errors and crimes, but that we may always be and remain *temples of God, and vessels of mercy*. Amen.
