## §11. DE LIBERO ARBITRIO — On Free Choice.

Of this doctrine in the first part of the *Paedagogia* we have discoursed copiously. Now therefore we shall briefly recapitulate what seems necessary — omitting the intricate and perplexed disputations.

**First** it is asked what is called *free choice*. **Then**, when the man had free choice in all things perfect and least impeded. **Afterward**, whether after the fall of the first parents there is left in man either integral free choice, or some part of it — and how far man hath free choice, and how far he hath it not.

Free choice is named in man **the faculty by which the will in man of its own accord, and not coerced, chooseth and desireth, or rejecteth, what reason judgeth**. The Greeks named it *αὐτεξούσιον* — to which pertaineth also *the faculty of the powers for performing either good or evil* which reason discerneth and the will chooseth.

This free choice was **part of original righteousness before the fall**, and was *in all things perfect and least impeded*. For the judgment of reason was sound; the will prompt; and the powers apt for acting. And therefore free choice was integral, because the judgment was integral and the will not impeded, and the powers were sufficient.

But since after the fall the judgment of reason has been depraved and the will corrupted, and all the powers weakened, and *the malum originis has more occupied the human nature than fire can occupy and penetrate iron* — it is customarily asked what has been left to man after the fall, and whether man has free choice, and how far.

Here we retain the *categorical response of Luther*, which is in the second chapter of Genesis. The words are these: *"We have indeed in some way free choice in those things which are below us. For we have been constituted by the divine mandate as lords of the fishes of the sea, of the fowls of the heaven, and of the beasts of the field. We kill them when we please, we enjoy the foods which they supply, and other commodities. But in those things which pertain to God and are above us, man has no free choice, but is truly, like clay in the potter's hand, placed in a mere passive potency and not an active one. For there we choose not, we do nothing — but we are chosen, prepared, regenerated, we receive — as Isaiah saith: 'Thou art the potter, we are Thy clay' (Isa. 64)."* And in the thirteenth chapter thus he saith: *"Man hath liberty in external functions. For it is free to take at table either pears or apples, to drink Zithum or wine, to go to this or that friend. In such things man hath election; and it is certain that these free works can be worships of God and please God, if thou walk in faith and remain in the precepts of God, or in good conscience."* ¹⁶²

That the whole matter may be better perceived and set in a certain order, first it must be known that as often as in Churches and schools **free choice is called *mind and will conjoined*, it is rightly answered that man hath free choice, because he hath mind and will**. Of the *substance of mind and will*, or (as they call it) of *free choice*, there is no question.

But when it is asked **of what quality free choice is, and what faculty of the will remains in the corrupted nature of man** — the answer cannot be given in a single word, but a distinction is needful, which the sacred letters themselves show us.

This is certain: **free choice is by no means integral, but miserably corrupted, weakened, and so prostrated that man in his whole life more truly creeps upon the ground than walketh upright**. Now we say: *Either the actions of man are common with the brutes* (which namely pertain to the preservation of species and nature — as begetting, rearing offspring, eating, drinking, going, standing, sleeping, keeping vigil, building); *or actions of reason — political, economic, public and private* (as discharging the office of magistrate, doing the external works of the Law, living honestly, injuring no one, giving each his own, loving and defending discipline, being incumbent on a certain study, cultivating fields, contracting, sailing, and the like); *or actions Ecclesiastical pertaining to the preservation of the ministry* (as teaching and hearing the Word, using certain ceremonies, giving and receiving the Sacraments, and similar external works which come into the exterior senses); *or actions and motions spiritual and utterly divine works — which God has either commanded in the Law, or which are proper to the Gospel* (as fulfilling the Law of God, knowing, fearing, and loving God, loving enemies, rightly invoking God, rightly serving and obeying God, believing, being converted unto God, doing true penitence, and persevering in faith); *or it is a question of events and successes of vocation and of actions in the whole life*. Unto these severally and in order response must be made if a certain and non-ambiguous sentence of free choice is to be held.

### The Five Grades of Human Action.

**As concerneth the first grade of actions**, it is certain that the rational nature is not worse than the brutes in its species. Man therefore has free choice, and can be carried by natural impetus to the actions of nature — and hath this prerogative over other animals, *that he hath a free will either of acting or not acting, either of eating or fasting*, according to the reasoning of his will (either good or evil) and the judgment of his reason (either right or perverse, either obeying nature or not obeying).

**As concerneth the second grade** — political, economic, public, and private actions — there is indeed free choice, but very greatly impeded. *That there is a liberty of will in this genus* two things show:

(a) **Manifest experience**, which testifies that the will differs from a stone (by reason of the *subject*: for naturals arise from matter and form or nature and temperament, or qualities — as heating from fire; but voluntary things arise from a *thinking and free potency*); (by reason of the *mode of action*: naturals act on the object presented; voluntaries can act or not act, and can suspend action); (by reason of *constancy and variety of action*: naturals act in one and the same mode, and are determined to one thing, *κατ᾿ ἐπιδότητα τῆς ὕλης* — as fire always heats; but voluntaries do not act in one mode — as Alexander is now clement, now cruel).

(b) **The justice of God**: for God is not the author of sin, nor of the evil actions which arise from the free will of man. And detestable is the opinion of the Stoics, who say all things (both good and evil) come to pass *fatally and necessarily, God so willing* — which is blasphemous and contumelious against God, and hurts the morals of men's life.

The **causes of the liberty of the human will** are:

- That there may be an evident distinction between *free and non-free agent*.
- That God may be established as most free agent.
- That in society and human life there may be some *governance and external discipline*, either *δεσποτικῶς* (by rule) or *κατὰ προαίρεσιν* (by voluntary choice). The *imperium δεσποτικόν* is that by which *the will obedient to reason commandeth the locomotive*; the *προαιρετικόν* is that by which *spontaneously the will prefereth honest actions, and eagerly and freely doth what is right*. Discipline coerceth men *δεσποτικῶς*. And discipline is necessary because of the mandate of God, punishment, public peace and tranquillity, and in the Church because of care of piety.

Between *προαίρεσις* and *τὸ αὐτεξούσιον* there is a distinction. *Προαίρεσις* is *a firm purpose and election μετὰ λόγου καὶ διανοίας* of doing something spontaneously and freely. *Τὸ αὐτεξούσιον* is *a free faculty of choosing and doing anything, or of casting off and omitting*. Hence Basil saith: *"Gabriel the Angel stood before the sight of God διηνεκῶς — continuously, constantly, perpetually. But Satan, an Angel, fell out of his own station παντελῶς — utterly. Him προαίρεσις kept in the celestial things ἐν τοῖς ἄνω; but this one his αὐτεξούσιον cast down — of which Satan abused against God."*

But it must be known that in this second grade man is often impeded by two things: his own infirmity, and the tyranny of the Devil. Neither is the judgment in this grade so right and integral, nor the will so alert, as in the first genus — as even the Gentiles noted. Hence that of Medea (Ovid, Met. 7): *"Cupido persuadeth one thing, mind another: I see the better, and approve; the worse I follow."* And: *"We strive always for the forbidden; we desire what is denied. Whatever is kept, we desire more; and the very prey calls the thief."* And Paul saith Eph. 2 that *the Devil is efficacious in the sons of unbelief, or in the impious* — as the examples of Saul, Judas, Nero, and of all tyrants, heretics, and countless others show. God therefore must be prayed with ardent vows, that He clemently assist us and help us, nor allow the Devil for his lust to work upon us.

That which is customarily objected from Sirach 15 — *"God left man in the hand of his own counsel"* — of this we have spoken above in the first place on the image of God. For Sirach speaks of the liberty of *integral nature*.

**As concerneth the third grade** — Ecclesiastical external actions — we are content with the same response as was given for the second. There is free choice in man in pure external things, whatsoever they be — namely, a certain carnal will and carnal zeal even in divine things — which yet man cannot rightly incept, follow through, or perfect, unless the Holy Spirit illuminate, help, and govern our carnal will and endeavours. As *Nicodemus* (John 3) carnally understands Christ and His kingdom. *Peter*, out of carnal affection, promiseth he will die for Christ.

**As concerneth the fourth grade** — spiritual actions — the response is plain and true: **man left to himself can do nothing at all, nor has he right judgment, nor a docile will, nor sufficient powers** — as David and Paul testify (Ps. 14 and 53, Rom. 3): *There is not one just, not even one; there is none who understandeth, none who seeketh God. All have gone aside; together they are made useless.* What he says — *that not even one is just* — Paul explains Rom. 8, saying: *τὸ φρόνημα τῆς σαρκὸς* — that is, *λόγος καὶ ὁρμαί* — *is θάνατος, a thing damned, and* ἔχθρα εἰς θεόν, *enmity or feud against God*. And 1 Cor. 2: *ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος* — that is (as Chrysostom rightly interprets), *ὁ διὰ σαρκὶ ζῶν, καὶ μήπω φωτισθεὶς τὸν νοῦν διὰ πνεύματος, ἀλλὰ μόνην τὴν ἐμφυτον καὶ ἀνθρωπίνην σοφίαν ἢ σύνεσιν ἔχων* — *does not perceive those things which are of the Spirit of God*. What he says — *there is none who understandeth* — takes away integrity and rectitude of judgment. *There is none who seeketh God* — takes away goodness of will and right zeal of true piety. *All are made useless* — takes away powers and endeavours.

But here again the studious must be admonished: **while we deny judgment, will, and powers unto good and right acting, we do not deny the *substance* of judgment, mind, will, and powers — but the *habit***. For to judge, to will, and to act (after creation, by the counsel, gift, and goodness of God) are proper to nature. As to judge evilly, to will evilly, and to act evilly are to be imputed to depraved nature, so *to judge rightly, to will rightly, and to act rightly in spiritual and divine things are benefits of divine grace*.

### The Man in Conversion — Passive Aptness.

Certain questions arise here — not indeed too necessary if what has been said be rightly received, but not to be passed by, since they have been often moved in Church and schools and in our age have been raised again: namely, *what a man can do before conversion; whether he is in some way apt to apprehend the grace of God offered; what he does in the act of conversion, whether he does anything or cooperates, or is a synergist or utterly ἄεργος; what a man renewed can do after conversion — how in true faith he may be kept and remain σκοπὸς λευκός*.

**As concerneth the first question**: it has been answered thus far *what man can do in three grades of actions — natural, political, and Ecclesiastical*. In these there is liberty of will in the reasoning we have said — or (as Paul names in 1 Cor. 7 on contracting marriage) *ἐξουσίαν περὶ τοῦ ἰδίου θελήματος* — no sane person can deny.

But **in divine and spiritual actions**, man — who ought to have been a polished mirror and the express image of God — has become through the fall of the first parents the *mask of the Devil, an enmity against God, or God's enemy fleeing God, averted from God, and a son of wrath*, who *perceiveth not what is of the Spirit of God* (1 Cor. 2). No natural aptness therefore, no other capacity unto the grace of God, is ascribed to man — except insofar as *man has been made by God and hath mind and will* — meriting nothing in divine matters, nay not even fit or efficacious of himself without the grace and help of God. **Luther calls this *passive aptness***. And as an enemy — though he be capable of reconciliation, because he is a man — yet as long as he is and remains an enemy, acteth as an enemy; so man once made God's enemy acteth as enemy — even though he hath mind and will — and so long acteth as enemy, until reconciliation with God be made: *not out of any aptness or capacity of human nature unto grace, nor out of the dignity of the man or of his works, but simply out of the mere grace and goodness of God through and for the sake of the Son the Mediator*.

Wherefore man can perform nothing whereby he obtains the good of grace. For since man did not remain in the justice and sanctity in which he was conditioned — even though God still preserves the order which yet remains in nature, and aids (as the heroic motions even in Gentiles manifestly show) — yet by this order he cannot stand before the judgment of God, since he is polluted by contagion of the person, and holds himself no otherwise than a bad tree, which sometimes produceth a fair fruit which — though it smile — yet does not prove the tree to be good. Whence memorable is the saying of Augustine: *"Human righteousness compared to divine righteousness is unrighteousness, because even a candle in darkness is beheld to shine, but placed in the sun's beam is darkened."*

Let this suffice concerning the first question.

**To the second question** Luther on Gen. 12 thus responds: *"That Abraham was liberated from idolatry is not from his own merits or powers, but only from the mercy of God calling him — as Moses also admonisheth his people that he was chosen by the Lord, not because they had deserved it, but because the Lord loved them and kept His oath given to the fathers. What else is Abraham than an auditor of the calling God — that is, a merely passive person, and only matter into which the divine mercy acts? This place therefore serves for confirming the doctrine of grace against the dignity of merits or works, which reason so extols. For if thou ask what Abraham was before he was called by the merciful God, Joshua answers (Ch. 24) that he was an idolater — that is, that he had merited death and eternal damnation. But in this misery the Lord doth not cast him off, but calls him, and by that calling — out of him, who is nothing — makes all. Easily do I believe that Abraham, if any consider civil virtues, was an honest man, and (as far as nature allows) the best of men, who indulged not lust, avarice, and other foul desires, but by moderation conquered or governed the blind impetuses of vitiated nature."* And a little later: *"Abraham then is nothing except matter — which the divine majesty by the Word, whereby it calls him, seizes and forms into a new man, and into a Patriarch — that this universal rule may stand: **Man of himself is nothing, can nothing, hath nothing, save sin, death, and damnation. But omnipotent God by His own mercy causeth him to be something, and to be freed from sin, death, and damnation through Christ the blessed Seed.**"* ¹⁶³

Elsewhere also Luther admits not in divine matters the Scholastic definition — that *man is a rational animal* — since reason plainly avails or performs nothing in the matters and mysteries of faith. Nay, the wiser someone is, and the more instructed in the judgment and dexterity of reason, the more easily he is offended by the preaching of the Gospel and mocks and despises it — unless he be illuminated and taught by the benefit and grace of the Holy Spirit, in which case he is called the *new man*.

*It is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that showeth mercy* — that is, there is no dignity, no efficacy, no sufficiency, no action or operation truly right, either of reason or of the human will *per se*, of zeal, care, labour, or dignity of works — but whatever is required unto our salvation, all of it is conferred, given, and granted unto us out of the mere mercy of God through and for the sake of the Son. And we are, in this matter, **passive matter** (that we may use Luther's words rightly understood) — that is, all dignity, sufficiency, and efficacy, and true action, we ascribe to the merciful God, acting on us through the Word and Holy Spirit; and nothing we claim for ourselves save what we *suffer*, that is, that we *let God act on us*, and simultaneously receive the benefits of God offered to us — we do not resist Him contumaciously and perseveringly, but let reason and mind be instructed and taught, will be reformed and bent, affections governed, life and actions ruled, and directed to the glory of God — through the Word, through the Holy Spirit, through the cross, and through all other means whereby God wills and by which He acts on us, either mediately, or sometimes also immediately, as often is done in the cross.

And although the depravity of our nature is so great that *the thought of the human heart is evil from its youth* (Gen. 8), and *the sense of the flesh is enmity against God* (Rom. 8), and manifoldly contumaciously fights God (as in the doctrine of original sin is more copiously shown) — yet **in the very conversion the Holy Spirit so reforms the reason and renews the will, moves and bends it, that man — by nature enemy of God and son of wrath — becomes friend of God and son and heir of God**; he understands, and gladly embraces, the goodness and grace of God; he assents to the promise; and subjects himself in all things to the will of God — *not indeed from nature of reason and human will, but from grace and the efficacious action of the Holy Spirit* who instructs and illuminates reason, heals and reforms the will — yet so that reason and will are not idle but simultaneously *patiens*, and now converted, *doing something in their own order*, and (to use Luther's words) *cooperating with the Spirit working in us and recreating us without us* — that is, not contumaciously resisting or spurning, but already having the Holy Spirit and receiving His benefits, and obeying and serving God, with the Holy Spirit as mover and helper. ¹⁶⁴

**The beggar-analogy:** A beggar receiving from a rich man an offered gift does nothing else save that *he stretches forth his hand to apprehend and receive the gift*. This beggar is *passive matter* — that is, the gift is given him by the richer. But *he does not contumaciously turn away his face; he doth not resist the giver; he doth not draw back his hand — but receives the offered gift*. And in that (which even a blind, lame, and deaf man could do by the leading and grace of the giver) he is said *to do something*. For if he did not do this, he would not receive the gift, but would be contumacious and ungrateful, and would repel the giver and irritate him and spurn the gift. But of this will and action of the beggar receiving the gift, or letting the giver give, the dignity and efficacy is nothing at all — but the whole is the giver's benefit; nor can the beggar say, *I stretched forth my hand for myself, and so I was made worthy of this gift* — but he must confess that out of the commiseration and beneficence of the giver he has received and has whatever he has.

We all after the fall of the first parents lie in a deep slough, nor by any reasoning of our labour or of another's work and help can we be extracted. Out of the mere goodness and mercy of God the Father toward us therefore, He sends and gives us His Son, who *calls us by His voice — "Come unto me, all"* — and offers us His help, and extracts us out of the slough, that we may not perish. Here we do nothing else save that we *hear the calling, and offer even our finger to His efficacy, that we may be extracted; nor turn our face from Him, nor spurn His benefits, nor resist His grace*. And to this the Son of God Himself looks at John 6, saying: *No one can come to me except the Father draw him. But everyone who hears and learns from the Father cometh unto me.* And this the customary sayings mean (rightly understood of the regenerate man — for of the non-regenerate they are false and Pelagian). Of Chrysostom: *"ἕλκει θεός, ἀλλὰ τὸν βουλόμενον ἕλκει"* — *"God draweth, but He draweth the one willing."* Of Basil: *"μόνον θέλησον, καὶ θεὸς προαπαντᾷ"* — *"Only will, and God cometh before."* Of Nazianzen: *"God saveth not the unwilling, nor doth He will thee unwilling to be won, nor doth He compel thee to hope."* And elsewhere: *"δέδοται τοῖς καλομένοις, καὶ τοῖς οὐκ ὀκνοῦσι"* — *"It is given to those who are called, and who hesitate not."* And Augustine: *"Faith is like an open vessel's mouth; infidelity is like a cover by which the vessel is stopped, so that it may not admit the liquor divinely poured in."* And Apoc. 3: *Behold, I stand at the door and knock: if any man hear my voice and open the door, I will come in unto him.*

When therefore it is said that in conversion the man holds himself *merely passively*, this is to be understood of *dignity, efficacy, sufficiency, and true, right, and solid action*. But it does not take away the reasoning of the order which God Himself has instituted and requires — that man hear the Word. Nor did Luther ever will his words to be so understood, as if by *passive subject* he denies that the renewed human will thereafter *doth act and receive the benefit of God*. But **he denies merit and dignity, and ascribes all to the mercy of God**. For the merit of Christ is the first, middle, and last cause in conversion, justification, and salvation.

D. Luther makes mention of *the cause without which not* (*causa sine qua non*), and so names the *knowledge and confession of sin* — and if any of the pious speak thus, he doth not disapprove, as is clear from his exposition of Ps. 51. Formerly in the schools they used with the same reasoning the word *συνεργία*, as is clear from Clement of Alexandria in his *Stromata*: *"ὃ μεθ᾿ ἑτέρου ποιεῖ, ἀτελὲς ὂν καθ᾿ ἀυτὸ ἐνεργεῖν φαμὲν καὶ συναίτιον"* — *"What one does with another, being incomplete of itself, we call this a co-worker and joint-cause."* And this word Paul also uses when he speaks of the ministry of preaching the Gospel (1 Cor. 3): *θεοῦ γάρ ἐσμὲν συνεργοί* — *"For we are God's fellow-workers."* Hence customarily three causes of a right and good action are set: *the Word of God, the Holy Spirit, and the human will now regenerate*, which is not resisting the Word of God and not casting out the Holy Spirit (as Saul cast Him out by his own act). ¹⁶⁵

*Zeal therefore must be stirred up in us, and the persuasion of enthusiasm and rapture — as also of coercion — must be shunned; and the sloth and security of men must not be confirmed*. Let us not be secure and slothful, but *invoke God, ask help from Him, and by the exercises of penitence prove and confirm our faith; frequently hear the Word of God; use the means proposed by God; hear and follow God speaking and calling us*, as Paul heard Christ and subjected himself to Him. Nor let us cast out the Holy Spirit by sins against conscience, nor cast the guilt of our destruction upon God, nor make Him a *προσωπολήπτης* — which certainly those do who feign enthusiasms, coercions, and contumacious repugnances in the very conversion of man (as we have said in the *Christian Paedagogy on the Holy Spirit*).

**But what man renewed can do after conversion**, all the pious experience in the exercises of faith and penitence. *Without Thy divinity, nothing is in man, nothing innocent.* There is a perpetual strife of the flesh and the Spirit, of the old and new man, in which man would utterly be conquered by the flesh unless he were sustained by the Spirit and preserved. To Whose admonitions he himself hearkens and follows, that he may not rush into errors and crimes. Therefore Peter saith: *Through faith ye are kept by the power and virtue of God unto salvation* — that is, *ye are preserved not by your own virtue in true faith and piety, but the help of God must be present*; therefore *ye ought to implore God's help*, that He rule you, preserve you, and confirm you in true faith and piety. As the sweetest verses admonish:

> *Nil sum, nulla miser novi solatia, massam*
> *Humanam nisi quod tu quoque Christe geris.*
> *Tu me sustenta, fragilem me Christe guberna,*
> *Fac ut sim massae portio parva tuae.*

And memorable is Bernard's saying: *"To have confidence in oneself is not of faith but of perfidy, not of confidence but of diffidence. But he truly believeth who neither believeth himself nor hopeth in himself — having become to himself as a lost vessel — but hath all consolation and hope in Christ."*

### The Fifth Grade — Events and Outcomes.

Now of the fifth grade a few things. It is certain that *there is an election of the will in the matter which it foresees*, even though the events and outcomes do not agree with the will and purpose — because there are many *arcane causes* on account of which many things happen otherwise than we had thought. As Jer. 10 saith: *I know, O Lord, that the way of man is not his; nor is it of a man to direct his steps.* By *way* he names *vocation*, of which it is certain that *not all perils can be foreseen, and that events and outcomes are not in our power*, nor is governance felicitous unless God help — as it is written Ps. 127: *Unless the Lord build the house, in vain they labour who build it.* And John 3: *Man can take nothing on himself unless it be given him from heaven.*

> *Ardua cura perit, successum functio nescit,*
> *Conatus nihil est, studium perit omne, laborque*
> *Ni Deus è caelo faveat, vitam que gubernet,*
> *Quo duce cuncta potest homo sumere, quo duce cassus*
> *In peius ruet, et retro sublapsus egebit.*

Likewise Prov. 16: *The heart of man disposeth his way, but of the Lord it is to direct his steps.* Hence the proverb: **Homo proponit, Deus disponit — Man proposeth, God disposeth**. And thence sayings of the wise even among the Gentiles — as Cicero's *"Omen — never [scoff at] the wise!"* — for many are the sad errors even of all the wise, and many lapses befall which beget inexplicable difficulties for human counsels, as not only the ancient histories of Pompey, Brutus, Antony, King Ahab, Saul, and others, but even recent events of our age everywhere testify. Many unforeseen and inextricable things offer themselves beyond the opinion of men — as David foresaw not the sedition of his son. And it is vulgarly said: *"Thou knowest not what the late evening brings."* *"The sun hath not yet run its course to evening."* And the sentence of King Philip is known, which Livy recites (Dec. 4 Bk. 9): *"The sun of all days has not yet set."* And of Solon: *"ὅρα τέλος μακροῦ βίου"* — *"Behold the end of a long life."* Likewise:

> *πολλὰ μεταξὺ πέλει κύλικος καὶ χείλεος ἄκρου.*
> *"Many things fall between the cup and the outermost lip."*

The Latins say: *"Between mouth and morsel."* Likewise: *"Meanwhile something may happen."* And the Mime's famous saying: *"Thou knowest not what evening may bring."*

Wherefore in the last grade also, we must all pray God to keep us — and know that *the whole of our life, and every outcome of it, hangs upon divine providence*.

### Closing Prayer of Locus II.

O eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, together with Thy Son and the Holy Spirit — the one and only true God — we beseech Thee, in true and salutary penitence and by the confidence of the Son the Mediator, so instruct, direct, and rule us — that we may fear Thee, love Thee, invoke Thee, seek Thee, know Thee, serve Thee — and unto Thee alone all the days of our life ascribe the glory of every good; that so, being converted and sanctified in Thy truth, we may bear the fruits of righteousness which please Thee, and that at the last we may be received by Thee unto Thy eternal Kingdom of glory. Amen.

# Locus III. De Libertate Christiana · On Christian Liberty.

**Christian Liberty** is not named *licence*, or *dissolution*, or *the confirmation of security*, or *the neglect of laws and discipline* — as many secure and Epicurean have thought, that the doctrine of Christian liberty establisheth *carnal licence of living at pleasure, of plundering ecclesiastical goods, of coupling to oneself many wives, of contemning all Mosaic Laws and even the Decalogue itself*. So certain Princes and Doctors have abused the doctrine of Christian liberty — saying that Moses ought to be sent to the gallows, prohibiting the Law from being taught, polluting themselves with various commixtures, taking away the authority of the magistrate — as the Anabaptists have done. Against these foul dreams, let us know:

**First**, Christian liberty is not political, civil, carnal, and secure liberty (of which rightly is said: *"O love of liberty, how thou deceivest a foolish world!"*) — but is a **spiritual manumission**, procured by the blood of the Son of God, which the Gospel offereth unto believers in Christ.

**Secondly**, this Christian Liberty consisteth *in the liberation from sin and from the malediction of the Law, and in the donation of the Holy Spirit* or *vivification* — efficacious for performing those works which the spiritual life requireth. Likewise, in **liberation not only from the Mosaic rites but also from all human traditions**, as far as concerns the conscience.

Rightly therefore is Christian Liberty defined thus: **Christian Liberty is a spiritual manumission, procured by the blood of Christ, which the Gospel offereth unto those believing in Christ — through which we, being freed from sin, from the damnation of the Law, and from human rites, are endowed with the Holy Spirit for pacifying our consciences and being instructed with true consolation in every cross — certain that our Liberator will shortly snatch us out of all evils.**

### The Four Grades of Christian Liberty.

Four grades of Christian liberty are recited — joined indeed by nature, but for teaching's sake to be distinguished, which consist in the merit and efficacy of Christ.

**The First Grade is called Grace** — that is, *liberation from sin, from the wrath of God, from the malediction of the Law, from eternal condemnation*. As it is written Rom. 8: *The law of the Spirit of life through Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death.* And Gal. 3: *Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the Law.*

**The Second Grade is Gift-through-Grace** — that is, *the efficacy of the Son of God in believers, or the donation of the Holy Spirit, vivification, consolation, inception of new obedience, defence and preservation of the Church, and mitigation of calamities*. This liberty is *liberation from the works of the flesh* (that we may not indulge in them), *and from legal fear-sorrow, from despair, and from the tyranny of the world*. For it is written 2 Cor. 3: *Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.*

**The Third Grade is from Ceremonies and forensic Mosaic Laws** — which, the Mosaic polity being now abolished and the types and figures ended, bind no one, as above in the doctrine of the Law has been said.

**The Fourth Grade is liberation from human traditions in the Church**. For no creature is permitted to institute worship of God, or a new law not agreeing with the divine Law. For it is written: *In vain do they worship me by the mandates of men*. And Col. 2: *Let no man judge you in food, drink, or on the alternation of the festal days.* But the distinction of times and lessons in the Church — which for order's sake because of public assemblies must be retained — is to be made without an opinion of worship and of necessity unto salvation. For outside the case of scandal such rites can without sin be omitted, as below on Ceremonies shall be said.

Whenever the discourse of Christian Liberty is instituted, always let there be held and considered the saying of Christ, John 8: *If the Son shall make you free, ye shall be truly free.* **Truly**, He saith — not in an empty title or in a shadow of liberty, but in fact: *sin abolished, the wrath of God appeased, death done away, all human calamities taken away, eternal righteousness, light, life, and glory bestowed*. For Christ embraceth the *integral liberty*, which He hath brought and begotten for His Church by His death. And with this liberty (which is of grace) is always joined the *liberty of gift*, which in this life is incepted, but in the resurrection shall be integral — when, all evils being blotted out, the Church shall enjoy the eternal and sweet familiarity of God and of our Saviour Jesus Christ. Unto that eternal and in consummation-heavenly integral liberty let us look with the mind, as often as we hear the name of Christian Liberty — and simultaneously let us think that it is *incepted in this life*.

Let us also remove the *dreams of the Jews* concerning political liberty and empires. Above also in the doctrine of the Kingdom of Christ we have shown the distinction between mundane empires and the liberty which the Gospel proposeth. Of this whole doctrine we remit the Reader to the *Loci Communes of D. Philip our Preceptor* — in the first place to the *sermons of D. Luther on the fifth chapter of the Epistle to the Galatians*, where is expounded this saying: *In the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, stand* — that is, *be ye firm*. And of Peter: *Be ye sober and vigilant.* ¹⁶⁶

Let us also execrate the figments of the *Libertines, Anabaptists, and Monks*, who say that only certain rudiments are contained in the sacred letters, and that one can choose certain kinds of holy life, and perform *works of supererogation*, and even (without the Word and mandate of God) write new Decalogues and live at will. Let us know these all — partly vain, partly plainly blasphemous — and pray the Son of God that He preserve for us the liberty procured by His blood, and by the liberty consummated at length by His coming grant us to celebrate Him with free and spontaneous Spirit, without any sin. Amen.
