## DOCTRINA DE PRAEDESTINATIONE — On the Doctrine of Predestination.

The universal doctrine of the providence and predestination of God — comprehended in certain themes and once set before the studious of piety — it pleaseth me now to recapitulate in this place.

**I.** **The Providence of God is an action of the divine will**, whereby God not only seeth and knoweth all things past and future, but also sustaineth, governeth, and moderateth the things by Him conditioned, and the order by Him instituted — and imparteth unto His work *light, motion, and life*.

**II.** Although many furiously deny that there is providence, yet against this delirium of the Epicureans God confirmeth us — both by Scripture and by illustrious testimonies of nature — and convinceth us to confess that there is providence.

**III.** Manifest and most certain testimonies of providence are: *the whole theatre of the entire nature of things, the very figure of the world, the sky, the lights, the order of motions, the alternations of times, the earth's site and fecundity, all things arising from the earth, the variety and perpetuity of species, propagation, the mode of generation, man himself* ὁ μικρόκοσμος, *and the very minds of men — and in these the knowledge concerning God, the distinction of the honest and shameful, the judgment of conscience in things done rightly and otherwise, the regular events by which atrocious offences are followed by atrocious punishments*. Likewise, *the wondrous signs added to the bodies of the slain, which point out the authors of murders, the heroic motions by which empires and arts are restored, the significations of future things (as predictions of the change of kingdoms), and prodigies*, and other similar many testimonies in nature — of which some are more, others less illustrious.

**IV.** These testimonies are not overturned by the *inequality of judgment* which some object — namely, that tyrants and other impious often live impune and have bloodless ends (as the elder Dionysius, Sulla, Tiberius, and others), while the good and just often live miserably and are put to death.

**V.** Rightly Isocrates saith: *The rule is not overturned by few and rare examples*; and *because of a few examples one is not to hope for impunity*.

**VI.** In the Church we know this very *dissimilitude* is a *testimony of the future judgment* and *of immortality* — in which the just distinction of good and evil shall remain.

**VII.** We execrate therefore the madness of the Epicureans who *remove God from governance*, and ascribe the cause of good and evil events only to *matter or the will of men, or fortune or chance*.

**VIII.** We do not indeed altogether exclude from all events the *matter and will of men*, but we constitute God as the *first Governor of things*, unto whom human affairs are a care, and who heareth and preserveth His own — even when *secondary causes* fail — He who also holdeth all secondary causes under Himself, and either moderateth them by His will, or by *certain permission* alloweth them to act.

**IX.** Rightly and customarily are numbered **six principal causes** when we speak of human actions and of the events which befall men: (1) *God*, either immediately without secondary causes or mediately acting something; (2) *The stars*; (3) *Temperaments*; (4) *The will of man, morals, zeals, education, and discipline*; (5) *The fury and potency of devils in impelling the impious*; (6) *External violence*.

**X.** Although the human mind hath certain arguments *proving that God is present as Moderator*, yet the assent is more difficult and languid than when it is convinced *that the world hath been made by God*.

**XI.** By divine testimonies therefore faith must be *stirred up and confirmed* in the souls — without which human assent is very languid, as we see even in Aristotle and in others.

**XII.** The sacred letters set before us **three grades or modes of providence and divine administration**.

**XIII.** **The first grade** (for teaching's sake) can be named ***universal Providence***, by which God preserveth safe the whole nature by Him conditioned, and the inclination and mode of acting of nature — that is, the order of motions, the alternations of times, the fecundity of the earth, of animals, and other things useful and necessary for the sustentation and preservation of life.

**XIV.** Of this first mode the sacred letters speak in many places — as Ps. 104, which is entirely a thanksgiving for the creation and preservation of things, from whose perpetuity (as Augustine speaketh) — that is, from their preservation and duration — is known in some way *the eternity of God*; and from the magnitude of the power of God, from the order and disposition of the wisdom of God, from the governance, *the goodness and justice of God*. Matt. 10: *Two sparrows are sold for a farthing, and one of them falleth not upon the ground without your Father.* Acts 17: *In Him we live and move and are* — that is, *through Him our life is given, sustained, and cherished*. Col. 1: *In Him all things consist*. 1 Tim. 6: *ὁ θεὸς τὰ πάντα ζωοποιεῖ*. Heb. 1: *φέρει τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ*. Hither pertain also many sayings in the Psalms — Ps. 24: *The earth is the Lord's and the fulness thereof* — Ps. 33: *He gathereth the waters of the sea as into a wine-skin, and layeth up the deeps in treasures* — Ps. 74: *Thine is the day and Thine is the night; Thou hast made the light and the sun, Thou hast fashioned all the bounds of the earth; summer and winter, Thou hast formed them*. Ps. 145: *The eyes of all wait upon Thee, O Lord, and Thou givest them meat in due season*.

**XV.** **The second grade** can be named ***special Providence***, by which God not only *seeth and heareth all things*, and is *everywhere*, and sustaineth and preserveth the nature by Him conditioned — but *moreover so moderateth all things according to His will* that all creatures obey Him commanding and willing, and execute His mandate, and serve God — that they may be instruments *either of the goodness of God, or of His justice and judgment*, according to the *promises and comminations* set before us in the Word.

**XVI.** For we must not look to the *Stoic necessity*, which errs in two ways: (a) *because it bindeth God to the secondary causes* and feigneth that He cannot act otherwise than those causes know; (b) *because it saith the will of men is simply impelled by God unto good and evil*, and thus constituteth God the *author of evils*.

**XVII.** Since this false opinion is contumelious against God and hurts the morals and life of men, it ought not to have place in the Church or in any assembly of honest and good men — nor must we look to the Stoic necessity in events, but to the promises and comminations of God.

**XVIII.** For God, by a certain *special providence* of His own, addicteth creatures unto His obsequy, and useth their ministry according to His good and just will — which effecteth both *goods* and *evils of punishments* (as rains, thunders, ices, hails, droughts, inundations of waters, *λιμόν καὶ λοιμόν* [famine and pestilence], war, exiles, peace, abundance or lack of things, and countless similar things) — by which He either aideth His own, or punisheth the evil, or chastiseth the pious.

**XIX.** Of this obedience of creatures to the nod and will of God Sirach saith (Ch. 39): *ἐστὶ πνεύματα ἃ εἰς ἐκδίκησιν ἔκτισται, καὶ ἐν θυμῷ αὐτῶν ἐστερέωσε μάστιγας αὐτῶν* — *There are winds or spirits ordained for punishment, and by their impetus they smite; and when calamity impendeth, then they tumultuate and blast the earth with whirlwind, and execute the wrath of Him who created them. Fire, hail, hunger, death — all these have been created for vengeance; beasts, scorpions, serpents, sword — are also created for vengeance, for destroying the impious — which, as rejoicing, energetically perform His mandate, and are prompt if ever God wills to use their operations on the earth; and when the hour cometh, they cease not.*

Hither be referred those sayings: Isa. 45: *I am the Lord, making peace and creating evil* — that is, *destroying the impious and punishing the contumacious*. Likewise Amos 3: *There is no evil in the city which the Lord hath not done.* Zeph. 1: *The Lord doth well and evil.*

**XX.** For there are to be held in the Church for teaching's sake the appellations *malum culpae* and *malum poenae* — which Augustine also useth — and which in the sacred letters are expressed by the voice *Raah*: which sometimes signifieth *culpa* (that is, *sin itself and vitium* opposed to *justice and honest good*); sometimes *poena* (justly imposed upon the offenders — opposed to the good or useful or sweet, or to both).

**XXI.** From God we by all modes remove **the evil of guilt**, who by nature is good, and neither willeth nor approveth nor aideth sin — as expressly it is written Ps. 5: *God, willing not iniquity, art Thou.* Likewise: *He who doeth sin is of the Devil.* Likewise: *All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.*

**XXII.** But **the evil of penalty is from God** — as Lam. 3: *Who is he that saith it is done, the Lord not commanding? Do not both evils and goods proceed from the mouth of the Most High? Why doth the living man murmur? Let him murmur against his own sins. Let us search our ways, and seek Him and return unto the Lord.*

**XXIII.** This distinction of words most greatly profiteth us for retaining the true sentence, founded in the express Word of God, in which God hath clemently and evidently patefacted His will (as far as it was necessary for us to know) — lest we err from the way and true target of truth, unto scrutinising the inscrutable, but that we retain the Word of God as a lamp unto our feet, and in events consider the divine promises and comminations.

**XXIV.** We often fall into diseases; often we undergo other perils, horrid tempests, thunders, famine, wars, seditions, exiles, and the like evils. Thieves are strangled, homicides beheaded, robbers and ravishers are put on the wheel, and others suffer other punishments for enormous crimes. Today the savagery of the Turks must be feared — and certainly atrocious punishments remain, which shall come upon us, our bodies, goods, faculties, families, and without doubt Churches and schools.

**XXV.** In these things we must look not to the *Stoic necessity*, or only to certain unknown *secondary causes*, but to the *divine promises and comminations* — such as are Prov. 3: *Poverty is in the house of the impious from the Lord, but the habitations of the just shall be blessed.* 1 Sam. 2: *Whoever shall honour me, I will glorify him; but those who contemn me shall be ignoble.* Ps. 107: *Fools are afflicted because of the way of their crimes and iniquities.* Likewise: *The impious and bloody shall not halve their days* (Ps. 45). Hos. 2: *She knew not that I gave her corn; therefore will I take away my corn again.* Prov. 10: *He who curseth his parents, his light shall be extinguished in the midst of darkness.* And Lev. 20 God threateneth *extermination from His people* upon the wicked. Hither pertain all the *ἐπιτιμητικαί* discourses of the Prophets (whereby they upbraid lapses), and *ψεκτικαί* (whereby they reproach improbity), and *ἀπειλητικαί* (whereby they threaten and inject fear), and *μεμπτικαί* (whereby they desire in us the offices of piety and vocation), and *ὀνειδιστικαί* (whereby they object our ingratitude and contempt of the divine Word), and *κατηγορικαί* (whereby they reprove sins of every kind, evil examples, and not only external lapses, wickedness, and manifest malice, but also *internal evils*).

**XXVI.** As for what many object — the *dissimilitude* and *inequality of judgment*, in that often the evil fare well and the good fare ill — and so wish to deny God's *special providence*: to this it hath been answered above; and this is more copiously handled when the locus on the Cross and calamities must be expounded, wherein the causes of our miseries are recited.

**XXVII.** Let us hold the saying of Psalm 75: *A cup is in the hand of the Lord, full of red wine mixed, and He poureth from it — yet all the impious of the earth shall drink and shall suck out the dregs* — that is, great is the discrimination between the affliction of the pious and of the impious. **The affliction of the pious floweth from the paternal love of the heavenly Father, and exerciseth the pious unto their own good, and endureth for a short time. But the punishments of the impious proceed from the wrath of God — and not returning to their senses, they perish; and even in this life these are the preludes of eternal punishments.**

**XXVIII.** As for what some also complain — namely, since God by His providence hath addicted all creatures unto His obsequy, why happen so many evils in nature and so many sins are perpetrated? — this requireth no other answer save that of Ecclesiastes 12: *All things which are done, God shall bring into judgment for every fault, whether it be good or evil*.

**XXIX.** Let us hold also the words of Augustine, *tract. 97 on John*: **God permitteth things so foul in opinions, cults, and morals to happen — that everywhere His judgments may be to be feared; and that by comparison of impure wickedness the most pure discipline may sweeten; and that unto Him may be given honour, but unto him fear or shame, who in this evil or under yonder governor hath not fallen, or, being lifted up by yonder deliverer, hath risen.**

**XXX.** **The third grade** can be named ***peculiar Providence of God***, which is *of the elect* or *of those believing in the Son of God* — by which, namely, God liveth and reigneth in His Church, and in her living members teacheth, consoleth, confirmeth, defendeth, raiseth, and cherisheth the believers; justifieth them through and on account of the Son, reformeth and regenerateth them, and bendeth their minds and wills unto His acknowledgement, fear, invocation, and obedience — that they may be and remain *temples of the Holy Spirit*.

**XXXI.** Of this mode of the providence of God speak these and similar sayings: Ps. 1: *The Lord knoweth the way of the just.* Deut. 30: *He is thy life and the length of thy days.* Matt. 10: *All the hairs of your head are numbered.* Ps. 91: *He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High shall abide under the protection of God.* Rom. 8: *There is now no condemnation unto them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit.* Ps. 36: *They shall not be confounded in the evil time, and in the days of famine they shall be satisfied.*

**XXXII.** When these three grades of divine providence are considered, at the same time also the *modes of God's presence* must be considered — which show how God is present unto things and sustaineth all. Now **four grades of divine presence** are customarily numbered.

**XXXIII.** **The first grade is the general action of God, or universal presence**, by which God is present unto all His creatures and most freely preserveth them, so long as either by His order and institution, or according to His promises and comminations, He willeth to preserve them. And hither pertain the sayings: Isa. 66: *Heaven is My seat and the earth is the footstool of My feet.* Jer. 23: *Do not I fill heaven and earth, saith the Lord?* Ps. 139: *If I ascend up into heaven, Thou art there; if I strew my bed in hell, behold Thou art there. If I take the wings of the dawn and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there is Thy hand,* etc. Likewise the verse: *"Everywhere present is God, and everywhere powerful."* — ἐστὶ θεὸς πάντῃ, ἔν τ᾽ ἐν καλοῖς τε κακοῖς τε πάντα ἔχει μὲν ὁ πάντα βλέπει τε θεὸς. *"Filling all things, God hath poured Himself into every mass — and even one herb reporteth God present."* Lucan: *"Jove is whatsoever thou seest, whithersoever thou movest."* ¹⁶⁷

**XXXIV.** This first grade of God's presence they name ***repletive being everywhere*** — which belongeth to God alone, since the remaining things (spiritual) are said to be in place *definitively*, corporeal things *circumscriptively*. And of this first grade let there be held the illustrious sentence of Gregory: **God abideth within all things, Himself outside all things, Himself above all things, Himself beneath all things: higher by power, lower by sustentation, exterior by magnitude, interior by subtlety; ruling from above, containing from below, encircling from without, penetrating within — He is never absent, and yet is far off from the cogitations of the unjust; nor yet is He absent thence where He is far off — because there He is not present by grace, but by vengeance.** And Augustine unto Dardanus saith: **God, without labour ruling and containing the world, is wholly in heaven, wholly on earth, and wholly in each; and contained by no place, but wholly everywhere in Himself.** ¹⁶⁸

**XXXV.** **The second grade** is that whereby God is present in His Church in this life *according to His promise and evident Word*, and by *His ministry* is present, and in the administration and use of the Sacraments is at hand according to His Word and institution — and through these means is efficacious in the hearts of believers, and effecteth in them motions pleasing to Himself, the Holy Spirit being given (who through the Word moveth minds and hearts, and constituteth for Himself temples in them) — as it is written: *We will come unto him, and will make our mansion with him.* And Wis. 7: *The throne of Wisdom is the soul of the just.* Likewise: *Where two or three are gathered together in My Name, I am in the midst of them.*

**XXXVI.** But God is present unto His creatures — and also unto the regenerate in this life — *separably and invisibly*. For often He destroyeth natures not pleasing (as in the deluge He destroyed the greatest part of the human race); and often He departeth from those who *against conscience rush into wickedness and errors*, and, willing, shake off the Holy Spirit — as He departed from Saul and from Judas, and even from David the adulterer, until he was converted unto God.

**XXXVII.** In the explication of this second grade, and in this whole doctrine of the providence of God, it is customarily inquired concerning ***predestination*** — which is *the election of the divine will* by which God chooseth those to be saved *through grace in Christ His Son*, and ordaineth them and calleth them by the voice of His Gospel according to His good pleasure unto the adoption of His sons through Christ — in whom the elect believe, and are gifted with the Holy Spirit, and in sanctity and purity of life bring forth the fruits of faith, and have and retain the *true doctrine* and the *true use of the Sacraments*, and thus in fear and true invocation expect the promised salvation.

**XXXVIII.** Whosoever concerning this eternal predestination of God wish to speak rightly and piously, ought to consider — and always to have before their sight — these **seven rules**:

1. **Outside the Word of God we ought to decree nothing concerning the will of God.**
2. **The promise of God concerning grace is universal**, as it is written: *He hath concluded all under sin, that He might have mercy upon all.* Rom. 11.
3. **With God there is no** *προσωποληψία* (respect of persons).
4. **In God there are no contradictory wills.** 1 Tim. 2: *God willeth all to be saved.*
5. **Grace overfloweth above sin.** Rom. 5.
6. **As in Adam all fell, so in Christ all rise again and are quickened.** 1 Cor. 15.
7. **God hath predestined none unto** *the evil of guilt*, nor unto eternal ruin by His eternal will — because it is written: *I live, saith the Lord, I will not the death of the sinner.* Ezek. 33. And Hos. 13: *Thy perdition is from thyself, O Israel; but thy salvation is from Me.*

**XXXIX.** Whoso observeth these rules, he cannot be dragged into the Stoic opinions; nor is he secure or slothful for apprehending the grace of God — which is offered unto all, and from which no one is excluded save he who by his own malice and unbelief excludeth himself. He is also certain that he hath been truly predestined by God unto eternal life, and hath testimonies of certitude of his own — *both in the vocation* (as Paul saith Rom. 8: *Whom He hath chosen, these also He hath called*), *with his own faith*, which the Holy Spirit effecteth (who is the *pledge of our inheritance*, Eph. 1); *both in sanctity or newness of life*, or in good works, *by which we make sure our calling and election*, as Peter speaketh; *both, finally, in the use of the Sacraments* — which are the *seals of grace* and *testimonies of our predestination*.

**XL.** This doctrine taketh away from us the confidence of our own merits, and stirreth us up to *make much of the ministry of the Word and Sacraments* (through which we are called), and impelleth us unto *gratitude for the immense goodness of God*, and consoleth us in the cross, and lifteth us up, and rendereth us undismayed *whatsoever indeed shall befall*, even should the whole world collapse — as Paul saith, 2 Tim. 2: *The foundation of God standeth firm, having this seal: The Lord knoweth those who are His.* And John 10: *My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me; and I give unto them eternal life, and they shall not perish for ever; and no one shall snatch them out of My hands.*

**XLI.** But the sum of this doctrine is this: **All who live and die in faith in Christ the Saviour, Redeemer, Mediator, and Justifier — are foreseen, elected, designated, called, justified, and destined unto glory, life, and eternal salvation, through and on account of the Son, out of the mere** *εὐδοκία*, **mercy, philanthropy, and love of God** — as rightly it is said: **God giveth. Christ meriteth or impetrateth. The Holy Spirit sealeth and confirmeth. Faith receiveth. Good works testify.** On the contrary, **all who either live or die without faith in the Son of God, are rejected and damned, and blotted out of the book of life or the catalogue of the just — not by God's fault** (who assuredly hath created no men unto ruin, if the counsel of creation and formation be considered) — **but by their own fault**, in that they have not believed in the only-begotten Son of God, as it is written.

**XLII.** **The third grade of God's presence** is that God is present unto the *blessed Angels and men in heaven*, and filleth them with His light, righteousness, and eternal life — giving Himself to be seen *visibly and immediately*, and never departing from them, even if He were only associate with them by that society whereby He is all in all.

**XLIII.** **The fourth grade** is *of the Son of God alone*, assuming *human nature* inseparably and by *personal union* — so that all the fulness of Divinity dwelleth in Christ the Son of Man *σωματικῶς* (bodily), Col. 2. And **Christ, the Son of God and Son of Man, is one person, without confusion of natures and without severance of natures and person, always and everywhere**. For He never and nowhere layeth down the human nature which He hath once assumed. And **Christ, wheresoever He is, is God and man — everywhere, the property of each nature being retained; and nowhere is He absolute God, but everywhere God incarnate**. ¹⁶⁹

**XLIV.** Moreover, the end of this doctrine of the providence of God is this: that we commend ourselves unto God, believe Him, obey Him, give Him thanks, fear, invoke, and celebrate Him; and that we despise the threats of the world and the Devil, and, in confidence of the care of God for us, discharge the offices of our vocation.

**XLV.** **The use consisteth in these**: if we have received anything good from God, that we celebrate Him with thanks; if any adverse thing hath befallen, that we be patient, and institute *examination of our life*, and acknowledge our sins, and amend. Let us also always fear God and invoke Him, and ask of Him to be aided, ruled, defended, and preserved — and let us be certain of the paternal care of God for us, we who have faith in His promises.

### CERTAIN OBJECTIONS OF THE STOICS, AND OF OTHERS, AGAINST THE DOCTRINE OF THE PROVIDENCE OF GOD.

**First.** *"It is impossible for two contradictories to be simultaneously true. This is true: 'Cicero shall be Consul.' Therefore its contradictory — 'Cicero shall not be Consul' — is not true. And consequently this — 'Cicero shall be Consul' — is necessarily true."*

**I answer to the minor.** The minor, insofar as it is a proposition concerning a *future contingent*, is not by any means determinately true. For *truth followeth the being of the thing*: as the thing is, so is the proposition true. Now the future contingent is as yet in reality itself *uncertain*; therefore also the proposition concerning the future contingent is uncertain. And even if afterward the event corresponds, yet the proposition *"Cicero shall be Consul"* is not true prior to the event's corresponding — save only by *necessity of consequence*. ¹⁷⁰

**Second.** *"Causes are connected — as the heat of the Sun, the earth, and fruits. But connected things act necessarily. Therefore there is necessity of motions and of actions."*

**I answer to the major.** The major is true concerning things acting *naturally*, not concerning voluntary things — because the *will is free*, and can assent to objects or resist them, and can rule the locomotive [faculty], as Basil saith: *τὰ ἔξω οὐκ ἐγὼ, ἀλλὰ ἐμὰ* ("Outer things are not mine, but my own [choices are]").

**Third.** *"Divine determination is immutable and necessary. All things happen with God determining. Therefore all things happen necessarily and immutably."*

**I answer to the minor.** All things happen with God determining, but *diversely*. For divine determination dependeth either upon the will of God Himself (as God determineth the future resurrection, and many other things, by His most free will), or is moved by our will (as God, foreseeing our sins, determineth how far He is going to permit them, and constituteth for us a *boundary* which it is not lawful to transgress). This foresight and divine determination is said to be *immutable and necessary — by necessity of consequence*, as to the event, not that it is the *cause* of the event, but because it concludeth the cause with a certain event. Wherefore the foresight and determination of God bringeth no necessity to our will acting ill, even if it bringeth necessity to the event by necessity of consequence — if we retain a depraved will of acting ill, and follow it. For God setteth a *term* to sins, and in His own time punisheth the contumacious. Hence Origen said: **Not because God foreknoweth something as future shall it therefore be — but because it is future, therefore is it known by God before it be done.** And hither in some way agreeth that similitude: Astrologers foresee the eclipse of Sun or Moon, conjunctions of the Planets, comets, and other things. Here the Mathematician's foresight is not the *cause* that such things happen, but because such things are to come, therefore are they foreseen. Foresight is thus as it were a *middle between the cause and the event*.

There is also to be held this distinction: **God foreseeth good things by knowledge, good pleasure or** *εὐδοκία*, **and disposition; but evil things He foreseeth only by knowledge and determination — how far He shall be about to permit them.**

**Fourth objection.** *"God's foresight is not deceived. But God's foresight would be deceived if those things did not happen which He foresaw. Therefore God's foresight is the cause of events."*

**I answer to the minor.** I deny the minor as it pertaineth to evil things. For God's foresight would not be deceived — rather it would be more confirmed and commended — if the man, God foreseeing and admonishing of the event of sins, should obey. But the foresight of God would be deceived if it itself were the cause of both the actions and the events — which since it is not, it is altogether false that it can be deceived. For also — by that saying which is said to be either done *in vain*, or to be nothing — God's providence is confirmed, God is affected with glory, and the Angels are made glad — namely, when an evil which God foresaw doth not befall, the man being converted unto God, which otherwise would have happened, if the man had not repented and turned unto God — as the example of the Ninevites showeth, who hear God foreseeing and indicating the punishments, and take away the cause of the punishments, and thus placate God, and avert the punishments themselves, which otherwise would have come, if they had not been converted unto God.

This too is true: that the foresight of God, by which He foreseeth our punishments and our ruin, is a *testimony of divine commiseration* — whereby God hath mercy on us, and admonisheth us unto penitence, and willeth *not our death but our life* — as Christ weepeth foreseeing the ruin of Jerusalem, Luke 19, and deploreth the blindness and *ἀναλγησίαν* (insensibility) of His people. Now therefore to say that the foresight of God is deceived, if that be changed which He foreseeth as future and hath signified to us if we be not converted — is the property of ingratitude, and in a certain manner *blasphemous*, as all the pious testify.

**Fifth.** *"If future things are the cause of God's foresight, and foresight doth not simply dispose and determine future things, then the knowledge of the Creator dependeth on creatures. But the knowledge of God is eternal, and dependeth not on creatures. Therefore future crimes and other future things are not the cause of foresight — but God Himself simply, as they ought to be and to happen, disposeth and determineth all things."*

**I answer to the minor.** The knowledge of God is eternal in a *twofold respect* — of divine omnipotence and of created things. For God, wise and omnipotent, from eternity foreknoweth and foreseeth all things which have been, which are, and which shall be for ever; and hath the first, most perfect, and most absolute *cognition of all things* — even of those which are not yet. But knowledge directed unto things which now exist and have been created by God — although it be from the prior knowledge, yet is by us better understood than the prior. Of this therefore we here speak, and say that *knowledge is proportioned to the being of the thing*. As the thing is, so is the knowledge of the thing. If the thing were other, the knowledge would also be other. Thus God seeth and knoweth future things — because they are such as future, He of Himself, according to His omnipotence and wisdom, foreseeth and foreknoweth them, and dependeth not on their event or condition.

But *how great is the malice*, willing to say that God's knowledge simply dependeth on the condition of future things — even as the Stoics bound God's power to secondary causes? God's eternal knowledge would be from eternity to eternity — wisdom and omnipotence — even if no thing ever had been created. But now, since He hath created things by His most free will, He knoweth them; and from head to foot, within and in the skin, all their *circumstances, conditions, fortunes, cases, and duration, actions, and events* He foreseeth.

I remember a certain wicked man was to be strangled, whose father, to liberate his son, approached the Emperor Charles V. — then dwelling in that place — and as suppliant interceded for his son. The Emperor, taking pity on the decrepit father's plight and on the grave and pious man, granted the son's life, and dismissed him free — commanded that he be restored to his father, with no severer discipline applied, save that he keep himself at home with his father and shun evil companies. The son, being freed, afterward often reproached his aged father with this very thing, saying: **"But thou wouldest never have been worthy of such honour as to speak with the Emperor, hadst it not been I."** Such, meseems, is the objection of those who say: **"But God would not foresee our actions, and there would be no knowledge in Himself concerning our things, if we did not do such things — we who are the cause that He knoweth and seeth these things."** This is the perversity and ingratitude of evil men, and a *contumely against God*. But if any wish to name the evil things future the *cause of God's foresight* — and understandeth "cause" as it is called *sine qua non* (without which not) — we do not fight with him, provided piety and modesty be present.

**Sixth.** *"He who foreseeth an evil impending, and can by no trouble avert it though able, and averteth it not, seemeth to delight in sin. God foreseeing evils could most easily avert them according to His omnipotence, yet averteth them not. Therefore God seemeth to delight in lapses."*

**I answer to the minor.** *In this doctrine, the power of God must altogether be distinguished from the will of God.* God could correct all things in one moment and restore them to right order. But His will is not violent — as though by one impetus it should destroy all things which are evil — but His will is: **First**, that the *rational creature*, which He hath endowed with liberty, should retain liberty and the *discrimination and election of good and evil*. **Then**, that through the Son may take place the *destruction of all the works of the Devil*, and that all believers in the Son may avoid *sins against conscience* and pursue righteousness. **Afterwards**, that in the *last judgment* there may be *visitation, examination, and separation* of the good and the evil — and evils be cast away for ever, goods remain for ever. This will hath been patefacted to us, in which we ought to acquiesce, and to bring against God no cause of any evil of guilt.

**Seventh.** *"He who sustaineth a sinning nature and doth not blot it out when He could, seemeth to delight in sin. God sustaineth the impious, and doth not straightway snatch them to punishment. Therefore He delighteth in sin."*

**I answer.** This is the same as the prior argument, even if in some way it seemeth other. The consequence must be denied, since it is *fallacia secundum non causam ut causam* (the fallacy of non-cause as cause). For the *created nature* must be distinguished from *impiety*. God sustaineth the *subject*, as His own work, even if against *impiety* (which is the destruction of the subject) He is vehemently angered. And hence appeareth *the immense goodness of God and* φιλοστοργία (paternal affection) — who seeth manifold blemishes and foulest leprosy in us, yet doth not straightway cast us away; but as a farmer in his orchard tolerateth sterile trees for some while, hoping that they may become tame by cultivation, so God granteth us space of doing penitence very prolix, and doth not straightway hasten unto extreme punishment — until, since we remain incurable, He rooteth up entirely and oppresseth; and, as before in our sustentation He gave His long-suffering to be beheld, so in punishment He seriously declareth His wrath against sin.

**Eighth.** *"Either it can happen otherwise than God hath foreknown, or not otherwise. If otherwise, then God's foreknowledge can be deceived and changed. If not otherwise, then all things happen necessarily."*

**I answer.** The argument is compounded of two questions — of which the prior is: *whether things foreseen by God can also be changed*, and *whether divine determination is immutable and necessary*. The latter is: *whether God's foreknowledge is deceived, if things do not happen as they were foreseen.*

Of the prior question it hath been said above in the solution of the third objection. Things foreseen by God, whose origin is drawn from our will, happen not otherwise — namely by *necessity of consequence*, when they have already been done. But they *can happen otherwise* before they be led out unto the foreseen event. God foreseeth the crimes of Nero, and determineth how far He shall be about to permit them. And Nero is punished, because he perpetrateth those crimes, and persevereth in them. Yet Nero ought to have and *was able* to omit those crimes and turn himself unto God — that he might not rush into crimes and fall into punishments.

Of the latter question it hath been said above in the solution of the fourth objection. God's foreknowledge is not deceived — since this very foresight of evils always hath joined to itself the *ratio, condition, and harmony of mercy and justice*. For God foreseeing crimes decreeth that He is going to punish them by reason of His justice, and to destroy the impious and those not turning to God; He decreeth also that He is going to *mitigate the punishments* through and on account of the Son, and to have mercy on all who, believing in the Son, do penitence and abstain from sins — as the examples of *Manasseh*, of the *Ninevites*, and others show. In this manner the foresight and determination of God in those things which principally arise from our will *always taketh place with the exception of penitence and conversion to God*, as it is written, Luke 13: *Unless ye do penitence, ye shall all likewise perish.* And Jer. 26: *If ye hearken unto Me, and desist from your evil ways, then will it repent Me of the evil which I thought to do unto you for your iniquities.*

**Ninth.** *"The second cause acteth not without the first. The second acteth necessarily. Therefore also the first."*

**I answer to the major.** The second acteth not without the first — namely, the *sustaining and preserving* one. The minor is too ambiguous. For if it be understood of things acting *naturally*, it is true: fire heateth iron applied to it by its nature. But if it be received concerning *voluntary things*, it is by no means true: an artisan doth not necessarily apply iron to fire. This ambiguity being shown, the objection of itself falleth. Also the consequence must be denied, since there is more in the conclusion than in the premises. For it doth not follow: *Fire necessarily heateth iron applied by the artisan; therefore the artisan necessarily applied it.* For the *prior and more potent cause* can act otherwise than the posterior and weaker cause.

**Tenth.** *"The second cause is efficacious of evil actions. Therefore also the first."*

I deny the consequent — and the reason is the same as in the prior argument. There is more in the conclusion than in the antecedent. **God aideth not evil actions**, even if He sustaineth the nature by Him created. Nor is He bound to secondary causes, whether they be celestial or natural or voluntary.

**Eleventh.** *"God often punisheth sins by sins — by tyranny, wars, and other modes. Therefore God willeth sin."*

**I answer.** God punisheth sins, and willeth the punishment by *the law of talion* — but willeth not sin. But as touching that the execution of the penalty is not without sin — the fault is not God's, but theirs who execute the penalty. **The law of legitimate penalty is of God's will. But the transgression of the law is of men**, who abuse their power, and therefore at length are punished by God, and are cast into the fire *as an useless rod which the father of the family hath used for the chastisement of his children* — as it is written of Assyria, Isa. 10: *O Assyria, rod of My fury, and staff of My wrath. Unto a hypocritical people I will send him, that he may trample them as the mire of the streets. But he thinketh not so, neither doth his heart conceive so; but he is cruel and proud, and arrogateth all things to himself; therefore at length, when I have accomplished My work, I will visit him and crush him.*

**Twelfth.** *"God willeth the evil of penalty. Therefore He willeth also the evil of guilt. The reason is: where guilt is, there is also penalty, and conversely — and he who willeth the one, willeth the other."*

**I answer.** This is a puerile argument or *enthymeme*, whose falsity is discerned in the omitted major: *"He who willeth the penalty, he willeth also the guilt."* This major is manifestly false. For God, magistrates, and judges will the penalty *because they will not the guilt* — and therefore punish the contumacious, that others being admonished may beware for themselves of sins and crimes, by which they merit the like penalties. Even the wicked themselves, *willingly rushing* into sin, do not therefore *will* the penalty.

**Thirteenth.** *"Many pious are pressed by various crosses which surely are from God — as the cross of Job. Therefore many evils are from God."*

The response is easy. **The cross of the pious is either exercise, or martyrdom, or punishment.** But every cross of the pious *conduceth to the good of the pious*, as is copiously shown in its place. Now the *evil of guilt* and the *evil of penalty* must be distinguished, as above hath been said. For if nature lacked sin, no cross would press the pious.

**Fourteenth.** *"It is written: I will harden Pharaoh's heart. And we pray: Lead us not into temptation. And Ps. 79: Thou dissipatest the covenant of Thy servant; Thou hast defiled his crown,* etc. *Therefore also the evils of guilt are from God."*

**I answer to the antecedent.** *Active verbs* in the Hebrew tongue very often signify *permission* and not *effection*. Therefore "I will harden" is: *I will suffer to be hardened, and Pharaoh to be carried away by his own impetus, since he willeth not to hear Me* — because God draweth him that is willing, not the resister.

**Rabbi Abraham**, author of the *Fasciculus Myrrhae* (Bundle of Myrrh), answereth: **Pharaoh was to himself the cause of his own hardening, and not God. Indeed God was a cause — but not otherwise than a stone in the way, upon which the incircumspect one striketh. For Pharaoh would not acknowledge the Lord, and by this very thing he was to himself the cause of his own perdition.**

**Rabbi Salomon** thus saith: **Pharaoh willed to act impiously and to irritate Me, therefore he was not worthy that My Spirit should descend into him and give him a tractable and perfect heart.** This explication pleaseth me greatly, because it showeth that those who *knowingly and willingly* act contumaciously against God rush therefrom into the depth of sins, and neither care for God nor for the Word of God — as many examples today among us show — and have hearts prefract, stony, iron, and are destitute of the Spirit of God.

**Aben Ezra** saith: The Lord hardened Pharaoh's heart *through many those signs* which He did in Egypt — whence Pharaoh was rendered worse, even though he sensed the open virtue of God; yet he willed not to give Him the glory due.

**Munster** saith: *"I will harden"* is the same as if God had said: **I know that Pharaoh's heart is to be hardened, and I shall use his hardening for your salvation unto My glory. I will object My Word and miracles unto him, from which he shall be more hardened — because he is impious by nature; and where the Word of God is proposed to the impious, he becometh more impious.** ¹⁷¹

But we retain — for the sake of the truth and the audience's capacity — the customary explication concerning *permission*, as above in the doctrine of Justification we have shown. For **God draweth back His paternal hand and permitteth the obstinate to be carried away by their own impetus, exposed to the power of the Devil** — even as the father repudiateth and disinheriteth an extremely contumacious son.

An example of this permission is 2 Kings 24: *The wrath of the Lord incited David to number the people.* And 1 Chron. 21: *Satan insufflated David to number Israel.* **What indeed is the "wrath of God"? It is when God permitteth us, who are evil, to be carried away by our own impetus, and to be exposed to the Devil, since we will not obey the Word of God.**

**Fifteenth.** *"All our hairs are numbered. Therefore all things happen necessarily."*

**I answer to the antecedent.** *The saying of Christ is a consolation proposed to the pious, and is not a Stoic axiom.* Nor doth it pertain to the impious and secure, who think that whatsoever happeneth, happeneth necessarily, and live basely.

**Sixteenth.** *"No one can believe in the Son of God unless he be led by the Spirit of God. Therefore our study, our care, and our labour are not required."*

**I answer to the antecedent.** We are led by the Holy Spirit — namely, *mediately through the Word* — not compelled, but hearing the Word and not contumaciously, of set purpose, and perseveringly resisting it. And John 6, the Son of God Himself saith: **No man cometh unto Me except the Father draw him** (namely, out of his miseries and the infernal pit); **and every one that heareth and hath learned of the Father, cometh unto Me.**

**Seventeenth.** *"Many are called, few are chosen. Therefore God by His eternal will willeth some to be damned."*

**I answer to the antecedent.** The saying of Christ is true — but not by reason of the will of God as *first cause of rejection*, but from *the malice and fault of man*. For **God willeth all to be saved**; but as for that this is not, it is the fault of men, evil by their own nature and *not hearing the Son of God* — as it is written: *He that believeth in the Son hath eternal life; he that believeth not is already judged, and the wrath of God abideth upon him.*

Let these sayings suffice concerning the providence of God — from which the younger may learn what is the sounder judgment, and, for the glory of God, may flee opinions and expressions *contumelious to God* and *harmful to life and morals*.

### On Those Assailed by the Temptation of Doubting Their Predestination.

At the end I shall add somewhat concerning that class of men who — assailed by grave temptations — complain that they are ignorant *whether they be certainly in the number of the predestinated*.

Now it is certain that among all temptations there is not one more difficult and more perilous than this very one, which concerning predestination falleth into a man's mind — whereby the man beginneth to *doubt whether he himself be in the number of the elect and inscribed in the book of life*. **Many even by this temptation fall into lethal diseases**, as examples everywhere testify; **many are consumed by sadness** whilst they *cry out of the depths* — as David in the Psalms (especially the 6th and 88th) complaineth; **many also, overcome by that diabolical temptation, are oppressed and driven unto despair** — of which tragedy I shall recite one example only, which happened in the year **1562**.

When a certain *Rector of a School*, despairing and ending his life by a noose on July 22, left behind after himself this writing:

> **"Sin against the Holy Spirit is: for a man, by sinning, to play with God — and so to be held on every side constricted by the sentence of the divine Law, that whither to escape he knoweth not, but pronounceth himself guilty of eternal damnation. This hath now happened to me, wretched, that I, addicted to eternal damnations, am thrust down to the never-ending Tartarus. By an external sanctity we cannot deceive God. Oh, most unhappy me of all — to whom it were better never to have been born!**
>
> **True it is, that the number of the saved is certain. This is from me: but what to me? Was it thus so necessarily to happen? I am of the number of the damned, and can never be ascribed to God — damned from the beginning. Therefore I go, eternal disgrace of my fatherland, a figment and vessel formed for ignominy. The magnitude of all sins hath assailed me, and the horror of the Devil. I depart unto the infernal lakes. Unto God I commend you, whose mercy hath been denied to me. Now more hidden is the cause of this thing than that human reason can look through it,"** etc.
>
> **Most lost — P. I. — himself subscribed.**

A like blasphemy also befell in the year **1548 at Cittadella in the Paduan territory, of the Venetian dominion** — where **Franciscus Spira** began to despair of the mercy of God, crying out that he was destined unto eternal torments, and that he could not love God but had a horrible hatred of Him — and this wretched man, rejecting all consolations from his despair, ended his life. ¹⁷²

These and many other things — such as the tragic examples of **Judas, Latomus, Hofmeister**, and the like — admonish us that we be most modest in feeling and speaking of the arcane mysteries of God; and that we pray God to sanctify us in His Word which is the truth — from which those lying and blasphemous spirits recede, and by their own fault and impudence (whereby they charge God with lying) rush into eternal punishments: not by God's eternal counsel, but by their own despair and repugnance and blasphemy. ¹⁷³

But *how* we should succour the consciences of the weak, lest they either stick in doubt of their election and of obtaining God's mercy, nor can extricate themselves therefrom; or drag others with themselves into the same peril; or plainly give place to the Devil and fall into despair — this the whole doctrine of the Gospel showeth, proposing to us the Son of God the Mediator, and *the Book of Life* which is: *He that believeth in the Son hath eternal life. I believe. Therefore I have eternal life.* For **the Book of Life is named the Gospel; the Book of Death is the Law itself, damning all the disobedient**; there is also the judgment of the Gospel: *He that believeth not in the Son, the wrath of God abideth on him.*

But there are *three things* by which we can rightly direct and overcome the temptations concerning predestination, through the grace of God: **First**, is the *true doctrine* sought from the Word of God. **Second**, is the *norm and rule* which can render our minds certain that we are not excluded from the number of the elect. **Third** are the *arms* by which in the very wrestling with the Devil we ought to come forth victors. Of these three we shall add a few things.

### 1. As to Doctrine — Three Rules.

As to what pertaineth to *doctrine*, these three rules are to be held:

**First:** *Nothing can or ought to be thought or said concerning predestination outside the manifest Word of God.* Therefore we must not indulge our own speculations, nor must attention be given to what others opine — but *unto the Law and the testimony*, that is, unto the Word of God (in which God hath patefacted Himself and His will unto us), we must run.

**Second:** *Whatsoever indeed is said concerning those to be saved and those to be damned, and concerning the eternal predestination or election unto goods and unto life, and the eternal reprobation of the impious*; likewise, *of the names and number of the saved and of the damned*, and of *immutable necessity*, and of some other things — which Christian piety and modesty forbid: whatsoever, I say, be said of these things — *always yet the mind, heart, spirit, and all the cogitations of man ought to be directed unto the certain and infallible scope which the doctrine of the Gospel showeth — that is, unto Christ, in whom whoso believeth, and departeth piously in faith, he from eternity is predestined unto life*. Nor have we any other interpreter or executor of predestination save the Son of God, in whom *all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid*. And there is no other Book of Life in which the saved may be contained, save the Book of the Gospel.

**Third:** It is most certain that *whosoever are saved, are saved by the gratuitous mercy of God through and on account of the Son*, in whom they have believed. On the contrary, *whosoever are damned, are damned by the just judgment of God by their own fault* — in that they have not acknowledged nor received Christ nor believed in Him.

By these rules is shown what predestination is, and how far we may rightly feel and speak concerning it. For **Predestination is that whereby God chose us in Himself, or in Christ, before the foundations of the world were laid, that we should be holy and irreprehensible in His sight through charity — that He might adopt us as sons through Jesus Christ in Himself, according to the good pleasure of His will**. Eph. 1.

But the questions — how God from eternity hath chosen us unto life, and how some are predestined unto salvation, others reprobated unto death, and this *from the goodness and justice of God so willing and ordaining*; likewise, whether some of the predestined can perish and be damned, and on the contrary whether some of the reprobates can at some time be saved; likewise, whether even sins themselves cooperate for good to the predestined, and virtues themselves fall out for evil to the reprobate; likewise, whether it is the sole will of God alone that maketh one to be chosen and another to be reprobated: **these and similar questions, either — as rocks and labyrinths — for the glory of God and the ratio of our conscience and the integrity of faith let us shun, or piously and modestly according to the norm of the Gospel let us explain** — of which now it must be said.

### 2. The Norm of the Gospel — Six Things.

The norm of the Gospel, according to which the consciences of the weak (contending in spiritual conflict, and desiring to be more certain of their predestination) must be counselled and succoured, consisteth chiefly in **six things**, which are:

1. **The** *εὐδοκία* (Good Pleasure) **of God.**
2. **Certitude of Vocation.**
3. **The Universal Promise of Grace.**
4. **The Doctrine of Justification and things connected with it.**
5. **Faith in Christ.**
6. **Consolations and Examples from Sacred Writings.**

**Of the** *εὐδοκία* **of God** it is said, Ezek. 18 and 33: *I will not the death of the sinner, but that he be converted and live.* And Matt. 3: *God is able of these stones to raise up sons unto Abraham.* And: *This is My beloved Son, in whom* εὐδόκησα (I have been well pleased). And Titus 2: ἐπεφάνη ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ, ἡ σωτήριος πᾶσιν ἀνθρώποις — *the grace of God hath appeared unto all men, salvation-bringing*.

**Of the certitude of vocation** Paul, Rom. 8, saith: *Those whom He predestined, these also He hath called.* Since therefore thou art called through the grace of God, and hearest the Gospel — know: **God willeth thou be saved; else He would not propose unto thee the voice of His Gospel.**

**Of the universal promise of grace** these evident testimonies are to be held, that with God there is no *προσωποληψία* (respect of persons): Deut. 10; Isa. 42; Job 34; 2 Chron. 19; Acts 10; Eph. 6; Rom. 2; Col. 3; Matt. 11: *Come unto Me all ye*. John 3, 6: *Everyone who believeth*. Joel 2 and Acts 2: *Everyone who shall have called upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.* Acts 10: *Unto Him all the Prophets bear testimony, that all who believe in Him receive the remission of sins through His name.* Acts 13: *In Him everyone that believeth shall be justified.* Rom. 3: *the righteousness of God through faith of Christ, unto all and upon all.* Isa. 38; Rom. 10: *Everyone that trusteth in Him shall not be shamed.*

And this most true rule is to be held: **As the comminations are universal and pertain unto all who have sinned, so the promises are universal and pertain unto all who believe in Christ.**

**Of the doctrine of justification** it is certain that as often as it is set forth, faith is felt in our souls, and joy — or some *motion, sparks and flames* — which however small they be, provided they lean upon the divine promises, testify with certainty *that we are in the number of the sons of God*. And there accede the *Sacraments, which are seals of righteousness*.

**Of faith in Christ** I shall add the most sweet words of **Gerhard**:

> **No way is open by which thou mayest attain how thou art elect, save that thou humbly descend unto the humble Christ — to whom the Father hath committed all judgment — nor that thou believe on the same Christ, in whom alone the Father revealeth the hidden sentence of His predestination. In vain doth he labour concerning predestination, whosoever seeketh its cognition outside Christ. For the Father judgeth no one, but hath given all judgment to the Son (John 5); in which Son whosoever truly believeth, let him not doubt that he is transcribed into the catalogue of those to be saved. All that the Father giveth Me — saith Christ, John 6 — shall come unto Me, and him that cometh unto Me I will not cast out. And a little after: This is the will of Him who sent Me, the Father: that of all which He hath given Me I lose nothing, but should raise it up at the last day. And this is the will of Him who sent Me: that everyone who seeth the Son and believeth on Him have life eternal, and I will raise him up at the last day. What need of many words? Such as thou understandest thyself truly to be in Christ, such do thou esteem thyself to be in God the Father also: and if thou truly believe in Christ, thou shalt have eternal life, and the Father acknowledgeth thee in the number of those to be saved,** etc. ¹⁷⁴

Let us also hold these as it were **heads**:

1. If we hear the doctrine of the Gospel — that is, are in the assembly of the called, where is the voice of the Gospel and the use of the Sacraments.
2. If we believe in the Son of God, Redeemer, Justifier, Mediator, and our Saviour.
3. If we acknowledge the imbecility of our faith, and deplore it, and pray God to increase and confirm our faith and make us temples of the Holy Spirit.
4. If we would willingly and from our soul obey God.
5. If we rejoice in the most sweet name of Jesus.
6. If in the cross we are patient and constant, and commit our will to the divine will.
7. If it grieveth us as often as we perceive we have failed and have offended God, and we flee unto the *Asylum* — the Son of God — etc.

**All these are infallible testimonies that we are the sons of God.**

**Of examples and consolations** it is said copiously elsewhere. Let there be held in readiness the illustrious examples of *David, Peter*, and the *thief on the cross*. Consolations abound in the doctrine of the Gospel — as are Isa. 53: *Truly our languors He hath borne.* 1 Tim. 1: *This is a certain word and worthy of all acceptation: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners.* 1 Tim. 2: *He gave Himself* ἀντίλυτρον (as a ransom). Matt. 11: *Come unto Me all ye,* etc. John 3: *So God loved the world.*

### 3. Luther's Four Rules — Arms Against Diabolical Fiery Darts.

Now since hitherto this doctrine hath been copiously stated, how the fiery darts of the Devil are to be shaken off, and by what arms these temptations concerning predestination are to be conquered, we shall show by **four rules which D. Luther, by the peculiar Spirit of God, delivered**.

**I. RULE.** — It is certain that *perilous cogitations concerning predestination are the snares and assaults of the Devil* — and, according to that saying, Prov. 25: *The scrutinizer of majesty shall be oppressed by glory.* And Sir. 3: *Seek not things higher than thyself, but those things which God hath commanded thee, those care for.* And David, Ps. 131, complaineth that he hath ill counselled himself as often as he willed to explore sublime things, saying: *If I did not humbly feel, and restrain my soul, then were I made like a child weaned from his mother.*

**II. RULE.** — *Nowhere hath God commanded that we should render ourselves solicitous concerning election and the ratio and way of our salvation* — but He only willeth that we ourselves be *hearers*, as He saith: *I am the Lord thy God.* Likewise, *This is My beloved Son, hear ye Him.*

**III. RULE.** — The mind and heart of man ought to fix its foot **not in speculations or in labyrinths of disputations, but in the express Word and mandate of God**.

**IV. RULE.** — **The greatest mandate of God is: that we hear the Son — in whom, as in a mirror, we contemplate the immense love of God toward us.**

According to these rules the devil is to be driven away; and thus can victory be obtained against spiritual temptations and doubts, the Holy Spirit consoling, confirming, and lifting up the soul and conscience. And let this only be said of the *first class of men beginning to doubt* concerning the grace of God and their own salvation.

But if beside these there befall temptations *concerning unworthiness*, let us know that **Christ came into the world that He might make sinners saved** — and let us consider the example of the *Canaanite woman* (Matt. 15) crying: *Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David.* But if we complain of defect of faculty and impotence, this hindereth nothing. For that very fact that thou *willest* to believe, however languid it be, is the most certain testimony **that thou art the domicile and temple of the Holy Spirit**. For it is God who worketh in us, both to will and to accomplish. And **to will to be just is the highest justice; and to be able to pray, *Lord I believe, but help Thou my unbelief* (Mark 9) — this indeed is the infallible** τεκμήριον **(sign) of the presence and efficacy of the Holy Spirit**. Let us pray therefore that we may believe, and know: so long as we are *able to pray*, all things with us are yet safe, and faith is kindled in us, and we are truly the sons of God.

# Locus IV. De Ecclesia · On the Church.

We have comprehended the doctrine of the Church integrally in the *Second Part of our Paedagogia* and in the *second tractate of the Analecta*. Therefore here we shall be briefer, and shall only add as it were *paralipomena* (things left over) to what we there more prolixly discussed, and it pleaseth us to institute an *anacephalaeosis* (recapitulation). Of these things therefore we shall treat briefly, with God's help. ¹⁷⁵

### The Ten Questions.

1. Of the **word Ecclesia**, and *what the Church is*.
2. Of the **Church before the Fall**, and after the Fall of man.
3. That there is **but one Church**.
4. Of the **signs that show the true Church**.
5. Of the **doctrine of the Church**.
6. Of the **one and perpetual Head of the Church, Christ**, and of the *government of the Church, or the Kingdom of Christ*.
7. Of the **power and authority of the Church**.
8. Of the **primacy of the Roman Church**.
9. Of the **ecclesiastical ministry**.
10. Of **traditions**.
