## V. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.

We are all **debtors of God**, on many accounts. God committeth unto us — to be rightly used and administered as unto servants and stewards — the *soul, reason, will, life; the body, members, health, ears, eyes, hands, feet, tongue; Word, Law, Gospel, and Sacraments; vocation in the Church, in polities, in families; conscience; temporal goods; the neighbour also — to be aided in whatever pious mode we can*. And of all these things, of which we are by no means lords but *dispensers unto the glory of God and unto our own and the neighbour's use* — according to the prescription of God, *a most severe ratio* is to be rendered, namely: *in the Word, in the sermon of the Law, likewise in conscience, in the cross also, in diseases and perils, and in the last agony, and finally in the last judgment*. But we cannot be *solvent* — yet as before we remained debtors of *office and dispensation*, so now we remain debtors of *solution or satisfaction* — obligated unto solution which we cannot however render.

**Debts** therefore are called **sins** by which we offend God and merit God's wrath. And any transgression of the Law is called a **debt** which obligateth unto satisfaction, unless there be a gratuitous remission. For *the whole life of man is damnable, contemptible, and unfruitful*. And *every tree which maketh not good fruit is cut down and cast into the fire*. And every debtor who is not solvent *is incarcerated, until either he satisfy or have intercessors*.

**Because of the infinite debts, therefore, we are all and each *sons of wrath* and *liable to eternal punishments*** — so that even the innocent before God is not innocent. *Unto Thee, O Lord, is justice, but unto us the confusion of face.* And we all hear the *sentence of the Law*: *Cursed is every one who hath not done all things which are written in the Law.*

There is need therefore of a **confession of debts** — ingenuous, open, humble, and suppliant — in which we must flee unto the *mercy of God exhibited in the Son, through the Son, and on account of the Son*. *Have mercy on me, O God. Enter not into judgment with Thy servant. Be propitious to me, a sinner. Remember not, O Lord, the delicts of my youth and my folly. A contrite and humble heart Thou wilt not despise. Convert me, and I shall be converted; heal me, and I shall be healed. Remit sins.*

**On account of the Son, therefore, God gratuitously remitteth to all believing in the Son and fleeing unto the mercy shown in the Son — all and every sin and debt** — so that each may say: *I believe the remission of sins* — as the Son of God saith: *Trust, my son; thy sins are remitted unto thee.* For *the blood of Christ cleanseth us from all iniquity*.

### On the Second Part of the Petition — "As we forgive our debtors."

But that our faith be not *hypocritical, dead, and idle*, there is need of a *declaration of faith*, or of *fruits toward our neighbour* — a consort with us of the same grace of God, of life, and of salvation. **Unto the neighbour therefore we ought to remit the debt** — that is, *offences and many injuries*. Now here it is not said of *contracts*, nor are the offices of vocation taken away — as of ministers of the Word, of the political magistracy, of preceptors and parents — but it is prescribed to each severally that they *remit and condone unto the neighbour hurts and offences*, and imitate *the immense mercy of God* — who, since He hath remitted to us *sixty tons of gold*, willeth that we remit to the neighbour *ten crowns* — as in the parable Matt. 18 is shown, where Christ, to Peter asking whether it be enough to remit seven times to the neighbour, responded: *Not seven times, but seventy times seven.*

Hither pertaineth the *integral doctrine on sin, on the Law, on the mercy of God, on confession, on the remission of sins and the justification of man before God, and on the mutual condonation of errata* which are wont to occur.

Of **original sin** and its propagation into the whole human race, and likewise of *actual sin*, it hath been said above. And always the gravity of sin must be estimated seriously — from the punishment which followed Adam's lapse; from our public and private calamities; especially from the *dignity of the price* by which we have been redeemed from the right of sin; and finally from the *comminations of eternal punishments* which God threateneth seriously against the non-converted or non-penitent.

We have also spoken **On the Law** in its place, and shown why no man can satisfy it. For in the Law we see who is our *Creditor* — namely, God Himself — and what a ratio He exacteth of us, and how great is the sum of our debt, and how great our inopia and misery, malediction also, and damnation.

**On the mercy of God** in the doctrine of the Gospel it is always said: *So God loved the world.* — *There hath appeared the philanthropy and benignity of God the Saviour unto all men.* — *The mercy of God from progeny into progeny unto them that fear Him.* — *I live, saith the Lord, I will not the death of the sinner.*

**On confession** above, in the locus on penitence, we have said somewhat. For God willeth that we *acknowledge and confess our sins in true humility, and ask pardon in true faith*, as it is written: *I said, I will confess my transgressions unto the Lord, and Thou hast remitted the impiety of my sin — for which every saint shall pray unto Thee.*

**On the remission of sins** in the doctrine of justification it hath been said. *Our Creditor God remitteth our debts* — that is, *He looseth the obligation unto eternal death and damnation*, and *condoneth the debt-due penalty*, and, sins being condoned, *receiveth man into grace out of mere mercy on account of the Son the Mediator* — as Isa. 45 it is written: *I, I am He who blot out thine iniquities before Me, and shall not remember thy sins.* And Ps. 103: *As far as East is from West, He hath made our iniquities far from us.* And Col. 2: *He hath blotted out the handwriting which was against us, which was contrary to us.*

As often as we hear the voice of the **remission of sins**, let us know that we are always admonished of these greatest things:

1. **Of sin**, which even all the saints carry about with them in this life.
2. **Of faith**, or firm confidence in God's mercy — conceived from His promise through the Holy Spirit — by which each firmly establisheth that unto him, believing in this life, is *certainly given the remission of sins on account of the victim of the Son*.
3. **Of grace and gift.** Gratuitously we are absolved from sins, and Christ's righteousness is imputed to us, and we are accepted unto eternal life on account of Christ. Being justified we are also *gifted with the Holy Spirit and regenerated*, that we may be a *new creature*, and live according to God's will, warring the good warfare, retaining faith and a good conscience.
4. **Of the certitude and immoveable truth of the divine promise**, which is daily new and fresh, and by *continuous course remitteth guilt and eternal punishment* to all believers.
5. **Of the precious λύτρον (ransom) of the victim of the Son of God**, by whose merit, virtue, and benefit we are received into grace.
6. **Of the open gate of salvation** unto miserable and afflicted consciences.
7. **Of the fount of all consolation** in all adversities and temptations, and in the agony of death.
8. **Of the eversion of all human merits.**
9. **Of the errors of the Monks**, which are: *doubt of remission, satisfactions, purgatory, confidence in works*. Likewise of the **Novatians**, on the *denied return of the lapsed unto grace*.

These and more the word *Remission* proposeth for us to consider. But with the faith of the remission of sins is conjoined the **mutual condonation of errata**, whereby some condone to others sins and offences without *affect of private vengeance* — and so, even if by office (or in the Church, as in excommunication, or in polity) there be need of *just and serious animadversion*, yet let *commiseration not be absent*, and if it be possible, let ἐπιείκεια (equity) be applied, and let all things be undertaken more unto *correction and edification than unto destruction*. Unto this mutual condonation let these causes impel us:

1. **The mandate of God.**
2. **The example of God.**
3. **The state of the Kingdom of heaven**, in which sins are remitted gratuitously.
4. **The consideration of our fellow-servants and brethren.**
5. **The exiguous debt**, respect of the sins remitted to us.
6. **The good example** which is offered to others by benignity.
7. **The tranquillity of conscience** and the integrity of reputation.
8. **The augmentation of divine blessing.** For God favoureth the placid.
9. **The corporal and eternal punishments of the irreconcilable.** They fall from God's grace, and at last fall into the hands of the tormentors, who are the Devils.
10. **Public tranquillity.**
11. **Vengeance to be committed unto God.**
12. **The instability and fragility of life.**

**The sum of the fifth petition is this:**

> *Our sins and offences, by which we have offended and irritated Thee, God our Father, and are liable to eternal punishments — remit unto us. For we confess ourselves most wretched sinners to have infinite sins, and manifoldly to have failed and to fail, and we grieve with our whole breast that we have offended Thee, and we pray that on account of Thy Son our Lord Jesus Christ, crucified for us and resuscitated, Thou wilt have mercy on us, and remit unto us all our sins and all impurity — and justify us through and on account of Thy Son our Lord Jesus Christ, whom Thou hast willed to be for us a victim,* καὶ μεσίτην καὶ ἱκέτην, *by wonderful and inenarrable counsel, and by immense wisdom and goodness — and sanctify and regenerate us by Thy Holy Spirit, alive, chaste, and truthful — that we may truly acknowledge Thee — the omnipotent true God, the eternal Father of our Lord Jesus Christ — and Jesus Christ Thy Son our Lord, and Thy Holy Spirit alive, chaste, and truthful — and truly fear Thee, truly believe in Thee, rightly invoke Thee, truly obey Thee, give Thee thanks, serve Thee, and see Thee propitious in all eternity. Convert us, eternal God, unto righteousness and eternal life, and teach, rule, and aid us, and make us vessels of mercy, salutary organs for our souls and for Thy Church. Give increase of faith. Give that we may prefer obedience toward Thee above all the goods of the world, in prosperities and adversities. Rule us by Thy Spirit, that we may take in good part the errors of others, and interpret unto the better part — that we be not calumnious censors, or rash — but that we may first acknowledge the beam in our own eyes before we try to extract the mote out of the eye of our neighbour. Give us mild, humane, and placid affects, that willingly, by Thine example and mandate, we may remit unto others who have hurt us their offences. Cohibit and repress in us whatsoever is proud, turgid, ambitious, arrogant, iracund, and avaricious. Let not the sun set upon our wrath. And O Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, bend our souls unto consideration and imitation of Thy voice: "Learn of Me, because I am meek and humble of heart." Restore and preserve peace and salutary concord among the members of the Church, that we may be and remain one in Thee.*

**Antithesis.** **Sins of weakness and ignorance. For the just falleth seven times a day. Rigour** καὶ ἀκριβοδίκαιον **or strict justice in inquiring into others' errata. For the highest right is the highest injury. Pride. Iracundity. Impatience. Tyranny. Cruelty. Morosity and difficulty in morals. Inhumanity. Pertinacity of wrath, envy, hatred, livor, rancor. Discord and dissensions in the Church. Iniquitous delations, calumny, lies, private vengeance,** σκυθρωπὸν καὶ ἀδιάλλακτον **or being irreconcilable**, etc. All these we deprecate in the fifth petition.

Furthermore this too must be added: our remission by no means can be called *the cause of divine remission*, because that is *gratuitous*. Wherefore to the argument (*"Remit and it shall be remitted unto you; therefore our condonation meriteth remission"*) rightly is answered: *this sentence is a discourse of penitence*, of which discourse the parts are two — **precept** and **promise**. Now, the promise being heard, the mind beholdeth the *doctrine on remission promised gratuitously on account of Christ*. But it signifieth that this work is required — namely, *our condonation*, as also our other works — and that it *pleaseth*: not because there is no nevus in the soul at all, but that *the pious mind resisteth malevolence and hatred on account of the mandate of God and the concord of the Church*, and acknowledgeth that *this moderation pleaseth God on account of Christ*, even if some *scar and imbecility remain in us*.

## VI. And lead us not into temptation.

**Temptation** is *a solicitation and impulsion of man, arising either from the flesh, or from the world, or from the Devil, unto something which displeaseth God and bringeth eternal ruin*.

**"To lead into"** — by Hebrew phrase — is *to suffer or permit a man both to fall into temptations, and to be conquered by them, and to be impelled unto sinning*. To be tempted *through itself* is not evil. *For what things doth an untempted man know?* But that we be not *involved in evil temptations perilous to our salvation and be overwhelmed by them*, we ask.

Now customarily is recited a threefold temptation: (1) **of seduction**, (2) **of presumption**, (3) **of probation**.

**Temptation of seduction** against the Law of God is either *intrinsic*, arising from evil concupiscence and the flesh; or *extrinsic*, arising either from *the vanity and improbity of the world alluring man unto sinning*; or *from the Devil the tempter, who by corruptions of doctrine and wicked-life examples and occasions assaileth men insidiously, seeking whom he may devour*; or *from things surrounding us* — as before us: *death, God's judgment, and hell*; behind us: *past sins, commissions and omissions*; on the right: *power, riches, honour*; on the left: *perils, persecutions, scandals, external form of the Church*.

**Temptation of presumption** is that by which man tempteth God, *abusing the longanimity, patience, and mercy of God, and the liberality and divine benefits*.

**Temptation of probation** is good, and hath God as author, who — that we may be rendered *more approved unto ourselves* — tempteth us *in doctrine, in morals, and in signs of wrath*.

- **In doctrine** God tempteth us when He permitteth *false doctors* to come and to propose various erroneous dogmas — as it is written, Deut. 13: *The Lord your God tempteth you, that it may be manifest whether ye love Him or not in your whole heart and in your whole soul.* For thus are made *manifest the hearts of many* — as today we see, full either of *ignorance and negligence, of security, of levity and inconstancy, of doubts,* καὶ ἀπιστίας ἢ κακοπιστίας. And this temptation is ascribed to God insofar as it is *of probation*, not insofar as it is *of seduction* — for *δοκιμασίαι* have God as author, not *τιμωρίαι* (punishments).
- **In morals or obedience** God proveth His own, when He *imposeth certain exercise of cross* upon them — as when He commandeth Abraham to sacrifice his only-begotten son, and when He afflicteth Job manifoldly. For it is written, Deut. 5: *The Lord tempteth thee, that it may be known what is in thy heart, whether thou shouldst walk in His mandates or not.*
- **In signs** God often tempteth us, when He *proposeth in heaven, earth, sea, horrid signs of His wrath*, by which the souls of the pious are shaken — as it is written, Exod. 20: *Fear not, for God is come that He might tempt you, and that the terror of Him might be in you, that ye should not sin.*

**The sum of the sixth petition therefore is this:**

> *We beseech Thee — O eternal God — to illumine and sanctify us; and so rule our minds that we may think those things which are approved by Thee and which are salutary unto us. Create in us a clean heart, and a firm and new Spirit in our inwards. Kindle in us clean affects which may respond to pious and holy cogitations; and bend the consent of the will unto piously-thought things — that we may always think, speak, and do pious, holy, and chaste things. Preserve, augment, confirm in us meditation and memory of pious matters. Grant us victory against the flesh, the world, and the Devil. Aid us: we perish. Preserve us: we are overthrown. Free us, rule, defend, govern — that we may avoid the fiery darts of the Devil, who** ἀσπόνδως **waketh war against Thee and Thy Church. Adjoin unto us Thine Angels, companions and defenders of our life against the devils. Let none snatch us — Thy sheep — from Thy hand. Let us not fall into errors and into wickedness — withdraw not Thy hand from us — but make that we be and remain Thy temples, and triumph against the flesh, the world, the Devil, and death.*

**Antithesis.** **Impure cogitations. Depraved and vitiated affects. Impure will. Depraved companies, and occasions of sinning. The various techne of the Devil and of the world, and its enticements. Likewise terrors, mockeries, manifold temptations, sadness, doubt of God's grace, distrust: idolatry, superstition, profane security, wickedness and tragic ruins.**

## VII. But deliver us from evil.

**Deliverance** signifieth both *mitigation and final deliverance*. But **evil** is here understood *of punishment*. For evil is twofold: **of guilt** (which hitherto we have deprecated), and **of penalty** (which we here deprecate).

**Evil of penalty** is the *tyranny of devils and every other calamity by which the Church and her members in this life are pressed* — either privately, in soul, body, reputation, fortunes, life — or publicly, in the common society: *through wars, scandals, heresies, seditions, hypocrisy, sophistic*.

Of the discrimination between *the evil by which the Church is pressed*, and *the evil by which the impious are affected*, it hath been said in the locus on calamities and the cross. The discrimination is taken:

- From the **efficient causes**. Of the pious it is written: *The Lord chasteneth those whom He loveth* — namely, by paternal love. But the impious He punisheth *by just indignation as Judge*.
- Then from the **final causes**. The pious are *proved and corrected*. The impious are *coerced and destroyed*.
- Afterward from the **effects**. The pious *give thanks to God in the cross*; the impious *fret and impatiently grieve and are confounded, and despair*.
- Likewise from **time and place**. The pious for a *short time* in this world bear the cross imposed on them by God. The impious are involved in *perpetual evil*, and their fire is never extinguished.

**And God freeth His Church and all the pious in a twofold way — by aiding and by fully freeing.** For He mitigateth the *present evil* and giveth *strength to bear it patiently*, and observeth a certain *vicissitude*, mingling *gladness with sadness and sadness with gladness*, and often by *internal and spiritual goods compensateth the bitterness of external evil*. But on the *last day* He shall fully free us not only from every evil, but even from *fear and peril of every evil*.

**The sentence of the petition therefore is this:**

> *Give us, O propitious Father, peace of the whole Church, spiritual and corporal, and private tranquillity and quiet: safety, good health. Mitigate the calamities by which we are justly pressed for sins. Correct us in judgment, and not in fury, lest we be reduced to nothing. Console and confirm all the afflicted by Thy Holy Spirit, give lightening and make placid exits. Adjoin unto us the Angels' guards, and preserve us in all our ways. Govern the course of our life amid perils unto the desired exit. When from this life we must depart, give us a placid migration — that in true acknowledgment and invocation of Thee we may placidly die, and not be long tortured; and receive our soul into Thy hands, and transfer us into eternal life and felicity.*

**Vida:** ¹⁹⁹

> *Give, Father, when the last hour of life shall come,*
> *Thyself to me present, with no shades terrifying,*
> *And in Thine embrace to pour forth my soul exulting —*
> *This only add to me, though others may desire more.*

**Antithesis.** **Wars, public and private scandals, seditions, schisms, and heresies: diseases, sorrows of soul, obtrectation, infamy, misfortune: the kingdom of Satan, of sin and of death: sudden and tragic death, despair, eternal damnation.**

## Doxology: Thine is the Kingdom, and the Power, and the Glory, for ever.

This confirmation and κορωνίς (crown) hath **three members**, of which:

- **The first** is taken from the **office of the King**, who ought to protect and cherish his subjects.
- **The second** from the **power of God**, which is opposed to our infirmity and indigence, and rouseth God to commiseration — who alone can aid us miserable.
- **The third** from the **final cause**, which is *the glory of God* — that is, the *confession, celebration, and preaching of the divine aid* — by which at the same time the devils and enemies of God are refuted, when God is present and aideth the Church, as it is written, Ps. 6: *The Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping — let all mine enemies be ashamed and troubled*, etc.

## Amen.

This is the **voice of faith**, and *the sealing of the petitions*, signifying **certitude, or certain hearing, and firm faith and hope** — opposed to all diffidence and doubt — and leaning upon the promise of Christ saying: *Amen, amen I say unto you, whatsoever ye shall have asked the Father in My Name — that is, in acknowledgment and invocation of Me — He will give you.*

**Thou willest to give what we have asked, because Thou art King and our Father, we the people are Thy people and Thy sons. Thou canst give what we have asked, because Thou art omnipotent — God the Father, Son the** θεάνθρωπε, **and Holy Spirit — we are weak and wretched. Thou hast said, Thou hast promised. Thy saying is the same as its being done. Thou through Thy Word hast been made our debtor. Thou owest, because Thou hast promised. Once Thou hast said,** *Let it be*. Therefore that which Thou hast said shall be done. **We believe Thy Word, and certainly know that we are heard and saved. Therefore we say Amen with joyful and strong soul.** *Lord, we believe; but help our weakness.* We say **Amen** — believing, wishing, hoping. **Do Thou** say **Amen** by commanding — that is: *Let it be. Let it be unto us according to Thy Word. Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us. Say unto us the word which Thou saidst to the Syrophenician woman: "Let it be unto thee as thou wilt." Hear us, if not according to our will, certainly unto our salvation. Great is Thy faithfulness. Thou art our portion, O Lord — sayeth our soul — therefore we hope in Thee. In Thee, O Lord, I have hoped — let me not be confounded for ever. Amen.*

### A Recapitulating Amen-Prayer.

**Our Father, exalted in creation, sweet in love, rich in inheritance: Who art in heaven — mirror of eternity, crown of jocundity, treasure of felicity.**

**Hallowed be Thy Name** — that it may be to us *honey in the mouth, harp in the ears, ardour in the heart*.

**Thy Kingdom come** — *jocund without permixture, tranquil without perturbation, secure and stable without loss*.

**Thy will be done, as in heaven so also on earth** — *that what Thou hatest, we may shun; what Thou lovest, we may love; what Thou willest and commandest, we may do, Thee giving*.

**Give us this day our daily bread** — *necessary unto the sustenance of life, not superfluous, not deficient*.

**And forgive us our debts, whatsoever against Thee we have committed, or against the neighbour, or against ourselves — as we also forgive our debtors, who have offended us in words, or in persons, or in things.**

**And lead us not into temptation** of the world, of the flesh, of the demon.

**But deliver us from evil**, *present, past, and future*. **Amen.**

# Locus V. Doctrina de Sacramentis · The Doctrine of the Sacraments.

**The merciful God hath added to His Word from the beginning of the world always certain external signs, incurring the eyes of men, that they might be *testimonies and seals of the promise of grace comprehended in the Word*** — as were all the *ceremonies of the Old Testament*, which as it were *in type* signified the future *Seed of the woman*, and in the souls of the holy Fathers always sounded that promise made to our first parents: *The Seed of the woman shall crush the head of the serpent* — as were **circumcision, the slaying of the paschal lamb**, and similar ceremonies, whose unique end was that they might be *signs of the will of God toward us*, and, as Paul calleth them, ***σφραγίδες τῆς δικαιοσύνης τῆς πίστεως*** — that is, *testimonies added to the promise of grace, which is to be apprehended by faith*.

And as in the Old Testament ceremonies were added to the promise of grace, so also in the New Testament certain external signs have been added to the *promise of the remission of sins, of righteousness, and of eternal life given us now on account of Christ* — signs which certify us of the promise of grace, in which are offered to believers *the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life on account of the Son*. And there are two chief external rites of this sort in the New Testament added to the promise of grace: namely, **Baptism** and **the Lord's Supper** — of which we shall speak separately, having first premised the exposition of the very word *Sacrament*.

## The Definition of Sacrament.

A simple description of the word, as we speak in the Church, is this:

> **A Sacrament is a sacred ceremony or action instituted by God, in which God by His immense goodness and mercy exhibiteth unto us something eximious and singular — consisting of *Word and integral element* — to which action there is added a *promise which is proper to the doctrine of the Gospel* — that it may confirm and seal faith in the living.**

That the whole definition may be more rightly understood, its particles are severally to be considered.

### "A Sacrament is a sacred action" —

Here first a puerile discrimination must be held, which discerneth ***sacrifices*** from ***Sacraments***. For these two words do not signify the same thing:

- **Sacrifices** are said [to be] *actions divinely instituted, in which we render unto God certain works — to this end, that we may affect Him with honour* — sacrifices which please God if they are made in *acknowledgment and faith of the Son of God*, and are *principally referred unto this end, that God may be affected with honour* — as *prayers, labours, studies, and all the works of our vocations*.
- **Sacraments** are *actions divinely instituted, in which — or through which — God exhibiteth to us promised goods through and on account of the Son*: namely, *the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit regenerating us, righteousness, and eternal life*.

### "A sacred action instituted by God" —

In these particles many matters are contained. For first, the *Sacrament is discerned* from all other actions *natural or physical, and political*. The water of Baptism, by which the *formale of sin* is washed away, hath not *physical causes*, but resteth solely upon the *Word* — which if it be absent, the water is water and remaineth water. *On account of the Word*, saith **Augustine**, *it is a bath: withdraw the Word, what shall the water be but water?* So the *Lord's Supper* is a sacred action, not physical or natural — because it inhereth in the *Word*, and without the Word it is nothing but bread; it is no longer the very Body of Christ, nor is the wine any longer the very Blood of Christ, but is an element differing in nothing from the rest of breads and wines. **For the efficacy of the Sacraments is founded not in the element, but in the Word.**

Then, the Sacraments are not *civil actions* — that is, not only are they *notes of certain professions* by which Christians join themselves distinctly from other men (Jews, Turks, and other professors of something else) — nor are they *allegories of certain works, of calamities, of mutual dilection, of charity*, etc. — as the *Anabaptists* feign.

But **chiefly** it is added in the definition: **the Sacrament is such a sacred action as is instituted by God**. For God is (as we customarily speak) the **cause efficient of the Sacraments**, and He willeth to be obeyed — He willeth those things which He hath instituted to be preserved and celebrated *just as He hath instituted them*, and as *in His Word they have been proposed*. And hence at length emergeth **the foundation of the whole Christian Church** — which is: *out of the sole Word of God all things in the Church must be judged*. And this is the *Lydian stone* by which we can prove all spirits, and by which we discern *true worships of God from superstitions and other things which have not the express mandate of God* — as are the **idols**.

For an *idol* is *what is said either to be God, and is not God; or to which God is bound, without the express Word* — as in the Supper of the Lord a manifest idol is the *circumgestation* of the bread. For the Sacrament is transferred to another use than that unto which God instituted it. **But God willeth not to be bound to anything without His Word** — that is, He willeth these worships alone to be performed unto Him, and willeth those alone to be approved by Himself which He Himself by His Word hath instituted — as the rule testifieth (extant in Isaiah, and by Christ repeated): *No work is a worship of God which God commandeth not by His Word*. For thus Christ saith: *In vain do they worship Me by the mandates of men.* And Deut. 4 God severely commandeth, saying: *Ye shall not add above the Word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish from it.* And Deut. 12 the same sentence is repeated: *Whatsoever I command, observe to do it: thou shalt not add anything upon it, nor diminish from it.*

**Great blasphemy therefore it is to transfer to another use than that unto which they were instituted by God, the things which God hath instituted.** *Eat*, saith Christ, *and drink*. This action of *eating and drinking* in the Church must be retained — not others feigned by men, and by the mere tyranny of the more powerful obtruded upon the inferior.

Often we wonder — or rather shudder — when we hear and read *the idols of the Gentiles*, which men ignorant of the true doctrine concerning God feigned. But so severe and hard a judgment is not to be expected from them as from those who *have God's Word*, from which they can learn *what the will of God is, what worships He willeth to be attributed to Himself, and how He willeth to be celebrated* — and yet dare, against the *manifest Word of God*, and against the manifest truth and the expressed will of God in the Word, to erect worships altogether *fictitious, empty, and Gentile* — which not only God doth not approve, but averteth and hateth as the *extreme βδέλυγμα* (abomination). *Knowingly and willingly* they commit that impiety with which the Ethnics were polluted. Therefore also their punishment without any doubt shall be greater than that of the Gentiles.

### "God bestoweth on us something singular and eximious" —

Furthermore it is set down in the definition, that *God in this action which is called a Sacrament bestoweth on us something singular and eximious*. For these particles contain the **causa formalis** (as they call it) — not external, but which is hidden in the external species, and through which God is efficacious — as it is said, *The Gospel is the power of God* — that is, the Gospel is the *canal and instrument through which alone God is efficacious in the minds of men by His Holy Spirit*. For the Holy Spirit *through the Word and Sacraments* truly *vivifieth, regenerateth the breasts of men*, and announceth unto them the *remission of sins on account of the Son of God*.

### "Consisting of Word and integral element" —

This too is necessarily to be added to the definition: that a **Sacrament consisteth of Word and integral element**. By this particle is set forth the **material cause**, of what it consisteth in itself.

- **Word** is called the *institution and mandate of God, requiring of us obedience which agreeth with His will* — that is, that *the native sentence of the institution be preserved*.
- **Element** is called the *visible external thing, the external use — as water, bread, wine*.

This element ought to be ***integral***, as Christ instituted in these words: **Eat, drink.** The other part is not to be withdrawn — as the **Papists** try to withdraw the other species, as though it were enough if Christ had extended only the Body to His disciples, whereas the Body cannot be without the Blood. O human wisdom, folly before God — which even the God of infinite wisdom thou triest to inform! But we diligently observe: **The Sacrament consisteth of Word and integral element — not of a mutilated or divided element — even as Christ Himself instituted: Eat, drink.** And this sentence of Christ we hold with firm breasts, though the whole world from heaven should collapse; and we know that, *if an Angel come from heaven and bring another voice than Christ hath sounded, he is anathema.*

### "That it may confirm and seal faith in the living" —

And as a Sacrament ought to consist not of a mutilated but of an integral element, so it is not to be applied to other things or creatures, but to *living men*. Therefore in the definition it is said that *the Sacrament confirmeth faith in the living*. For **neither Christ nor His Apostles exhibited a Sacrament to the dead or to other things destitute of sense, but to the living** — nor is any mandate of Christ extant that a Sacrament should be applied for the dead. **Manifest therefore is the error and extreme profanation of the Sacrament — that it is applied in the Mass for the dead**; likewise that a bell and other things lacking life, sense, and reason are *baptised*. These all are *corruptions of Christ's institution*. And these corruptions were before this time — before the merciful God through His elect organ, D. **Martin Luther**, restored the light of His Word truly and integrally — so frequent, that Sacraments were applied to just anything.

**I myself have heard at Wittenberg some twenty years ago from a certain soldier, of long age worn out**, that in the Neapolitan war there was great scarcity of drink, nor was there water in the army left, which they could drink; therefore the *sacrificers* gave an *ass* a consecrated bread to devour, and cast it into the sea. How great this blasphemy was, no human voice can enough express: but he added, that thence such rains arose that all thought they must die and perish in the waters. **This was the work of the Devil**, who like a lion prowleth around, watching whom he may devour. But had those sacrificers learned the use of the Sacraments unto which God instituted them, doubtless into so great and foul errors they would not have fallen. **The Sacrament — whether of Baptism or of the Altar — ought to be applied to and profit the living and only men, as Christ instituted. Whoever changeth the mandate of Christ, sinneth horribly.**

### The Final Cause: to Confirm and Seal Faith.

The final cause of the Sacraments is placed in the definition as these words: ***that they may confirm and seal faith***.

For the Sacraments are principally instituted unto this end — **that they may be pledges, certifications, testimonies, seals, or σφραγίδες and signs of the New Testament** — that is, of the promise, in which unto all believers is offered and exhibited the *remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life through faith on account of the Son*. Rightly therefore we say that *the reception of the Sacraments takes place chiefly for this cause — that faith be confirmed*. For as *faith is preserved, augmented, nourished, and excited by the Word*, so the *Sacraments admonish us of the promise of the New Testament*. **The Word (invisible)** invisibly through the Holy Spirit working in the minds of men confirmeth faith. But the **Sacraments — which are visible signs and external rites, incurring the eyes** — *concerning the promise of grace* (that is, of the remission of sins, donation of the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life) *render believers certain*.

Although however the *Sacraments confer nothing per se* — that is, if only we accede unto them, that we may enjoy them simply *without a good conscience, without faith*, or, as they say, ***ex opere operato*** — yet if they be received *by a faithful and believing mind*, they are altogether **testimonies and infallible pledges of the promise, which is proper to the Gospel** — which is felt and impetrated only by faith.

Therefore Paul saith that **circumcision** for Abraham was the *seal of the righteousness of faith* — that is, of that righteousness which was imputed to him on account of *faith in the future Messiah*. Such a seal Paul saith circumcision to have been — that is, a *testimony by which God testified that He had received Abraham the believer into grace*. As often therefore as Abraham beheld the sign of circumcision impressed on his body, he was ever admonished of the grace of God: *Behold, by this sign God testifieth (which thou bearest impressed on thy body) that He hath given thee the promise of the blessed Seed, and willeth thee to believe that thou art received on account of that Seed, and heard, and that thou hast remission of sins,* etc. Thus this sign or note was *a perpetual admonition of the will of God, of the promise*, and *was the confirmation of faith in the mind of Abraham* — by which faith in the future Seed he was just — not because of that seal impressed on the body (which was only, as I said, an admonition of the will of God, and a testimony of the righteousness of faith).

And this was the cause why Abraham (Gen. 24) sweareth his servant and biddeth him place his hand under the thigh. For by this rite of oath he testified that he believed in *the blessed Seed promised* — of which matter a certain testimony existed in his body, namely *circumcision around the region of the thigh*.

### Baptism and the Supper — Testimonies of Spiritual Goods.

So **Baptism is a certain κριτήριον and τεκμήριον**, that these spiritual goods — namely, the *remission of sins, the donation of the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life* — are exhibited and given to every one who is baptised in the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit — and there ariseth between God and the baptised a certain ***ἐπερώτησιν*** (interrogation), that is, *a stipulation of a good conscience with God*, even as such an association is entered between bridegroom and bride *by rings and other ornaments*. As often therefore as we are present at Baptism, let us think of this *last covenant of Christ* which He hath entered with us, and let us be admonished of the promise — that we be *washed from every sin and purged* — that is, we have the *remission of sins, we are just on account of the Son*, etc.

**In the same mode it is written in the words of the Supper of the Lord:** *This cup is the new Testament in My blood, which for you is shed.* Here the word *Testament* signifieth nothing else than *the promise of the remission of sins, of the Holy Spirit, of righteousness, and of eternal life, sealed by the blood of the Son of God — who is the Testator, and bequeatheth these eternal goods to believers, or to those receiving the testament by faith*. And He addeth a *testimony* — namely, the *cup or the reception of His body and blood*, that we may be certain that these spiritual goods are truly exhibited unto us believing. Admonished therefore by this cup, let us believe that the remission of sins is given to us *not on account of this work, but on account of the Son of God*, and by this pledge or seal let us confirm our faith.

### The Order of Consideration.

The **first and principal end** of the Sacraments therefore is that they be *signs of the will of God toward us*, or *testimonies of the promised grace* — that is, of the *remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life*.

Then this too — as it were a *general hypothesis* — must most firmly be fixed in weak minds in the reception of the Sacrament: **that just as it is necessary to receive the promise by faith, so also in the use of the Sacraments there must accede faith which looketh upon the promise** — as Christ saith in the words of Baptism: *He that believeth and shall have been baptised shall be saved.* And in the Supper: *This cup is the new Testament, the blood shed for you.* Therefore, since this ceremony admonisheth us of the Gospel and of the whole benefit of the New Testament, faith must plainly accede — because the promise requireth faith. Hence rightly is it agreed to say: **Not the Sacrament, but faith in the Sacrament justifieth.** And: *He that believeth in Him eateth Him.*

Therefore *those err also* who say the *Sacrament is a cause*, not only the *seal of grace*. For manifestly from what hitherto we have said, it followeth that ***execrable is the error*** of those who teach *the Sacraments have been ordained and instituted unto this use — that they should confer grace ex opere operato* — and, as they speak, *without any good motion of the user*, or that *the Sacraments of the new law give grace in those who put no obstacle*. So the **Monks** speak. And this erroneous sentence manifestly the sayings refute: *The just liveth by his faith. Being justified by faith we have peace with God. Whatever is not of faith is sin.* And **there is no work which ex opere operato through itself meriteth for the doer, or for others, remission of sins**.

### Water and Word — Both Necessary as Signs.

Then it must be known in this place that **God is efficacious through Word and through Sacraments**. Although the Word is more excellent and more necessary — as Paul saith: *The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth* — yet great also is the necessity of the Sacraments, but *as signs only, when they can be had*. For God willeth in this mode to gather Himself the Church, as also through the Word: He willeth not the signs to be contemned, when they can be had. Therefore also **Cornelius** was baptised, because God willed him to be a member of the Church, and willed this Baptism to be the confirmation of faith in him. But the **thief on the cross** was not baptised by the customary rite, because he could not have the rite; and yet in the same mode, as though he had been baptised, he obtained the *fruit of Baptism* — namely, the remission of sins, the Holy Spirit, righteousness, and eternal life. Wherefore the ancients rightly said that some receive **the Sacrament, and at the same time the *res sacramenti***, that is, the *fruit* — as Cornelius baptised received the Sacrament and the *res*, that is, the remission of sins and other spiritual gifts gratuitously on account of the Son. Some indeed receive **the Sacrament, but not the *res*** — such as are all the impious *without faith*, taking to themselves, as Paul saith, *judgment*. And some finally **not the Sacrament itself, but the *res* of the Sacrament** — as the thief on the cross. So also of the martyrs it hath been said, that they are baptised *in their own blood*.

And hence too it may in some way be gathered how much is conceded us — that ***infants*** in the Church who die before they are brought to Baptism, because they cannot have the customary rite, obtain by God's immense goodness on account of the Son *the res of the Sacrament*, as though they had been baptised — and can by their own faith be justified and saved, according to the promise: *I will be thy God, and of thy seed for ever.* But this we leave to the judgment of God, which yet in the Church we know to be *paternal and most clement*.

Enough on the definition of the Sacrament.

## On the Number of the Sacraments.

**Commonly in the Papacy seven Sacraments are numbered**: *Baptism, Confirmation, Eucharist, Penitence, Extreme Unction, Order, and Matrimony*.

But since it is altogether necessary that those *ceremonies which Christ instituted in the New Testament be discerned from other things* which either were instituted *before Christ came, in the Old Testament*, or *pertain not properly to the New Testament* — therefore **rightly are there numbered only two Sacraments — Baptism and the Lord's Supper**. For these ceremonies were in the New Testament first *instituted by Christ*, and are *external signs of the will of God toward us*.

But as touching the word ***Sacrament***, many things can be called by this name — namely, all things which are *mandated by God and commended by promises* — as *prayer, patience in calamities, alms, the condoning of injuries*, and many others. For these works are *divinely enjoined and commanded to men*, unto which also *illustrious promises* have been added. **Of prayer** there are everywhere in Scripture mandates and promises: Ps. 50: *Invoke Me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify Me.* Matt. 7: *Ask, and it shall be given you.* And there is added a universal: *Every one that asketh receiveth.* Ps. 145: *The Lord is near unto all invoking Him, unto all invoking Him in truth. The will of them that fear Him He will do, and their deprecation He will hear.* And that most sweet voice in **Ecclesiasticus 35** existeth: *The prayer of him that humbleth himself shall penetrate the clouds, and shall not depart until it draw near, and shall obtain consolation; nor shall it retire, until the Most High shall look upon it. And the Lord will not delay, but shall judge the just* — that is, *shall approve the just, and show them to be truly just and pleasing to Himself*. And Isa. 65: *Before they cry, I shall hear; while they yet speak, I shall hear.* With which sentence agreeth that most sweet saying of **Tauler**: *"The soul of man is never so avid of receiving as God is more avid of giving."* ²⁰⁰

**Of patience in calamities** it is said, 1 Cor. 11: *When we are judged, by the Lord we are corrected, that we may not be damned with this world.* Ps. 118: *It is good for me that Thou hast humbled me, that I might learn Thy justifications.* Ps. 71: *Precious is their blood before Me,* etc.

**Of alms** the precepts and promises are known: Luke 6: *Give and it shall be given you.* Isa. 58: *Break thy bread to the hungry, and lead the wandering poor into thy house. If thou seest one naked, cover him — and from thy flesh, that is, thy kinsman, do not hide thyself.* And there are added perspicuous promises. **First:** *Then shall thy light break forth as the dawn* — that is, thou shalt obtain and find consolation and aid in time of necessity. **Second:** *And thy health shall speedily arise* — that is, God shall again bless thee, and whatever thou first didst spend in aiding the needy, opulently He shall restore to thee, in this life and also in another life. **Third promise:** *And thy righteousness shall go before thee* — that is, not only shalt thou thereby procure a good name, that thou be called *just and observant of equity*, but God shall defend thee, and *temporal calamities He shall either altogether take from thee, or certainly mitigate*, and He Himself shall help thee bear the burden imposed on thee, on account of that mercy by which thou didst succour the needy. **Fourth:** *And the glory of the Lord shall receive thee unto itself* — that is, in thy prayer, when thou askest something from God, thou shalt be heard — as followeth: *Then shalt thou invoke, and the Lord shall respond; thou shalt cry, and He shall say: Behold, here I am.* And that this promise may more penetrate the souls of men, God repeateth the same: *If thou hast granted thy own to the hungry as they find, and hast satisfied the afflicted soul, thy light shall rise in the darkness, and thy shadow shall be as noon. And the Lord shall lead thee always, and shall satisfy thy soul in drought, and shall strengthen thy bones, and thou shalt be as an irrigated garden, and as a fountain of waters, which never denieth its waters*, etc.

**Of the condoning of injuries** everywhere also exist testimonies — as in the Lord's Prayer: *Remit unto us our debts, as we remit unto our debtors.* Likewise Luke 6: *Remit, and it shall be remitted unto you.* Hither pertaineth also the saying, Matt. 5: *If thou shalt offer thy gift at the altar, and there shall remember that thy brother hath aught against thee, leave there thy gift before the altar, and go — first be reconciled to thy brother — and then coming offer thy gift.*

And in this mode also **marriage can be called a Sacrament**, because it is both *mandated by God*, and *hath promises added to it* — as below on marriage we shall say in a peculiar place.

### The Reason for Restricting the Word "Sacrament" to Ceremonies of Christ.

But since it is necessary to distinguish *the promises of the Law* — which are *conditional*, that is, exhibited *on account of the condition of the fulfilled Law* — **from the promises proper to the Gospel, which are gratuitous** — therefore also the *mandates of God which endured in the Law before Christ's coming, or the legal ceremonies*, must be discerned from the *mandates of Christ first proposed in the Gospel, and from the ceremonies which declare the promises of the Gospel*.

Wherefore it is both *useful and necessary* to restrict the general vocable *Sacrament* to a certain **species** — namely, to the *ceremonies instituted in the preaching of Christ* — that men may be taught what is *proper to the Gospel*, what benefits Christ hath brought to us, and by what external testimonies He hath confirmed these.

And in this mode the appellation *Sacrament*, understood customarily, is defined:

> **A Sacrament is an external, visible ceremony, instituted by Christ, that it may be a testimony of the promised grace, or a sign of the will of God toward us, and a pledge of the applied promise, according to the ordination and the Word of the institution.**

**Customarily therefore, and rightly, only two Sacraments are numbered — namely, Baptism and the Lord's Supper.** For these two consist of *elements* (that is, a certain *visible creature incurring the eyes*), and have joined to them the *Word which proposeth the promise of grace* and addeth to those external rites this power — that they may be truly *testimonies of the will of God toward us*.

There is added by some also **absolution**, which rite — although it have no element or visible creature joined to it — yet is an *external rite which is part of the vocal ministry*, and is a *sign of the whole Gospel, or a testimony and announcement of the remission of sins and of reconciliation* — of which chiefly it is said in the customary definition: *A Sacrament is a sign of grace* — that is, *of gratuitous reconciliation which is given on account of Christ and preached in the Gospel*. And absolution is founded in this Word: *I give unto you the keys of the heavens; and whatsoever ye shall bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven; whatsoever ye shall loose on earth shall be also loosed in heaven.*

But before we say anything on Baptism and the Lord's Supper, we shall premise most briefly a few things on the remaining ceremonies — namely, *ordination, confirmation, and unction* — which the adversaries call Sacraments.

## On Ordination.

Now when it is spoken **of ordination**, is understood *the vocation unto the ministry of the Gospel, which is by the authority and mandate of God* — either **immediately from God** (which properly is the *Prophetic and Apostolic vocation*, of which Paul saith that he was called *neither from men nor through men*); or **mediately through men by divine mandate** — as were those whom Scripture nameth *sons of the Prophets*, that is, disciples who were instructed by the Prophets, that they too might be fit for teaching. Thus were constituted by the Apostles the *bishops and priests of the Churches*, and afterwards from the Church *ministers are elected and ordained*.

### The Priesthood of All Christians and the Ordained Ministry.

Although however all Christians are ***priests*** — in respect of the *priesthood of Christ*, the primary priest, whose members are all Christians, and unto whose priesthood all and each ought to bring their own offices — each one in his own vocation (as the father of the family should institute his children and family in the true doctrine, the magistracy should care that its subjects be taught in the true doctrine, and thus each in his own kind should offer *spiritual hosts to God* and invoke the Name of God, as it is said, 1 Pet. 2: *Ye are a royal priesthood, that ye should preach the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His admirable light,* etc.) — **yet not all are ministers of the Church**, as the *Anabaptists* dream. For *no one usurpeth honour for himself*, but he who is *called by God, whose organ is the Church*, through which God calleth apt men unto the ministry, and *publicly approveth and commendeth them*.

And there are *divine testimonies always to be had in sight of all Christians*, by which Christ commendeth the ministry of His Church — some of which I shall subjoin, that they may admonish the studious *of the dignity and efficacy of the ministry of the Gospel*:

- John 20: *As the Father hath sent Me, so also I send you. Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins ye shall have remitted, are remitted unto them.*
- Matt. and Luke 10: *He that heareth you heareth Me; and he that despiseth you despiseth Me; but he who despiseth Me despiseth Him who sent Me.*
- Mark 16: *Going into the whole universe, preach the Gospel to every creature.*
- Matt. 28: *Going, teach all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.*
- John 17: *And not for these do I pray only, but also for those who shall believe through their word on Me.*
- John 15: *Ye bear witness.*
- Acts 1: *Ye shall be My witnesses unto the ends of the earth.*
- 2 Pet. 1: *For prophecy came not of old by the will of man; but the holy men of God spoke as they were moved by the Holy Spirit.* — He plainly affirmeth the words of God's ministers to be made *by the impelling Holy Spirit*, and to be *the Words of God*, of which no one can doubt.
- Rom. 1: *The Gospel is the power of God unto every believer.*
- John 15: *I am the vine, ye are the branches. He that abideth in Me, and I in him, beareth much fruit.*
- 2 Cor. 5: *God hath placed in us the Word of reconciliation. For Christ therefore we do an embassy, as though God were exhorting through us.* How great this is — that *God exhorteth through the ministers of the Gospel*, and that *their words are the very Words of God*.
- 2 Cor. 3: *He hath made us ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit.* By **letter** he calleth any sort of obedience, likewise ministry without the Holy Spirit — that is, *without true fear, without faith, true invocation, and acknowledgment of Christ*. By **Spirit** he nameth the whole ministry which is perfected *by the governing Holy Spirit, working in hearts new light, wisdom, righteousness, and life pleasing to God, and ardent with the motions of the Holy Spirit* — namely, *fear, faith, invocation, dilection, true acknowledgment of the Son of God*, etc. Likewise by **letter** he nameth *the Law*, or *philosophic discipline without the notice of the Gospel* — which as *letter only effecteth errors*, or is (as Paul saith in the same place) the *ministry of death, bringing not life but death* — since it is done *without the true fear of God and faith invoking God in the acknowledgment of Christ*. And by **Spirit** he nameth the ministry of life, *consolation, new light, and life kindled in hearts, which sinners acknowledge to have been received into grace on account of the Son*.

And it is profitable to remember many testimonies — which the studious ought carefully to collect into a heap from daily lections: for they admonish us of the ministry, which God willeth to preserve in His Church, and to build His Church upon it, that the *gates of hell may not prevail against her*, as He saith: *Behold, I am with you to the consummation of the world.*

### The Church's Power of Calling.

Unto so great a function and so great a ministry — of teaching the Gospel, administering the Sacraments, announcing the remission of sins, excommunicating the contumacious *without corporal force* — **the Church hath power of calling certain men apt and idoneous for so great an office**, who avail *in judgment and erudition, and are endowed with honest and pious morals*: *not avaricious, adulterers, whore-mongers, given to wine and gluttony — but faithful and holding the ministry of faith with pure conscience*, as Paul prescribeth.

**This vocation which is made through the Church, today is called *ordination*** — and by others the *Sacrament of Order*. But as I said above, that ***λογομαχίαι*** (word-battles) must not be borne on grave matters — so altogether again *the rude* must be admonished: if the vocable *Sacrament* be taken *generally*, then a Sacrament can be called *any thing or ceremony which hath an express mandate of God in Scripture* — nay, all works whose sum is proposed in the Decalogue, and therefore also *ordination*. But why this ought not to be done, it hath been said above — namely, that *the promises of the Gospel may be exactly discerned from the promises of the Law*, and that it may be known *what ceremonies are testimonies or seals of our salvation, and what not*.

These things I willed to premise concerning the *dignity and efficacy of the ministry* before I should speak concerning the rite, and I willed also in passing to admonish the younger sort concerning the vocable *Order* — whether it be to be called by the name of Sacrament or not. Now I come unto the rite, and to the errors annexed to the rite.

### The Rite of Ordination.

**The rite of ordination** can by no one of sane mind be reprehended, nor was it ever by us called into doubt whether it ought to be retained; and in our Churches it hath been always with great care preserved. For it appeareth that ***the imposition of hands*** hath been received by the holy Fathers and propagated unto us — which was a *sign of a thing destined unto the worship of God*, as flocks were ordered by this rite unto this office, that they should become victims (Exod. 29). Thus Moses ordaineth Joshua unto the government of the people of God (Num. 27). It was also a *sign of blessing*, as Jacob blesseth by this rite the sons of Joseph; Christ the boys, etc. And especially the *signification and type* must be considered in the rite of victims, which designed *Christ*. God the eternal Father *imposed hands on Christ* — that is, chose Him, blessed Him, anointed Him — that He might become the *victim for the whole human race* — as Christ saith, Isa. 61: *The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me, because He hath anointed Me,* etc. Luke 4 and Ps. 2: *I have installed My King upon Zion, My holy mountain.* Afterwards this same signification is rightly transferred unto ministers. Christ, anointed by the Father, breatheth into His disciples the Holy Spirit, imposeth hands upon them — that is, chooseth them by the voice of the Church, as it is written, Eph. 4: *He ascended, He gave gifts to men — Prophets, Apostles, Pastors, Doctors,* etc. Here the same rite is commended to us by Paul, 1 Tim. 4: *Neglect not the gift or grace which is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy with the imposition of the hands of the presbytery or priesthood.*

**Altogether therefore it is necessary to retain the ordination of priests**, and those magistrates are to be reprehended who *admit whatever men without exploration of doctrine unto the ministry*. Today the more powerful in many places elevate unto the government of the Church those whom they favour — *unlearned and slothful*, and (as **Basil** complaineth) *most vile of all servants — glutton-teachers*, more studious of the belly than of the Word or the salvation of their flock. It would be useful and salutary for all Churches that *first the doctrine of those who wish the way of the ministry to be opened for themselves, should be explored*. Let pious magistrates think it their office therefore that they should be *nourishers of the Church*, and study to preserve the true doctrine, and care that their subjects be instructed in the true doctrine *by intelligent men — knowing the controversies of doctrine, and knowing what the errors are and what the true doctrine is* — nor let them receive any into the ministry *without exploration of doctrine*, in which the *powers, erudition, and sentiment of each concerning doctrine* may be observed.

### Errors of the Adversaries Concerning Ordination.

Now I shall subjoin a few things concerning the errors of the adversaries.

**The first** is that they affirm that *priests can be ordained only by bishops*. But if the *bishops truly discharged their office*, and did not consider themselves commended with *polities but with the Churches of Christ*, and cared that the Gospel be purely and truly preached — then to them could be granted this power of ordaining others — *not by necessity, but for greater concord and charity*. For **necessity there cannot be**, because there is no mandate of Scripture, but a counsel of men. Now, although most bishops are unworthy of this name, and care nothing for the Gospel, and (as **Cyclops** in **Euripides** saith) *know no other God besides the belly* — they subject to themselves *political kingdoms, do not teach others, do not baptise, and perform no work or office mandated by Christ in the Church truly and integrally*; besides, they *persecute those who truly administer the Ecclesiastical functions, and excommunicate them as heretics* — yet **ordination is not to be omitted by us**, but by the *examples of the ancient Churches we ought to retain it diligently ourselves, and ordain persons idoneous for the ministry*. ²⁰¹

**The second error** is that the *bishops in ordination forbid marriage to priests* — which doctrine is called by Paul *a dogma of the Devil* (1 Tim. 4); and Paul prescribeth that *each should have his own wife, to avoid whoredom*. Likewise: *Better it is to marry than to burn.* By these and similar sayings priests are by no means excluded. Nay, Paul maketh mention of priests also when he saith unto Timothy: *Let the deacons be husbands of one wife, who rightly rule their children and their own families.* And in the same place: *A bishop ought to be irreprehensible, a husband of one wife.* And the same he repeateth to Titus. Wherefore it is a *fiction of the Devil* to deny marriage to priests — as Paul manifestly testifieth, 1 Tim. 4, that *there shall be in the latter times some who shall depart from the faith, and shall forbid to contract matrimony, and shall command to abstain from foods*, etc. And the adversaries well know that they can bring forth no truth against this article which affirmeth that *marriage is conceded to priests*.

**Pigghius** dared to sound this execrable voice: *"A priest polluting himself with whoredom sinneth less than one taking a wife."* Now it is certain that *whore-mongers and adulterers shall not enter into the Kingdom of God*, as often is said. Col. 3: *On account of fornication cometh the wrath of God.* Eph. 5: *No fornicator hath inheritance.* And most celebrated and preeminent cities have been destroyed on account of *vagrant lusts* — Sodom, Gomorrah, Troy, and many others. If in polities God so punished this sin, how much more atrociously will He punish, where priests have been polluted by whoredom or lusts, who ought to preside over the Word of God! For it is necessary that *most burn*, as Paul saith — that is, that they be *inflamed with vagrant lusts*. And that God will punish so great errors in the last judgment, must plainly be established by us — where *delay He shall compensate with gravity of punishment*.

**Siricius the Pope** — that I may also insert this in passing — when in Spain he had commanded priests to *leave their wives*, is read to have alleged the saying of Paul, Rom. 8: *Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.* In which place Paul nameth *flesh* the *whole man without the Holy Spirit* — not only the *sensitive appetite*, but *the mind and will without the Holy Spirit*.

**The third error** is that they feign *ordination is done for this — that Epistles and Gospels be read, and in the Mass they may sacrifice for the living and the dead* — by which error the fiction of *vigils, of Masses for souls, of purgatory, and of the idolatrous oblation* is confirmed, as below on the Mass we shall admonish.

There are also *many other errors annexed* — as of the *seven days or seasons of days* by which the priests to be initiated are laden, and many other things, partly *ridiculous*, partly *superstitious and idolatrous*.

### Warnings Against Anabaptists and Donatists.

Here the younger sort must also be admonished concerning the errors of the ***Anabaptists*** and the ***Donatists***. The former feign, like the *Enthusiasts* of old, that ***new revelations are to be expected***, and that they are to be sought *by many affections of the body* — and thus with the ministry they contemn also ordination. These deliriums let us shun. They think themselves *about to receive the Spirit without the Word, before they come to the Word*. And that they are afterwards *going to judge and interpret Scripture by their own imaginations* — as **Münzer** felt, and today many feign, who claim great acumen of judgment between the *letter and the spirit*. Let us therefore fix in our inmost minds this sentence of Paul: **The Gospel is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth** — that is, is *the instrument through which alone God is efficacious in the minds of men*. And **Athanasius**, book 3 *On the Holy Spirit* p. 54, piously saith: *Whenever the Spirit is said to be in anyone, He is understood to be in him through the Word giving the Spirit.* And although this sentence of Athanasius is properly to be understood *of the Son of God, whom after the manner of John he calleth Word or* λόγος, yet it may not incommodiously be received of the *vocal word, or of the ministry of the Gospel and the preaching of Christ* — as elsewhere the same [author] saith: *Not outside the Word is the Spirit.* Thus God willed *first to reveal Himself vocally to Moses in the burning bush, before He should send him to Pharaoh — He willed not to be patefacted to Moses by Enthusiastic numen.* Nor did any Prophet without the *vocal word receive the Holy Spirit*, etc. Wherefore the fictions of the Anabaptists are to be execrated, which arise from *false persuasions of the discipline of the Law and ignorance of the doctrine of faith*, or chiefly from *mere hypocrisy*. ²⁰²

Then also the ***Donatists*** are not to be borne in the Church — who *on account of the evil morals of ministers do not fear to cast away the whole ministry*, and dare to contend that *neither the Gospel nor any Sacrament is efficacious if the ministers' morals are vitious*. And on that account those who are *baptised by ministers whose morals are not integral, or by heretics, they baptise again* — which error the *Anabaptists* today have renewed, as the *Münsterite filth* showeth. Against this error let us first know that ***the dignity of the ministry dependeth not on the dignity of the minister***. For if the force of the Gospel and of the Sacraments depended on the dignity of the minister, *our faith would become uncertain*. Therefore, that our faith may be certain, let us altogether execrate the *fanatic delirium of the Donatists*.

This is the argument of **Augustine**, who in many books refuted the Donatists. And book 6 he saith: *Water is not profane or adulterous, over which the Name of God is invoked, even if by profanes and adulterers it be invoked.* And on John, *tractate 6*: *Baptism is such as He is in whose power it is, not such as he is by whose ministry it is given.* Refuted also by **Nazianzen** is the same error, who useth this similitude: *The figure of the seal is the same whether it be sculpted in a golden or an iron ring: so the same is the ministry whether good or evil hold it.* And Christ Himself, Matt. 13, comparerth the Church to a *net-drag* in which are good and evil fishes. He saith likewise that in the Church *tares are to remain unto the resurrection*, nor are they to be uprooted until He Himself come and uproot them. Likewise: *Upon the chair of Moses the scribes and Pharisees sit; whatsoever they shall bid you, do it.* Now it is agreed that the scribes and Pharisees were *hypocrites*, and yet Christ commandeth to obey them, and affirmeth their function to avail — if however they *sit upon the chair of Moses*, that is, teach the doctrine delivered by God, and *sit not upon another chair*, that is, teach not doctrine fighting with the faith, etc.

Diligently however here it must be observed: **we speak of evil morals and of not-enormous vices, not of manifest crimes or of evil doctrine.** For ministers who are *polluted with open crimes* are to be excommunicated by the common voice of the Church, unless they repent, and are to be punished by the magistracy who beareth the sword. Of such crimes, or of idolatry, we speak not, but rather of the *common infirmities in the morals of men*. One is *morose*, another is *iracund*, another *indulgent and less temperate than he ought*, prodigal, bibulous, tenacious, sordid, etc. — nor is any *without vices*. Of these common morals — if crimes accede not — let us follow the customary saying: *τρόπος φίλου γίνωσκε, οὐκ ἔχθαιρε* ("Know the ways of a friend; hate him not"). Likewise: *μὴ φίλον ἐχθαίρῃς ἁμαρτάδος εἵνεκα μικρῆς* ("Do not hate a friend on account of a small fault"). Likewise, *charity covereth all delicts*. Because indeed all have *certain infirmities of their own*, and no one is *without vices*, but God willeth *that we love one another mutually — that we wash one another's feet, as Christ commandeth* — that is, *heal such infirmities among us by mutual lenity*, according to that: *He who hateth vices, hateth men,* etc.

Let this suffice on ordination — and let the younger sort learn *reverently to feel of the ministry, and let all study to exhibit due honour to the ministers of the Gospel*, as Paul, 1 Thess. 5, prescribeth: *We beg you*, saith he, *that those who preside excellently ye think worthy of dilection on account of the ministry, and have peace with them.* And let *the fathers of families learn reverently to speak in their families concerning the ministers and concerning the whole ministry*, lest their families be scandalized and be confirmed in *profane contempt and carnal security*, but let them know that *the matter of their salvation consists in the ministry*, and let them more diligently hear the Word of God. Finally, let each *aid the ministry*, as is prescribed 1 Tim. 5: *That ye acknowledge* — that is, *aid, love, and defend* — *those who labour among you, and who are set over you in the Lord, and admonish you*. This voice also of **Solomon**, Prov. 3, is most worthy that it should always be in the sight of the pious: *Honour God from thy faculties, and thy barns shall be filled,* etc.

## On Confirmation and Unction.

**Confirmation** of old was the *exploration of doctrine, and public prayer and confession, with the imposition of hands added* — of which mention is made Acts 8, and 1 Tim. 4, likewise 2 Tim. 1, Heb. 6. There concurred therefore in the rite of confirmation:

1. **Exploration of doctrine.**
2. **Public profession of doctrine**, or a *recitation of the sum of doctrine*.
3. **Separation from Ethnics and heretics.**
4. **Instruction of the simpler and ruder.**
5. **Discrimination between profanes and pious.**
6. **Public prayer for the pious.**
7. **External imposition of hands.**
8. **Efficacy of the Holy Spirit augmenting His gifts and confirming faith and consolation in the pious.**

For the prayer was not empty. Now the rite of *imposition of hands* is most ancient — which the holy Patriarchs used *in prayers*, in which upon some person peculiarly the Name of the Lord was invoked, that by this rite that person might as it were *be offered to God, and placed in His sight* — with supplications added, that *God would deign to largess grace and blessing on him*. Thus therefore Jacob imposeth hands on the boys whom he blesseth. Thus *presbyters pray over the sick* (James 5). Thus Christ imposing hands *blesseth the little ones* (Mark 10). For that was the solemn *mode of the Saviour Himself of blessing* — by hand together with voice — when unto Him were offered *little ones, that He should impose hands and pray* — that is, *bless*.

This rite afterwards endured in the Church, not only in *blessing and prayer*, but also in the *public ordination of those who were legitimately called unto the ministry of teaching the Gospel and administering the Sacraments* — and this for these causes:

1. **That the person be publicly designated and denounced by the Church** — that *he had been legitimately elected and called* — as Moses (Deut. 34) by this rite solemnly introduceth Joshua to the people, and denounceth *him to be his successor*.
2. **That the one called be confirmed of his legitimate and divine vocation**, and be made certain of *the approval and consent of the whole Church*, and in his own conscience be more alacritous unto undertaking the ministry — which without vocation cannot be administered with a good conscience.
3. **That the one called be admonished** — *he is destined unto divine and spiritual worships*, and *separated from the world's unclean actions*; and *many perils are to be undergone and overcome by him for the glory of God*. For thus hands were imposed on victims.
4. **That it may be a public protestation of the Church before God**, and that in *election and vocation* be preserved the *rule and form prescribed by God Himself* — as Paul saith, 1 Tim. 5: *Hands lay quickly upon no one.*
5. **That it may be shown that vocation pleaseth God**, which is made *by the voice and testification of the Church according to the norm prescribed by the Holy Spirit in the Word*.
6. **That prayers and supplications may be made to God for blessing, grace, and fruit or success of labours unto the edification of the Church** — against the *plots and tyranny of the devil, the world and the flesh, of tyrants and of heretics who impede the course of true doctrine*.

These are the causes for which the rite of imposition of hands is still retained in the ordination of ministers of the Church — which rite however let us know **doth not imprint any singular character on the ordained**, nor doth the *right of teaching the Gospel and administering the Sacraments depend upon it*, or is the ministry of the ordained efficacious *on account of this rite* — but the rite is *added to vocation for the sake of public deliberation and approbation* — namely, that the *renunciation of the called person may be more illustrious*, and that *the suppliant prayer of all may accede*, and that *this rite may admonish of certain offices*.

### The Papal Corruptions of Confirmation.

But **now the rite of Confirmation which the bishops retain is a plainly otiose ceremony and ostentation, not lacking idolatry** — especially since to the ***consignation*** (as they call it) which is made by the bishop, they *bind the perception of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit*, as they speak.

### On Pontifical Unction.

**Such is also the Papal Unction**, in which those about to die *are anointed with consecrated and magic oil, and impious invocations of the dead are added* — with the promise attached, that *those about to die shall in this way obtain the remission of all sins which by external members they have committed*. This is *impious superstition, contumelious to the merit of the Son of God*. But **unction of old was a *medical curation and a gift of healing the sick*** — with which God adorned the Fathers, Prophets, and Apostles — and **oil was a symbol of the gift of healing** (James 5). But now, why should the symbol be, if nowhere is the gift extant any longer? But *that many are healed by the prayers of the Church*, and that *the health of the body is a gift of God to be sought from God and to be cherished with singular diligence*, let us know.
